case_title: R.S. India Wind Energy Pvt. Ltd. vs PTC India Financial Services Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant R.S. India Wind Energy Pvt. Ltd. (renewable energy company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956) versus Respondent No.1 PTC India Financial Services Ltd. and others, including Power Finance Corporation (PFC) as project funder, sister concern RSIGEPL (R.S. India Global Green Energy Pvt. Ltd.), sister concern of the Respondent (PEL), and a joint venture 'Proforma 10th Respondent'. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant was to set up a 99.45 MW wind power project at Satara, Maharashtra, costing Rs. 634 crores, with PFC funding the balance after the Appellant's Rs. 147 crore equity infusion. After the original turbine supplier withdrew, RSIGEPL entered an MOU dated 10 December 2008 with the Respondent's sister concern to set up an 80 MW wind project in Tamil Nadu through Proforma 10th Respondent, with an equity subscription agreement giving PTC Energy Ltd. 9% equity in RSIGEPL and the Appellant/RSIGEPL holding 55%/45% in Proforma 10th Respondent. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; the dispute did not concern a monetary default but alleged fabrication/discrepancy in corporate records. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board approvals for a Rs. 250 crore corporate guarantee and share pledge were passed on 30 June 2011; a criminal complaint was filed by Respondent No.1 before the EOW on 7 May 2015 (with a parallel complaint by PEL against RSIGEPL), both later closed after 7-8 months of investigation with no irregularities found; a CLB order dated 16 October 2015 directed that the main petition be heard uninfluenced by prima facie observations on minutes; documents were supplied by the Appellant on 1 February 2016; Respondent No.1 then filed C.A. No. 92/C-1/2016 before the newly constituted NCLT (functional from 1 June 2016), leading to the impugned order dated 22 September 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Alleged variances were pointed out between two sets of Board meeting minutes for roughly ten meetings held between February 2008 and June 2011, including differing CMD signatures, missing pages, and unsigned minutes; the Appellant countered with a tabular chart explaining each discrepancy (e.g., inadvertent photocopying omissions) and pointed to matching Audited Balance Sheets approved by the Board and AGM. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The application, originally filed under Regulation 44 of the Company Law Board Regulations, 1991 before Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 came into force, was decided by NCLT under Section 213(b) on 22 September 2016, directing investigation into the Appellant's affairs on grounds of apparent malpractice and mismanagement; the Appellant challenged this order before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether sub-clause (b) of Section 213 is wide enough to include contravention of any law; whether the Tribunal was bound to specifically record satisfaction of the ingredients under sub-clauses (i) to (iii) of clause (b); and whether those ingredients can be relied upon even in an application filed by members under clause (a) of Section 213, or only in applications by 'any other person' or suo motu action.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The requirement of Tribunal 'satisfaction' that circumstances exist suggesting one of the ingredients under sub-clauses (i) to (iii) of clause (b) of Section 213 applies uniformly to all applications for investigation into a company's affairs, regardless of whether the applicant falls under clause (a) (members) or clause (b) (any other person/suo motu). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Any other person' under clause (b) covers any aggrieved individual, including creditors and depositors, and the word 'otherwise' empowers the Tribunal to act suo motu; the section must be read as a whole rather than treating clauses (a) and (b) as wholly independent gateways. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: At the investigation-ordering stage the Tribunal need only find good grounds/prima facie material on record indicating misconduct or fraud; it is not required to reach a final, objective conclusion of guilt, as detailed evidence is to be gathered by the appointed inspector(s) during the investigation itself, though the Tribunal must disclose material and record reasons for its satisfaction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Tribunal had relied on record evidence, applied its mind, and recorded adequate grounds for ordering investigation into discrepancies in the company's minutes, the Appellate Tribunal found no reason to interfere with the impugned order.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for want of merit; there shall be no order as to costs.
summary: R.S. India Wind Energy Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi order dated 22 September 2016 directing investigation into its affairs under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013, following an application by PTC India Financial Services Ltd. alleging discrepancies and fabrication in Board meeting minutes from 2008-2011. The Appellant argued the Tribunal wrongly invoked Section 213(b) grounds without properly establishing the statutory ingredients, and that such grounds were inapplicable to member-filed applications. NCLAT held the satisfaction requirement under clause (b) applies uniformly to all applications, found the Tribunal had validly relied on prima facie record material warranting deeper probe, and dismissed the appeal with no order as to costs.

case_title: Sanjiv Gupta vs Getit Infoservices Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sanjiv Gupta, former Managing Director of Respondent No.1 company (Getit Infoservices Pvt. Ltd.), against Respondent No.1 company and other respondents including newly appointed Additional Directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not a commercial/lending transaction; this was a shareholder oppression and mismanagement dispute concerning corporate governance, control of the Board of Directors, and the Appellant's removal/resignation as Managing Director. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; no monetary default was in issue. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 122(ND)/2016 was filed on 22 August 2016 seeking relief under Section 241(1)(b) read with Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013; the matter was taken up on 24 August 2016 and then 30 August 2016, when the Tribunal recorded a consensus status quo order regarding the Board's constitution; an E-Form DIR 12 (SRN No. 8103S8538) intimating the Appellant's resignation (allegedly tendered on 12 August 2016) was filed with the Registrar of Companies via Straight Through Process on 30 August 2016; the Appellant filed C.A. No. 85(PB)/2016 under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules 2016 seeking clarification and to declare the DIR 12 form non est; the Tribunal's impugned order refusing clarification and further interim relief was passed on 5 September 2016, which was then appealed. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant held only 0.06% shareholding in Respondent No.1, raising a maintainability objection under Section 244; the Appellant argued the E-Form DIR 12 filing was suppressed from the Tribunal on 30 August 2016 and that his resignation had not been approved by the Board, making the DIR 12 filing improper; the Appellant also argued that as 'Managing Director' under Section 2(54), he was not covered by the resignation-effect provisions of Section 168(2). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Company Petition (alleging oppression/mismanagement and seeking to protect a proposed management buyout) was filed on 22 August 2016; interim relief and clarification were sought and refused by NCLT's order dated 5 September 2016 in C.A. No. 85(PB)/2016, which the Appellant challenged before NCLAT via this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should clarify or modify the Tribunal's interim order dated 30 August 2016 (status quo order) and whether the E-Form DIR 12 evidencing the Appellant's resignation as Managing Director should be declared non est, pending final adjudication of the maintainability of the underlying Company Petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not interfere with or clarify an interim status-quo order passed by the tribunal of first instance where the underlying question of maintainability of the petition (including shareholding threshold issues under Section 244) remains open and undecided on merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The effect of a director's resignation under Section 168(1) takes effect from the date the company receives the notice or a later date specified by the director, but whether a Managing Director (as defined under Section 2(54)) is covered by this provision was raised but left open for determination by the Tribunal at the maintainability stage rather than decided by the Appellate Tribunal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Disputed factual questions regarding suppression of the E-Form DIR 12 filing and the validity/approval of the resignation were treated as matters going to the merits of the underlying petition, not suitable for resolution via interim appellate intervention. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Finding no merit in the appeal against the refusal to clarify or modify the interim order, the Appellate Tribunal declined to interfere, while expressly preserving the Appellant's right to argue the maintainability question on merits before the Tribunal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for want of merit, with a clarification that the Appellate Tribunal's observations shall not prejudice the Appellant's right to contest the question of maintainability of the Company Petition before the Tribunal on merit.
summary: Sanjiv Gupta, former Managing Director of Getit Infoservices Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT order refusing to clarify an earlier interim status-quo order and refusing further interim relief in his oppression-and-mismanagement petition. He argued that an E-Form DIR 12 evidencing his resignation had been improperly filed and suppressed, and that as Managing Director he was not subject to Section 168(2)'s resignation provisions. NCLAT found no merit in the appeal, declined to modify or clarify the interim order, and dismissed the appeal—while clarifying that its observations would not affect the Tribunal's independent decision on the underlying petition's maintainability.

case_title: Global Leisure and Recreation Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs Ms. Punita Khattar & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Global Leisure and Recreation Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. (the respondent company and associated parties in the original petition) versus Respondents Ms. Punita Khattar & Anr. (the original petitioner(s) before NCLT, alleging oppression and mismanagement, with the petitioner referenced as having previously held Managing Directorship). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not a lending/commercial transaction; this is a shareholder oppression and mismanagement dispute concerning corporate governance and conduct of company affairs, including alleged failure to hold Board meetings within stipulated periods. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; no monetary default is at issue. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original Company Petition was filed by the Respondents under Sections 397, 398, 409, and 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013), alleging oppression and mismanagement; the Appellants filed an application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 seeking reference of the dispute to arbitration; this application was dismissed by NCLT's impugned order dated 21 November 2016 in C.A. No. 40/C-2/(ND)/2016, which was then appealed. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellants contended the dispute was arbitrable in nature due to an arbitration clause; the Respondents countered that the grievances (oppression, mismanagement, failure to hold Board meetings within stipulated time) fall exclusively within the Tribunal's jurisdiction under Sections 241-242 and cannot be adjudicated by an arbitrator; the Appellants also raised a counter-allegation that the original petitioner/Respondent herself committed oppression and mismanagement during her tenure as Managing Director. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Appellants' Section 8 arbitration application by order dated 21 November 2016; the Appellants challenged this dismissal before NCLAT, which is the subject of the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a dispute involving allegations of oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 (corresponding to Sections 397-398 of the 1956 Act) is arbitrable and ought to be referred to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, where the parties' agreement contains an arbitration clause.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Questions of oppression and mismanagement, including issues such as a company's failure to hold Board meetings within stipulated statutory periods, fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Tribunal under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, and are not matters that an arbitrator has jurisdiction to decide, even where the parties' underlying agreement contains an arbitration clause. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 does not mandate reference to arbitration where the substance of the dispute concerns statutory oppression/mismanagement remedies exclusively vested in the Tribunal, as opposed to purely contractual or civil disputes between parties. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Appellate Tribunal declined to make any determination on the merits of whether oppression or mismanagement had in fact occurred (including the counter-allegation against the original petitioner), holding that such fact-based determination on evidence is exclusively for the Tribunal to decide after hearing the parties. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the grievances raised are in the nature of oppression and mismanagement not amenable to arbitral determination, the Tribunal's order declining to refer the dispute to arbitration was upheld, and the appeal against that refusal was dismissed, without prejudice to either party's right to pursue arbitration separately for any other genuinely arbitrable dispute permitted under a separate agreement.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs. The Appellate Tribunal clarifies it has not decided the case on merits, which remains to be decided by the Tribunal; it is also open to the aggrieved party to move the appropriate forum for appointment of an arbitrator if any other dispute is permitted/agreed upon under a separate agreement.
summary: Global Leisure and Recreation Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT order dismissing its application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to refer an oppression-and-mismanagement dispute to arbitration. The original petitioners had filed a Company Petition alleging oppression and mismanagement, including failure to hold Board meetings on time. NCLAT held that such statutory oppression/mismanagement grievances fall within the Tribunal's exclusive jurisdiction under Sections 241-242 and are not arbitrable, and accordingly dismissed the appeal without costs, leaving the merits of the oppression/mismanagement petition to be decided by NCLT.

case_title: Pratosh Kumar Sharma vs M/S Bhanvi Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Pratosh Kumar Sharma (representing the company/appellant management) versus Respondent Nos. 1 and 2, M/S Bhanvi Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. and another (contesting respondents), with other respondents being formal parties. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not a lending/commercial transaction; this concerns an interim order appointing an Interim Administrator over the appellant company in connection with a pending Company Petition, and the scope of that Administrator's powers over the company's assets, properties, and books of accounts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; no monetary default is at issue. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: An earlier Interim Order was passed on 4 March 2016; the impugned order under appeal was passed on 21 October 2016 by NCLT New Delhi in Company Application No. S-CL-I/2016 in Company Petition No. 50(ND) of 2016, directing appointment of an Interim Administrator and interim custody of the company's assets, properties, books of accounts, vouchers, and papers. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal's prima facie observations at paragraphs 8, 9 and 10 of the impugned order formed the basis for appointing the Interim Administrator and directing custody of assets; the Appellate Tribunal treated these as tentative, prima facie views not binding on the final merits determination of the Company Petition. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Company Petition No. 50(ND) of 2016 remains pending before NCLT for final decision on merits; the Appellant challenged the interim order dated 21 October 2016 (appointing Interim Administrator and directing interim custody of assets/properties) before NCLAT via this Company Appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal's interim order appointing an Interim Administrator and directing interim custody of the company's assets and properties (in addition to its books of accounts) was justified and warranted at the interim stage, pending final adjudication of the Company Petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While an interim order appointing an Interim Administrator to prepare a report for the Tribunal may validly require custody of a company's books of accounts, vouchers and papers, it need not extend to interim custody of the company's broader assets and properties where such custody is not necessary for the limited purpose of submitting that report. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The time-bound disposal framework under Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 was invoked to expect expeditious final adjudication of the underlying Company Petition, reinforcing that interim measures should not preempt or substitute for the final merits determination. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prima facie observations made by the Tribunal at the interim stage (for the limited purpose of deciding on appointment of an Interim Administrator) cannot be treated as concluded findings and must not influence or be relied upon during final hearing or judgment on the Company Petition, which must be decided strictly on the evidence on record and the Interim Administrator's report. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The interim order was partly modified — the direction for interim custody of the company's assets and properties was set aside, while the direction for custody of books of accounts, vouchers, and papers was upheld, with safeguards imposed requiring intimation to the Interim Administrator and Respondents before any sale, mortgage, or encumbrance of company assets.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 21 October 2016 is modified to the extent that the direction to hand over interim custody of the company's assets and properties is set aside, while the direction to hand over books of accounts, vouchers and papers to the Interim Administrator is upheld; the Appellant is permitted to access books of account for maintaining current entries; any proposed sale, mortgage, alienation or encumbrance of company assets must be intimated to the Interim Administrator and Respondent Nos. 1 and 2, with proceeds recorded in the company's books and deposited in its bank account with details furnished to the Administrator; the appellants are directed to cooperate with and hand over records to the Interim Administrator immediately; the Tribunal is expected to decide the Company Petition expeditiously per Section 422 timelines, uninfluenced by the prima facie observations in the interim order. The Company Appeal stands disposed of accordingly.
summary: Pratosh Kumar Sharma appealed an NCLT interim order appointing an Interim Administrator and directing interim custody of the company's assets, properties, books of accounts and papers in a pending oppression/mismanagement-related Company Petition. NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, setting aside the direction for custody of assets and properties as unnecessary for the Administrator's limited reporting purpose, while upholding custody of financial records, and imposed safeguards for any future asset transactions. The Appellate Tribunal clarified that the Tribunal's prima facie observations must not influence final adjudication of the Company Petition, which remains pending on merits, and disposed of the Company Appeal with these modifications.

case_title: Khanakul Thana Krisijata Pannya Sarabarahakari & Babsayi Samitee Himghar Ltd. & Ors. vs Krishna Gopal Jana & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s Khanakul Thana Krisijata Pannya Sarabarahakari & Babsayi Samitee Himghar Ltd. and others, versus Respondent No.1 Krishna Gopal Jana (Applicant No. 1/original petitioner before NCLT, described as Borrower in a Memorandum of Agreement) and Respondent No.2 Ms. Sephali Jana (Applicant No. 2 before NCLT, an independent shareholder holding 15.61% of shares, who was not a party to the Agreement). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Memorandum of Agreement (Annexure-A to the Company Appeal) was reached between the Appellant (as Lender) and Respondent No.1 Krishna Gopal Jana (as Borrower); however, Respondent No.2, an independent 15.61% shareholder, was not a signatory to this Agreement. The underlying dispute is a shareholder oppression/mismanagement petition under Sections 397-398 of the Companies Act, 1956. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable within the scope of this appellate order; the appeal concerned the maintainability of the Company Petition rather than a monetary default determination. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned order was passed by NCLT on 29 August 2016; the Memorandum of Agreement between the Appellant and Respondent No.1 was executed and placed on record as Annexure-A to this Company Appeal. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The key evidence was the Memorandum of Agreement (Annexure-A) between the Appellant and Respondent No.1, which the Appellant argued should place the underlying petition in abeyance; however, Respondent No.2 (Ms. Sephali Jana), an independent shareholder holding 15.61% shares, was not a party to that Agreement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original Company Petition under Sections 397-398 of the Companies Act, 1956 was filed jointly by Applicant No.1 (Krishna Gopal Jana) and Applicant No.2 (Sephali Jana) before NCLT; NCLT's order dated 29 August 2016 was challenged by the Appellant (the company/Lender) before NCLAT via this Company Appeal, arguing the petition should be treated as not maintainable or held in abeyance in light of the Agreement with Respondent No.1.
legal_issues: Whether a Memorandum of Agreement executed between the company (Appellant) and one of two joint petitioners (Applicant No.1) in an oppression-and-mismanagement petition under Sections 397-398 of the Companies Act, 1956 renders the petition non-maintainable or liable to be kept in abeyance, where the second petitioner (an independent shareholder) was not a party to that Agreement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A settlement or agreement reached between a company and only one of multiple joint petitioners in an oppression-and-mismanagement petition does not affect the independent right of a co-petitioner who is not a party to that agreement to maintain and pursue the petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The maintainability of a petition under Sections 397-398 of the Companies Act, 1956 filed jointly by multiple applicants is assessed independently for each applicant; a settlement affecting one applicant's claim does not extinguish or hold in abeyance the substantive rights of a co-applicant who holds the requisite shareholding and did not join the settlement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Agreement (Annexure-A) was examined solely to determine its parties and scope; since the non-signatory co-petitioner independently held 15.61% shareholding (sufficient standing), the petition's maintainability at her instance was unaffected regardless of the Agreement's terms as to the other petitioner. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the petition remains maintainable at the instance of the non-signatory shareholder-petitioner irrespective of any arrangement between the company and the other petitioner, the appeal challenging the Tribunal's order was found to be without merit and was dismissed, upholding the impugned order, without prejudice to the rights and contentions of the parties including the first Respondent.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed for want of merit; the impugned Order dated 29 August 2016 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal is upheld. The Order is passed without prejudice to the rights and contentions of the parties, including first Respondent Krishna Gopal Jana.
summary: The appellant company challenged an NCLT order refusing to treat a shareholder oppression-and-mismanagement petition as non-maintainable or held in abeyance, based on a Memorandum of Agreement it had reached with one of the two joint petitioners, Krishna Gopal Jana. NCLAT held that since the second petitioner, an independent shareholder holding 15.61% shares, was not a party to that Agreement, her right to maintain the petition under Sections 397-398 of the Companies Act, 1956 remained unaffected. Finding no merit in the appeal, NCLAT dismissed it and upheld the impugned NCLT order, without prejudice to the rights of the parties including the first Respondent.

case_title: Prag Bosimi Synthetics Ltd. vs 3A Capital Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Prag Bosimi Synthetics Limited versus Respondent No.1 3A Capital Ltd. and others, the original petitioner before the erstwhile Company Law Board. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not addressed in this order; the appeal concerned solely a jurisdictional/maintainability question and did not reach the substance of the underlying Company Petition (CP No. 89/2011). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; no default amount or date is addressed in this order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The order under appeal was passed by the erstwhile Company Law Board, Kolkata on 9 May 2016 in CP No. 89/2011; the National Company Law Tribunal was constituted with effect from 1 June 2016; the present appeal against the pre-1 June 2016 Company Law Board order was filed before NCLAT thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: No evidence on the merits of the underlying dispute was considered; the sole basis for decision was the statutory appeal route applicable to orders passed by the Company Law Board before the constitution of the NCLT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Company Law Board, Kolkata passed an order on 9 May 2016 in CP No. 89/2011 filed by Respondent No.1; the Appellant filed the present appeal before NCLAT under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, without appearing at the hearing on 12 July 2016.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against an order passed by the erstwhile Company Law Board (before the constitution of the National Company Law Tribunal on 1 June 2016) is maintainable before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, or whether such an appeal must instead be filed before the High Court under Section 434(1)(b) of the Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against an order of the National Company Law Tribunal lies to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal under Section 421(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, but this remedy applies only to orders passed by the Tribunal after its constitution; orders passed by the erstwhile Company Law Board prior to the notified transfer date are appealable, if at all, only to the High Court under Section 434(1)(b). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 434(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 specifically provides that a person aggrieved by a decision or order of the Company Law Board made before the notified transfer date may file an appeal to the High Court within sixty days (extendable by a further sixty days on sufficient cause), on a question of law arising from such order — this is a distinct and exclusive remedy separate from Section 421 appeals to NCLAT. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: No evidentiary determination was required; the question was purely one of statutory forum and maintainability based on the date of the impugned order relative to the NCLT's constitution date of 1 June 2016. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the impugned order was passed by the erstwhile Company Law Board on 9 May 2016, prior to the constitution of the National Company Law Tribunal, an appeal against it does not lie to NCLAT under Section 421 and is not maintainable before it.
operative_order: The appeal is held not maintainable and is accordingly dismissed.
summary: Prag Bosimi Synthetics Ltd. appealed before NCLAT against an order dated 9 May 2016 passed by the erstwhile Company Law Board, Kolkata in CP No. 89/2011. Nobody appeared on behalf of the Appellant at the hearing. NCLAT held that since the impugned order was passed by the Company Law Board before the National Company Law Tribunal's constitution on 1 June 2016, any appeal against it lay to the High Court under Section 434(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013, and not to NCLAT under Section 421. The appeal was accordingly held not maintainable and dismissed.

case_title: Vinod Muktinath Sharma vs M/s Sharma Realty Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Vinod Muktinath Sharma, a shareholder (claimed 33.5%, disputed by Respondents as 2.5%) in Respondent No.1 M/s Sharma Realty Pvt. Ltd., a family company comprising the Appellant, another brother, and their father as shareholders/managers; Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 being the other brother and father. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute concerns two major properties of Respondent No.1 company — the Khandelwal Herman Property and the NIC (National Industrial Corporation) Property — and competing claims over development rights in the NIC property arising from cross-suits between Respondent No.1, Ackruti City Limited, and others (Suit Nos. 1358/2008 and 2392/2009 pending before the Bombay High Court), including a proposed settlement allegedly allocating development rights partly to Ackruti City Limited and partly to Respondent No.1. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; no monetary default is in issue — the dispute concerns alleged oppression via disposal of company property/development rights. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original Company Petition No. 74(ND)/2015 was filed by the Appellant alleging oppression; the Company Law Board had earlier restrained the Respondents from dealing with the Khandelwal Herman Property, and by order dated 29 October 2015 the Board rejected the Respondents' contention on shareholding percentage; the Bombay High Court Division Bench, by an order (partially illegible date, cited as '2219' in OCR, likely 2015), directed status quo over the NIC property asset; the impugned NCLT order was passed on 15 June 2016 in C.A. No. 05(MB)/2015, directing the Respondents to maintain status quo over development rights and any money arising from settlement in the pending suits, which was then appealed via this Company Appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant alleged the Respondents colluded with Ackruti City Limited to secure a consent decree in the Bombay High Court suits that would allocate roughly 20% of NIC property development rights to Ackruti without consideration and the remaining amount to Respondent No.1, with Respondent No.1 in turn potentially entering a joint venture with Ackruti without specified consideration; the Tribunal's counsel for Respondent No.1 could not give a specific answer on the consideration amount for any proposed transfer of development rights. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Company Petition No. 74(ND)/2015 remains pending before NCLT; the Appellant's application for interim relief (status quo over the NIC property) was partly addressed by NCLT's interim order dated 15 June 2016 directing status quo over development rights and settlement proceeds; the Appellant, dissatisfied that broader status quo was not granted, appealed this interim order to NCLAT under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal's interim order dated 15 June 2016, directing the Respondents to maintain status quo over development rights and settlement proceeds arising from pending Bombay High Court suits concerning the NIC property, adequately protected the Appellant's interest, or whether a broader status quo order restraining any dealing with the NIC property itself was warranted pending final disposal of the Company Petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will decline to modify an interim protective order passed by the tribunal of first instance where that order already directs maintenance of status quo over the disputed rights and any proceeds arising from a settlement, and where the underlying petition is shortly listed for further hearing, since such a direction is sufficient to safeguard the interests of all parties pending final adjudication. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Where a company's board itself has resolved that any dealing with development rights or interest in a disputed property requires the Board's approval, and the Tribunal's interim direction already mandates maintaining status quo over development rights and settlement proceeds and requires the Respondents to communicate proposed transactions to the applicant, this operates as an adequate interim safeguard without needing to extend to a blanket restraint on the property itself (particularly where a coordinate court, the Bombay High Court, has already directed status quo over the property asset in parallel proceedings). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Appellate Tribunal examined whether the Respondents could specify a consideration amount for any proposed transfer of development rights to a third party; the absence of a clear answer and the absence of any concluded settlement or consent decree before the High Court meant that the existing interim safeguard (status quo over development rights and proceeds) was deemed adequate at this interim stage, without requiring further appellate intervention. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Tribunal had already directed maintenance of status quo over development rights and settlement proceeds, and the Bombay High Court had separately directed status quo over the NIC property asset itself, and the Company Petition was due to be taken up shortly, the Appellate Tribunal found no reason to modify the interim order and disposed of the Company Appeal on that basis.
operative_order: The Company Appeal stands disposed of with no order as to costs, on the basis that the Tribunal's interim order dated 15 June 2016 (directing the Respondents to maintain status quo over development rights and settlement proceeds, and to communicate proposed transactions to the Appellant) is not modified and shall continue to protect the interests of all parties, including the Appellant, until the Company Petition is taken up for further orders.
summary: Vinod Muktinath Sharma, a shareholder in family-owned Sharma Realty Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT interim order that directed the Respondents to maintain status quo over development rights and settlement proceeds concerning the disputed NIC property, arguing a broader restraint on dealing with the property itself was necessary given alleged collusion with a third party, Ackruti City Limited, in pending Bombay High Court suits. NCLAT found the existing interim safeguard—combined with a parallel Bombay High Court status quo order over the property asset—adequate to protect all parties' interests pending final hearing of the Company Petition, declined to modify the interim order, and disposed of the Company Appeal with no order as to costs.

case_title: Upper India Steel Manufacturing & Engineering Company Ltd. & Ors. vs Shri Gurlal Singh Grewal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Upper India Steel Manufacturing & Engineering Company Ltd. & Ors. (respondents in the original Company Petition) versus Respondents Shri Gurlal Singh Grewal & Ors. (original petitioners before the erstwhile Company Law Board). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not addressed in this order; the appeal concerned solely a procedural transfer application and did not address the substance of the underlying Company Petition (CP No. 48 of 2007). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; no monetary default is addressed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Company Petition (CP No. 48 of 2007) was filed by the Respondents before the erstwhile Company Law Board in 2007 and was taken up for hearing by the concerned Member only after almost six years, on 11 September 2015; counsel for the Petitioners (Respondents herein) argued for fourteen days between 11 September 2015 and an unspecified date in January (OCR garbled); counsel for the Appellants argued for six days up to 13 March 2016 (OCR garbled year); the Petitioners' counsel then argued in reply for six days; judgment was reserved on 11 September 2015 but remained undisposed even six-and-a-half months later; the Appellants then sought transfer of the matter to the Mumbai Bench (CA 72/PB/2016) via the same Member who had earlier heard the matter as a Company Law Board Member, which application was dismissed by NCLT's impugned order dated 24 August 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellants' transfer application relied on the fact that the same Member (Shri B.S.V. Prakash Kumar) had already heard the matter extensively as a Company Law Board Member and had reserved judgment; NCLT rejected the transfer application, holding the matter was not so complicated as to require transfer to Mumbai Bench, and that the Technical Member would in any case need to hear the arguments afresh. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT's order dated 24 August 2016 dismissed the transfer application (CA 72/PB/2016) seeking transfer of CP No. 48 of 2007 (with attendant applications) to the Mumbai Bench; the Appellants challenged this dismissal before NCLAT via the present Company Appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal erred in dismissing an application to transfer a long-pending Company Petition to the Mumbai Bench, where the same presiding Member had earlier heard extensive arguments on the matter while it was pending before the erstwhile Company Law Board and had reserved judgment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A transfer application seeking to have a long-pending company law matter heard by the same Member who had previously heard it in a different judicial capacity or forum does not warrant transfer where the matter is not so factually or legally complicated as to necessitate transfer, particularly where the newly constituted Tribunal (with a Technical Member) would in any event need to hear arguments afresh. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 419 of the Companies Act, 2013 (concerning timely disposal by Benches of the Tribunal) was invoked to direct that the matter, having been left pending before the appropriate Bench (Chandigarh Bench), should be disposed of expeditiously in terms of that provision, rather than being transferred based on prior familiarity of a particular Member with the case. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Appellate Tribunal weighed the history of prolonged hearings (fourteen days of arguments, six days of counter-arguments, six days of reply, followed by over six months without disposal after judgment was reserved) but found this history, by itself, insufficient to justify transferring the case to a specific Bench merely because a particular Member had previously heard it. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: No ground was made out to transfer the case to the Member at the Mumbai Bench; the parties were directed to pursue the matter before the NCLT Chandigarh Bench, where the matter was pending disposal, and the transfer application's dismissal by NCLT was upheld.
operative_order: The Company Appeal stands disposed of with the aforesaid observations, upholding the dismissal of the transfer application; the parties are directed to pursue the case before NCLT, Chandigarh Bench, where the matter is pending, and that Bench is directed to dispose of the matter in terms of Section 419 of the Companies Act, 2013. There shall be no order as to costs.
summary: Upper India Steel Manufacturing & Engineering Company Ltd. and others appealed an NCLT order dismissing their application to transfer a long-pending Company Petition (CP No. 48 of 2007) to the Mumbai Bench, where a Member who had previously heard extensive arguments on the matter as a Company Law Board Member was now sitting. NCLAT found no ground to warrant such transfer, holding the matter was not so complex as to require it and that the Technical Member would need to rehear arguments regardless. The appeal against the dismissal of the transfer application was disposed of, with the parties directed to pursue their case before NCLT Chandigarh Bench for expeditious disposal under Section 419, and no order as to costs.

case_title: Gulshan Kumar Garg vs Jaiprakash Associates Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Gulshan Kumar Garg, a depositor/creditor, versus Respondent Jaiprakash Associates Ltd., the company against which repayment of deposit was sought. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute concerned repayment of the principal amount along with interest due to the Appellant from the Respondent company under the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, specifically Rule 17 governing repayment of deposits. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Specific default amount not stated in the order (illegible/OCR-garbled); the Appellant confirmed at the hearing that he had received the amount due under Rule 17. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not specified in the order beyond the fact that repayment was made under Rule 17 of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, prior to the hearing on 18 October 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant himself stated before the Appellate Tribunal that he had received the amount due under Rule 17; counsel for the Respondent company submitted that the appeal had accordingly become infructuous. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Company Appeal was filed by the Appellant seeking recovery of the principal amount with interest due to him as a depositor; at the hearing on 18 October 2016, in view of the stand taken by both parties (that payment had already been received), the Tribunal disposed of the appeal without further orders on merits, while directing that Intervention Applications filed in this appeal be considered along with an analogous Company Appeal (AT) No. 6 of 2016.
legal_issues: Whether any further order is required on an appeal seeking recovery of a deposit repayment where the appellant has already received the amount due under Rule 17 of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, rendering the appeal infructuous.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where an appellant seeking recovery of a deposit amount confirms receipt of the amount due under the applicable statutory rule prior to final hearing, the appeal is rendered infructuous and no further substantive order on the merits of the claim is required. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 17 of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014 governs the repayment obligation of a company to its depositors, and satisfaction of that obligation (as confirmed by the depositor-appellant) extinguishes the live controversy in an appeal seeking such repayment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the appellant's own admission of receipt of payment, combined with the respondent's confirming submission, as sufficient basis to treat the matter as resolved without requiring further evidentiary inquiry into the original claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the underlying grievance (non-payment of deposit) had been remedied by payment under Rule 17, the Appellate Tribunal disposed of the Company Appeal without passing any further order on merits, while directing that pending Intervention Applications filed in this appeal be considered together with a related, analogous Company Appeal (AT) No. 6 of 2016.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is disposed of without any further order, the appellant having confirmed receipt of the amount due under Rule 17 of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, rendering the appeal infructuous; Intervention Application(s) filed in this appeal are directed to be considered along with the analogous Company Appeal (AT) No. 6 of 2016.
summary: Gulshan Kumar Garg, a depositor, had appealed against Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. seeking recovery of principal and interest due under the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014. At the hearing, the Appellant confirmed he had already received the amount due under Rule 17, and the Respondent's counsel submitted the appeal had become infructuous. NCLAT accordingly disposed of the Company Appeal without passing any further order on merits, while directing that pending intervention applications filed in this appeal be taken up along with a related, analogous appeal, Company Appeal (AT) No. 6 of 2016.

case_title: Suresh Goyal & Ors. vs Shakti Solvex & General Mills Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Suresh Goyal & Ors. versus Respondents Shakti Solvex & General Mills Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not specified in this order; the appeal involved a valuation dispute connected to the underlying company matter, with a Valuer's report being central to the appellant's decision to withdraw. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable/not specified in this order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not specified in this order beyond the fact that a report was filed by the Valuer prior to the hearing on 16 November 2016, and a petition for condonation of delay had also been filed alongside the appeal. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The key document referenced was a report filed by the Valuer, in view of which the Appellants' counsel sought permission to withdraw the appeal rather than press it further. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants had filed the Company Appeal along with a petition for condonation of delay, challenging an unspecified impugned order; at the hearing on 16 November 2016, in light of the Valuer's report, the Appellants' counsel sought to withdraw the appeal, which was allowed by NCLAT without liberty to file a fresh appeal against the same impugned order.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellants should be permitted to withdraw their Company Appeal (along with the accompanying petition for condonation of delay) in light of the Valuer's report, and whether any liberty should be granted to file a fresh appeal against the same impugned order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant may be permitted to withdraw a pending appeal at their own request, but such withdrawal, once allowed without liberty to re-file, operates as a final disposal precluding any further challenge to the same impugned order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Not applicable; no statutory provision was interpreted in this order beyond the procedural act of allowing withdrawal of the appeal and the connected condonation of delay petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Not applicable; no evidentiary determination was made, as the appeal was withdrawn at the Appellants' own request in light of the Valuer's report rather than being decided on merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants' request to withdraw the appeal was allowed, but expressly without liberty to file any fresh appeal against the same impugned order, rendering the withdrawal final and conclusive as to that order.
operative_order: The prayer to withdraw the appeal is allowed, without any liberty to file any appeal against the same impugned order. The appeal along with the petition for condonation of delay are dismissed as withdrawn.
summary: Suresh Goyal & Ors. sought to withdraw their Company Appeal against Shakti Solvex & General Mills Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., along with an accompanying petition for condonation of delay, in light of a report filed by a Valuer. NCLAT allowed the withdrawal but expressly barred the Appellants from filing any fresh appeal against the same impugned order. The appeal and the condonation of delay petition were accordingly dismissed as withdrawn, bringing finality to the matter.

case_title: Hasmukhlal Madhavlal Patel & Anr. vs. Ambika Food Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 272 of 2017 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 273 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Original Petitioners Manish and Krunal Patel formed the VP Patel Group (holding 24.20%); Original Respondents 2 and 3 Hasmukhlal and Dilipkumar Patel formed the HM Patel Group (holding 30.80%); Respondents 4 and 5 formed the Sheth Group (holding 45%) in Ambika Food Products Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and equity distribution within a closely held private company with an initial paid-up capital of Rs. 1 crore. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unilateral expansion of authorized capital to Rs. 2 crores, pre-emptive disproportionate share allotment to the HM Patel Group, and alleged siphoning of over Rs. 98.72 lakhs during 2008-2009. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting on 18.12.2009 proposed capital increase; notice issued 24.12.2009 for EOGM held on 27.01.2010; share allotment finalized 09.02.2010; rival requisition under Section 169 issued on 22.02.2010 culminating in an EOGM on 05.03.2010 removing Respondents 2 and 3. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered postal envelopes containing unrelated company papers instead of EOGM notices; share application forms dated 04.02.2010 wherein HM Patel Group members applied for equity far exceeding the 1:1 entitlement prior to authorization. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: TP 10/2016 was filed on 28.10.2010 and TP 197/2016 was filed in February 2012 alleging oppression and mismanagement; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 17.05.2017 upheld capital expansion, voided the directors' removal, ordered proportionate reallocation of shares as of 18.12.2009, and directed an audit for FY 2009-2010.
legal_issues: Whether the unilateral allotment of increased share capital disproportionately to a majority faction prior to offering unsubscribed shares constitutes an oppressive act, and whether calling an EOGM under Section 169 without convening a Board meeting renders the removal of directors void.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While a bona fide capital increase to fulfill institutional credit requirements is valid, allotting unsubscribed new shares disproportionately without first providing all existing shareholders a fair opportunity to subscribe in proportion to their holding is oppressive and void. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 169 mandates that a valid EOGM requisition must first be placed before the Board of Directors, and requisitionists acquire the statutory right to convene the EOGM directly only if the Board fails to act within 21 days from deposit. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The fiduciary duty of directors requires strict demonstration of good faith in share allocation; pre-planned over-subscription applications submitted prior to formal approval reveal mala fide conduct. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The share allotment resolution dated 09.02.2010 was invalid, requiring proportionate reallocation as of 18.12.2009, while the removal of directors on 05.03.2010 was legally void.
operative_order: Appeals partly allowed; paragraph 92(c) of the NCLT order modified to substitute the audit commencement period from 'financial year 2009-2010' to 'financial year 2008-2009', with all other substantive directions regarding share reallocation, director reinstatement, and share valuation affirmed without costs.
summary: Hasmukhlal Patel and Dilipkumar Patel appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order addressing cross-petitions for oppression and mismanagement in Ambika Food Products Pvt. Ltd. The primary disputes concerned an increase in authorized capital from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 2 crores, disproportionate share allotments to the HM Patel Group, and the removal of directors at an EOGM convened by the VP Patel Group. The Appellate Tribunal held that while the capital increase was justified, the share allotment was executed oppressively and required proportionate re-allotment. It also affirmed that the directors' removal violated Section 169. Modifying the audit scope to begin from FY 2008-2009, the appeals were disposed of.

case_title: The Statesman Ltd. vs. Emaar MGF Land Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Statesman Ltd. acted as the Objector/Appellant (alleged Judgment Creditor), Emaar MGF Land Ltd. as Demerged Company/Respondent No. 1, and MGF Developments Ltd. as Resulting Company/Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lease agreement dated 20.09.2006 for 162,520 sq. ft. of commercial space at Kolkata for 12 years with an option to renew for 9 years. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claims of Rs. 5,92,81,459 deducted as TDS and Rs. 24,90,87,095 for unmarketable commercial property allotted under a settlement, totaling an outstanding claim of Rs. 30,83,68,554 under an arbitral award. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitral award delivered on the evening of 12.05.2016; First Motion Scheme Application CA(M) 77/2016 filed earlier on 12.05.2016; High Court convened creditor meetings on 30.05.2016; Second Motion CP 689/2016 notices issued on 09.08.2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Creditor lists framed as of 29.02.2016, newspaper publications in Business Standard on 09.06.2016 and 15.06.2016, and Form 16A TDS certificates confirming statutory tax deductions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Petition No. 689/2016 was transferred from the Delhi High Court to NCLT New Delhi; NCLT approved the demerger scheme on 08.01.2018, holding that the arbitral debt stood satisfied and the objector lacked locus standi.
legal_issues: Whether a demerger scheme under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 is vitiated by suppression of material facts when an arbitral award is pronounced late on the same day the First Motion is filed, and whether an individual disputed creditor representing negligible debt value can obstruct a scheme approved by an overwhelming majority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Non-inclusion of a liability crystallized through an arbitral award delivered after the execution and swearing of a First Motion application based on a prior practicable cut-off date does not constitute fraudulent suppression of material facts. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 9(b) of the Companies Rules, 2016 and Section 230(4) intend that outstanding debt must reflect the latest audited statements not exceeding six months prior, and objection thresholds require at least five percent of total outstanding debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Public notice via paper publication provides constructive notice to all classes of creditors; a dissenting creditor must demonstrate that their vote could materially affect the collective statutory majority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant's claim represented less than two percent of total unsecured debt, could not alter the outcome, and remained unaffected since both companies survived the demerger.
operative_order: Appeal rejected with directions that the Appellant shall pay costs of Rs. 75,000/- to each of the two Respondents, without prejudice to the pending arbitral proceedings.
summary: The Statesman Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench order approving a Scheme of Arrangement for demerger between Emaar MGF Land Ltd. and MGF Developments Ltd. The Appellant contended that the Respondents suppressed an arbitral award of approximately Rs. 30.83 crores rendered on 12.05.2016 and failed to serve notice as a judgment creditor. The NCLAT held that filing the First Motion based on creditor records dated 29.02.2016 did not amount to suppression. Furthermore, constructive notice was given via press publications, and the Appellant's debt value could not influence the overwhelming majority vote. The appeal was rejected with Rs. 75,000 costs to each Respondent.

case_title: Vinod Kumar Sharma vs. M/s. Bhawani Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Review Application (AT) No. 01 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 22 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vinod Kumar Sharma as Applicant/Original Petitioner and M/s Bhawani Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. alongside three promoter-directors as Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation of a private company with an initial subscription of 40 shares of Rs. 100 each and transfer of 5 Pacca Bighas of land situated at Village Hajipur, Meerut for company project development. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Consideration of Rs. 2,80,000 paid by the company to the applicant on 03.06.1988, which was reciprocally remitted back and booked as unsecured debt rather than equity capital. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original land transfer effected 03.06.1988; Company Petition filed as CP No. 68/ND/2010 before the CLB alleging oppression and transferred to NCLT Allahabad as CA No. 23 of 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheets and Chartered Accountant reports from 16.08.1991 and 31.03.1994 listing Rs. 2,80,000 under unsecured loans from directors; AGM returns of 08.09.1996 reflecting transfer of the applicant's 10 subscription shares on 06.04.1996; absence of share certificates. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad on 18.11.2016 dismissed the petition for lack of maintainability under Section 399; NCLAT initially dismissed the appeal on 09.02.2017; the Supreme Court on 21.08.2017 granted liberty to seek review on the premise that NCLT found 14.017% holding.
legal_issues: Whether unallotted funds recorded consistently as unsecured debt in corporate books can be computed towards shareholding to fulfill the ten percent threshold under Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petitioner seeking to maintain an action for oppression and mismanagement must possess proprietary title to the statutory minimum paid-up equity as of right, and mere unadjudicated claims or advances recorded as unsecured loans cannot be treated as equity holding to satisfy eligibility. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 399(1)(a) requires an applicant to actually hold not less than one-tenth of issued share capital; a member cannot claim eligibility based on hypothetical shareholding that would arise only upon future conversion of debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical possession of share certificates or entries in the Register of Members is essential; contradictory claims regarding property transfers and refund promises destroy the credibility of alleged equity contributions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The applicant held at best 0.05% equity, failing the threshold of Section 399, and had misrepresented the lower tribunal's hypothetical computation as an affirmative factual finding.
operative_order: Review Application (AT) No. 01 of 2017 rejected and Company Appeal (AT) No. 22 of 2017 dismissed without costs.
summary: Vinod Kumar Sharma filed a review application following Supreme Court directions in a dispute concerning M/s. Bhawani Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. The Applicant contended that the NCLT recorded a finding that he held 14.017% shareholding, qualifying him under Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956. The NCLAT examined the balance sheets and records, establishing that a payment of Rs. 2,80,000 for land was entered as an unsecured loan rather than issued share capital, leaving his equity at 0.05% prior to transfer. Finding that the 14.017% figure was merely a rejected hypothetical argument and that no share certificates existed, the NCLAT dismissed both the review and the appeal.

case_title: Srei Infrastructure Finance Ltd. vs. Sumit Binani & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. as Financial Creditor and Resolution Applicant (H1 bidder); M/s Adhunik Alloys & Power Ltd. as Corporate Debtor; Sumit Binani as Resolution Professional; and Bhagwati Power & Steel Ltd. (BPSL) as rival Resolution Applicant (H2 bidder). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) triggered under Section 7 of the IBC by State Bank of India against the Corporate Debtor, followed by submission of competing resolution plans. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor under Section 7; competing resolution plans submitted by SREI (Rs. 300 Crores) and BPSL (Rs. 326 Crores with upfront cash consideration). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 03.08.2017; BPSL filed objection CA(IB) 289/KB/2018 on 12.04.2018; RP held SREI ineligible on 16.11.2017 based on Hyderabad NCLT ruling; NCLAT reversed Hyderabad NCLT ruling on 20.07.2018; 270-day CIRP period expired on 18.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT Hyderabad order dated 16.11.2017 treating SREI as a 'related party' in Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd. (DCHL) for holding over 20% equity; share allotment disclosures to BSE/NSE dated 14.01.2015; and NCLAT judgment dated 20.07.2018 finding Rs. 20 crore investment was never recognized as equity by RoC or Stock Exchanges. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed CA (IB) No. 377/KB/2018 on 26.04.2018 refusing to restrain CoC from approving BPSL's plan; SREI appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a finding of ineligibility under Section 29A(c) read with Section 29A(j) based on an Adjudicating Authority order survives after that foundational order is set aside in appeal, and whether a rival resolution applicant can re-agitate related party status when the appellate tribunal has definitively settled the issue.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An objection to a resolution applicant's eligibility under Section 29A that rests entirely upon an adverse judicial finding of 'related party' status collapses once that underlying finding is reversed on appeal by an appellate tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Connected person and related party disqualifications under Section 29A(c) and 29A(j) require actual, legally recognized shareholding or management control in an NPA entity; investments not legally converted or recognized as equity cannot sustain disqualification. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mixed findings of law and fact regarding corporate membership and equity status determined by an appellate tribunal attain finality and cannot be reopened or reviewed in collateral proceedings under the guise of statutory estoppel. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: SREI was an eligible Resolution Applicant; the pending approval of BPSL's resolution plan ceased to survive, and the RP was bound to submit SREI's approved plan to the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; BPSL's resolution plan held non-surviving; RP directed to place SREI's CoC-approved resolution plan before the Adjudicating Authority within seven days for approval under Section 30(6); the litigation pendency period from 18.05.2018 excluded from CIRP duration without costs.
summary: SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order that refused to halt the CIRP of M/s Adhunik Alloys & Power Ltd. SREI, the highest evaluated bidder (H1), had been disqualified under Section 29A of the IBC following an NCLT Hyderabad order treating it as a related party to Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd., an NPA entity. SREI's disqualification was overturned by NCLAT on 20.07.2018. The NCLAT held that the foundation of ineligibility had been completely effaced, rendering SREI eligible. Consequently, BPSL's plan ceased to survive, and the RP was directed to place SREI's plan before the NCLT for approval.

case_title: Supriya Das & Ors. vs. Sova Tea Company Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Supriya Das (widow) and two daughters of Late Sujit Kumar Das (original petitioners) as minority shareholders against Sova Tea Company Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1) and Anjan Kumar Das (Respondent No. 2, nephew and managing director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operation and ownership of tea garden business under a private company incorporated in 1989, originally held 50:50 between the two family branches (1141 shares each). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Expansion of authorized share capital from Rs. 5,00,000 to Rs. 15,00,000; issuance of 12,718 equity shares exclusively to Respondents 2 to 4 on 20.01.2004; cessation of Rs. 20,000 monthly director remuneration/rent in 2008; unpaid share agreement balance of Rs. 7,00,001. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share transfer agreement dated 06.05.1998; capital increase on 28.07.2003; share allotment on 20.01.2004; vacation of directorship on 02.12.2007 under Section 283(1)(g); Company Petition filed in 2010. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered postal receipts (receipt No. 5794 dated 05.12.2003); board minutes dated 28.10.2002 granting sole management authority to Respondent No. 2; board minutes of 02.12.2007 noting 24 consecutive meeting absences and non-compliance with Section 266D (DIN filing). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed Company Petition No. 426(KB)/2010 on 07.07.2017 citing acquiescence, unclean hands, and delay/laches, while directing transmission of undisputed shares; petitioners appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether capital expansion, share allotment to meet lender collateral requirements, relocation of registered office, and statutory cessation of directorship due to consecutive absences and lack of DIN constitute acts of oppression and mismanagement when challenged after gross delay.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Capital expansion and equity allotments undertaken bona fide to procure commercial finance in corporate interest cannot be characterized as oppressive where complaining members were served notice and showed no willingness to subscribe. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 283(1)(g) operates by operation of law to vacate a director's office when they absent themselves from consecutive board meetings without obtaining leave of absence and fail to comply with mandatory DIN requirements under Section 266D. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Equitable relief under Sections 397/398 requires clean hands and prompt assertion; long-standing acquiescence with knowledge bars claims under the doctrine of delay and laches. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The respondents acted within corporate necessity and legal bounds; the petitioners failed to prove any act of oppression or mismanagement, and vacation of directorship was statutory and valid.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the order of NCLT Kolkata dated 07.07.2017 upholding the company transactions and directing transfer of admitted shares left by the deceased to legal heirs affirmed without costs.
summary: Legal heirs of Late Sujit Kumar Das appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dismissing their petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 against Sova Tea Company Pvt. Ltd. and Anjan Kumar Das. Appellants challenged the 2003–2004 increase in share capital, allotment of 12,718 shares to respondents, registered office relocation, and vacation of their directorships. The NCLAT held that capital was expanded lawfully to secure credit facilities, notices were duly served, and directorships stood vacated by law under Section 283(1)(g) due to 24 consecutive absences and failure to obtain DIN. Finding no oppression or mismanagement, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Dr. M.A.S. Subramanian & Ors. vs. T.S. Sivakumar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Dr. M.A.S. Subramanian and family members (controlling majority and directors) against Respondents 1 to 5 (original petitioners, minority shareholders), M/s Vee Pee Estate and Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (purchaser/Respondent No. 6), and M/s Hotel Mass Pvt. Ltd. (Company/Respondent No. 7). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation of a hotel enterprise in 1982 wherein late founder M.A. Shanmugam was allotted 12,180 shares against conveyance of 52 Kuzhies and 14 Veesams of land; subsequent unlawful sale of the hotel's entire assets and business to an outsider. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Sale of company buildings, fixtures, and movables for Rs. 3,93,80,706 (substantially lower than book value), appropriation of land worth Rs. 58.50 crores, and clandestine transfer of 3,15,860 equity shares (97.83% stake). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form No. 2 share return filed 14.03.1983; land lease agreement created by MD on 16.09.1998; composite sale deed executed on 31.10.2011; sale deed registered as Doc No. 1844 of 2013 on 07.10.2014; Company Petition filed on 25.10.2014. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Balance sheet notes for FY 1987-1988, 2005-2006, and 2010-2011 reflecting the land as a fixed asset of the company; self-dealing lease deed executed by Appellant No. 1 acting simultaneously as lessor and lessee; total absence of general body notices or special resolutions authorizing asset alienation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai in TCP 157/2016 ordered appointment of an independent auditor and PCS on 03.10.2017; Appellants appealed seeking to validate the sale.
legal_issues: Whether a majority managing director holding company property in trust under part performance can treat corporate immovable assets as personal property, and whether disposing of the entire undertaking and transferring majority shares to an outsider without pre-emption notice violates fiduciary duties and constitutes severe oppression and mismanagement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Corporate controllers stand in a fiduciary position as trustees of company assets held under part performance; alienating the entire corporate substratum and disposing of equity to non-members without pre-emptive notice violates the Articles of Association and constitutes actionable oppression and mismanagement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Broad discretionary powers granted to directors under articles regulating share capital cannot override mandatory pre-emption clauses in articles governing transfer of shares, nor can they circumvent statutory requirements for shareholder consent to sell a company undertaking. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Self-dealing contracts executed by a director in a dual capacity without general body sanction fail the fiduciary duty test; book entries and balance sheet disclosures consistently acknowledging asset ownership bind the company's directors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The alienation of the hotel undertaking and share transfers were executed in breach of trust and oppression of minority shareholders, requiring nullification of the sale deed and share transfers.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of by quashing and setting aside share transfers in favor of third parties; restoring shareholding as of 29.09.2011; declaring sale deed dated 31.10.2011 non-binding on the Company; upholding independent audit; and directing NCLT to immediately appoint an Administrator and new Directors under Section 242(2)(k) without costs.
summary: Controlling directors of M/s Hotel Mass Pvt. Ltd., led by Dr. M.A.S. Subramanian, appealed against an NCLT Chennai order that instituted an investigation into the sale of the company's entire hotel undertaking and majority shareholding to M/s Vee Pee Estate and Hotels Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT held that the land and hotel building formed the company's primary substratum, held in trust and reflected in balance sheets since 1983. The managing director breached fiduciary duties by executing a self-dealing lease deed and surreptitiously alienating corporate assets and shares without EOGM approval or pre-emptive offers to minority members. NCLAT set aside the sale deed and share transfers, restored shareholding to 29.09.2011, and ordered appointment of an Administrator.

case_title: Avance Logistics & Trading India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Bell Finvest (India) Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 336 of 2017, 07 of 2018 and 10 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Bell Finvest (India) Ltd. as Financial Creditor across three proceedings; Naveen Luthra (shareholder of Corporate Debtor M/s Luthra Water Systems Pvt. Ltd., CA 336/2017), M/s Avance Logistics & Trading India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, CA 07/2018), and Intercon Container Survey & Commodities Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, CA 10/2018). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Short-term commercial loan agreements carrying upfront interest deductions (flat 10% to 24% p.a.) coupled with contractual default penal interest provisions stipulated at 1% per day (365% p.a.). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in loan facilities; Intercon Container defaulted on repayment of Rs. 58,55,500 as on 20.06.2017; Luthra Water disbursed Rs. 1,37,66,400 after upfront deduction of Rs. 34,41,600; all corporate debtors failed to pay contractual principal and accrued interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Sections 433/434 Companies Act 1956 issued on 11.09.2016; Section 7 petitions admitted by NCLT Mumbai on 15.11.2017 (Luthra Water) and 11.09.2017 (Avance Logistics); Intercon petition rejected by NCLT Mumbai on 15.09.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, promissory notes, personal and corporate guarantees, disbursement records reflecting net payouts after deducting advance interest, and default computation sheets showing 1% per day penal interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted Section 7 petitions against Luthra Water Systems and Avance Logistics, but rejected the petition against Intercon Container holding the penal interest to be usurious; appeals were consolidated before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under Section 7 of the IBC has the jurisdiction to investigate, adjudicate, or reject an insolvency petition on the ground that the contractual penal interest claimed by a financial creditor is usurious or extortionate under the Usurious Loans Act, 1918.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency proceeding under Section 7 of the IBC is not a money claim, suit, or debt recovery mechanism, and the Adjudicating Authority lacks statutory competence to reopen contracts or scale down interest under usury laws. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 3 and 4 of the Usurious Loans Act, 1918 apply strictly to civil suits and court-administered insolvency proceedings; by virtue of the jurisdictional bar in Section 231 of the IBC, usury statutes have no application to Section 7 or 9 proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Section 7(5), the Adjudicating Authority is confined to ascertaining whether the application is complete and whether there is an existing financial debt and default; disputes regarding quantum or extortionate interest cannot preclude admission when default on principal is undisputed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The admissions in CA 336/2017 and CA 07/2018 were lawful and sustained, while the rejection in CA 10/2018 was erroneous as the Adjudicating Authority could not invoke the Usurious Loans Act to dismiss a valid petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 336 of 2017 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 07 of 2018 dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 10 of 2018 allowed, order dated 15.11.2017 set aside, and matter remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to admit the application after notice if default is not cleared, without costs.
summary: Consolidated appeals were filed challenging orders of NCLT Mumbai Bench regarding Section 7 IBC petitions initiated by Financial Creditor Bell Finvest (India) Ltd. Corporate debtors contended that contractual penal interest of 1% per day (365% p.a.) was extortionate and void under the Usurious Loans Act, 1918. The NCLAT held that Section 7 proceedings are for corporate resolution and not recovery suits, rendering the Usurious Loans Act, 1918 inapplicable. Because existence of debt and default on principal was established, the Adjudicating Authority was obligated to admit the petitions. The appeals against admission were dismissed, while the order rejecting admission was set aside.

case_title: Palaniandavar Benefit Fund Ltd. vs. Registrar of Companies, Chennai
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Palaniandavar Benefit Fund Ltd. (Appellant/Original Petitioner), a non-banking benefit fund incorporated in 1991, represented by Director Maickavel Ravichandran, against Registrar of Companies (ROC), Chennai (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operating a benefit fund to receive deposits and issue small-ticket micro-loans (up to Rs. 15,000) against gold/silver jewels and securities in Nagapattinam, Tamil Nadu. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total failure to file statutory Annual Returns and Balance Sheets with the ROC for six consecutive financial years from 2010-11 to 2015-16, alongside reporting Nil income tax liability for AY 2016-17 and 2017-18. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Show cause notice in Form STK-1 issued on 20.03.2017 allowing 30 days for representation; striking-off notification published in Gazette of India on 15-21 July 2017 (S.No. 12077); representation sent to ROC on 18.08.2017; IT returns filed belatedly in February/March 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Non-filing on MCA portal; statutory notices published in English and vernacular newspapers; Income Tax Return Acknowledgements reflecting Nil tax/income for AY 2014-15 through AY 2017-18; company's claim of professional accountant abandonment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed CP No. CP/65/(IB)/2018 on 13.04.2018, categorizing the company as a non-operating shell company based on Nil tax returns; the company appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the striking off of a company's name under Section 248 of the Companies Act, 2013 was procedurally valid when notice was served and published, and whether filing belated Nil income tax returns establishes that the company was carrying on business or in operation to justify revival under Section 252.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Failure to submit statutory financial records for more than two consecutive financial years justifies a statutory presumption of non-operation under Section 248, and filing Nil income tax returns after striking off cannot prove that a company was carrying on business as a going concern. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 248 read with Rule 7(1) requires substantial service via direct notice (Form STK-1) and wide public notice in English and vernacular gazettes/newspapers; a Nil return of income tax must be legally interpreted as a 'Nil return of business'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The evidentiary burden under Section 252 to prove active business operation cannot be satisfied by blaming professional consultants or asserting lack of legal awareness when promoters have maintained decades of prior corporate filings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ROC adhered strictly to statutory procedure, natural justice was satisfied, and the appellant company was non-operational and shell in character, warranting dismissal.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Chennai Bench dated 13.04.2018 upholding the striking off of the company's name from the Register of Companies affirmed without costs.
summary: Palaniandavar Benefit Fund Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dismissing its petition under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking restoration to the Register of Companies.
