The ROC Chennai struck off the company's name in July 2017 following continuous failure to file statutory balance sheets and annual returns from FY 2010-11 onwards. The company contended lack of notice and blamed its accountant, claiming it was an operational benefit fund. The NCLAT held that statutory notices in STK-1, STK-5, and newspaper publications fulfilled natural justice. Furthermore, belatedly filed Income Tax Returns declaring Nil tax equated to Nil business, confirming non-operation. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: MJM Industries Pvt. Ltd. vs. The Registrar of Companies, Andhra Pradesh & Telangana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: MJM Industries Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Original Applicant), a private company with three directors and paid-up capital of Rs. 5,00,000, against Registrar of Companies (ROC), Andhra Pradesh & Telangana (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate incorporation to manufacture, trade, export, and assemble industrial goods and LPG-fueled iron boxes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Absolute failure to file statutory annual financial statements (Section 137) and annual returns (Section 92) with the ROC since the date of incorporation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: STK-1 notice issued to the company and two directors via speed post on 17.03.2017; Form STK-5 published on 05.05.2017; STK-5A published in English and Telugu newspapers on 15.05.2017; strike-off notice STK-7 issued 21.07.2017; dissolution gazette published 19.08.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Speed post postal dispatch records and BNPL expenditure receipts totaling Rs. 33 lakhs incurred by ROC; unfiled balance sheets and auditor reports for FY 2013-14 to 2017-18; Form DIR-12 appointing a third director filed on 14.03.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench rejected restoration application CA No. 95/252/HDB/2017 on 19.09.2017 holding the appeal casual and devoid of supporting record; company appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether omission to serve individual Form STK-1 notices on a newly appointed third director invalidates a striking-off action under Section 248(1) when the company and two existing directors were served via speed post and public notice in newspapers was effected.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of statutory strike-off notice upon the registered company and a majority of its directors on record constitutes substantial compliance with natural justice; omitting an individual director does not vitiate the removal where constructive and public notice is established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 248(1) read with Rule 3(2) of the Companies Rules, 2016 and Section 27 of the General Clauses Act requires dispatch to available recorded addresses; service upon the corporate entity constitutes notice to all constituent directors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: When official dispatch proof and newspaper publications (Form STK-5A) are produced by the statutory authority, failure by the company or directors to respond creates a rebuttable presumption of knowledge and non-operation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant failed to file statutory returns since incorporation or respond to public and personal notices, justifying the conclusion of dissolution and rejection of the appeal.
operative_order: Appeal rejected; the impugned order dated 19.09.2017 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench in CA 95/252/HDB/2017 upheld without costs.
summary: MJM Industries Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Hyderabad Bench rejecting its application under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 against ROC Andhra Pradesh & Telangana. The company's name was struck off under Section 248(5) after it completely failed to file annual accounts and returns since incorporation. The company argued that the strike-off was defective as its third director was not individually served notice under Rule 3(2). The NCLAT held that speed post dispatch to the company and two directors, along with extensive newspaper publication in STK-5A, amounted to substantial notice. In the absence of timely objections or statutory filings, the strike-off was valid, and the appeal was rejected.

case_title: VLS Finance Ltd. vs. Southend Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 57 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 370 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: VLS Finance Ltd. (Appellant/Third-Party Intervener), Southend Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 Company), Dinesh Kumar Gupta & family (Respondents 2-5), and Vikrant Puri (Respondent No. 22/Original Petitioner). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial equity investment agreement dated 12.07.2007 by VLS Finance in BMS IT Institute Pvt. Ltd. to develop a 34,275 sq. meter IT plot in NOIDA, resulting in an arbitral award against BMS and its promoters. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default under an arbitral award dated 02.03.2015 obtained by Appellant; high court injunctions against alienation of property at B-319, Okhla Industrial Area Phase-I; development rights transferred via conveyance deed dated 10.06.2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court injunction issued 27.04.2012; arbitral award rendered 02.03.2015; Company Petition CP 24/2016 filed under Section 397/398; impleadment denied on 04.09.2017; petition withdrawn on 19.12.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: High Court and Supreme Court interim orders restraining disposal of Southend's 47.5% constructed share; share transfer records showing promoter stakes shifted to Vikrant Puri; withdrawal application CA 459/2017 filed under Rule 82. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench permitted intervention only to VLS Finance on 04.09.2017 (subject of CA 370/2017), and allowed the original petitioner to withdraw the petition on 19.12.2017 citing amicable settlement; VLS Finance appealed against the withdrawal.
legal_issues: Whether a non-member third party granted leave to intervene can prevent the original petitioner from withdrawing a company petition under Section 241/Rule 82, and whether NCLT must keep an oppression petition alive to protect third-party arbitral decree holders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition alleging oppression and mismanagement is an internal action maintainable solely by a statutory member; an intervener who is not a shareholder possesses no vested legal right to compel continuation of the petition when warring shareholders settle and seek withdrawal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 82 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 vests the Tribunal with discretion to grant leave to withdraw a Section 241 petition; that discretion cannot be hijacked by an outside third party to convert the Tribunal into an enforcement or monitoring forum. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Apprehensions of future collateral breaches of independent court orders do not confer locus standi under Section 399/241; non-mention of pending appeals in procedural forms does not invalidate a voluntary withdrawal where all parties are represented. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT did not act arbitrarily in granting leave to withdraw, and the appellant must pursue remedies for enforcement or contempt before the High Court and Supreme Court.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 57 of 2018 dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) No. 370 of 2017 disposed of as infructuous, without costs.
summary: VLS Finance Ltd. appealed against an order of the NCLT Principal Bench allowing Vikrant Puri to withdraw his petition under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 against Southend Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. following an amicable settlement. VLS Finance, an external arbitral decree-holder with restraint orders from the Delhi High Court and Supreme Court, was permitted to intervene but denied impleadment. It opposed withdrawal, asserting collusion and potential violations of High Court injunctions. The NCLAT held that oppression proceedings cannot be kept alive at the behest of a non-member lacking statutory locus standi. Concluding the NCLT exercised sound discretion under Rule 82, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: K. Vaidyalingam vs. S. K. Ganesan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant K. Vaidyalingam (director and shareholder representing the Vaidyalingam Group) against S.K. Ganesan and family (Respondents 1-5 representing Ganesan Group), Balaji Rubber Industries Pvt. Ltd., Bidar Rubber and Reclaims Pvt. Ltd., and Eswar Rubber Products Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint ownership and management of rubber manufacturing businesses across multiple closely held corporate entities governed by family arrangements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational and managerial disputes concerning oppression and mismanagement, leading to an attempted private settlement via an unperformed Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MOU entered on 20.07.2011; MOU cancelled by respondents via letter dated 10.11.2011; company petitions CP 71/2012, CP 80/2012, and CP 45/2013 filed in 2012 and 2013; Section 8 applications filed in 2012 and 2013. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOU dated 20.07.2011 containing Clause 19 arbitration agreement; cancellation communication dated 10.11.2011; failure to produce original or certified copy of MOU; non-signatory status of the corporate entities and multiple shareholder respondents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Single Bench Chennai dismissed Section 8 applications CA 159/2012, CA 190/2012, and CA 1/2013 on 31.08.2017 (formal order 03.10.2017); Vaidyalingam appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement can be referred to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 when the arbitration agreement is contained in an unproduced, cancelled MOU to which neither the corporate entities nor all litigating shareholders are parties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application to refer disputes to arbitration cannot be maintained where the subject matter involves statutory claims of oppression and mismanagement that extend beyond arbitrable private disputes, particularly where there is no identity of parties between the arbitration agreement and the company petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Mandatory reference under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 requires strict compliance with Section 8(2) through the production of the original arbitration agreement or a certified copy; failure to produce the same is fatal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An arbitral tribunal has no jurisdiction to bind non-signatory third parties or corporate entities that have neither signed nor adopted the agreement; once an MOU is cancelled and uncontested, it ceases to be an enforceable arbitration agreement. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 8 applications were rightly dismissed due to non-joinder of necessary parties to the agreement, failure to file the original document, and the broader statutory scope of Sections 397/398.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 319, 320, and 321 of 2017 dismissed; NCLT Chennai directed to dispose of the underlying company petitions expeditiously under Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 without costs.
summary: K. Vaidyalingam appealed from an NCLT Chennai order rejecting applications under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 that sought to refer three oppression and mismanagement petitions to arbitration. The Appellant relied on an arbitration clause in an MOU dated 20.07.2011. The NCLAT held that the subject companies and several litigating shareholders were not signatories or parties to the MOU, which had been cancelled on 10.11.2011. Furthermore, the appellant failed to produce the original or certified agreement under Section 8(2). Holding that statutory oppression claims under Sections 397/398 exceed arbitral jurisdiction, the NCLAT dismissed the appeals.

case_title: M. Nandagopal vs. Virtuous Urja Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Virtuous Urja Ltd. (Operational Creditor/Respondent), Nandha Energy Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and Mr. M. Nandagopal (Appellant/Managing Director of Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational dealings giving rise to an alleged trade debt, leading to the initiation of winding-up proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of alleged operational dues leading to winding-up action on grounds of inability to pay debts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Notification of Transfer of Pending Proceedings Rules issued on 07.12.2016; transfer of winding up petition from Madras High Court to NCLT Chennai; 60-day compliance window under Rule 5 expired without filing Form 5 or Section 8 demand notice; NCLT orders passed on 31.07.2017 and 29.08.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Total absence of a statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) in Form 3/4; omission to provide Part IV particulars or documentation of default under Form 5; challenge to Rule 5 pending before the Madras High Court. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A winding up petition under Sections 433/434 of the Companies Act, 1956 transferred from Madras High Court to NCLT Chennai under Rule 5 was admitted under Section 9 of the IBC on 29.08.2017 with moratorium and IRP appointment; Managing Director appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a winding-up petition transferred from a High Court to the NCLT under Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 can be admitted under Section 9 of the IBC without mandatory service of a demand notice under Section 8(1) and submission of Form 5 particulars within sixty days.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Transferred winding-up proceedings under Rule 5 cannot be treated as valid applications under Section 9 of the IBC unless the operational creditor strictly complies with prerequisite statutory mandates, including serving a Section 8 demand notice and filing prescribed Form 5 particulars. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules, 2016 is mandatory; failure by a transferred petitioner to furnish required statutory information within sixty days of the notification causes the transferred proceeding to abate automatically by operation of law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Service of a demand notice under Section 8(1) is a non-negotiable jurisdictional condition precedent to the maintainability and admission of an operational debt insolvency application under Section 9. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no Section 8 notice was issued and Form 5 details were omitted, the application abated, rendering the order of admission and appointment of the IRP illegal and void ab initio.
operative_order: Appeals allowed; impugned orders dated 31.07.2017 and 29.08.2017 set aside; winding up petition declared abated and proceedings closed; moratorium vacated; Corporate Debtor released to operate independently; NCLT to determine IRP fees payable by Corporate Debtor; liberty granted to Respondent to serve a fresh Section 8 notice without costs.
summary: M. Nandagopal, Managing Director of Nandha Energy Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Chennai order admitting a transferred company winding-up petition under Section 9 of the IBC filed by Virtuous Urja Ltd. The Appellant contended that the transferred petition violated Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 as no Section 8 demand notice or Form 5 particulars were submitted. The NCLAT held that serving a Section 8 demand notice is an indispensable jurisdictional prerequisite for Section 9 proceedings. Because the creditor failed to comply within sixty days of transfer, the proceedings abated. The NCLAT set aside the admission order and released the Corporate Debtor from moratorium.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. V. Ramakrishnan & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Financial Creditor/Appellant), Mr. V. Ramakrishnan (Respondent No. 1/Personal Guarantor and Director), and M/s Veesons Energy Systems Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by the Corporate Debtor secured by personal guarantee and mortgage of personal collateral securities executed by the Director in favor of SBI. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to a SARFAESI demand of Rs. 61,13,28,785.48 as of 04.08.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued 04.08.2015; Section 13(4) possession notice issued 18.11.2016; Corporate Debtor's Section 10 IBC petition admitted with moratorium; SBI issued SARFAESI auction sale notice on 12.07.2017 against guarantor's property; guarantor filed IA 05/2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of personal guarantee, Section 13(2) demand notice, symbolic possession notice, and auction sale notice dated 12.07.2017 issued during the currency of CIRP moratorium. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench on 18.09.2017 allowed IA No. 05/2017, restraining SBI from proceeding under SARFAESI against the Personal Guarantor until the moratorium expired; SBI appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the statutory moratorium declared under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 operates to restrain a financial creditor from enforcing security interests against the personal assets of a personal guarantor to the corporate debtor during the CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory moratorium declared under Section 14 upon the admission of an insolvency petition applies comprehensively, prohibiting financial creditors from taking coercive recovery measures against the personal properties of a personal guarantor during the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reading Section 14(1) alongside Section 31(1) and Section 60(2)-(4), an approved resolution plan is expressly binding on guarantors, meaning personal guarantors are integrally bound to the corporate resolution process, extending the protective shield of moratorium to them. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once a corporate debtor is admitted into CIRP under Section 10, any simultaneous independent enforcement actions under the SARFAESI Act against security interests created by a surety must yield to the statutory moratorium. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in restraining SBI from auctioning the personal guarantor's mortgaged assets until the conclusion of the corporate moratorium.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the order of the Adjudicating Authority Chennai Bench dated 18.09.2017 restraining the State Bank of India from proceeding against the Personal Guarantor during the moratorium period affirmed without costs.
summary: State Bank of India appealed against an NCLT Chennai order that stayed its SARFAESI auction proceedings against the personal property of Mr. V. Ramakrishnan, Managing Director and Personal Guarantor of Corporate Debtor M/s Veesons Energy Systems Pvt. Ltd., during the currency of an IBC moratorium. SBI argued that Section 14 applies exclusively to the assets of the Corporate Debtor and not to personal guarantors. Construing Section 14 with Section 31(1) and Section 60, the NCLAT held that the moratorium extends to the property of personal guarantors to ensure comprehensive corporate resolution. The appeal was dismissed. (Note: This ruling was subsequently reversed by the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 3595 of 2018).

case_title: Shailesh P. Gonawala & Anr. vs. Shree Saisang Associates Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shailesh P. Gonawala (Appellant No. 1/Original Petitioner No. 1, founding director) and Rameshchandra A. Morawala (Appellant No. 2/Original Petitioner No. 2) against Shree Saisang Associates Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 Company) and Shailesh U. Vakharia & Ors. (Respondent directors 2 to 8). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project involving 35,511 sq. meters of land in Surat plotted into 179 plots and developed as Sai Unity Row Houses. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Board authority granted on 15.12.2009 to Appellant No. 1 to execute conveyance deeds was revoked on 02.05.2013; Appellant No. 1 nevertheless executed 12 subsequent deeds (7 in his own name) conveying 1039.59 sq. meters; FIR lodged for siphoning Rs. 134.44 lakhs; High Court granted bail upon cash deposit of Rs. 1,33,44,000. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Authority revoked and new Chairman elected on 02.05.2013; Appellant arrested from 11.12.2014 to 02.01.2015; Board meeting held 17.04.2017 to call EOGM; EOGM conducted 20.05.2017 removing Appellant No. 1 from directorship; Company Petition filed 22.05.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Postal dispatch receipt dated 25.04.2013 proving service of 02.05.2013 Board meeting notice; dispatch proof for 17.04.2017 Board meeting; Form ADT-3 resignation filed by former statutory auditor M/s S.B. Vaidya & Co.; audited financial statements subsequently compiled and filed with ROC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed CP No. 68/241&242/NCLT/AHM/2017 on 23.11.2017 holding no oppression or mismanagement established; Appellants appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the revocation of a director's conveyancing authority and subsequent removal from the Board pursuant to shareholder requisitions constitute oppression and mismanagement, and whether delayed compilation of annual accounts caused by internal management disputes and auditor non-cooperation justifies intervention under Section 242.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Lawful withdrawal of administrative or conveyancing authority and subsequent removal of a director carried out after due notice and statutory process cannot be categorized as acts of oppression and mismanagement, particularly where the aggrieved director acts in breach of fiduciary duty by executing unauthorized self-dealing conveyances. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Delayed compilation or filing of annual financial statements under Section 129 is a regulatory default for which statutory penalties lie, but it cannot be invoked as an act of mismanagement under Section 241 by a sitting director who was equally responsible for corporate governance during the relevant periods. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Dispatch receipts from the postal department establish valid service of meeting notices; an intentionally absent director cannot allege denial of natural justice or falsification of minutes where quorum was complete. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant failed to demonstrate any actionable oppression or mismanagement and had acted in bad faith by executing unauthorized deeds in his own favour without disclosure under Section 297, justifying dismissal.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the impugned order dated 23.11.2017 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in CP No. 68 of 2017 affirmed without costs.
summary: Shailesh P. Gonawala and another appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench's dismissal of their petition alleging oppression and mismanagement in Shree Saisang Associates Pvt. Ltd. The appellant challenged the Board's resolution revoking his conveyancing authority, his subsequent removal from directorship, and the delay in compiling annual accounts. The NCLAT found that valid notice was served for all relevant Board and shareholder meetings and that the appellant deliberately abstained while continuing to execute unauthorized land conveyances, including several in his own name without disclosure. Holding that delayed accounting did not constitute mismanagement at the instance of a responsible director, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Valuefab Solutions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Registrar of Companies, Karnataka
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Valuefab Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant Company incorporated on 21.02.2012) against Registrar of Companies, Karnataka (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Private limited software and product development company that ceased generating revenue after June 2013 and remained completely inactive. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to file statutory Balance Sheets and Annual Returns for three consecutive financial years from FY 2013-14 to 2015-16; bank account with HDFC Bank closed as on 31.03.2016; absence of non-current or fixed assets; negligible cash balance of Rs. 1,79,023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Notice STK-1 issued 16.03.2017; representation dated 20.02.2017 stating the company was in the process of closure; consolidated STK-5 notice published in Official Gazette on 20.05.2017 and newspapers on 13.05.2017; STK-7 strike-off published 17.07.2017 and gazetted 29.07.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MCA-21 portal default records; company's letter dated 20.02.2017 admitting product development ceased in June 2013; bank account closure letter dated 31.03.2016; profit and loss account for FY 2016-17 reflecting zero revenue and Rs. 45,875 expenditure. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench dismissed restoration petition CP No. 200/2017 on 26.02.2018 holding that reviving a non-functional company solely for winding up contradicts Section 252(3); the company appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a company struck off under Section 248 for continuous statutory non-filing can be restored to the Register of Companies under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 solely to enable it to complete voluntary winding up or formal closure proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory phrase 'otherwise it is just' in Section 252(3) is designed to protect active, viable companies or their creditors; it cannot be interpreted to permit the revival of an admittedly defunct and non-operational entity solely to undergo formal voluntary winding-up procedures. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(3) requires objective satisfaction that the company was either carrying on business or in operation at the time of strike-off; where bank accounts are closed and no business operations exist, restoring the name defeats the statutory object of Section 248. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Misleading advice received from third-party online advisory portals or collateral consequences such as director DIN deactivation do not constitute a 'just cause' under Section 252. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ROC followed statutory notice requirements, and because the company was non-operational and admitted its defunct state, no legal justification existed for restoration.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Bengaluru Bench dated 26.02.2018 dismissing CP No. 200/2017 affirmed without costs.
summary: Valuefab Solutions Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an order of the NCLT Bengaluru Bench refusing to restore its name to the Register of Companies under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. The company had been struck off by ROC Karnataka in July 2017 for failing to file balance sheets and annual returns since FY 2013-14. The appellant conceded that it was non-operational, had closed its bank accounts in 2016, and had no commercial assets, but sought revival solely to execute formal winding-up proceedings. The NCLAT held that Section 252 is meant to safeguard operating companies and cannot be used to restore defunct companies solely for closure. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Shree Kumar Mundhra vs. Spell Organics Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shree Kumar Mundhra (Appellant/Original Petitioner) against Spell Organics Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 Company), Suresh Kumar Mundhra (Respondent No. 2, Managing Director and brother), and Registrar of Companies (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate guarantee and personal indemnity provided by Respondent No. 1 and Respondent No. 2 to Celica Developers Pvt. Ltd. to secure commercial loans availed by Apsom Turner Pvt. Ltd., an entity controlled by Appellant and his wife. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Apsom Turner resulting in an arbitral award dated 13.02.2015 against it; Respondent No. 1 discharged Rs. 1.20 crores under the corporate guarantee and instituted CS(OS) No. 3169 of 2015 to recover the same from Appellant; disputed retention of 87,010 equity shares under Folio No. S-026. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitral award rendered 13.02.2015; General Diary of lost shares lodged 20.04.2015; duplicate share request made 20.04.2015; police complaint alleging share theft lodged 01.12.2015; CP No. 15/04/2016 filed before NCLT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Police General Diaries alleging contradictory claims of lost certificates versus subsequent theft by brother; RTGS records confirming payment of Rs. 1.20 crores by Respondent No. 1; Annual Returns for FY 2015-16 reflecting lien/pledge encumbrance on shares. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissed CP No. 15/04/2016 on 10.05.2018, holding that the petition was beyond the scope of Sections 46/56 and that the company had a valid right to retain the pledged certificates until debt satisfaction; petitioner appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a shareholder who deposited physical share certificates as collateral security for a corporate guarantee discharged on his behalf can compel delivery of the certificates or issuance of duplicate share certificates under Section 46 or Section 56 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for issuance of duplicate share certificates or delivery of original certificates under company law cannot be utilized to circumvent a lawful contractual deposit or possessory pledge of shares securing financial obligations discharged by a third party. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 46(2) provides relief exclusively where share certificates are proved to have been lost, destroyed, defaced, mutilated, or torn; it does not empower a shareholder to bypass an ongoing commercial pledge dispute or possessory lien. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relief under summary company jurisdiction requires clean hands; a petitioner who fabricates police reports claiming loss of shares, followed by allegations of theft after being confronted with proof of security deposit, is barred by inequitable conduct. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The respondents established legitimate possession of the share certificates as security for Rs. 1.20 crores discharged under guarantee, placing the dispute squarely within the civil court's jurisdiction.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT New Delhi Bench dated 10.05.2018 affirmed; Appellant directed to pay costs of Rs. 1,00,000/- to Respondent No. 1.
summary: Shree Kumar Mundhra appealed against an NCLT New Delhi Bench order dismissing his petition under Sections 46 and 56 of the Companies Act, 2013 against Spell Organics Ltd. and its Managing Director. The Appellant sought delivery of original share certificates for 87,010 shares or issuance of duplicates, claiming the certificates had been lost and subsequently stolen by his brother. The respondents proved that the certificates had been deposited as security for a corporate guarantee under which the company had paid Rs. 1.20 crores on behalf of the appellant's enterprise. The NCLAT held that Section 46 cannot be invoked to defeat a possessory security, condemned the appellant's contradictory police complaints, and dismissed the appeal with Rs. 1 lakh costs.

case_title: M/s Relisys Medical Devices Ltd. vs. D. Raju Reddy & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Relisys Medical Devices Ltd. (Appellant Company) against D. Raju Reddy (Respondent No. 1, non-resident investor) and Registrar of Companies, Hyderabad (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of 1,92,441 Compulsory Convertible Debentures (CCDs) of Rs. 10 each at a premium of Rs. 60 to Respondent No. 1 on 01.12.2011, with subsequent conversion into equity shares on 06.08.2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Erroneous conversion of 1,92,441 CCDs into 4,29,419 equity shares at an undervalued premium of Rs. 21.37 (FMV was Rs. 64.22), resulting in excess allotment of 2,19,658 equity shares in violation of FEMA valuation norms; RBI issued compounding directives on 01.03.2017 to unwind excess shares. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CCDs issued 01.12.2011; converted 06.08.2013; compounding application submitted to RBI on 09.09.2016; RBI directive letter issued 01.03.2017; CP No. 35/59/HDB/2017 filed under Section 59. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RBI compounding advisory letter No. HY.FE.FID/1755/14.04.542/2016-17; balance sheets for FY 2014-2016 reflecting erroneous paid-up capital; ROC report dated 25.07.2017; affidavit-cum-undertaking to reallocate capital and securities premium. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed CP No. 35/59/HDB/2017 on 05.10.2017 holding that cancelling excess shares amounts to a capital reduction requiring procedure under Section 66; company appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the cancellation of excess shares allotted through an incorrect conversion ratio of CCDs to rectify FEMA non-compliance constitutes a capital reduction under Section 66 or a rectification of the Register of Members under Section 59 where total capital funds remain preserved in the securities premium account.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An internal accounting re-allocation between paid-up share capital and the securities premium account to correct a defective conversion price does not constitute a reduction of share capital under Section 66 when the aggregate consideration received by the company remains unaltered. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013 (Section 78 of the 1956 Act), the securities premium account is treated for all practical purposes as paid-up capital; unwinding erroneously allotted shares and re-crediting the difference to securities premium is a rectification under Section 59. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where regulatory directives from the Reserve Bank of India require unwinding excess share allotments to cure foreign exchange non-compliance, and the allottee raises no objection, the Tribunal has jurisdiction under Section 59 to rectify the corporate register. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in classifying the unwinding as a Section 66 capital reduction; the company was legally entitled to cancel 2,19,658 excess shares and adjust its books.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of; impugned order of NCLT Hyderabad dated 05.10.2017 set aside; Appellant directed to cancel 2,19,658 excess shares, adjust consideration to 2,09,761 equity shares of Rs. 10 at a premium of Rs. 54.22, credit securities premium, and refile audited balance sheets without prejudice to RBI proceedings.
summary: Relisys Medical Devices Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad Bench order dismissing its application under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013. The company had erroneously converted CCDs held by an NRI into 4,29,419 equity shares at an undervalued premium, resulting in an excess allotment of 2,19,658 shares in contravention of FEMA regulations. Following RBI directions to unwind the excess shares, the company petitioned for register rectification. The NCLT dismissed it as an impermissible capital reduction. Overturning the decision, the NCLAT held that reallocating amounts between paid-up equity and the securities premium account does not diminish capital, qualifying as rectification under Section 59.

case_title: Usha Holdings L.L.C. & Anr. vs. Francorp Advisors Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Usha Holdings L.L.C. and affiliate (Appellants/Alleged Operational Creditors) against Francorp Advisors Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Undated 2008 Memorandum of Understanding and franchise licensing agreements for the operation of franchise consulting services under the mark 'FRANCORP' in India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under a US District Court decree dated 05.10.2015 awarding USD 1,661,743, stemming from claims of breach of licensing agreement, USD 10,000,000 conversion, and punitive damages. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Commercial dispute initiated in US District Court on 14.12.2012; preliminary jurisdictional order dated 27.03.2014; US default decree entered 05.10.2015; CP (IB) 196 (PB)/2017 filed before NCLT under Section 9 of IBC. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Uncertified copies of US District Court judgment and decree; undated draft franchise licensing agreements; uncertified commercial agreement lacking proof of reciprocity under Section 44A of CPC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissed Section 9 petition on 11.12.2017 on grounds of inexecutable foreign decree, non-compliance with Section 44A CPC, and absence of operational debt; Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under the IBC possesses jurisdiction to adjudicate the legality and conclusiveness of a foreign court decree, and whether damages awarded by a foreign court for breach of licensing and conversion agreements qualify as an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority under the IBC is not a civil court and has no jurisdiction to evaluate, enforce, or determine the legality and validity of a foreign decree. However, claims arising out of breach of licensing covenants or unliquidated tortious damages do not qualify as 'operational debt'. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(21) of the IBC, an operational debt is strictly confined to a claim in respect of the direct provision and supply of goods or employment and services; foreign decree damages for breach of partnership covenants fall outside this definition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An applicant invoking Section 9 must demonstrate a direct nexus between the claimed financial liability and the actual supply of operational goods or services rendered to the corporate debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the NCLT's findings regarding the legality of the foreign decree were null and void for want of jurisdiction, the petition was non-maintainable as the appellants were not operational creditors.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority's findings regarding the foreign decree declared null for lack of jurisdiction, but the dismissal of the Section 9 petition upheld due to lack of an operational debt, without costs.
summary: Usha Holdings L.L.C. appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against Francorp Advisors Pvt. Ltd. The claim was based on an uncertified ex parte decree of USD 1,661,743 from a US District Court for breach of an undated franchise license agreement. The NCLT had rejected the petition citing non-executability under Section 44A CPC. The NCLAT clarified that the Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to evaluate the legality of foreign decrees. However, because the claimed liability arose from licensing breaches and damages rather than the supply of goods or services, it did not constitute an operational debt, making the petition non-maintainable.

case_title: K.S. Rangasamy vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent No. 1, State Bank of India, is the Financial Creditor; M/s Summer India Textile Mills Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Appellant K.S. Rangasamy is a Shareholder, Promoter, and Director of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit/loan facilities extended by the Financial Creditor (and State Bank of Patiala) to the Corporate Debtor for textile manufacturing operations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was declared an NPA on 28th October, 2012; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice dated 10th October, 2013 claimed Rs. 105,66,05,078/-, whereas the Form 1 Section 7 petition claimed an aggregate debt of Rs. 131,63,86,382.66/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recovery proceedings under RDDB Act Section 19 and SARFAESI Section 13 notices initiated between 2013 and 2015; stay orders issued by Supreme Court, DRT Madurai (March 2015), and Madras High Court (22nd September, 2015); Form 1 petition filed on 7th June, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor alleged lack of prior notice under Rule 4(3) due to a local holiday on 12th June, 2017 before admission on 13th June, 2017, and alleged improper inclusion of debts of an affiliate (Summer India Weaving and Processing Mills Pvt. Ltd.); however, the Corporate Debtor admitted default and offered to pay Rs. 3,365 lakhs in 12 equal monthly instalments with 9% interest per annum. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed on 7th June, 2017 and admitted by NCLT Chennai Bench in CP No. 515 of 2017 on 13th June, 2017, which admission was challenged by the promoter on appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC can be admitted despite pending stay orders in DRT/SARFAESI/RDDB proceedings and whether the admission order was void for violation of natural justice/Rule 4(3) where debt and default were undisputed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Pendency of parallel debt recovery proceedings or interlocutory stay orders under recovery statutes does not bar insolvency admission under Section 7 where financial debt and default are established; further, remanding an admitted default on technical grounds of natural justice constitutes a useless formality. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC operates independently of Section 19 of the RDDB Act and Section 13 of the SARFAESI Act; where a complete application establishes debt and default, admission is mandatory. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the occurrence of default and liability of debt are admitted or undisputed by the Corporate Debtor, no prejudice is caused by procedural dispatch, fulfilling the 'useless formality' exception to the rules of natural justice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The admission of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process by the Adjudicating Authority was lawful and required no interference, as debt and default were explicitly conceded.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 13th June, 2017, while granting liberty to the Financial Creditor to consider any settlement proposal if the Resolution Applicant offers less favorable terms.
summary: The promoter of Summer India Textile Mills Pvt. Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Chennai admitting State Bank of India's Section 7 IBC application for a default exceeding Rs. 131 crores. The appellant contended that parallel DRT and SARFAESI proceedings had been stayed, that natural justice was violated due to lack of adequate notice before admission, and that claims were inflated. The NCLAT held that stays in recovery proceedings do not impede Section 7 proceedings where debt and default are established. Given that the corporate debtor conceded liability and default, remanding for procedural compliance was deemed a useless formality, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Aditya Enterprises vs. Rajratan Exim Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Aditya Enterprises claimed the status of Financial Creditor; Respondent Rajratan Exim Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant claimed to have lent an aggregate sum of Rs. 1,00,00,000/- to the Corporate Debtor in two tranches of Rs. 50,00,000/- each on 8th September 2014 and 10th September 2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default was asserted for non-repayment of the Rs. 1,00,00,000/- loan; specific date of default was unspecified beyond non-payment post-disbursement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding up petition under Section 433(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 1956 filed before the High Court; transferred to NCLT Mumbai pursuant to Notification dated 7th December, 2016 and treated as a Section 7 IBC application. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant produced bank receipts confirming fund transfers; however, no record, agreement, or evidence demonstrated that the funds were borrowed for commercial business purposes or carried consideration for time value of money, while Respondent asserted complete repayment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the application on 23rd April 2018 holding that mere receipt of money without demonstrating the underlying purpose does not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8).
legal_issues: Whether a mere monetary transfer/receipt without proof of borrowing for business purposes or consideration for the time value of money constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) capable of triggering Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Mere disbursement or receipt of funds, absent proof that the borrowing was for business purposes or contains the essential element of consideration for the time value of money, does not constitute a financial debt under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(7) and Section 5(8)(a) require an applicant to demonstrate that money disbursed falls squarely within the statutory definition of borrowing against the time value of money, failing which the claimant cannot be classified as a financial creditor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Producing mere transaction/receipt confirmations is insufficient; primary documentation establishing loan purpose, commercial terms, and payable status must be placed on record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The existence of a valid financial debt was not established, and given the dispute over liability and alleged repayment, no default under Section 7 occurred.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 23rd April, 2018 rejecting the petition.
summary: Aditya Enterprises appealed the dismissal of its transferred winding-up petition, treated as a Section 7 IBC application, against Rajratan Exim Pvt. Ltd. by NCLT Mumbai. The appellant alleged default on an advance of Rs. 1 crore disbursed in September 2014. The corporate debtor disputed the claim, stating the sum was already repaid. The NCLAT held that the mere receipt of money does not qualify as an operational or financial debt under Section 5(8) in the absence of evidence showing it was borrowed for business or entailed consideration for the time value of money. Finding no proof of financial debt, the appellate tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: United News of India & Ors. vs. Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: United News of India along with its directors/officers (including Vishwas Tripathi and Prafulla Maheshwari) are Appellants/Applicants; Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory corporate secretarial compliances concerning the timely convening of Annual General Meetings, laying of balance sheets, and filing of financial statements/annual returns. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaults spanning financial years 2012-2013 to 2014-2015 regarding non-compliance with statutory provisions; statutory compounding fees initially recommended by RoC aggregated multiple lakhs per applicant across default heads. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Suo moto compounding applications filed by the Appellants after rectifying the defaults; NCLT New Delhi Bench passed compounding orders on 11th December and 12th December, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RoC inspection/recommendation reports recommending maximum fines under Sections 129, 137, 92, and 96 of the 2013 Act and Sections 210 and 168 of the 1956 Act; proof that defaults were subsequently made good with no criminal prosecutions pending. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench compounded the offences by substantially reducing penalties to approximately 1/4th or 1/5th of the maximum penal amount (e.g., composite fine of Rs. 1.10 lakhs each in CA 45/2018; Rs. 1.25 lakhs each in CA 46/2018; Rs. 2 lakhs and Rs. 1.5 lakhs in CA 47/2018; Rs. 1.25 lakhs each in CA 48/2018); Appellants appealed citing inability to pay.
legal_issues: Whether financial inability/hardship of a company constitutes a valid legal ground to interfere with or further reduce compounding fees that have already been reduced by the NCLT to 1/4th or 1/5th of the statutory maximum.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Inability or financial difficulty of a company to pay a compounding fine does not render a judicial compounding order illegal nor justify appellate interference where the tribunal has already exercised equitable discretion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Compounding provisions under the Companies Acts permit the Adjudicating Tribunal to reduce fines based on gravity and duration of default; once substantially mitigated below statutory maximums, financial incapacity cannot void the levy. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Discretion exercised by the lower tribunal in mitigating penal provisions to a fraction of the maximum recommendation must be assessed on proportionality, not the subjective cash flow distress of the contemnors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The compounded fines determined by the Tribunal were just, equitable, and legally sound, leaving no ground for appellate relief.
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs, and the impugned orders dated 11th and 12th December, 2017 are confirmed.
summary: United News of India and its directors appealed against compounding orders passed by NCLT New Delhi under various provisions of the Companies Acts 1956 and 2013 regarding delayed AGMs and non-filing of balance sheets and annual returns for FY 2012-13 to 2014-15. The NCLT had compounded the offences and significantly reduced the statutory fines to 1/4th or 1/5th of the maximum penal amounts. The appellants sought further reduction or relief solely claiming financial hardship. The NCLAT held that inability to pay is not a valid legal ground to hold a compounding order illegal, affirmed the NCLT's discretion, and dismissed the appeals.

case_title: M/s. India Awake for Transparency vs. M/s. Hasham Investment and Trading Company Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s India Awake for Transparency is a Section 8 NGO non-member; Respondent No. 1 is M/s Hasham Investment and Trading Company Pvt. Ltd.; Respondents No. 2 to 5 include Azim H. Premji, Yaseem Premji, P. Srinivasan, and Azim Premji Trust. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Merger/amalgamation of respondent entities into Respondent No. 1, which the Appellant alleged involved transfer of assets for private benefit rather than public interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No financial default metric; allegations pertained entirely to acts of oppression and mismanagement prejudicial to public interest under Section 241. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 15 of 2017 filed before NCLT Bengaluru Bench seeking waiver under Section 244 to maintain a Section 241 petition. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant conceded that it was not a member of Respondent No. 1, arguing that being a Section 8 NGO vindicating public interest empowered it to seek waiver of all qualifying requirements under the proviso to Section 244(1). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench rejected the waiver application and dismissed Company Petition 15 of 2017 holding that a non-member cannot maintain a petition under Section 241 or seek waiver under Section 244.
legal_issues: Whether a non-member of a company can seek waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241 in the name of public interest.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The threshold requirement of being a member of the company is an absolute condition precedent for maintaining an oppression and mismanagement petition; the statutory power of waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) applies strictly to numerical or shareholding thresholds of existing members, and cannot be invoked by a non-member. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The opening words of Section 244(1) ('The following members of a company shall have the right to apply') read with the proviso ('so as to enable the members to apply') govern clauses (a) and (b); the words 'all or any of the requirements' relate solely to numerical/shareholding thresholds and do not eliminate the mandatory requirement of membership. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The prima facie locus standi test: if the applicant is not a registered member of the company, the waiver application must be rejected outright without entering into allegations of mismanagement or public interest. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant being an admitted non-member had no standing to apply under Section 241 or seek waiver under Section 244, and public interest grievances by non-members must be pursued through other statutory avenues such as Chapter XIV or Section 241(2).
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merit with costs quantified at Rs. 2,00,000/- to be paid by the Appellant to Respondent No. 1.
summary: M/s India Awake for Transparency, a Section 8 NGO and non-member, filed an application before NCLT Bengaluru for waiver under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241 against Hasham Investment and Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. and Azim Premji. The NCLT rejected the petition for lack of standing. On appeal, the NCLAT affirmed that the proviso to Section 244(1) empowers the tribunal to waive numerical or shareholding limits only for existing members, but does not waive the foundational requirement of being a member. The appeal was dismissed with costs of Rs. 2 lakhs.

case_title: Sriram Compounds Pvt. Ltd. vs. Shiva Drums Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sriram Compounds Pvt. Ltd. is an Operational Creditor/original petitioner; Respondent Shiva Drums Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/services giving rise to operational debt previously pursued through a winding-up petition under the Companies Act, 1956. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date of default not specified in the appellate order; pertained to unpaid debts underlying the winding-up petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding up petition filed before Delhi High Court under Section 433(e) of Companies Act 1956; transferred to NCLT Principal Bench pursuant to Rule 5 of Transfer Rules, 2016 (amended 29th June, 2017 requiring requisite IBC information within 60 days). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor failed to issue a statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC in Form 3/4 and failed to file Form 5 particulars (along with bank certificate and IRP written communication) within the stipulated 60-day transfer window. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi) dismissed/abated the transferred petition on 26th July, 2017 for non-compliance with Rule 5 and failure to issue Section 8 notice.
legal_issues: Whether a winding-up petition transferred from the High Court to the NCLT stands abated under Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 if the operational creditor fails to serve a demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC and submit Form 5 within sixty days.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For a transferred winding-up petition to be treated as an application under Section 9 of the IBC, service of a statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) and submission of all Form 5 information within sixty days are mandatory conditions precedent, failing which the petition abates by operation of law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016, failure to submit required information under the IBC within the 60-day notification window results in statutory abatement of the transferred proceeding. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance standard; in the absence of an annexure proving service of the Section 8 demand notice and Form 5 disclosures, the tribunal lacks jurisdiction to treat the petition as an application under Section 9. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transferred application was incomplete and not remedied within the statutory timeframe, rendering its dismissal/abatement by the Adjudicating Authority proper.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 26th July, 2017, with liberty granted to the Appellant to issue a fresh demand notice under Section 8(1) and file a fresh application under Section 9 of the IBC.
summary: Sriram Compounds Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissing its winding-up petition transferred from the Delhi High Court against Shiva Drums Pvt. Ltd. Following the transfer under Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016, the appellant failed to issue a mandatory Section 8(1) demand notice and did not submit Form 5 disclosures within the statutory 60-day period. The NCLAT held that non-compliance with Rule 5 and the absence of a Section 8 demand notice caused the transferred petition to abate by operation of law. The appeal was dismissed with liberty to file a fresh Section 9 petition.

case_title: Mahesh Kumar Sureka vs. SBER Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent SBER Bank is the Financial Creditor; Varrasana Ispat Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Appellant Mahesh Kumar Sureka is a Director of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit/loan facilities extended by the Financial Creditor and a consortium of lenders to the Corporate Debtor for industrial steel operations[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from failure to pay the debt within the stipulated time, giving rise to debt recovery proceedings under Section 19 of the DRT Act (specific monetary quantum not quantified in order)[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Joint Lenders Forum (JLF) convened on 30th July, 2014 where the Corporate Debtor proposed a Corrective Action Plan (CAP); Section 7 application filed under CP (IB) No. 543/KB/2017[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor argued absence of default under Section 3(12) due to pending restructuring/CAP before the Joint Lenders Forum and challenged the competence of the signatory of Form 1, which had been executed and signed by the Chief Executive Officer of the Financial Creditor[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 16th November, 2017, imposed a moratorium, and appointed an Interim Resolution Professional; the admission was appealed by the director[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 IBC application can be admitted during the pendency of a debt restructuring proposal before a Joint Lenders Forum, and whether Form 1 signed by the Chief Executive Officer of a bank is legally valid.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Restructuring discussions before a Joint Lenders Forum or the pendency of DRT proceedings do not bar admission under Section 7 of the IBC once financial debt and default are established; furthermore, an application signed by a senior designated officer such as the Chief Executive Officer of a financial institution is valid and competent[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Default under Section 3(12) is defined broadly as non-payment of a debt once it becomes due and payable in law or fact, and Section 7 mandates admission once the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that default has occurred and the application is complete[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Satisfaction of default based on undisputed non-payment of debt; signature on Form 1 by a bank's Chief Executive Officer fulfills authorization requirements under Form 1 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor failed to service its debt, the application was complete in all respects, and neither JLF deliberations nor signatory objections vitiated the admission[cite: 6].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs, upholding the admission order dated 16th November, 2017 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench[cite: 6].
summary: Mahesh Kumar Sureka, director of Varrasana Ispat Limited, appealed the admission of SBER Bank's Section 7 IBC application by NCLT Kolkata Bench[cite: 6]. The appellant contended that no default occurred under Section 3(12) as a Corrective Action Plan was pending before the Joint Lenders Forum, DRT proceedings were ongoing, and Form 1 lacked proper authorization[cite: 6]. The NCLAT rejected these contentions, holding that deliberations before the Joint Lenders Forum do not preclude insolvency resolution where debt and default are undisputed[cite: 6]. Further, Form 1 signed by the bank's Chief Executive Officer was valid[cite: 6]. The NCLAT affirmed the admission order and dismissed the appeal[cite: 6].

case_title: R. Manavazhagan vs. Registrar of Companies, Puducherry
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant R. Manavazhagan is a Director and shareholder of Educare Network Consultant Private Limited; Registrar of Companies, Puducherry is the Respondent[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Maintenance of corporate status and filing of statutory annual returns and balance sheets since incorporation in 2012[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to file statutory Annual Returns and Balance Sheets from incorporation in 2012 up to the date of striking off[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The company was struck off from the register of companies under Section 248(5) via notification dated 15th-21st July, 2017; RoC filed an affidavit before the Tribunal on 27th February, 2018 raising no objection to restoration[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Income tax returns filed showing 'Nil' tax payable; Appellant produced bank statements, balance sheets, and profit & loss accounts to establish ongoing business operations, and alleged lack of hearing before the Section 248(5) striking off[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench rejected the restoration application under Section 252(3) on 4th April, 2018 holding the company was a non-going concern and a 'shell company'[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can reject an application for restoration under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 by labeling a company a 'shell company' without identifying specific statutory violations under Section 248 or examining evidence of ongoing business operations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A company cannot be denied restoration under Section 252(3) through generic categorization as a shell company without adjudicating whether statutory grounds under Section 248 were met and evaluating documentary evidence demonstrating active operations[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 248(1) and Section 252(3), the Adjudicating Authority must objectively verify whether the company failed to commence business within one year or was not carrying on business for two preceding financial years, and must consider relevant financial records rather than dismissing the petition summarily[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proper judicial scrutiny requires consideration of all corroborative operational records including income-tax returns, bank statements, balance sheets, and profit and loss accounts[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT failed to identify the specific statutory violation under Section 248 and ignored evidence of active business, warranting that the rejection order be set aside[cite: 7].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed without costs; the impugned order dated 4th April, 2018 is set aside, and the matter is remitted to NCLT Chennai Bench to reconsider the restoration application within three months in light of all operational evidence[cite: 7].
summary: R. Manavazhagan, director of Educare Network Consultant Pvt. Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Chennai rejecting an application under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to restore the company's name[cite: 7]. The RoC had struck off the company under Section 248(5) for failure to file financial statements since its 2012 incorporation[cite: 7]. The NCLT rejected restoration labeling the entity a 'shell company' because its tax returns reflected 'Nil' tax[cite: 7]. The NCLAT set aside the rejection, holding that the Tribunal failed to examine whether statutory grounds under Section 248 existed or consider bank records and balance sheets showing ongoing business, and remitted the matter for redetermination[cite: 7].

case_title: Achenbach Buschhutten GmbH & Co. vs. Arcotech Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Achenbach Buschhutten GmbH & Co. is the Operational Creditor; Respondent Arcotech Limited is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement dated 23rd December, 2014 superseded by a Supply Contract Agreement dated 9th November, 2015 (amended 27th September, 2016) for the supply of a hot mill with electrical panels and switch cabinets[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant claimed unpaid operational debt of Euro 4,472,638.99 under various invoices dating between 13th April, 2014 and 23rd June, 2016[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8(1) issued on 7th February, 2017; Section 9 application filed on 31st March, 2017; subsequent legal notice issued on 5th May, 2017 granting 60 days for amicable dispute resolution under Article 36 of the contract[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor sent an email on 27th June, 2016 (prior to IBC enactment) disputing the advance payment guarantee issued by Hermes instead of a commercial bank as required by RBI regulations, requesting two months' extension, and warning that premature dispatch would incur over 1 million Euros in customs clearance costs[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed the Section 9 application due to existence of dispute and technical defects; on remand from the Supreme Court (following Macquarie Bank Ltd. ruling), NCLAT heard the appeal on merits[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding contract compliance and bank guarantee specifications existed prior to the issuance of the Section 8(1) demand notice, rendering the Section 9 application non-maintainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC cannot be admitted where a genuine, pre-existing dispute regarding contractual performance, regulatory compliance, or bank guarantee validity was communicated prior to the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 read with Section 8 requires the absence of any pre-existing dispute; a dispute raised via contemporaneous correspondence prior to the demand notice demonstrates that the claim is contested and unsuitable for summary insolvency proceedings[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of contemporaneous documentary evidence (such as emails pre-dating the statutory demand notice raising non-compliance of bank guarantees with central bank regulations) establishes a bona fide pre-existing dispute[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had raised a legitimate dispute as early as 27th June, 2016 regarding defective guarantees and premature dispatch, which was never remedied, justifying dismissal of the Section 9 application[cite: 8].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order rejecting the Section 9 application[cite: 8].
summary: Achenbach Buschhutten GmbH & Co. appealed the dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application against Arcotech Limited by NCLT Chandigarh regarding claimed dues of Euro 4,472,638.99 for supply of a hot mill and switch cabinets[cite: 8]. The matter was remitted by the Supreme Court for adjudication on merits[cite: 8]. The NCLAT found that the corporate debtor had sent an email on 27th June, 2016 raising objections regarding an unacceptable bank guarantee under RBI regulations and requesting dispatch delays to avoid substantial customs liabilities[cite: 8]. Holding that a genuine dispute pre-existed the Section 8 demand notice, the NCLAT affirmed the dismissal of the petition[cite: 8].

case_title: Dakshin Gujarat Vij Company Ltd. vs. M/s. ABG Shipyard Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Dakshin Gujarat Vij Company Ltd. is an essential utility/electricity service provider; M/s ABG Shipyard Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP represented by its Resolution Professional[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Continuous utility supply of electricity to the Corporate Debtor during the CIRP period[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor accumulated unpaid current electricity charges for September 2017, October 2017, November 2017, January 2018, February 2018, and March 2018, while December 2017 charges (Rs. 5 lakhs) were paid under interim tribunal directions[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Moratorium declared under Section 14 at the insolvency commencement date; interim directions issued on 15th January, 2018; moratorium set to expire by end of January 2018[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Professional contended that under Section 14(2) and Regulations 31 & 32, essential supplies could not be disconnected and that current charges must only be accounted as CIRP costs due to paucity of funds (only Rs. 7 lakhs available)[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority's proceedings restricted utility disconnection during CIRP, prompting the electricity board to appeal before NCLAT seeking payment of current consumption charges[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC exempts a Corporate Debtor from paying current charges for essential utility services (such as electricity) consumed during the CIRP period, or requires essential utilities to be supplied free of cost.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The moratorium under Section 14 bars recovery of past arrears but does not prohibit or bar payment of current charges for essential utility services consumed during the CIRP; essential supplies are not required by law to be provided free of cost[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 14(2) read with CIRP Regulation 32 prohibits termination or suspension of essential services, Regulation 31 cannot override the substantive provisions of Section 14 so as to force suppliers to provide utilities without current compensation[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Reconciliation of operational necessity; if a corporate debtor lacks funds to pay current charges for essential utilities, the Resolution Professional cannot keep operations running merely to accrue administrative debt on utility providers[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Current consumption charges incurred during the moratorium must be paid by the Resolution Professional in accordance with a prescribed schedule, and the supplier cannot levy late payment surcharges or disconnect during the CIRP[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of/allowed with directions ordering the Resolution Professional to pay outstanding current electricity charges for specified months between February and April 2018, while restraining the Appellant from levying late payment surcharges or disconnecting supply during the CIRP[cite: 9].
summary: Dakshin Gujarat Vij Company Ltd. appealed against the non-payment of current electricity dues by M/s ABG Shipyard Ltd. during its CIRP[cite: 9]. The Resolution Professional claimed that Section 14(2) and Regulations 31 & 32 prohibited disconnection of essential services and that current charges should merely be accounted as CIRP costs due to paucity of funds[cite: 9]. The NCLAT held that the Section 14 moratorium does not bar payment of current consumption charges, nor does it mandate that essential services be supplied free of cost[cite: 9]. The NCLAT set a payment schedule for current charges while restraining the utility from disconnecting electricity or levying late surcharges[cite: 9].

case_title: Machhar Polymer Private Limited vs. Sabre Helmets Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Machhar Polymer Private Limited is the Operational Creditor; Respondent Sabre Helmets Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying supply of goods/materials by the operational creditor to the corporate debtor giving rise to operational debt[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arising from non-payment of outstanding invoices; specific default quantum and default date not specified in the appellate order[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 1333/I&BP/2017 filed under Section 9 before NCLT Mumbai Bench[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor failed to appear despite paper publication in the 'Times of India' and 'Sandesh'; NCLT suo moto invoked Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to dismiss the petition as time-barred[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the Section 9 petition on 28th September, 2017 holding that the Limitation Act, 1963 automatically applies to IBC proceedings and dismissed the petition with liberty under Section 14 of the Limitation Act[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963 apply to an application for initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 of the IBC, and whether an application can be dismissed suo moto on limitation without granting an opportunity to explain delay or laches.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the then-prevailing NCLAT jurisprudence, the Limitation Act, 1963 per se did not apply to CIRP applications under Section 7 or 9 of the IBC; however, principles of delay and laches applied, requiring the Adjudicating Authority to provide the applicant an opportunity to explain any delay before rejecting a claim as stale[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 cannot be automatically invoked by the Adjudicating Authority to dismiss an IBC petition without evaluating whether there is a continuing cause of action or granting the applicant reasonable time to explain delay[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an application appears to involve delay beyond three years, the court must afford the applicant an opportunity to demonstrate the absence of laches or the existence of a continuous cause of action[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in summarily dismissing the application under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, requiring the dismissal to be set aside and remanded[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed without costs; the impugned order dated 28th September, 2017 is set aside, and the matter is remitted to NCLT Mumbai Bench to reconsider the Section 9 application after notice and opportunity to cure defects[cite: 10].
summary: Machhar Polymer Private Limited appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai dismissing its Section 9 IBC petition against Sabre Helmets Private Limited on the ground that it was barred by limitation under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 10]. The corporate debtor had remained ex-parte[cite: 10]. The NCLAT, relying on its precedent in Speculum Plast, held that the Limitation Act, 1963 was not per se applicable to CIRP applications under the IBC and that an applicant must be given an opportunity to explain delay and establish the absence of laches or a continuing cause of action[cite: 10]. The NCLAT set aside the rejection and remitted the petition for reconsideration[cite: 10].

case_title: BCL Homes Ltd. vs. Canara Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant BCL Homes Ltd. is the Corporate Applicant/Corporate Debtor; Canara Bank and other lenders/homebuyers are the Respondents/Financial Creditors[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project financed by credit facilities from respondent banks and advance consideration from homebuyers[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from inability to service bank liabilities and complete home deliveries (exact monetary figures not specified in appellate order)[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP(IB) No. 98/Chd/CHD/2017 filed by the Corporate Applicant under Section 10 of the IBC[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Canara Bank and homebuyers objected, alleging the debtor alienated large chunks of unencumbered land to directors' relatives months before filing without routing proceeds through the bank, leaving only mortgaged property[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench rejected the Section 10 application on 28th November, 2017 holding that the corporate debtor did not come with clean hands due to prior asset disposals[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can reject an application under Section 10 of the IBC on extraneous grounds such as alienation of assets prior to filing, alleged suppression of facts outside Form 6, or objections raised by creditors and homebuyers[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot reject a Section 10 application on extraneous grounds or prior transactions not required to be disclosed under statutory formats if the applicant is not disqualified under Section 11 and default is established[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10 read with Form 6 restricts the inquiry to whether debt and default exist and whether the applicant suffers any ineligibility under Section 11; non-disclosure of matters outside Form 6 does not amount to fraudulent suppression[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict statutory compliance; the tribunal cannot look beyond the disclosures mandated by Section 10 and Form 6 or require additional affidavits regarding pre-filing asset sales[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Allegations regarding past asset alienations are beyond the scope of Section 10 scrutiny, and where debt, default, and completeness exist without Section 11 disqualification, admission is mandatory[cite: 11].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed without costs; the impugned order dated 28th November, 2017 is set aside, and the matter is remitted to NCLT Chandigarh Bench to consider the Section 10 application afresh and grant time to cure defects if incomplete[cite: 11].
summary: BCL Homes Ltd. appealed against the rejection of its Section 10 IBC application by NCLT Chandigarh[cite: 11]. The NCLT had rejected the petition after financial creditors and homebuyers alleged that the corporate debtor transferred substantial land parcels to directors' relatives prior to filing rather than coming with clean hands[cite: 11]. The NCLAT set aside the rejection, holding that under Section 10 and Form 6, the Adjudicating Authority cannot evaluate extraneous allegations of pre-petition asset transfers or require disclosures beyond statutory formats[cite: 11]. As debt and default were evident and Section 11 was not attracted, the matter was remitted for fresh consideration[cite: 11].

case_title: K.S. Oils Ltd. vs. The State Trade Corporation of India Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s K.S. Oils Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor acting through its Resolution Professional Kuldip Verma; Respondent No. 1 is The State Trade Corporation of India Ltd., a Financial Creditor[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying commercial and trade finance transactions between the parties subject to an arbitration agreement under the Indian Council of Arbitration[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under commercial trading obligations leading to CIRP initiation against the Corporate Debtor (quantum and default date not specified in the order)[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Moratorium declared under Section 14 upon CIRP admission; Indian Council of Arbitration passed an order on 3rd August, 2017 deciding to proceed with arbitral proceedings despite the moratorium[cite: 12]. 5.
