FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Professional filed an application before the NCLT seeking to set aside the arbitral tribunal's order dated 3rd August, 2017 and halt arbitration[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 6th October, 2017 rejected the RP's application, holding it lacked jurisdiction to set aside an order passed by the Indian Council of Arbitration[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether arbitral proceedings pending against a Corporate Debtor can proceed after the declaration of a moratorium under Section 14(1)(a) of the IBC, and whether the NCLT has jurisdiction to set aside procedural orders of an arbitral tribunal[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An arbitral proceeding against a corporate debtor cannot continue during the moratorium under Section 14(1)(a), as the IBC overrides the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; however, the NCLT lacks jurisdiction to directly quash orders of an arbitral tribunal[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(a) explicitly interdicts the institution or continuation of pending arbitral proceedings against the corporate debtor; by virtue of the non-obstante clause in Section 238, the IBC prevails over the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Automatic stay rule; once an insolvency admission order under Sections 7, 9, or 10 is established, all parallel arbitral proceedings against the corporate debtor are stayed by operation of law[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly refused to set aside the arbitral order for lack of supervisory jurisdiction, but parties are legally prohibited from pursuing arbitration during the moratorium and must submit their claims and counterclaims to the Resolution Professional[cite: 12].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without interference with the NCLT's refusal to set aside the arbitral order, but ordering that arbitral proceedings before the Indian Council of Arbitration remain stayed during the moratorium, granting liberty to file claims before the Resolution Professional[cite: 12].
summary: K.S. Oils Ltd., through its Resolution Professional, appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad which dismissed its plea to set aside an order of the Indian Council of Arbitration that continued arbitral proceedings despite an IBC moratorium[cite: 12]. The NCLAT affirmed that while the Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to quash arbitral orders, Section 14(1)(a) read with Section 238 of the IBC completely stays all ongoing arbitral proceedings against the corporate debtor[cite: 12]. Directing the parties not to pursue the arbitration until completion of the moratorium period, the appellate tribunal permitted the parties to present their claims and counterclaims before the Resolution Professional[cite: 12].

case_title: R. Systems International Limited vs. Registrar of Companies / Unnamed Respondent
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is R. Systems International Limited, a company proposing a Scheme of Arrangement[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate capital restructuring involving a Scheme of Arrangement under Section 230 that specifically contemplated a reduction of share capital[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; matter pertains to internal share capital restructuring and reorganization under company law[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CA (CAA)-105 (ND)/2017 filed under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (CAA) Rules, 2016[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Scheme of Arrangement enclosed as Annexure 'A' providing for share capital reduction along with necessary auditor certifications and company disclosures[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissed the application on 8th December, 2017 as non-maintainable, ruling that reduction of capital is exclusively governed by Section 66 and cannot be sanctioned under Section 230[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether a company can effect a reduction of share capital as part of a Scheme of Compromise or Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 without being relegated to an independent application under Section 66[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A scheme of arrangement that includes or contemplates a reduction of share capital is fully maintainable under Section 230, and the procedural requirements of Section 66 do not bar or exclude such schemes[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Explanation to Section 230 expressly declares that Section 66 shall not apply to the reduction of share capital effected in pursuance of an order of the Tribunal under Section 230, establishing that Section 230 is an independent, composite statutory code[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory construction of plain language; the lower tribunal committed legal error by overlooking the express non-applicability carved out by the Explanation to Section 230[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in dismissing the application on maintainability, and schemes embodying share capital reductions are permissible under Section 230[cite: 13].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed without costs; the order dated 8th December, 2017 is set aside, and the matter is remitted to NCLT New Delhi Bench to decide the Section 230 application in accordance with law after notice and hearing[cite: 13].
summary: R. Systems International Limited appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissing its application under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 for sanctioning a Scheme of Arrangement involving reduction of share capital[cite: 13]. The NCLT had rejected the petition on the premise that reduction of capital is exclusively regulated by Section 66 and falls outside Section 230[cite: 13]. Setting aside the order, the NCLAT held that the Explanation to Section 230 expressly provides that Section 66 does not apply to capital reductions effected pursuant to Section 230 orders[cite: 13]. The matter was remitted to the NCLT for fresh consideration on merits[cite: 13].

case_title: Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. vs. Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Respondent Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan and housing financing facilities extended by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from failure to service debt liabilities (exact amount and date of default omitted from the order)[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding up proceedings were initiated and a winding up order was passed by the High Court of Bombay prior to the filing of the Section 7 petition[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record established that the High Court of Bombay had already ordered the winding up of the Corporate Debtor, and the proceedings were not transferred to the NCLT[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench on 18th May, 2018 dismissed the Section 7 petition as not maintainable on the ground that the Bombay High Court had already ordered the winding up of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is maintainable against a Corporate Debtor in respect of whom a winding-up order has already been passed by a High Court[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a company court has already ordered the winding up of a corporate debtor, a subsequent application for initiating corporate insolvency resolution process under Section 7 is not maintainable[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'winding up' under Section 2(94A) of the Companies Act, 2013 is synonymous with 'liquidation' under the IBC, and Section 11(d) bars insolvency initiation where liquidation/winding up has already commenced[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Stage of proceedings test; where the debtor has progressed to the second stage of winding up/liquidation, reverting to the first stage of CIRP is legally impermissible[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Bombay High Court had ordered the winding up of the Corporate Debtor, the Section 7 petition was rightly rejected as non-maintainable[cite: 14].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 18th May, 2018[cite: 14].
summary: Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Mumbai dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd.[cite: 14]. The NCLT rejected the petition because the Bombay High Court had already ordered the winding up of the corporate debtor[cite: 14]. Relying on the doctrine that winding up is synonymous with liquidation, the NCLAT held that once a winding up order has been passed, the process enters the liquidation stage, precluding creditors from reverting to the first stage of CIRP under Section 7[cite: 14]. The dismissal of the Section 7 petition was accordingly affirmed[cite: 14].

case_title: Ankit Patni vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent State Bank of India is the Financial Creditor; Impex Metal & Ferro Alloys Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Appellant Ankit Patni is the Promoter and Director of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Banking credit facilities extended by State Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor for industrial manufacturing operations[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid credit facilities (exact default amount and date of default not recorded in the order)[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed under CP (IB) No. 176/KB/2018; RBI issued circulars dated 22nd May 2017, 13th June 2017, and 12th February 2018[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor did not dispute the existence of debt or default, but argued that under the RBI Circular dated 12th February 2018, banks had to wait for a calibrated two-year period before referring medium-exposure accounts to IBC[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted the Section 7 application on 3rd July, 2018 in CA (IB) No. 366/KB/2018 in CP (IB) No. 176/KB/2018[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether Reserve Bank of India circulars issued under Sections 35AA and 35AB of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 curtail or override a financial creditor's independent statutory right to trigger Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: RBI circulars and regulatory frameworks for stressed asset resolution do not override the statutory right of a financial creditor to initiate insolvency resolution under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The IBC is an independent and complete code; guidelines issued under Sections 35AA and 35AB of the Banking Regulation Act cannot extinguish or suspend the immediate statutory rights of lenders under Section 7[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Satisfaction of debt and default; once the Adjudicating Authority finds that a financial debt is due, default is uncontroverted, and the petition is complete, admission must follow[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RBI circular dated 12th February 2018 did not apply retrospectively to a pre-existing filing and could not restrict the lender's right to pursue insolvency against an admitted default[cite: 15].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, confirming the admission order dated 3rd July, 2018 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench[cite: 15].
summary: Ankit Patni, promoter of Impex Metal & Ferro Alloys Limited, appealed against the admission of State Bank of India's Section 7 IBC application by NCLT Kolkata[cite: 15]. The appellant contended that the bank was mandated to adhere to RBI's stressed asset circulars (including the 12th February, 2018 framework) which allowed a phased two-year timeline before referring eligible non-performing accounts to the IBC[cite: 15]. The NCLAT held that RBI circulars cannot restrict or override the statutory right of a creditor under the IBC, which is a self-contained code[cite: 15]. Since the existence of debt and default was undisputed, the NCLAT affirmed the admission and dismissed the appeal[cite: 15].

case_title: Ruchita Modi vs. Mrs. Kanchan Ostwal & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mrs. Kanchan Ostwal (Sole Proprietor of J.K. Electricals) is the Operational Creditor; Mec Shot Blasting Equipment Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Appellant Ruchita Modi is an erstwhile Promoter, Director, and Shareholder of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Running supply of goods/electrical materials by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Debt acknowledged on 30-01-2016 via 97 cheques (some honored, some dishonored); total claimed operational debt was Rs. 1,33,55,795.40 (including principal, interest, and legal costs), settled at Rs. 60,65,668/-[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Insolvency petition CP (IB)/93/9/JPR/2018 filed under Section 9; NCLT Jaipur admitted the petition on 18-09-2019; NCLAT stayed CoC constitution on 26-09-2019; formal Deed of Settlement executed on 02-11-2019[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Duly executed Deed of Settlement dated 02-11-2019 marked 'X' providing for upfront payment of Rs. 15,00,000/- via Demand Draft No. 208958 and the balance in eight monthly installments through post-dated cheques[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench admitted the Section 9 application on 18th September, 2019 and appointed Anoop Kumar Goyal as IRP; the admission was challenged before NCLAT where parties arrived at a complete settlement prior to CoC constitution[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT can invoke its inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to take a settlement on record, set aside the CIRP admission order, and permit withdrawal of a Section 9 application before the Committee of Creditors is constituted[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal possesses inherent authority to permit the withdrawal of an insolvency application and set aside an admission order where a comprehensive bilateral settlement is reached prior to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 preserves the inherent power of the Appellate Tribunal to make such orders as may be necessary for meeting the ends of justice, including terminating CIRP upon pre-CoC settlement[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tender and verification of a bona fide, uncontroverted settlement deed accompanied by payment instruments prior to the formation of the Committee of Creditors[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Committee of Creditors having not been constituted, the settlement was accepted, the Section 9 petition was treated as withdrawn, and the corporate debtor was restored to normal management[cite: 16].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the admission order dated 18th September, 2019, appointment of IRP, and moratorium are set aside; Section 9 petition is dismissed as withdrawn; IRP fee fixed at Rs. 1,50,000/- plus actual CIRP costs to be paid within three weeks, with liberty to the creditor to revive CIRP in case of default[cite: 16].
summary: Ruchita Modi, shareholder of Mec Shot Blasting Equipment Pvt. Ltd., appealed the admission of a Section 9 IBC application filed by operational creditor Kanchan Ostwal[cite: 16]. Before the Committee of Creditors was constituted, the parties entered into a Deed of Settlement resolving the Rs. 1.33 crore operational claim for Rs. 60.65 lakhs, paying Rs. 15 lakhs upfront with the balance via post-dated cheques[cite: 16]. Exercising inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, the NCLAT accepted the settlement, set aside the insolvency admission and moratorium, discharged the IRP with fixed fees, and dismissed the petition as withdrawn[cite: 16].

case_title: Kailashchandra Ramgopal Lohiya vs. Suvas Reality Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kailashchandra Ramgopal Lohiya is the Appellant/Petitioner; Suvas Reality Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. are the Respondents[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance dispute regarding the convening and holding of shareholder and board meetings under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; matter pertains to interlocutory injunctions regarding corporate meetings[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interlocutory Application No. 270 of 2019 filed seeking stay of an Extra-Ordinary General Meeting (EOGM) scheduled for 8th November, 2019[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant failed to establish a prima facie case or balance of convenience to halt the scheduled corporate meetings, particularly in light of two prior orders passed on 28th January, 2019[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 26th November, 2019 dismissed IA No. 270 of 2019 refusing to stay the EOGM or restrain subsequent board/general meetings without bench permission; the applicant appealed[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether an interlocutory stay of an Extra-Ordinary General Meeting or a blanket restraint on holding company meetings can be granted in a Section 241-242 proceeding without establishing a prima facie case[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not interfere with the discretionary refusal of an interlocutory injunction staying corporate meetings in oppression and mismanagement proceedings unless a clear prima facie case and irreparable injury are demonstrated[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Discretionary interim relief under Section 242 requires demonstrable illegality or prejudice to corporate operations; meetings held in accordance with statutory provisions cannot be stayed as a matter of course[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Standard for interlocutory injunctions; the applicant must substantiate a compelling prima facie case of oppression or illegality[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT properly determined that the applicant failed to make out a case for injuncting the EOGM or restraining future meetings[cite: 17].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 26th November, 2019 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench[cite: 17].
summary: Kailashchandra Ramgopal Lohiya appealed an interlocutory order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench passed in an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 17]. The appellant had sought a stay of an Extra-Ordinary General Meeting convened for 8th November, 2019 and a blanket directive barring any board or general meetings without prior tribunal approval[cite: 17]. The NCLT refused interim relief after finding that no case was established[cite: 17]. Affirming the decision, the NCLAT found no ground to interfere with the lower tribunal's discretion and dismissed the appeal[cite: 17].

case_title: Deepak Gupta vs. Ved Contracts Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent M/s Ved Contracts Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor; M/s RG Infra Build Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Appellant Deepak Gupta is an interested party/promoter of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying contractual works and supply contracts executed between the operational creditor and corporate debtor[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default exceeded the statutory minimum threshold of Rs. 1,00,000/- for unpaid operational debt; exact claimed amount not specified in the appellate order[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 insolvency petition filed; NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted the application on 25th September, 2019; appeal filed with a 5-day delay[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant relied on corporate debtor's accounting entries across three consecutive years showing receivables from the creditor, asserting claims and counterclaims and requesting joint contract inspection; no pre-existing dispute had been raised prior to statutory notice[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted the Section 9 petition on 25th September, 2019, which admission was challenged on appeal[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether unadjudicated claims, counterclaims, or disputed invoice accounting raised during Section 9 proceedings defeat an operational debt exceeding the statutory threshold in the absence of a pre-existing dispute[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of a genuine pre-existing dispute raised prior to statutory notice, an Adjudicating Authority cannot determine complex claims, counterclaims, or invoice adjustments in summary Section 9 proceedings once an operational default exceeding the statutory threshold is established[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9, the tribunal is confined to ascertaining the existence of debt, occurrence of default, and absence of a pre-existing dispute, and is not an adjudicatory forum for resolving disputed contractual counterclaims[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pre-existing dispute standard; disputes regarding bills, quality, or reciprocal accounting must exist prior to the statutory notice and cannot be manufactured post-facto[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was payable and exceeded the threshold, and unadjudicated counterclaims did not establish a valid defense against insolvency admission[cite: 18].
operative_order: The 5-day delay in filing is condoned; the appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the admission order dated 25th September, 2019[cite: 18].
summary: Deepak Gupta appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi admitting an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed by Ved Contracts Pvt. Ltd. against RG Infra Build Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 18]. The appellant argued that the debtor's books showed amounts receivable from the creditor, alleging reciprocal claims and counterclaims requiring joint inspection[cite: 18]. The NCLAT held that summary proceedings under Section 9 cannot adjudicate counterclaims or accounting controversies[cite: 18]. Because default exceeded the statutory threshold and no dispute existed prior to the demand notice, the admission order was affirmed and the appeal dismissed[cite: 18].

case_title: Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave & Anr. vs. Hema Manoj Shah & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent Hema Manoj Shah is the Resolution Professional; Appellant Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave was a Director/Shareholder, and Appellant Vishal Dave was the son of a Director of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency administration and statutory obligation of suspended directors/promoters to cooperate and deliver physical possession of corporate assets to the RP[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from ongoing defiance of judicial orders to appear, surrender premises, and remit prior punitive costs of Rs. 1,00,000/-[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Contempt notices issued; NCLT summons issued directing personal appearance on 15.04.2019 along with the statutory auditor; appeal dismissed on 22nd April, 2019[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants repeatedly failed to appear before the NCLT, obstructed the RP, removed materials, tampered with company assets, disconnected electricity, and defaulted on prior cost orders while offering keys only during appellate hearings[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench initiated contempt proceedings on 28th March, 2019 for non-appearance and disregard of court orders; the suspended management appealed against the summon/contempt order[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether an appellate court should interfere with interlocutory summons issued in contempt proceedings against suspended management who obstruct a Resolution Professional, tamper with assets, and defy judicial directives[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate tribunals will not interfere with interlocutory summons or contempt processes initiated by an Adjudicating Authority to enforce attendance and safeguard corporate assets against recalcitrant management[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inherent and statutory compliance mechanisms require suspended management to cooperate with the Resolution Professional, and deliberate defiance warrants contempt scrutiny without premature appellate interference[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bad faith and contumacious conduct standard; persistent non-appearance, interference with assets, and non-payment of costs disentitle a litigant to discretionary appellate relief[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT acted properly in issuing summons to secure presence in contempt proceedings, and the appellants' obstructive conduct warranted punitive appellate costs[cite: 20].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; costs of Rs. 5,00,000/- are imposed on each appellant (total Rs. 10,00,000/-) payable within 30 days in addition to prior costs, leaving the pending contempt proceedings to be adjudicated by the NCLT[cite: 20].
summary: Gaurav Dave and Vishal Dave, suspended management of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against an order of NCLT Mumbai Bench summoning them and the statutory auditor in contempt proceedings for repeated non-appearance and non-cooperation with Resolution Professional Hema Manoj Shah[cite: 20]. The RP reported that the appellants tampered with assets, removed equipment, disconnected power, and failed to pay previously imposed costs[cite: 20]. The NCLAT refused to interfere with the pending contempt inquiry, reprimanded the appellants for contumacious conduct, dismissed the appeal, and slapped an additional cost of Rs. 5,00,000/- on each appellant[cite: 20].

case_title: Anil Syal vs. Sanjeev Kapoor & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent No. 1 Sanjeev Kapoor (Proprietor of Kapoor Logistics) is the Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 2 Flywheel Logistics Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (CIN: U60232DL2015PTC288609) is the Corporate Debtor; Appellant Anil Syal is the Ex-Director and Shareholder of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Service contract for providing freight logistics and running route vehicles in Freight Line Haul Operations between Pantnagar and Pune from January 2017 to August 2017[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor raised invoices totaling Rs. 66,00,860/-; received part payment of Rs. 35,68,484/- (last payment made on 22nd August 2017 of Rs. 12,02,266/-); balance claimed in Section 8 notice was Rs. 33,69,997/- along with an alleged email balance confirmation of Rs. 30 Lakhs dated 27th July 2018[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 in Forms 3 and 4 issued on 1st August 2018; C.P. No. (IB)-1488/ND/2018 filed under Section 9 and admitted on 2nd September 2019[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor's underlying invoices and billing documents were issued against an entirely separate legal entity, 'Flywheel Logistics Pvt. Ltd.' (CIN: U60200DL2009PTC192531), whereas the Section 8 demand notice was served on the Corporate Debtor 'Flywheel Logistics Solutions Pvt. Ltd.' (CIN: U60232DL2015PTC288609) without accompanying valid invoices raised against it[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted the Section 9 petition and initiated CIRP on 2nd September 2019, which admission was challenged by the suspended director on appeal[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether a demand notice issued under Section 8 of the IBC against a corporate debtor demanding payment for invoices raised against a separate sister concern or group company constitutes a valid statutory demand notice to maintain an application under Section 9[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC is invalid if the underlying invoices upon which the claim is founded were issued to an entirely separate corporate entity, and such a defect deprives the operational creditor of the statutory right to trigger CIRP under Section 9[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(1) mandates the delivery of a demand notice of unpaid operational debt along with copies of invoices demanding payment from the corporate debtor itself; demanding third-party/sister company debt does not satisfy statutory requirements[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict entity identity matching test; the name, corporate identity number (CIN), and registered address on the invoices must correspond to the corporate debtor upon whom the Section 8 notice is served[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the invoices were raised against Flywheel Logistics Pvt. Ltd. and not Flywheel Logistics Solutions Pvt. Ltd., the demand notice was legally invalid, and the Section 9 application could not be sustained[cite: 21].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the admission order dated 2nd September, 2019 is set aside; the Corporate Debtor is released from all rigours of CIRP and restored to its Board; NCLT directed to determine IRP fees and expenses to be borne initially by Corporate Debtor with right of recovery/execution against the Operational Creditor[cite: 21].
summary: Anil Syal, ex-director of Flywheel Logistics Solutions Pvt. Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi admitting an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed by Kapoor Logistics[cite: 21]. The operational creditor claimed unpaid freight charges of Rs. 33,69,997/- under a Section 8 demand notice served on the corporate debtor[cite: 21]. However, the invoices relied upon were raised against an entirely separate company, Flywheel Logistics Pvt. Ltd., which possessed a different CIN and registered address[cite: 21]. The NCLAT held that serving a Section 8 demand notice for dues of a separate sister entity does not fulfill statutory prerequisites[cite: 21]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the admission order and dismissed the CIRP proceedings[cite: 21].

case_title: Jagdambey International vs. Visa Powertech Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Jagdambey International (partnership firm through partner Amit Goel) claimed the status of Financial Creditor; Respondent Visa Powertech Pvt. Ltd. (represented by Director S.B. Agarwal) is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant transferred Rs. 28 lakhs on 20.10.2015 and Rs. 17 lakhs on 23.10.2015 via banking channels to the Corporate Debtor; Corporate Debtor repaid Rs. 5 lakhs on 26.11.2015, leaving an alleged balance of Rs. 40 lakhs[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged unpaid financial debt of Rs. 40 lakhs; no interest was agreed, charged, debited, or claimed (interest claim was formally given up in amended Form 1)[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Monetary transfers made in October 2015; Demand Notice demanding return sent on 25.09.2018; Respondent replied on 23.10.2018; CP(IB) 4023/I&BP/MB/2018 filed under Section 7[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant relied solely on an oral agreement and internal balance sheet entries where the amount was booked under 'other current assets' (2015-16) and later 'loans and advances'[cite: 22]; Corporate Debtor demonstrated by correspondence and ledgers that the sum was an equity contribution made on behalf of Sai Ysh Solar/R.K. Singh for commissioning a solar power project pursuant to a request dated 04.08.2015[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the Section 7 application on 06.03.2019 holding that the transaction did not qualify as a financial debt, which was challenged on appeal[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether an interest-free monetary advance made pursuant to an alleged oral agreement without consideration for the time value of money constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) capable of triggering Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance of funds cannot be classified as a financial debt under the IBC in the absence of evidence demonstrating that the disbursement was made against consideration for the time value of money[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) requires the essential commercial element of time value of money; mere ledger entries and balance sheet classifications of 'loans and advances' without interest stipulations or indirect commercial returns do not establish a financial debt[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluation of contemporaneous contractual terms; where no loan agreement exists, no interest is debited or charged, and the respondent demonstrates the funds were intended as project equity contributions, the burden of proving a financial debt is not discharged[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant failed to demonstrate that the money transferred created a financial debt and default, justifying the rejection of the Section 7 petition[cite: 22].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 6th March, 2019[cite: 22].
summary: Jagdambey International appealed the dismissal of its Section 7 IBC application against Visa Powertech Pvt. Ltd. by NCLT Mumbai[cite: 22]. The appellant claimed it had orally advanced an interest-free loan of Rs. 45 lakhs in October 2015, of which Rs. 40 lakhs remained unpaid[cite: 22]. The corporate debtor established that the funds represented equity contributions for a solar power project on behalf of a third party[cite: 22]. The NCLAT held that the transaction lacked the essential ingredient of consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8), as there was neither an agreement for interest nor any commercial return[cite: 22]. Finding no financial debt, the appellate tribunal affirmed the dismissal[cite: 22].

case_title: Madhusudan Sharma vs. J.D. Aneja Edibles Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Madhusudan Sharma is the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent is J.D. Aneja Edibles Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Resolution Applicant)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP proceedings involving statutory investigation into avoidance transactions and subsequent submission and approval of a resolution plan for an edible oil manufacturer[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; appeal concerned expungement of adverse judicial observations against the Resolution Professional[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Avoidance application IA No. 58/JPR/2018 filed by the RP on 15.10.2018 under Sections 43, 45, 50, and 66; Resolution Plan approved by NCLT Jaipur on 7th June, 2019[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Cause lists and order sheets established that IA No. 58/JPR/2018 was listed and taken up before the Adjudicating Authority eight times (25.10.2018, 30.11.2018, 04.01.2019, 07.02.2019, 14.02.2019, 22.02.2019, 28.02.2019, and 07.03.2019) without any substantive order being passed by the tribunal[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench approved the resolution plan on 7th June, 2019 but recorded adverse remarks in paragraphs 29 and 30 that the RP had not been vigilant and made no serious efforts to press the avoidance application[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority is justified in making adverse judicial strictures against the diligence of a Resolution Professional for non-disposal of an avoidance application when the application was repeatedly listed before the tribunal without orders being passed[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adverse judicial observations regarding lack of vigilance or diligence cannot be recorded against an insolvency professional where delays in hearing or adjudicating applications are attributable to the court's own docket and failure to pass orders on scheduled listing dates[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A(g) disqualification operates only when an order has been made by the Adjudicating Authority under the avoidance provisions; an RP cannot be faulted for procedural pendency outside their control[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Judicial record verification; examination of procedural order sheets showing repeated listing without judicial orders refutes allegations of professional delinquency[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the avoidance application was listed eight times without the NCLT passing orders, the negative strictures against the Resolution Professional were unmerited and liable to be expunged[cite: 23].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the adverse remarks and observations recorded against the Resolution Professional in paragraphs 29 and 30 of the order dated 7th June, 2019 are set aside and expunged[cite: 23].
summary: Madhusudan Sharma, Resolution Professional of J.D. Aneja Edibles Pvt. Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Jaipur Bench approving a resolution plan but containing adverse remarks against him in paragraphs 29 and 30[cite: 23]. The NCLT criticized the RP for failing to diligently pursue an avoidance application under Sections 43, 45, 50, and 66 prior to plan approval[cite: 23]. The NCLAT examined the record and noted that the application had been listed before the NCLT eight separate times without any orders being passed by the bench[cite: 23]. Holding that the RP could not be blamed for judicial delays, the NCLAT set aside and expunged the adverse remarks[cite: 23].

case_title: JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. & Ors. vs. M/s. Well-Do Holdings and Exports Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Appellant Resolution Professional represents Sevenhills Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Appellants Dr. B.R. Shetty and BRS Ventures Investment Ltd. (BRSVIL) are the Successful Resolution Applicants; M/s Well-Do Holdings and Exports Pvt. Ltd. is an unsuccessful applicant[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Sevenhills Healthcare Private Limited involving invitation of Expression of Interest (EoI) and evaluation of resolution plans[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total admitted debt of the Corporate Debtor collated by the Resolution Professional was Rs. 1,356.89 Crores; EMD fixed at Rs. 100 Crores[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 13th March, 2018; EoI invited on 14th May, 2018; CoC approved BRSVIL's resolution plan on 8th September, 2018; RP filed Section 31 approval application thereafter[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Out of 18 applicants who submitted EoIs, only BRSVIL deposited the required Rs. 100 Crore EMD and submitted a plan; ineligible promoter Dr. Jitendra Das Maganti (IA 409/2018), consortium member Well-Do Holdings (IA 410/2018), and a 49.9% shareholder (IA 450/2018) challenged the EMD condition as exorbitant only after plan approval[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench on 23rd January, 2019 refused to approve the CoC-approved plan and ordered de novo resolution starting with fresh EoIs, holding the Rs. 100 Crore EMD and forfeiture terms harsh and burdensome[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to reject a CoC-approved resolution plan and order de novo insolvency proceedings based on belated challenges to EMD conditions brought by ineligible promoters or defaulting participants after plan approval[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 31 read with Section 30(2), the Adjudicating Authority exercises limited quasi-judicial review to verify statutory compliance, and cannot interfere with the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in fixing criteria like EMD[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Locus standi and timeliness test; promoters ineligible under Section 29A lack standing to challenge EoI criteria, and participants who fail to challenge process documents prior to the submission deadline cannot assail them after approval[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exceeded its statutory remit by entertaining unmerited interlocutory challenges and ordering a de novo process rather than evaluating the approved plan under Section 31[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can set aside an approved resolution plan and direct de novo invitation of EoIs on the ground that the EMD condition fixed by the CoC was excessive, on applications filed by ineligible promoters and defaulting applicants after plan approval[cite: 24].
operative_order: The appeals are allowed; the impugned order dated 23rd January, 2019 is set aside; the matter is remitted to NCLT Hyderabad Bench to pass orders on the approval of BRSVIL's resolution plan under Section 31 in consonance with Section 30(2) within three weeks[cite: 24].
summary: Appeals were filed by the RP, financial creditor JM Financial ARC, and successful applicant BRS Ventures against an order of NCLT Hyderabad which refused to approve a CoC-approved resolution plan for Sevenhills Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. and directed de novo initiation of EoIs[cite: 24]. The NCLT had intervened on applications by ineligible promoters and an applicant who failed to deposit the Rs. 100 Crore EMD[cite: 24]. The NCLAT held that promoters ineligible under Section 29A and applicants who did not submit plans within time have no standing to challenge EoI conditions after plan approval[cite: 24]. The NCLAT set aside the de novo order and remitted the plan for approval under Section 31[cite: 24].

case_title: Janak Dhawan vs. Famous Innovations Digital Creative Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Janak Dhawan (Appellant/Promoter), M/s Famous Innovations Digital Creative Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor), M/s Mode Advertising and Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), G. H. Prints Pvt. Ltd. (Intervener/Second Operational Creditor), Atul Tandon (Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged operational relationship based on an agreement between Respondent No. 1 and the Corporate Debtor, which the Appellant contended was a partnership agreement providing for a 35% profit share rather than pure supply of goods or services. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed by Respondent No. 1 in Form 5 totaling Rs. 17,47,436/- plus interest and TDS. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued under Section 8 of IBC; dates not explicitly specified in the order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Four Demand Drafts totaling Rs. 17,47,436/- alongside cheques covering interest and TDS handed over to Respondent No. 1's counsel; Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) executed on 13th December 2019 between the Corporate Debtor and G.H. Prints Pvt. Ltd.; Summary Suit pending by an employee (Ms. Rupa Gaur) for bounced cheques of approximately Rs. 4 Lakhs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition filed by Respondent No. 1 admitted by NCLT New Delhi Bench-II on 4th July 2019. A parallel Section 9 petition by G.H. Prints Pvt. Ltd. admitted on 15th October 2019 was recalled by NCLT on 5th November 2019 as infructuous due to the existing CIRP. Appellant appealed the admission order before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the CIRP initiated under Section 9 of the IBC can be set aside and the petition withdrawn under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016 where the Committee of Creditors has not been constituted and the Corporate Debtor has reached an amicable settlement with the creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In circumstances where the Committee of Creditors has not yet been constituted and the corporate debtor enters into a full and final settlement with the creditors, the appellate tribunal can exercise its inherent powers to set aside the admission of insolvency and dispose of the insolvency application as withdrawn. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Application of inherent powers under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016 allows the tribunal to make such orders as necessary for meeting the ends of justice, including terminating CIRP pre-CoC formation upon amicable settlement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that the Committee of Creditors has not been constituted, verified settlement of dues via cleared financial instruments/memorandum of understanding, and establishment that the corporate debtor is a functioning going concern. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no CoC was formed and the corporate debtor had settled the full dues of the operational creditors while remaining a going concern, continuation of CIRP was unjustified.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 4th July 2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-II is set aside[cite: 1]. The Section 9 application is disposed of as withdrawn and Company Petition No. IB-568/(ND)/2019 stands closed[cite: 1]. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigour of CIRP and assets/records are directed to be handed back to the Directors/Promoters[cite: 1]. The IRP's fee is assessed at Rs. 75,000/- per month for 5.5 months plus Rs. 85,000/- toward publication and legal costs, with the balance to be paid by the Appellant within three weeks after adjusting Rs. 1,68,500/- already paid[cite: 1].
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order admitting a Section 9 IBC application against the Corporate Debtor, M/s Mode Advertising and Marketing Pvt. Ltd[cite: 1]. Prior to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors, the Appellant reached an amicable settlement with the Operational Creditor by delivering demand drafts of Rs. 17,47,436/- plus interest and TDS[cite: 1], and executed an MOU with another creditor[cite: 1]. Exercising its inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, the NCLAT set aside the admission order, dismissed the insolvency application as withdrawn, released the Corporate Debtor from CIRP, and determined the final remuneration payable to the Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 1].

case_title: Manjit Commercial LLP vs. SPM Auto Pvt. Ltd. (In Liquidation) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Manjit Commercial LLP (Appellant/Prospective Bidder), SPM Auto Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor in Liquidation), Dry Nut Enterprises (Respondent No. 2/Auction Purchaser). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: E-auction sale of liquidation assets of the Corporate Debtor, specifically land and building situated at Plot No. B-169 and 170, RIICO Industrial Area, Phase-II, Delhi Jaipur Highway, Behror, Rajasthan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation valuation metrics: original first auction reserve price was Rs. 7.24 Crores, which failed to attract buyers; second auction reserve price set at Rs. 6.15 Crores with EMD of Rs. 61,54,122/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First e-auction held from 15.02.2019 to 15.03.2019; second e-auction notice issued on 10.04.2019; bidding forms and EMD due 10.04.2019 to 12.04.2019; second e-auction conducted on 15.04.2019; successful bidder announced on 16.04.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Newspaper advertisement published in 'Business Standard' (Delhi and Jaipur editions) on 10.04.2019; e-mail sent by Appellant on 15.04.2019 offering to buy at a higher price without participating in the bid; e-mail dated 20.04.2019 by ex-Director Vikrant Mahajan alleging collusion. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant challenged the second e-auction before NCLT New Delhi (Bench-II) in CA No. 551/ND/2019, alleging arbitrary reduction of reserve price and truncated bid window; NCLT dismissed the application on 10.06.2019, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Liquidator violated the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 by reducing the reserve price by 15% after a failed auction and shortening the bidding submission window to three days in the second e-auction.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party that abstains from participating in an officially advertised public e-auction has no locus standi to subsequently derail the liquidation process through unverified allegations, and a liquidator possesses statutory discretion to reduce the reserve price up to 75% upon failure of a prior auction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 4 of Schedule I of the Liquidation Process Regulations permits reduction of the reserve price by up to 75% when an earlier auction fails; reducing it by 15% is well within lawful authority. Clause 3 of Schedule I empowers the liquidator to determine terms, conditions, and timelines of sale without rigid mandatory duration constraints under the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Presumption of regularity in official acts where newspaper publication complies with Regulation 12, unsupported by evidence of collusion under Regulation 33(3). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator acted strictly in conformity with statutory liquidation rules and timelines to avoid protracted proceedings, rendering the challenge baseless.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, and the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 10th June 2019 upholding the second public e-auction is affirmed[cite: 2].
summary: Manjit Commercial LLP appealed against an NCLT order that rejected its challenge to the second e-auction of an immovable property belonging to the Corporate Debtor (in liquidation), SPM Auto Pvt. Ltd[cite: 2]. The Appellant contended that the Liquidator improperly reduced the reserve price from Rs. 7.24 Crores to Rs. 6.15 Crores and curtailed the bid submission duration to three days[cite: 2]. The NCLAT upheld the auction, observing that the Liquidator was legally empowered under Schedule I of the Liquidation Process Regulations to reduce the reserve price following a failed auction and determine marketing schedules[cite: 2]. The appeal was dismissed because the Appellant failed to participate in the auction and raised unsubstantiated objections[cite: 2].

case_title: Kavita Anil Taneja vs. ISMT Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kavita Anil Taneja (Appellant/Shareholder-Director), M/s ISMT Limited (Respondent/Purported Operational Creditor), M/s Fieldspares Sales & Services Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Work order dated 7th January 2012 for the supply of 10,000 Metric Tons of Indonesian Thermal Coal for ISMT Limited's 40 MW captive power plant, under which ISMT Limited paid 50% advance against security to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt default of Rs. 2,10,00,000/- out of an initial advance of Rs. 2,60,00,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8(1) of IBC issued by ISMT Limited; date of notice not stated in the order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Work order dated 7th January 2012; settlement proposal letter dated 9th August 2018 written by Corporate Debtor acknowledging unfulfilled supply, cost sharing, mutual adjustments, and offering to repay Rs. 80 Lakhs over 10 months. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed by ISMT Limited in CP No. 1206/IB/9(MB)/2017 admitted by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 13th September 2017 on grounds of demand notice issuance and default. Appellant appealed the admission order.
legal_issues: Whether an advance payment made by an entity as a purchaser/joint venturer for the supply of goods constitutes an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) enabling the purchaser to initiate CIRP as an 'operational creditor' under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity that only advances money for the procurement of goods or services without actually supplying any goods or rendering any services does not qualify as an 'operational creditor' holding an 'operational debt' under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(20) read with Section 5(21) mandates that an operational debt must strictly arise out of the provision of goods or services; funding or advancing consideration for a purchase or joint venture is outside the operational creditor framework and may at best represent a financial debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Direct examination of the contract/work order obligations demonstrating that the creditor was the customer/financier and not the vendor or service provider. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since ISMT Limited advanced funds and never provided goods or services, it is not an operational creditor, rendering its Section 9 petition fundamentally non-maintainable.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 13th September 2017 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside[cite: 3]. The application under Section 9 of the IBC is dismissed[cite: 3]. Moratorium, appointment of IRP, freezing of accounts, and all consequential actions are declared illegal and vacated[cite: 3]. The Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP to function under its Board of Directors[cite: 3]. NCLT is directed to fix the IRP's fee to be paid by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 3]. Liberty granted to Respondent to claim as a financial creditor before the appropriate forum if default persists[cite: 3].
summary: ISMT Limited advanced Rs. 2.60 Crores under a work order for the procurement of 10,000 MT of Indonesian Thermal Coal and subsequently filed a Section 9 IBC application against the supplier, Fieldspares Sales & Services Pvt. Ltd., alleging default of Rs. 2.10 Crores[cite: 3]. The NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the application[cite: 3]. On appeal, the NCLAT held that because ISMT Limited merely paid advance consideration and did not supply goods or provide services, it did not satisfy the statutory definition of an operational creditor under Section 5(20) and 5(21)[cite: 3]. The NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission, dismissed the petition, and restored the Corporate Debtor's management[cite: 3].

case_title: Tanya Bhatnagar vs. Mohamed Hesham Amin Basha Mashaa'l & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tanya Bhatnagar (Appellant/Director), Mohamed Hesham Mohamed Amin Basha Mashaa'l (Respondent No. 1/Purported Operational Creditor), M/s Global Energy Talent Private Limited (Respondent No. 2/Corporate Debtor - Indian entity), Global Energy Talent, Mauritius (Foreign contracting entity), Mohinder Singh (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported service engagement or contractual arrangement entered into exclusively between Respondent No. 1 and Global Energy Talent, Mauritius; no contractual agreement or privity existed with the Indian company M/s Global Energy Talent Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt default amount not quantified in the judgment text; RP expenses incurred were roughly Rs. 6 Lakhs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice issued under Section 8(1) of the IBC addressed to M/s Global Energy Talent Private Limited; date of notice not mentioned in the order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lack of any contract or privity between Respondent No. 1 and the Indian entity; proof of out-of-court settlement directly between Respondent No. 1 and Global Energy Talent, Mauritius, including payment of Rs. 2 Lakhs by the Mauritius entity towards RP expenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition filed by Respondent No. 1 was admitted by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III on 19th December 2018. Tanya Bhatnagar appealed against the admission order before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable against an Indian corporate entity when the operational debt arose exclusively from an arrangement with an independent foreign entity, and whether such filing constitutes fraudulent or malicious initiation under Section 65 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for insolvency resolution under Section 9 of the IBC is non-maintainable in the absence of privity of contract establishing a debtor-creditor relationship between the applicant and the target corporate debtor, and initiating proceedings against an unrelated entity attracts scrutiny for malicious prosecution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 requires a direct operational creditor and corporate debtor relationship; deploying insolvency provisions against a distinct legal entity constitutes initiation for purposes other than resolution, warranting inquiry under Section 65. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Establishing lack of privity of contract through undisputed corporate records and conduct indicating debt resolution executed with an entirely separate overseas affiliate. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: There was zero contractual privity between Respondent No. 1 and the Indian company, rendering the Section 9 petition non-maintainable and maliciously instituted.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19th December 2018 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III is set aside[cite: 4]. The Section 9 application is dismissed, all moratorium and appointment orders are annulled, and the Corporate Debtor is restored to its Board of Directors[cite: 4]. The Corporate Debtor is directed to pay Rs. 6 Lakhs to the RP (after adjusting Rs. 2 Lakhs paid by the Mauritius entity) within three weeks, with liberty to recover the sum from Respondent No. 1[cite: 4]. The matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to issue notice and determine whether penal orders should be passed against Respondent No. 1 under Section 65 of the IBC[cite: 4].
summary: Respondent No. 1 filed a Section 9 IBC application against an Indian entity, M/s Global Energy Talent Private Limited, which was admitted by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III on 19th December 2018[cite: 4]. The Appellant established on appeal that the Respondent's contractual arrangement was solely with Global Energy Talent, Mauritius, and that the parties had independently settled the dispute[cite: 4]. The NCLAT held that in the absence of privity of contract establishing an operational debtor-creditor relationship, the petition was non-maintainable and appeared maliciously filed[cite: 4]. The NCLAT set aside the admission, quashed the CIRP, and remitted the matter for consideration of penalties under Section 65 against Respondent No. 1[cite: 4].

case_title: Axis Bank Ltd vs. Ashish Rathi, Resolution Professional & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Axis Bank Limited (Appellant in Comp. App. 590/2018), Runh Power Corporation Ltd. (Appellant in Comp. App. 641/2018 / Equipment Supplier), Ind-Barath Power (Madras) Limited (Corporate Debtor), Ashish Rathi (Resolution Professional), China Bank (Issuing Bank), Bank of Baroda (Intermediary/Advising Bank). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply Agreement dated 31st August 2010 for 1 No. 660 MW BTG executed between Corporate Debtor and Runh Power for setting up a thermal power plant in Tuticorin, Tamil Nadu, requiring advance Bank Guarantees for receiving 5% advance payment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Second Bank Guarantee No. 37003020000267 for USD 6,846,000 issued on 25th November 2011; First Bank Guarantee for USD 4,564,000 issued on 22nd September 2014; both expired on 30th September 2018 during the moratorium. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Supply agreement executed 31st August 2010; foreign court injunction granted by Jinan Court, China on 23rd February 2018; liquidation application filed by RP on 25th October 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Advance Bank Guarantees issued by China Bank via Bank of Baroda (not Axis Bank); injunction order dated 23rd February 2018 passed by Jinan Court, China restraining remittance under the Bank Guarantees. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP in CP(IB) No. 150/9/HDB/2017. RP requested Axis Bank to invoke both BGs; Axis Bank invoked the first but refused the second. RP filed IA No. 153/2018 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench, which on 12th September 2018 directed Axis Bank to encash the second Bank Guarantee. Axis Bank and Runh Power appealed against this direction.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction to direct a bank to invoke a foreign bank guarantee issued through an entirely different financial institution, especially where a competent foreign court has issued an injunction restraining remittance.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot issue directions compelling a bank to invoke or encash a bank guarantee where the bank is neither the issuing nor the intermediary bank through which the guarantee was established, nor can it ignore a pre-existing foreign court injunction on remittance. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 and adjudicatory powers under the IBC do not extend to coercing a non-guarantor banking entity into undertaking extra-legal encashments contrary to banking law and binding international court injunctions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of bank guarantee documents identifying the issuing bank and routing institution (Bank of Baroda, not Axis Bank) and verified judicial restraint orders from the foreign court of jurisdiction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in directing Axis Bank to encash a Bank Guarantee routed through Bank of Baroda and subject to an operative foreign injunction.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 12th September 2018 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench in I.A. No. 153 of 2018 is set aside to the extent it directed Axis Bank to encash the Bank Guarantee[cite: 5]. Both appeals are allowed without costs, leaving it open to the concerned party to seek relief before an appropriate forum[cite: 5].
summary: Under a 2010 BTG Supply Agreement, Runh Power Corporation procured two advance bank guarantees from China Bank via Bank of Baroda in favor of Ind-Barath Power (Madras) Limited[cite: 5]. During the Corporate Debtor's CIRP, the NCLT Hyderabad directed Axis Bank to invoke the second Bank Guarantee of USD 6,846,000[cite: 5]. Axis Bank and Runh Power appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 5]. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's direction, holding that Axis Bank could not be commanded to encash a guarantee issued through Bank of Baroda, particularly given an existing injunction issued by the Jinan Court in China restraining payment remittance[cite: 5].

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Punjab National Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Appellant in Comp. App. 329/2018 / Financial Creditor), Punjab National Bank (Appellant in Comp. App. 529/2018 / Financial Creditor), Corporate Debtor (entity under CIRP), Committee of Creditors (CoC participants), Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Letters of Credit facility and margin money kept separately in a Fixed Deposit (FD) account of the Corporate Debtor prior to initiation of CIRP for making payments to Operational Creditors against Letters of Credit. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary default sums and interest figures not explicitly quantified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated and statutory moratorium under Section 14 came into effect; NCLT Division Bench Chennai passed the underlying direction on 23rd May 2018; PNB's appeal filed with a delay of 50 days beyond the initial 30-day statutory period. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Fixed Deposit account maintained in the name of the Corporate Debtor containing margin money funds; bank records showing debit transactions executed by State Bank of India from the said FD account during the moratorium period. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: State Bank of India debited the FD account during moratorium; the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chennai) directed SBI on 23rd May 2018 to reverse the debits to restore parity among CoC members regarding voting rights. SBI and PNB appealed the order to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a financial creditor is legally permitted under Section 14 to debit margin money from a Corporate Debtor's Fixed Deposit account during the statutory moratorium period, and whether the Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to condone an appeal delay exceeding the statutory cap under Section 61(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any asset or margin money belonging to the Corporate Debtor and held in its bank accounts constitutes property protected by the statutory moratorium, precluding unilateral debits or appropriations by financial creditors during CIRP, while the appellate tribunal lacks power to condone an appeal filed beyond the outer statutory limit. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The moratorium under Section 14 operates as an absolute statutory freeze protecting corporate debtor assets against encashment or debit adjustments; Section 61(2) sets an inflexible limitation threshold permitting condonation only up to 15 days past the initial 30-day timeline. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of asset ownership demonstrating that margin money held in the Corporate Debtor's fixed deposit belongs to the Corporate Debtor, and mathematical calculation of filing delay exceeding the outer limitation cap. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: SBI's debits from the corporate debtor's FD during moratorium were impermissible and required reversal, while PNB's appeal was strictly barred by limitation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 329 of 2018 is dismissed without interference with the NCLT order dated 23rd May 2018, granting SBI liberty to take appropriate steps after the moratorium and permitting the RP to utilize the funds towards resolution costs to maintain the debtor as a going concern[cite: 6]. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 529 of 2018 is dismissed as barred by limitation without costs[cite: 6].
summary: State Bank of India appealed an NCLT Chennai direction requiring it to reverse debits made from a Corporate Debtor's Fixed Deposit account during CIRP to preserve voting parity within the Committee of Creditors[cite: 6]. SBI argued the funds constituted pre-CIRP margin money for Letters of Credit[cite: 6]. The NCLAT held that because the margin money belonged to the Corporate Debtor, debiting the account during the Section 14 moratorium was impermissible[cite: 6]. The NCLAT dismissed SBI's appeal while clarifying the Resolution Professional could deploy the money towards CIRP costs[cite: 6]. A companion appeal by Punjab National Bank was dismissed as time-barred under Section 61(2)[cite: 6].

case_title: Axis Bank Ltd. vs. Sixth Dimension Project Solution Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Axis Bank Ltd. (Appellant / Financial Creditor / CoC Member), M/s Sixth Dimension Project Solution Limited (Corporate Debtor), Ms. Rama Subramaniam (Operational Creditor), Mr. S. Gopalakrishnan (Interim Resolution Professional / Continuing RP), Mr. Santanu T. Ray (Proposed Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying default arising from an operational claim admitted under Section 9 IBC, leading to CIRP where Axis Bank was a member of the Committee of Creditors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default figures in the Section 9 petition not stated in the order; CIRP had run for approximately 180 days without substantial progress. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 petition admitted in CP No. 587/I&BP/2018; CoC meeting resolving replacement held on 3rd October 2018; NCLT rejection order passed on 13th March 2019; initial 180 days of CIRP expired. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC resolution dated 3rd October 2018 approving replacement of Mr. S. Gopalakrishnan with Mr. Santanu T. Ray passed with 100% voting share; failure of the IRP to file the Information Memorandum or report corporate non-cooperation to the Adjudicating Authority within statutory timelines. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CoC applied to NCLT Mumbai Bench for replacement of RP under Section 22/27 and extension of CIRP; NCLT rejected the replacement application on 13th March 2019 on the ground that the CoC provided no tenable, valid, or genuine reasons. Axis Bank appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors is required to assign or substantiate specific grounds/reasons when exercising its commercial wisdom to replace a Resolution Professional under Sections 22 and 27 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory scheme of the IBC vests the Committee of Creditors with unfettered commercial authority to replace a Resolution Professional by requisite majority vote without the requirement of stating specific reasons or proving allegations of misconduct. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 22 and 27 of the IBC do not mandate that the CoC specify or prove valid grounds for replacing an RP; requiring the Adjudicating Authority to conduct an inquiry into reasons causes unnecessary delay detrimental to CIRP timelines. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the requisite statutory voting threshold (100% CoC approval) and confirmation that the proposed Resolution Professional has no disciplinary proceedings pending against him. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by demanding proof of valid grounds for RP replacement when the CoC had resolved the change by a unanimous 100% voting majority.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 13th March 2019 is set aside[cite: 7]. The CoC is permitted to engage Mr. Santanu T. Ray as Resolution Professional subject to no pending proceedings against him[cite: 7]. Mr. S. Gopalakrishnan is directed to hand over charge and submit evidence of his fees/costs to the CoC for adjustment from resolution costs[cite: 7]. CIRP timeline is prospectively extended by 90 days from the date of receipt of the certified order, and the pending extension application before NCLT stands disposed of[cite: 7].
summary: Axis Bank appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting a 100% CoC-approved resolution to replace the Resolution Professional, Mr. S. Gopalakrishnan, with Mr. Santanu T. Ray under Sections 22 and 27 of the IBC on the ground that no valid reasons were substantiated[cite: 7]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the rejection, ruling that the IBC does not require the CoC to provide or prove reasons for replacing an RP, as adjudicating such reasons causes unwarranted delay[cite: 7]. The Tribunal sanctioned the appointment of the new RP, ordered payment of verified fees to the outgoing RP, and granted a 90-day extension to the CIRP[cite: 7].

case_title: Sarita Vishal vs. Anupam Enterprises & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sarita Vishal (Appellant / Director-Shareholder), M/s Aarti Security Services (Respondent in Comp. App. 909/2019 / Operational Creditor), Anupam Enterprises (Respondent in Comp. App. 929/2019 / Operational Creditor), M/s Shahi Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), Kailash Chander Jain (Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of security and operational services by the Operational Creditors to the Corporate Debtor under respective commercial contracts/invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed by Aarti Security Services settled for Rs. 40,00,000/- (Rs. 10 Lakhs paid immediately + Rs. 30 Lakhs deferred); operational debt claimed by Anupam Enterprises settled for Rs. 3,00,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned admission orders passed by NCLT on 22nd August 2019; settlement with Anupam Enterprises executed on 30th November 2019; settlement agreement with Aarti Security Services executed on 3rd December 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Agreement dated 3rd December 2019 and signed affidavit between Sarita Vishal and Brahm Pal Singh (Aarti Security Services); cheque of Rs. 10 Lakhs delivered in court; Settlement Agreement dated 30th November 2019 confirming full receipt by Anupam Enterprises; receipt of Rs. 2 Lakhs by IRP towards costs and fees. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench New Delhi admitted separate Section 9 petitions against the Corporate Debtor on 22nd August 2019 in CP No. IB-1066(PB)/2019 (Aarti Security) and CP No. IB-1566(PB)/2018 (Anupam Enterprises). The Appellant challenged both orders before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to quash Section 9 CIRP admission orders when the Corporate Debtor concludes complete settlement agreements with operational creditors prior to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Prior to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors, the Appellate Tribunal is empowered under its inherent jurisdiction to set aside an order of admission under Section 9 of the IBC if the debtor has amicably settled all outstanding liabilities with the petitioning operational creditors and cleared the IRP's expenses. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Exercise of inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 is valid and appropriate to terminate insolvency proceedings where no third-party creditor rights have accrued via CoC constitution and the dispute stands fully settled. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of executed settlement agreements, confirmation of payment receipts/cheques before the court, and formal acknowledgment by the IRP of full fee satisfaction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Settlements having been finalized with both operational creditors and the IRP fees fully disbursed before CoC formation, continuing CIRP serves no purpose and must be set aside.
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 22nd August 2019 passed in C.P. No. IB-1066(PB)/2019 and C.P. No. IB-1566(PB)/2018 are set aside[cite: 8]. Both Section 9 petitions stand disposed of, the IRP is directed to return records and assets to the Board of Directors, the Adjudicating Authority shall close proceedings, and the Corporate Debtor is released from the rigour of CIRP to function independently[cite: 8]. Both appeals are allowed without costs[cite: 8].
summary: Two separate Section 9 IBC applications filed by M/s Aarti Security Services and Anupam Enterprises against Shahi Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. were admitted by NCLT Special Bench New Delhi on 22nd August 2019[cite: 8]. The Appellant director appealed both orders[cite: 8]. Before the Committee of Creditors was constituted, the Appellant entered into formal settlement agreements with both operational creditors—disbursing settled amounts including a Rs. 10 Lakhs cheque in court—and paid Rs. 2 Lakhs to the IRP for accrued costs and fees[cite: 8]. Exercising inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, the NCLAT set aside both admission orders, dismissed the insolvency petitions, and restored the Corporate Debtor's management[cite: 8].

case_title: Amrit Feeds Ltd. vs. S.S. Enterprises
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amrit Feeds Ltd. (Appellant / Corporate Debtor), S.S. Enterprises (Respondent / Operational Creditor), Agarwal Industries Pvt. Ltd. (Prior Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational transactions involving supply of goods/services by S.S. Enterprises to Corporate Debtor giving rise to an unpaid operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date of default not quantified in the text of the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Prior CIRP initiated in CP(IB) No. 333/KB/2018 on 15th January 2019; parallel petition CP(IB) No. 1238/KB/2018 disposed of on 25th January 2019; prior CIRP set aside on settlement by NCLAT on 11th February 2019 in Comp. App. 102/2019; restoration ordered by NCLT on 10th May 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Demand notice under Section 8(1) issued by S.S. Enterprises; suppression of fact by Amrit Feeds' promoters before NCLAT that S.S. Enterprises' Section 9 petition had been disposed of on technical grounds with directions to file a claim with the earlier IRP; restoration application Misc. A. 302/KB/2018 (MA 302/KB/19). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: S.S. Enterprises' Section 9 petition was disposed of on 25th January 2019 by NCLT Kolkata as infructuous because a prior CIRP initiated by Agarwal Industries was active. After the promoter settled with Agarwal Industries and had that CIRP quashed without disclosing S.S. Enterprises' claim, S.S. Enterprises sought restoration. NCLT Kolkata restored the petition on 10th May 2019 under Rule 11. Amrit Feeds appealed the restoration order.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to restore a Section 9 petition disposed of on technical grounds when an earlier CIRP against the Corporate Debtor is terminated upon settlement, without necessitating a fresh Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an operational creditor's Section 9 petition is dismissed or disposed of purely as infructuous due to a pre-existing CIRP against the corporate debtor, the Adjudicating Authority retains inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11 to restore the petition if that pre-existing CIRP is subsequently terminated pursuant to a settlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inherent power under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 empowers the tribunal to recall or restore an application disposed of on technical grounds to avoid grave injustice; the creditor is not required to issue a fresh Section 8(1) demand notice because the original cause of action and statutory default remain extant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof that the initial petition was disposed of solely because of an ongoing CIRP and evidence demonstrating suppression of outstanding claims by the debtor when terminating the prior CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no error or illegality in invoking Rule 11 to restore the Section 9 petition to its original file, as the debtor will be accorded full opportunity of hearing on merits.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Kolkata order dated 10th May 2019 restoring Company Petition No. CP (IB) No. 1238/KB/2018 to its original file[cite: 9]. The Adjudicating Authority shall hear the Appellant Corporate Debtor after due notice before passing substantive orders on merits[cite: 9].
summary: S.S. Enterprises filed a Section 9 application against Amrit Feeds Ltd., which NCLT Kolkata disposed of on technical grounds on 25th January 2019, directing the creditor to file a claim in an already-existing CIRP initiated by another creditor[cite: 9]. After the promoters settled the first CIRP without disclosing S.S. Enterprises' pending claim, NCLAT terminated that CIRP[cite: 9]. S.S. Enterprises then applied for restoration of its Section 9 petition, which NCLT Kolkata granted under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016[cite: 9]. Amrit Feeds appealed, arguing lack of power to review/recall and demanding a fresh Section 8 notice[cite: 9]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the restoration as lawful and within inherent powers[cite: 9].

case_title: Urban Infrastructure Trustees Limited vs. Neelkanth Realty Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Urban Infrastructure Trustees Limited (Appellant / Purported Financial Creditor / Debenture Holder), Neelkanth Realty Private Limited (Respondent / Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debentures issued by the Corporate Debtor that matured in 2011, held or claimed by the Appellant as a debenture holder. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under Form 1 including an admitted claim amount of Rs. 7,23,34,059/- alongside an additional disputed amount; debentures matured in 2011. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Debentures matured in 2011; NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the Section 7 petition on 25th January 2019; settlement negotiations recorded before NCLAT on 26th September 2019 offering staggered payments until 31st January 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheet containing an entry acknowledging liability towards a generic class of debentures; failure of the Appellant to produce original/duplicate debenture certificates establishing title and entitlement to redemption. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Urban Infrastructure Trustees filed a Section 7 petition which NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected on 25th January 2019, holding that entries in balance sheets do not prove default of specific titleholders without producing debenture certificates. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
