Furthermore, Section 238 of the IBC overrides the NHB and RBI Acts, and the commercial wisdom of the CoC in distributing plan proceeds in accordance with Section 30(2)(b) is non-justiciable.

case_title: Dr. P. Mahalingam vs. Muthoot Fincorp Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 146 of 2020 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1121 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. P. Mahalingam (Appellant/Suspended Director & Personal Guarantor); Muthoot Fincorp Limited (Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor); DCB Bank Limited (Respondent No. 2/Financial Creditor); Santosh Hospitals Private Limited (Respondent No. 3/Corporate Debtor through Liquidator Ms. Deepa Venkat Ramani); Greater Chennai Corporation (Respondent No. 4 in connected appeal). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility of Rs. 42 Crores sanctioned by Muthoot Fincorp to Santosh Hospitals Pvt. Ltd., secured by personal guarantee and equitable mortgage of hospital land and a 5-storey building at Besant Nagar, Chennai, executed via registered Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds by the Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default admitted by the Corporate Debtor in Form-VI under Section 10 of the IBC was Rs. 39,00,00,000 owed to Muthoot Fincorp (total default Rs. 39,52,24,076); Appellant later undertook to pay Rs. 57,50,00,000 as full settlement but defaulted entirely. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 04.04.2019 under Section 10; 180-day CIRP period expired on 04.10.2019; NCLT extended CIRP by 15 days expiring on 19.10.2019; CoC voted for liquidation on 18.10.2019; NCLT ordered liquidation on 04.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Settlement Deed dated 28.09.2002 conveying title to the Appellant personally; registered Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds dated 17.08.2016; unregistered/miscellaneous 'Deed of Solemn Undertaking' dated 05.11.2002 attempting to declare the asset as corporate property; Advocate Commissioner reports confirming the hospital was non-operational since 2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor filed Section 10 application admitted on 04.04.2019; IRP filed MA 363/2019 for possession of the mortgaged hospital; Appellant repeatedly breached judicial undertakings to settle debt; on 18.10.2019, CoC resolved by 73.44% majority to liquidate; NCLT Chennai passed liquidation order on 04.12.2019, and on 17.12.2020 directed GCC to restore possession to Muthoot Fincorp, both challenged by the Appellant.
legal_issues: Whether an order of liquidation passed by the Adjudicating Authority pursuant to a 73.44% CoC vote is valid when the statutory CIRP period has expired without any resolution plan, and whether an immovable property owned personally by a promoter-guarantor and mortgaged to a secured creditor forms part of the corporate debtor's estate to attract the Section 14 moratorium.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon expiration of the maximum corporate insolvency resolution period without the approval of a resolution plan, the adjudicating authority is statutorily mandated to order liquidation based on the commercial wisdom of the committee of creditors, and personal assets of third-party guarantors do not vest in the corporate debtor's estate or enjoy protection under the moratorium. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 33(2) of the IBC, the CoC is empowered to resolve to liquidate the corporate debtor at any time before confirmation of a plan; under Section 14(3)(b) read with Explanation (a) to Section 18(1)(f) and Section 36(4), the moratorium and corporate estate do not encompass assets owned by third-party personal guarantors, even if reflected in balance sheets without valid conveyance deeds. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Legally valid registered conveyance under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act; an informal solemn undertaking or balance sheet entry cannot override registered title deeds establishing personal ownership and valid mortgages enforceable under SARFAESI. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC validly resolved to liquidate the defunct corporate debtor with a 73.44% majority, and the Appellant's repeated failure to honour settlement undertakings rendered liquidation inevitable; furthermore, Muthoot Fincorp as mortgagee of the personal guarantor's asset was entitled to retain possession.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 146 of 2020 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1121 of 2020 are dismissed without costs. The liquidation order dated 04.12.2019 and the order directing handover of keys to Muthoot Fincorp dated 17.12.2020 are confirmed. All connected interim applications are closed.
summary: Appellant, promoter and personal guarantor of Santosh Hospitals Pvt. Ltd., appealed NCLT Chennai's orders directing liquidation under Section 33(2) and restoring possession of the hospital premises to secured creditor Muthoot Fincorp. Appellant contended the hospital was corporate property and should have been revived as a going concern. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that the CoC validly exercised its commercial wisdom to liquidate the hospital after the CIRP period expired without a resolution plan and following repeated breaches of settlement undertakings. Moreover, title to the mortgaged property belonged to the Appellant personally, excluding it from the Corporate Debtor's estate under Sections 14 and 18.

case_title: Kiran Shah, RP of KSL and Industries Ltd. vs. Enforcement Directorate, Kolkata
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kiran Shah (Appellant/Resolution Professional of KSL and Industries Ltd.); Enforcement Directorate, Kolkata (Respondent/Statutory Authority under PMLA); KSL and Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Tayal Group entity). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated against KSL and Industries Ltd. under Section 7 of the IBC by financial creditors; commercial mall asset ('Empress Mall', Nagpur) owned by the CD was previously mortgaged to a consortium of banks led by Bank of India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from credit facilities aggregating Rs. 524.61 Crores availed by Tayal Group entities and laundered through shell companies; ED provisionally attached the Empress Mall valued at Rs. 483,16,35,696 as equivalent value of proceeds of crime. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: FIRs registered by CBI in 2015-2016; ECIR recorded on 19.10.2016; ED issued Provisional Attachment Order under Section 5 PMLA on 08.05.2019; NCLT admitted Section 7 petition on 06.09.2019; Adjudicating Authority PMLA confirmed the attachment on 24.10.2019; RP filed IA 81/2020 before NCLT on 10.01.2020; NCLT dismissed the application on 31.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Conveyance deed dated 07.02.2005 showing CD acquired Empress Mall; mortgage deeds dated 05.09.2008 with banks; ED investigation records demonstrating laundering of bank funds through shell entities; PAO dated 08.05.2019 and confirmation order dated 24.10.2019; pendency of Appeal No. 3387/2019 before the Appellate Tribunal PMLA. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution Professional filed IA 81/2020 before NCLT Ahmedabad seeking to quash the PMLA attachment orders and regain custody of Empress Mall; NCLT dismissed the application for want of jurisdiction, holding that PMLA is a special criminal statute outside Section 60(5) of the IBC, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) exercising jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC possesses the statutory power to quash or set aside a provisional attachment order confirmed by the PMLA Adjudicating Authority, and whether the Section 14 moratorium applies to criminal attachment of proceeds of crime under the PMLA prior to plan approval.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory moratorium and general omnibus jurisdiction of company tribunals under insolvency legislation do not override criminal attachments of proceeds of crime undertaken by special statutory authorities under anti-money laundering laws, and challenges to such attachments must be pursued strictly before the specialized appellate hierarchy created by the penal statute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC bars civil debt recovery actions and pecuniary claims against the debtor, but does not interdict statutory penal actions under the PMLA aimed at confiscating tainted proceeds of crime; Section 32A(2) immunity only activates post-approval of a resolution plan by the adjudicating authority and confers no pre-approval protection; Section 60(5) cannot be stretched to confer judicial review over specialized quasi-judicial authorities acting under public criminal law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Distinction between civil creditor enforcement and sovereign criminal confiscation; government confiscating proceeds of crime does not act as a creditor recovering a debt, thereby negating any statutory conflict between IBC and PMLA during ongoing CIRP prior to plan approval. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly held that it lacked jurisdiction to invalidate the PMLA attachment order; the Resolution Professional having already elected his statutory remedy by filing an appeal before the PMLA Appellate Tribunal under Section 26 cannot bypass that specialized forum via Section 60(5).
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 817 of 2021 is dismissed without costs. Connected Interlocutory Applications (IA Nos. 2778 and 2194 of 2021) are dismissed. The Resolution Professional is granted liberty to pursue its statutory appeal before the PMLA Appellate Tribunal in accordance with law.
summary: The Resolution Professional of KSL and Industries Ltd. appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing his application to quash a PMLA attachment order over the Corporate Debtor's primary asset ('Empress Mall', Nagpur, valued at Rs. 483 Crores), which had been attached as proceeds of crime. The RP argued that the Section 14 moratorium and Section 238 override PMLA attachments. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the Section 14 moratorium does not shield proceeds of crime from penal confiscation under PMLA, and Section 32A immunity applies only after a resolution plan is approved. The NCLT lacks jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to review PMLA attachment orders, and the RP must pursue remedies before the PMLA Appellate Tribunal.

case_title: Mr. Naresh Kumar Dasari vs. Competition Commission of India
appeal_number: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 24 of 2022 with Competition Appeal (AT) No. 26 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Naresh Kumar Dasari (Appellant in Comp. App. 24/2022 and Managing Director of Macromedia Digital Imaging Pvt. Ltd.); Macromedia Digital Imaging Pvt. Ltd. / MMDI / OP-6 (Appellant in Comp. App. 26/2022); Competition Commission of India (Respondent); Diamond Display Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (OP-1); AGX Retail Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (OP-2); Opal Signs Pvt. Ltd. (OP-3); Avery Dennison Pvt. Ltd. (OP-4); Amreesh Neon Pvt. Ltd. (OP-5); Hith Impex Pvt. Ltd. (OP-7). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tender floated by SBI Infra Management Solution Pvt. Ltd. (SBIIMS) on 28.03.2018 for the supply and installation of new LED back-lit signages and replacement of existing signages for branches, offices, and ATMs across 13 metro circles in India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bid-rigging, collusive manipulation of e-reverse auction prices, and geographical allocation of metro circles; penalty of Rs. 51,77,659 imposed on MMDI (OP-6) at 1% of average relevant turnover, and penalty of Rs. 46,468 imposed on Naresh Kumar Dasari at 1% of average income. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Complaint received on 28.06.2018; Suo Moto Case No. 2/2020 registered; e-reverse auction conducted on 04.06.2018 and 05.06.2018; CCI passed the final cease and desist order and penalty on 03.02.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Incriminating emails dated 02.06.2018 and 04.06.2018 sent by Naresh Kumar Dasari containing an Excel workbook titled 'Bbi_Bid_4June18.xlsx' detailing cut-off prices, circle categorizations, pre-decided L-1 bidders, and bidding sequences matching actual reverse auction outcomes; Call Data Records (CDRs) proving continuous coordination during the bidding window; admission of cartel conduct by OP-4 under Section 46 lesser penalty application; subsequent subcontract execution of tender works by MMDI in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: DG investigated under Section 26(1) and found OP-1 to OP-7 and their executives guilty of cartelization; on 03.02.2022, the CCI held MMDI liable under Section 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) and penalized Naresh Kumar Dasari under Section 48, which was appealed under Section 53B before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an enterprise that did not directly participate as an official bidder in an e-reverse auction can be held liable for bid-rigging under Section 3(3)(d) of the Competition Act, 2002, and whether its Managing Director who formulated collusive bidding matrices can be penalized under Section 48 as having acted in an individual capacity.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Actual formal participation in a tender process is not a prerequisite to establish bid-rigging or cartel liability where an enterprise, through its management, colludes with competitors to fix prices, allocate territories, or manipulate the competitive bidding mechanism. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002 prohibits any concerted action or understanding that directly or indirectly results in bid-rigging or eliminates competition; under Section 48(1) and 48(2), key persons responsible for the conduct of the business of the company cannot escape vicarious liability by setting up a plea of individual or unofficial capacity when the company itself participates financially or executes subcontracted tender works. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Preponderance of probabilities based on holistic assessment of direct and circumstantial evidence; exact mirroring of pre-shared bidding sequences and cut-off prices in actual tender results constitutes conclusive proof of meeting of minds rebutting any contention of a mere tutorial. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: MMDI and its Managing Director actively orchestrated the collusive bidding sequence and derived commercial benefits through execution of works, fully satisfying the ingredients of Section 3(3)(c), 3(3)(d), and Section 48 of the Act.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 24 of 2022 and Competition Appeal (AT) No. 26 of 2022 are dismissed. The impugned order of the Competition Commission of India dated 03.02.2022 in Suo Moto Case No. 02 of 2020 is confirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellants, Macromedia Digital Imaging Pvt. Ltd. (MMDI) and its Managing Director Naresh Kumar Dasari, challenged the CCI's order dated 03.02.2022 penalizing them for bid-rigging and cartelization under Section 3(3) and Section 48 of the Competition Act, 2002 in an SBIIMS signage tender. Appellants argued that MMDI was not an official bidder and Dasari had merely acted as an informal advisor in his personal capacity. The NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that formal participation is not a prerequisite under Section 3(3)(d). Dasari's circulation of pre-planned bidding charts and MMDI's execution of subcontracted work established collusive orchestration, making both the company and the Managing Director liable.

case_title: Union Bank of India vs. M/s. Rajdeep Clothing & Advisory Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union Bank of India on behalf of Committee of Creditors (Appellant/Lead Financial Creditor); M/s Rajdeep Clothing & Advisory Pvt. Ltd. and 12 other corporate entities (Respondents No. 1 to 13/Unsecured Financial Creditors); Brijesh Kumar Mishra (Respondent No. 14/Erstwhile RP); Ravi Kapoor (Respondent No. 15/Replaced RP); Krishna Knitwear Technology Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unsecured financial loan facilities and corporate guarantees extended to Krishna Knitwear Technology Ltd. by the respondent financial creditors, which were admitted as financial debt during the CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the Corporate Debtor in servicing credit facilities leading to CIRP initiation under Section 7 by Andhra Bank (now Union Bank of India); subsequent unilateral reduction of principal and interest claims of Respondents by the RP based on a Transaction Audit Report. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 13.01.2020; claims invited by 13.02.2020; 1st CoC meeting held on 29.02.2020; Transaction Auditor appointed on 17.07.2020 and reported on 29.08.2020; RP excluded Respondents from CoC via email on 14.10.2020; NCLT Ahmedabad passed the impugned order on 06.04.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Duly verified Form-C claim submissions accompanied by Form-26AS tax deductions; absence of common directors between Corporate Debtor and the Respondents in statutory registers; reliance by RP on an obsolete 2014 SAT order under SEBI regulations concerning 'persons acting in concert' to classify them as related parties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed IA No. 953/2020 and IA No. 13/2021 before NCLT Ahmedabad challenging claim reduction and exclusion from the CoC; on 06.04.2021, NCLT held Respondents were not related parties, directed reconstitution of CoC with full voting rights, replaced the RP under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, and referred him to IBBI; Union Bank of India appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional possesses the statutory power under the IBC to unilaterally determine, reduce, or reject admitted financial claims and de-list financial creditors from the Committee of Creditors as related parties without prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority, and whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Rule 11 to suo motu replace the Resolution Professional for grave procedural illegalities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional functions merely as an administrative facilitator without adjudicatory powers and cannot unilaterally review, reduce, or reject admitted financial claims or de-constitute the Committee of Creditors on allegations of related-party status without prior judicial determination by the Adjudicating Authority; where an insolvency professional commits flagrant illegalities paralyzing the CIRP, the Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent powers to order their replacement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1)(b) and Section 21(2) require the RP to collate claims and constitute the CoC comprising all financial creditors; the proviso to Section 21(2) restricts voting rights of related parties but does not empower the RP to unilaterally strip membership or exclude creditors; Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, 2016 confers inherent jurisdiction on the Tribunal to replace an RP to prevent abuse of process when the statutory mechanisms under Section 22 or 27 cannot resolve an administrative impasse. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict statutory criteria for 'related party' under Section 5(24); third-party forensic reports or ten-year-old market regulator orders regarding 'persons acting in concert' cannot substitute objective corporate shareholding and directorship records. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP exceeded his brief and violated natural justice by arbitrarily disqualifying financial creditors based on an inconclusive external audit; NCLT properly exercised its inherent powers to replace the RP and direct the reconstitution of the CoC.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 399 of 2021 is dismissed without costs. The interim order staying the operation of the impugned order stands vacated. Reconstitution of the CoC and replacement of the Resolution Professional by Mr. Ravi Kapoor are confirmed.
summary: Union Bank of India, representing the CoC of Krishna Knitwear Technology Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad dated 06.04.2021, which held that 13 unsecured financial creditors were not related parties, ordered their re-induction into the CoC with voting rights, and replaced the Resolution Professional under Rule 11 for exceeding his authority. The RP had unilaterally excluded the creditors and reduced their claims based on an inconclusive transaction audit and an old SAT ruling. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the RP has no adjudicatory power to remove members from the CoC or alter admitted claims without tribunal approval, and upheld the NCLT's inherent jurisdiction to replace an errant RP.

case_title: Pawan Jagetia vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
appeal_number: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 16 of 2021 with Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 18, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26 & 27 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: United Breweries Ltd. / UBL (OP-1), Crown Beers India Ltd. (OP-2), SABMiller India Ltd. (OP-3), Carlsberg India Pvt. Ltd. / CIPL (OP-4), and All India Brewers Association / AIBA (OP-5); Pawan Jagetia, Nilesh Patel, Shekhar Ramamurthy, Kalyan Ganguly, and other corporate executives (Individual Appellants); Competition Commission of India (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Production, marketing, distribution, and commercial sale of beer across various States and Union Territories in India, commanding an aggregate 88% domestic market share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Horizontal cartelization, collective price alignment of Ex-Brewery Price (EBP) and Maximum Retail Price (MRP), supply restrictions, and second-hand bottle procurement price-fixing; aggregate penalty of Rs. 751.83 Crores levied on UBL (after 40% leniency reduction), Rs. 120.56 Crores on Carlsberg (after 20% reduction), and individual penalties at 3% of average incomes under Section 48. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lesser penalty application filed by SABMiller on 26.07.2017; Suo Moto Case No. 06/2017 registered and Section 26(1) order passed on 31.10.2017; DG dawn raids on 10-11.10.2018; UBL and Carlsberg filed leniency applications on 12.10.2018 and 15.10.2018; CCI passed the final cease, desist, and penalty order on 24.09.2021 (rectified on 04.11.2021). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Thousands of internal emails, WhatsApp chats, and cost cards exchanged among executives discussing common MRP targets; admissions in leniency applications under Section 46 disclosing cartel operation; recorded statements of executives admitting price coordination before state excise authorities; evidence of collective supply curtailment in Odisha, Maharashtra, and West Bengal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI held UBL, SABMiller, CIPL, and AIBA guilty under Section 3(3)(a), 3(3)(b), and 3(3)(c) read with Section 3(1), granted SABMiller 100% penalty immunity, granted UBL 40% reduction, and granted CIPL 20% reduction, alongside penalizing individual directors under Section 48; Appellants preferred appeals under Section 53B before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the absence of a Judicial Member vitiates the final orders passed by the Competition Commission of India under Section 27, whether a leniency applicant under Section 46 can contest cartel liability on merits after admitting anti-competitive conduct, and whether state regulatory control over liquor prices negates an appreciable adverse effect on competition under Section 3.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An enterprise or individual that admits its participation in an unlawful horizontal cartel to secure statutory leniency and a reduction in financial penalties cannot subsequently resile from its confession to challenge the finding of liability on merits before an appellate tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Section 9 of the Competition Act, 2002 do not mandate the presence of a Judicial Member on the Commission, and Section 15 expressly validates proceedings notwithstanding any defect or vacancy; Section 46 and the Lesser Penalty Regulations constitute a sui generis disclosure code where 'vital disclosure' serves as admission of guilt; government price administration in an alcoholic beverage market does not exempt brewers from Section 3 since an 'attempt' to fix prices or exchange commercially sensitive data under Section 2(c) triggers a statutory presumption of AAEC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Presumption of Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC) under Section 3(3); once collusive horizontal agreements and price alignments are established through emails and admissions, the statutory presumption applies and cannot be rebutted by subjective economic consultant reports. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CCI acted strictly in accordance with law in utilizing leniency disclosures and corroborative raid evidence to establish nation-wide cartelization, and the penalties imposed were proportionate, lenient, and legally sound.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 16, 18, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, and 27 of 2021 are dismissed without costs. The orders of the Competition Commission of India dated 24.09.2021 and 04.11.2021 are confirmed in their entirety.
summary: Major domestic beer manufacturers (United Breweries, Carlsberg, AIBA) and their key executives appealed against a CCI order imposing penalties totaling over Rs. 870 Crores for nation-wide cartelization and price-fixing between 2009 and 2018 under Section 3(3) and Section 48 of the Competition Act, 2002. Appellants argued that the lack of a Judicial Member invalidated the order, that state alcohol price regulations negated any anti-competitive impact, and that leniency applications under Section 46 could not be used to establish liability. The NCLAT dismissed all appeals, holding that judicial members are not mandated under Section 8, and parties obtaining leniency cannot resile from admissions on appeal. State price regulation does not shield collusive price coordination from statutory antitrust prohibitions.

case_title: Mr. R. P. Khosla & Anr. vs. Ascot Hotels & Resorts Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 31 of 2022 with Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 32 & 33 of 2022 and Contempt Case (AT) Nos. 05 & 12 of 2019, 08 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: R. P. Khosla and Vineet Khosla (Appellants/Khosla Group); Ascot Hotels & Resorts Ltd. and Vikram Bakshi (Contesting Respondents/Bakshi Group); Montreaux Resorts Pvt. Ltd. / MRL (Subject Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint venture agreement and MoU dated 21.12.2005 and 31.03.2006 to develop a luxury hospitality resort at Kasauli, Himachal Pradesh, involving transfer of 51% equity in MRL to Vikram Bakshi and appointment of nominee directors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate deadlock, contested board meetings dated 11.12.2007 and 18.12.2007 altering shareholding and directorships, and mutual allegations of fraudulent diversion of corporate assets and fabrication of minutes. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 114 of 2007 filed before CLB; Supreme Court ordered status quo on 08.05.2014; fresh CP No. 144 of 2016 filed under Sections 241-242 of Companies Act, 2013; Section 8 arbitration application (CA 553/2020) filed by Bakshi Group on 22.09.2020; NCLT referred parties to arbitration on 31.05.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clause 29 of the Agreement dated 31.03.2006 providing for private commercial arbitration; conflicting board minutes and statutory filings regarding directorships of MRL; interim status quo orders of the CLB and Supreme Court. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Court No. IV allowed Vikram Bakshi's CA 553/2020 on 31.05.2021, referring the oppression and mismanagement petition to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration Act, while NCLT Acting President dismissed Transfer Petition TP 07/2021 and rejected Vineet Khosla's impleadment application (CA 731/2020); appeals were preferred under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether disputes and statutory claims of oppression and mismanagement arising under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 are non-arbitrable, and whether the NCLT erred in referring such statutory company proceedings to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory petitions alleging oppression and mismanagement in a company's affairs involve rights in rem and require statutory remedies exclusively within the domain of specialized company tribunals, rendering such disputes non-arbitrable and incapable of being referred to an arbitral tribunal under commercial arbitration clauses. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 confer plenary and discretionary statutory powers upon the NCLT that cannot be exercised by a private arbitrator; Section 430 explicitly bars the jurisdiction of civil courts over matters determinable by the Tribunal, which implicitly extends to private arbitral tribunals under the doctrine of non-arbitrability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Distinction between rights in rem and rights in personam; while purely contractual rights may be referred to arbitration, petitions seeking corporate governance remedies, alteration of registers, or regulating future corporate affairs under Section 242 cannot be contracted out via arbitration agreements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed a fatal legal error in allowing the Section 8 application and referring the Section 241-242 petition to arbitration; an order allowing a Section 8 application is appealable before the NCLAT under Section 421 of the Companies Act, justifying setting aside the reference.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 32 of 2022 is allowed; the NCLT order dated 31.05.2021 allowing CA No. 553 of 2020 under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is set aside. Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 31 & 33 of 2022 and Contempt Case (AT) Nos. 05/2019, 12/2019, and 08/2021 are dismissed. The NCLT is directed to decide CP No. 144 of 2016 on merits on the existing record within six months, and both parties are restrained from filing further interlocutory applications.
summary: Appellants belonging to the Khosla Group appealed NCLT New Delhi's order dated 31.05.2021 allowing an application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and referring their oppression and mismanagement petition (CP No. 144 of 2016) regarding Montreaux Resorts Pvt. Ltd. to private arbitration. Allowing Company Appeal No. 32 of 2022, the NCLAT held that petitions under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 involve statutory rights in rem and non-arbitrable issues reserved exclusively for company tribunals under Section 430. An appeal against such a reference is maintainable under Section 421 of the Companies Act. The reference to arbitration was set aside, and the NCLT was directed to decide the company petition on merits.

case_title: Startree Retailors Private Limited vs. Mr. Anil Kumar Birla & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 49 of 2021 with I.A. No. 121 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Startree Retailors Private Limited (Appellant/Unsuccessful Bidder); Anil Kumar Birla (Respondent No. 1/Liquidator of Ennore Coke Limited); Linkstar Infosys Private Limited (Respondent No. 2/E-Auction Service Provider); Mahalaxmi Wellman Fuel LLP (Respondent No. 3/Successful Auction Purchaser); Ennore Coke Limited (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Electronic public auction of the liquidation assets (leasehold land, building, plant & machinery, furniture, fixtures, and vehicles at Haldia) of Corporate Debtor Ennore Coke Limited with a reserve price of Rs. 16.20 Crores conducted under Schedule I of IBBI Liquidation Regulations[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation of Ennore Coke Limited under Section 33 of the IBC; disputed auction closing metrics where Appellant placed its 9th bid of Rs. 17.80 Crores at 17:37:33 hrs and Respondent No. 3 submitted the final winning bid of Rs. 17.90 Crores at 17:41:01 hrs[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Expression of Interest and Process Memorandum issued on 24.12.2020; e-auction conducted on 21.01.2021 from 15:00 hrs with auto-extensions until closure at 17:46:00 hrs; sale certificate issued to Respondent No. 3 on 17.02.2021; NCLT Chennai dismissed IA No. 74/2021 on 18.03.2021[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: System-generated audit logs and Bids History Reports establishing continuous session participation of Respondent No. 3 and 20-minute inactivity/logout of Appellant between 17:37:34 and 17:57:59 hrs; admission transcripts proving Appellant simultaneously logged in via multiple browsers and shared its active auction screen on Zoom in breach of auction protocols; screen captures produced by Appellant lacking mandatory certification under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 74/2021 under Section 60(5) of IBC before NCLT Chennai seeking to set aside declaration of Respondent No. 3, declare itself successful bidder, or direct a re-auction to maximize asset value; NCLT dismissed the application on 18.03.2021; Appellant appealed under Section 61 along with IA No. 121 of 2021 to introduce third-party technical reports[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether an electronic auction sale conducted in accordance with IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations can be reopened or set aside at the instance of an unsuccessful bidder offering a higher subsequent price under the guise of asset value maximization when no fraud or material irregularity is proved, and whether uncertified electronic screenshots under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act can substantiate allegations of bid tampering[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A confirmed public auction sale conducted transparently under statutory liquidation regulations cannot be reopened or set aside merely because an unsuccessful bidder subsequently offers a higher amount under the pretext of maximizing asset value, provided no fraud or material irregularity is established[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Schedule I read with Regulation 33 of IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 and Section 35(1)(f) of the IBC vests the liquidator with the duty to conduct public auctions in a time-bound manner; once full sale consideration is remitted, the sale stands completed under Clause 13 of Schedule I and the proceeds must be distributed under the Section 53 waterfall without exposing concluded transactions to unending collateral challenges[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance with Section 65B(4) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; electronic screenshots tendered to substantiate alleged auction portal manipulation are legally inadmissible without a contemporaneous supporting certificate[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The system audit logs established that Appellant remained inactive and logged out for over 20 minutes while Respondent No. 3 placed a valid incremental bid within the auto-extension window; the auction was conducted fairly without fraud, and the issuance of the sale certificate cannot be disturbed[cite: 21].
operative_order: I.A. No. 121 of 2021 seeking to introduce additional evidence is dismissed[cite: 21]. Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 49 of 2021 is dismissed without costs, confirming the order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 18.03.2021[cite: 21]. All connected pending applications are closed[cite: 21].
summary: Startree Retailors, an unsuccessful bidder in the liquidation auction of Ennore Coke Limited, appealed against an NCLT Chennai order confirming the sale of the assets to Mahalaxmi Wellman Fuel LLP for Rs. 17.90 Crores[cite: 21]. The Appellant alleged bid tampering, asserting that its bid of Rs. 17.80 Crores was the highest visible bid before the portal closed, and offered to submit a higher bid to maximize asset value[cite: 21]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that screenshots tendered by the Appellant were inadmissible without Section 65B Evidence Act certification, and audit logs demonstrated the Appellant was logged out and inactive for 20 minutes when the winning bid was placed[cite: 21]. A concluded auction sale cannot be set aside without proof of fraud merely because an unsuccessful bidder offers more money post-auction[cite: 21].

case_title: M/s. Ambadi Investments Limited vs. Ms. Valli Arunachalam & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 54 of 2021 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) Nos. 4 & 6 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ambadi Investments Limited (Appellant in Comp. App. 54/2021/Murugappa Group holding company); Alagappan Arunachalam Murugappan & other directors (Appellants in Comp. App. 4/2022); M.V. Subbiah (Appellant in Comp. App. 6/2022); Ms. Valli Arunachalam and Ms. Vellachi Murugappan (legal heirs of deceased petitioner Mrs. M.V. Valli Murugappan/Respondents No. 1 and 2/M.V. Murugappan branch). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging systemic oppression, prejudice, and mismanagement against minority female branch members holding an 8.21% equity stake in Ambadi Investments Limited, accompanied by an application under Section 244(1)(a) seeking waiver of the statutory 10% shareholding requirement[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory disqualification from filing an oppression petition without waiver under Section 244; procedural disputes concerning stamp paper dates (08.02.2021) versus affidavit execution dates (27.01.2021) in the initial waiver application[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First waiver application (CP/29/CHE/2021) filed on 08.02.2021; second waiver application and fresh petition (CP/95/CHE/2021) filed on 09.08.2021; withdrawal application (MA/79/CHE/2021) filed on 31.08.2021; NCLT Chennai allowed withdrawal and took CP/95/CHE/2021 on record on 29.09.2021[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interlocutory applications alleging perjury and defective verifying affidavits in CP/29/CHE/2021; death of petitioner Mrs. M.V. Valli Murugappan on 21.01.2022 resulting in statutory abatement of criminal/perjury claims under Section 394(2) CrPC; draft petitions establishing that CP/29/CHE/2021 was never formally admitted or numbered under Section 241[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed MA/79/CHE/2021 under Rule 44 read with Rule 11 of NCLT Rules to withdraw defective waiver application CP/29/CHE/2021 and proceed with fresh application CP/95/CHE/2021; NCLT Chennai allowed withdrawal and closed pending ancillary applications on 29.09.2021, prompting company and director appeals under Section 421[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether the withdrawal of a pre-admission waiver application filed under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 is governed by generic withdrawal rules under Rule 44 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 or by the stringent requirements of Rule 82 regarding petitions under Section 241, and whether filing a fresh waiver application prior to formal withdrawal of the first is barred by Order II Rule 2 or Order XXIII Rule 1 of the CPC[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application seeking waiver under Section 244 of the Companies Act is a distinct threshold proceeding and does not constitute an instituted petition in rem under Section 241; consequently, withdrawal of such an application prior to adjudication is governed by Rule 44(2) and inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 rather than Rule 82[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal is guided by principles of natural justice and is not bound by the technicalities of the Code of Civil Procedure; the technical bars of Order II Rule 2 and Order XXIII Rule 1 of the CPC do not apply to summary company proceedings, particularly where a fresh waiver application incorporates subsequent causes of action and is instituted before the earlier defective application is withdrawn[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Stage of hearing; 'hearing' under Rule 44(2) means the judicial application of mind to the merits of the controversy, and where pleadings are incomplete and no hearing on merits has commenced, an applicant possesses the right to withdraw defective threshold applications[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly permitted the withdrawal of CP/29/CHE/2021 and properly took the fresh waiver petition CP/95/CHE/2021 on file for subsequent determination of maintainability and waiver merits[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 54 of 2021, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 4 of 2022, and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 6 of 2022 are dismissed without costs[cite: 22]. The order of the NCLT dated 29.09.2021 is affirmed, and all connected interim applications are closed[cite: 22].
summary: Ambadi Investments Ltd. and its directors appealed an NCLT Chennai order permitting minority shareholders (Valli Arunachalam and family) to withdraw their initial Section 244 waiver application (CP/29/CHE/2021) under Rule 44 and proceed with a fresh waiver application and oppression petition (CP/95/CHE/2021)[cite: 22]. Appellants contended that withdrawal required compliance with Rule 82, was barred by Order II Rule 2 and Order XXIII Rule 1 CPC, and evaded pending perjury applications regarding notarization dates[cite: 22]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that an unadmitted Section 244 waiver application does not constitute a Section 241 petition, making Rule 82 inapplicable[cite: 22]. In addition, Section 424 frees the NCLT from rigid CPC procedural bars, and Rule 44 read with Rule 11 fully empowers the Tribunal to permit withdrawal of defective threshold filings[cite: 22].

case_title: Santanu T. Ray, Resolution Professional Of Zicom SAAS Private Limited vs. Tata Capital Financial Services Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Santanu T. Ray is the Appellant and Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Zicom SAAS Private Limited; Tata Capital Financial Services Limited is Respondent No. 1 (Lessor/Operational Creditor); Central Bank of India, Union Bank of India, and Punjab National Bank are Respondents No. 2, 3, and 4 (Members of CoC); Khemani Distributors and Marketing Limited is Respondent No. 5 (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Master Lease Agreement dated 14.05.2015 executed between CD and R-1 alongside 23 Lease Summary Schedules leasing Honeywell security systems and equipment to CD for periodic lease rentals, with the last lease ending on 30.06.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: R-1 initially filed an operational claim of Rs. 1,05,71,482.26 (Rs. 10,52,940.05 lease rental dues + Rs. 43,54,502.92 fair market value of assets), out of which RP admitted Rs. 95 Lakhs; subsequently, R-1 asserted an enhanced additional claim of Rs. 11.79 Crores on 23.04.2021 (delayed by 256 days), later claiming Rs. 12,49,19,520 in IA 1511 of 2021, of which Rs. 3,14,81,158 was claimed as CIRP costs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 18.03.2020; public announcement on 13.08.2020 setting claim deadline of 25.08.2020; 90-day outer limit expired on 09.11.2020; R-1 filed initial claim as FC on 17.11.2020, revised Form B on 13.01.2021, and lodged an additional claim on 23.04.2021; RP rejected the additional claim via emails dated 26.04.2021 and 21.05.2021; CoC approved the Resolution Plan on 11.06.2021 with 98.85% voting share; RP filed Plan approval application IA No. 1300 of 2021; R-1 filed IA No. 1511 of 2021 on 05.07.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease Summary Schedules confirmed lease tenures expired by 30.06.2020 before the public announcement; equipment had completed its useful economic life; CD derived no rental income from the equipment during CIRP; R-1 raised no invoices for deemed extension rentals as required under Clause 2(g) of the Master Lease Agreement; the claimed sum of Rs. 3,14,81,158 duplicated Rs. 43.54 Lakhs of Fair Market Value already admitted within the Rs. 95 Lakhs claim. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench in IA No. 1511 of 2021 vide order dated 02.09.2021 disallowed Rs. 8.65 Crores pre-CIRP arrears due to the 90-day delay under Regulation 12(2), but erroneously directed the RP, CoC, and SRA to include Rs. 3,14,81,158 as dynamic CIRP costs under Section 5(13)(e) and Regulation 31(b) on the ground that the leased equipment was used during CIRP.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority possessed jurisdiction to unilaterally admit an unverified, belated claim of Rs. 3,14,81,158 as Insolvency Resolution Process Cost without verification by the Resolution Professional or approval and ratification by the Committee of Creditors. 2. Whether an additional claim submitted beyond the mandatory 90-day outer limit under Regulation 12(2) of the CIRP Regulations, and after approval of the Resolution Plan by the CoC, can be entertained and directed to be paid as CIRP cost. 3. Whether lease rentals arising from expired lease agreements, unsupported by invoices and involving equipment from which no revenue was generated during CIRP, can constitute essential supplies or CIRP costs under Section 5(13) read with Regulations 31 and 32.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate upon or compel the inclusion of unverified, unratified commercial or contractual claims as Insolvency Resolution Process costs post-approval of a Resolution Plan by the Committee of Creditors; any belated or enlarged claim that surfaces after plan approval upsets the frozen baseline and violates the clean-slate doctrine. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: CIRP costs under Section 5(13)(e) read with CIRP Regulations 31 and 32 are strictly confined to essential goods and services (electricity, water, telecommunications, and IT services not directly feeding operational output) and costs directly incurred in running the CD as a going concern that are formally ratified by the CoC; Regulation 12(2) operates as an absolute outer temporal limit of 90 days from the insolvency commencement date, leaving no residual or inherent discretion to condone delays in CIRP claim submissions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To qualify as valid CIRP operational or lease expenditure, the claimant must produce contemporaneous invoices mandated by the underlying contract and establish that the leased assets were actively utilized during CIRP to preserve corporate value and generate actual revenue; unbilled claims and duplicate amounts covering fair market values already accounted for cannot be treated as process costs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because R-1's lease had expired, no invoices had been raised, no income was generated during CIRP, and the additional claim of Rs. 11.79 Crores was submitted after an unjustified 256-day delay and after CoC approval of the plan, the NCLT's direction to include Rs. 3,14,81,158 as CIRP cost without RP verification and CoC approval was unsustainable in law.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 951 of 2021 is allowed. The impugned order dated 02.09.2021 passed by the NCLT Mumbai Bench in I.A. No. 1511 of 2021 in C.P. (IB) No. 219 of 2019 is set aside in toto. All pending interlocutory applications and interim orders stand disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Zicom SAAS Private Limited appealed against an NCLT order directing him to include an unverified, belated claim of Rs. 3,14,81,158 from lessor Tata Capital Financial Services Limited as CIRP cost in the approved Resolution Plan[cite: 1]. Tata Capital filed its initial operational claim belatedly, of which Rs. 95 Lakhs was admitted, but subsequently lodged an inflated claim of Rs. 11.79 Crores with a 256-day delay post-plan approval[cite: 1]. NCLAT held that the 90-day deadline under CIRP Regulation 12(2) is non-extendable, and the NCLT cannot bypass RP verification or CoC commercial wisdom to impose unbilled, post-expiry lease damages as CIRP costs[cite: 1]. Consequently, NCLAT set aside the impugned order and allowed the appeal[cite: 1].

case_title: Union Bank of India on behalf of the Committee of Creditors of Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited vs. National Housing Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union Bank of India representing the Committee of Creditors of Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited (DHFL) as Appellant; National Housing Bank (NHB), an apex statutory housing refinance institution, as Respondent No. 1; DHFL (Corporate Debtor/FSP) represented through Administrator R. Subramaniakumar as Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Memorandum of Arrangement dated 27.02.2004 along with subsequent sanction letters executed between DHFL and NHB granting financial assistance and housing refinance facilities against identifiable, earmarked individual housing loan portfolios. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following defaults during 2018-2019, NHB recalled the entire facility and filed Form C for an admitted financial debt of Rs. 2,436.67 Crores (constituting a 2.81% voting share in the CoC), claiming the entire sum as tagged receivables held in statutory trust under Section 16B of the NHB Act. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI superseded DHFL's Board on 20.11.2019 and filed Company Petition No. 4258 of 2019 under FSP Rule 5(a)(i) on 29.11.2019; NCLT admitted CIRP on 03.12.2019; MCA issued Notification S.O. 464(E) on 30.01.2020; NHB filed IA No. 1104 of 2020 with an additional affidavit on 07.08.2020; interim arrangement between NHB and CoC recorded on 03.12.2020 ring-fencing Rs. 2,436,67,20,412; CoC approved Piramal's resolution plan on 15.01.2021 by 93.65% majority; NCLT allowed NHB's application IA 1104 of 2020 and approved the resolution plan via separate orders dated 07.06.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Refinance agreements and sanction letters specifically provided that individual tagged loans disbursed by DHFL were earmarked to NHB and could not be transferred or encumbered without consent; Adverse Balance Certificates submitted semi-annually by DHFL and certified by Statutory Auditors confirmed the tagged loan pool was unencumbered and held in trust; NHB filed Form C expressly reserving its statutory trust rights under Section 16B alongside security interests. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed IA No. 1104 of 2020 on 07.06.2021, declaring that tagged receivables held under Section 16B are deemed third-party assets held in trust, excluded from the moratorium under Section 14 and FSP Rule 10, making the consent terms dated 03.12.2020 absolute; CoC appealed under Section 61 asserting priority conflict under Section 238.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that the National Housing Bank is entitled to enforce its rights under Section 16B of the NHB Act after the commencement of CIRP against a Financial Service Provider. 2. Whether the relationship between DHFL and NHB is solely a debtor-creditor relationship governed by the Code, or whether NHB is a sui generis financial creditor entitled to statutory trust protection over tagged receivables. 3. Whether tagged receivables refinanced by NHB constitute third-party assets held in trust under Rule 10 of the FSP Rules read with MCA Notification S.O. 464(E), thereby falling outside the scope of DHFL's estate, the Section 14 moratorium, and Section 238 of the Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Assets and recoveries held by a Financial Service Provider that are statutorily impressed with a trust for a refinancing developmental institution do not constitute the corporate debtor's property, and the non-obstante clause of Section 238 of the Code cannot override third-party ownership or trust rights over such non-debtor assets. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 16B of the NHB Act creates a mandatory statutory fiction whereby any sums and securities received by a borrowing institution in realization of refinanced loans are received 'in trust' for the NHB to the extent of outstanding accommodation; Rule 10 of the FSP Rules, read with MCA Notification S.O. 464(E), expressly exempts funds and assets required to be held in trust for third parties from the operation of the Section 14 moratorium and CIRP estate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where underlying loan documentation, sanction letters, and auditor-certified Adverse Balance Certificates establish that a pool of receivables was specifically earmarked, tagged, and held unencumbered as statutory trust property, the institution's claim over those earmarked sums is legally substantiated as a third-party asset. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because tagged receivables were impressed with a statutory trust under Section 16B of the NHB Act and excluded from the moratorium under Rule 10 of the FSP Rules, NHB is a sui generis financial creditor entitled to full repayment of its admitted claim of Rs. 2,436.67 Crores from those ring-fenced third-party funds, warranting dismissal of the CoC's appeal.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 461 of 2021 is dismissed. The order of the NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 07.06.2021 in IA No. 1104 of 2020 is affirmed, upholding the absolute operation of the interim arrangement dated 03.12.2020. No order as to costs.
summary: Union Bank of India, representing DHFL's Committee of Creditors, appealed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order declaring tagged loan receivables refinanced by the National Housing Bank to be third-party assets held in trust under Section 16B of the NHB Act[cite: 2]. The CoC argued that NHB was merely a commercial financial creditor whose rights were subsumed under the Code's waterfall priority via Section 238[cite: 2]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that Section 16B creates a statutory trust over refinanced receivables, which are ring-fenced from the Section 14 moratorium under Rule 10 of the FSP Rules and MCA Notification S.O. 464(E)[cite: 2]. Consequently, Section 238 does not extinguish NHB's beneficial ownership over non-debtor assets[cite: 2].

case_title: Sesa Group Employees Provident Fund & Ors. vs. Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 677 of 2021 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 800 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SESA Group Employees Provident Fund, SESA Mining Corporation Ltd. Employees Provident Fund, SESA Resources Ltd. Employees Provident Fund, and BALCO Employees Provident Fund (Appellants/Trusts); Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1); Committee of Creditors of DHFL (Respondent No. 2); Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant/Respondent No. 3); Catalyst Trusteeship Limited (Authorised Representative of NCD holders/Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellants are third-party employee provident fund trusts who, in the exercise of their investment powers under Paragraph 52 of the EPF Scheme, commercially invested trust funds into Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) floated by DHFL. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: SESA Trusts invested approx. Rs. 11 Crores and BALCO Trust invested approx. Rs. 19 Crores in DHFL's NCD issues; under the approved Resolution Plan, the NCD holders were allocated 40.12% of their admitted claims as assenting financial creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against DHFL; CoC approved Piramal's Resolution Plan on 15.01.2021 by a 93.65% majority and the Distribution Mechanism by 86.95%; NCLT approved the plan on 07.06.2021 while directing the CoC to reconsider the distribution for small investors/PF holders; in its 20th meeting on 17.06.2021, the CoC rejected modifications by an 89.19% majority; the plan was fully implemented on 30.09.2021 via reverse merger. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants filed claims in Form C as Financial Creditors through their Authorised Representative Catalyst; within the respective NCD ISIN classes, over 90% voted in favour of the plan; Appellants abstained from voting within their classes; no employer-employee relationship existed between DHFL and the beneficiaries of the Appellants' trusts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the Resolution Plan on 07.06.2021 with a request to reconsider PF distribution; following the CoC's formal rejection on 17.06.2021, the Appellants appealed to NCLAT under Section 61(3) demanding 100% reimbursement under the EPF Act and Section 36(4) of the Code.
legal_issues: 1. Whether third-party Employee Provident Fund Trusts that commercially invested trust funds in the debentures of a corporate debtor are entitled to priority or full repayment of dues under Section 11 of the EPF & MP Act, 1952 or Section 36(4)/Section 155 of the Code. 2. Whether an individual constituent of a class of financial creditors is bound by the vote of the Authorised Representative under Section 25A and estopped from maintaining an independent appeal challenging the approved Resolution Plan and Distribution Mechanism. 3. Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal possesses equitable jurisdiction under Section 61(3) to interfere with or modify the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors regarding fund distribution.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory priority and trust exclusion accorded to provident fund accumulations under social welfare and insolvency legislations protect exclusively the statutory dues owed by an insolvent employer to its own workers, and do not apply to voluntary commercial investments made by external, third-party employee trusts in the corporate debtor's debt securities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 11(2) of the EPF & MP Act, 1952 applies exclusively to contributions owed by an entity in its capacity as an 'employer'; Sections 36(4)(a)(iii) and 155 of the IBC exclude provident fund assets solely from the liquidation estate of the employer-debtor and do not apply during CIRP resolution or to unrelated corporate debenture issuers; under Section 25A(3A), the vote cast by an Authorised Representative reflects the collective will of the class, creating statutory estoppel against individual constituents. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Claimants submitting Form C as debenture holders, who voluntarily invest under portfolio management rules (Paragraph 52 of the EPF Scheme) where losses are contractually absorbed by the fund, rank as ordinary secured financial creditors and cannot claim parity with the debtor company's direct workforce. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because DHFL was not the employer of the trust beneficiaries and the class's Authorised Representative had voted in favour of the Resolution Plan by an overwhelming majority, the commercial wisdom of the CoC in allocating approximately 40% payout cannot be judicially reviewed or modified.
operative_order: Company Appeals CA (AT) (Ins) No. 677 of 2021 and No. 800 of 2021 are dismissed. The approved Resolution Plan and Distribution Mechanism stand confirmed without costs.
summary: Third-party employee provident fund trusts appealed against an NCLT order approving Piramal's resolution plan for DHFL, demanding 100% repayment of their Rs. 30 Crore debenture investments by invoking the EPF & MP Act and Section 36(4) of the IBC[cite: 3]. Dismissing the appeals, NCLAT held that statutory priority and insolvency exclusions apply strictly to dues owed by an insolvent employer to its direct workforce, not to third-party trusts making commercial debenture investments[cite: 3]. Furthermore, the Authorised Representative of the debenture holders had assented to the plan, legally binding all class members and precluding any judicial review of the CoC's commercial wisdom[cite: 3].

case_title: Mr. R. P. Khosla vs. Mr. Vikram Bakshi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. R. P. Khosla is the Appellant (Director and Shareholder of M/s. Montreaux Resorts Pvt. Ltd. / Petitioner No. 6 in CP No. 144 of 2016); Mr. Vikram Bakshi is the Respondent (Director and Principal Shareholder of Ascot Hotels & Resorts Ltd. / Respondent No. 2 in CP No. 144 of 2016). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint venture to develop a tourist resort on land owned by Montreaux Resorts Pvt. Ltd. in Kasauli, Himachal Pradesh, formulated under a Memorandum of Understanding dated 21.12.2005 and an Agreement dated 31.03.2006 transferring 51% shareholding in Montreaux Resorts Pvt. Ltd. to Vikram Bakshi, incorporating an arbitration clause under Clause 29. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; the proceedings arose out of intra-corporate disputes, allegations of deadlocks, invalid board meetings, unauthorized share allotments of 6.58 lakh equity shares, and acts of oppression and mismanagement rather than a monetary loan default metric. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 114 of 2007 initially filed on 13.08.2007 under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956; Company Petition No. 144 of 2016 filed under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013; Respondent filed Company Application No. 553 of 2020 on 22.09.2020 under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; NCLT heard arguments and reserved orders on 26.11.2020; NCLT pronounced its order allowing CA No. 553 of 2020 on 31.05.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement dated 31.03.2006 containing Clause 29 (arbitration mechanism); board minutes dated 30.09.2006, 11.12.2007, and 18.12.2007 concerning appointments of additional directors and cancellation/allotment of equity shares; records of High Court and Supreme Court orders directing the company tribunal to adjudicate the oppression and mismanagement disputes on merits. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench Court No. IV, New Delhi, allowed Company Application No. 553 of 2020 vide order dated 31.05.2021, referring the parties to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 contending that statutory petitions under Sections 241 and 242 are non-arbitrable.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an appeal lies under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 before the NCLAT against an order passed by the NCLT allowing an application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, given that Section 37(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act does not provide for an appeal against an order referring parties to arbitration[cite: 4, 5]. 2. Whether disputes and statutory claims of oppression and mismanagement raised in a company petition filed under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 are arbitrable and capable of being referred to an arbitral tribunal under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996[cite: 4, 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory petitions providing specialized remedies in rem or exclusive statutory powers entrusted to dedicated company tribunals cannot be referred to private arbitral fora under an arbitration agreement, as statutory regimes creating exclusive jurisdiction by necessary implication bar the arbitrability of such disputes[cite: 4, 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 is an overarching statutory appellate provision that entitles any aggrieved person to appeal any order passed by the NCLT to the NCLAT, irrespective of the negative stipulations contained in Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996[cite: 4, 5]; further, Section 242 confers broad statutory powers in rem (such as regulating future corporate conduct, removing directors, or terminating agreements) which cannot be exercised by a private arbitrator[cite: 4, 5], read alongside the explicit jurisdictional bar on civil courts under Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 4, 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an action is founded on statutory rights under Sections 241 and 242 seeking relief against oppression and mismanagement and invoking powers reserved exclusively to public tribunals as a matter of public policy, the dispute is non-arbitrable by necessary implication notwithstanding the presence of an arbitration clause in underlying contractual agreements[cite: 4, 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Oppression and mismanagement proceedings under Sections 241 and 242 are non-arbitrable; hence, the NCLT committed a fatal legal error in allowing the Section 8 application and staying the company petition, rendering the order dated 31.05.2021 unsustainable in law[cite: 4, 5].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 32 of 2022 is allowed[cite: 4, 5]. The NCLT's order dated 31.05.2021 allowing Company Application No. 553 of 2020 under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is set aside[cite: 4, 5]. The NCLT is directed to decide Company Petition No. 144 of 2016 on merits expeditiously, preferably within six months, on the basis of materials already on record[cite: 4, 5]. Both parties are restrained from filing any further Company Applications, Interlocutory Applications, or affidavits in CP No. 144 of 2016[cite: 4, 5].
summary: An appeal was preferred under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 against an order of the NCLT New Delhi Bench allowing an application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and referring oppression and mismanagement proceedings under Sections 241 and 242 to arbitration[cite: 4, 5]. Setting aside the NCLT order, the NCLAT held that appeals under Section 421 are maintainable against NCLT orders referring parties to arbitration[cite: 4, 5]. The Appellate Tribunal ruled that oppression and mismanagement claims involve statutory remedies and orders in rem under Section 242 that lie within the exclusive jurisdiction of the NCLT via Section 430, rendering such disputes non-arbitrable by necessary implication[cite: 4, 5].

case_title: Mr. Satyan Kasturi vs. State Bank Of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Satyan Kasturi is the Appellant (Personal Guarantor to the Corporate Debtor and an Australian citizen); State Bank of India is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor); M/s. PPS Enviro Power Private Limited is Respondent No. 2 (Corporate Debtor / Principal Borrower); Mr. PVB Sudhakara Rao is Respondent No. 3 (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities comprising Term Loans, Cash Credit, Corporate Loans, Letters of Credit, and Bank Guarantees totaling Rs. 225.94 Crores sanctioned and disbursed by State Bank of Hyderabad/State Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor, secured inter alia by a Personal Guarantee Deed for an overall limit of Rs. 149.35 Crores executed by the Appellant on 13.05.2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default amount of Rs. 237,94,44,380.77 as on 06.12.2017 plus contractual interest and costs; loan account of the Corporate Debtor was classified as Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 26.12.2015, and the debt was formally recalled as due on 18.10.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan recall legal notice issued on 11.10.2017 demanding payment within 7 days; CIRP initiated against the Corporate Debtor on 13.08.2019 in CP (IB) No. 407/2018; Section 95 statutory demand notice in Form B issued by SBI on 23.09.2020 and served on the Appellant on 06.10.2020; Section 95 petition filed on 16.10.2020; interim moratorium imposed on 28.07.2021; RP filed recommendation report under Section 99 on 15.08.2021; NCLT admitted the petition on 20.06.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Guarantee Deed for Overall Limit dated 13.05.2014 executed by the Appellant indicating an Indian residential address at West Mambalam, Chennai, with Clause 20 establishing service terms; Revival Letter dated 10.08.2016 executed by the Appellant acknowledging continuing liability; loan sanction letters, disbursement schedules across ten loan accounts, and certified bank statements of accounts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bench-I Hyderabad admitted SBI's application CP(IB) No. 401/95 of IBC/HDB/2020 vide order dated 20.06.2022, initiating the personal insolvency resolution process against the Appellant; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61 contending that foreign nationality invalidated the guarantee under FEMA Regulation 3A and that the claim was barred by limitation from the 2015 NPA date.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the personal guarantee executed by a foreign national/Australian citizen in respect of a rupee-denominated debt of an Indian corporate debtor is void ab initio under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 read with Regulation 3A of the FEMA (Guarantees) Regulations, 2000[cite: 6]. 2. Whether an insolvency petition under Section 95 of the Code against a personal guarantor is barred by limitation when the corporate debtor's account was classified as an NPA more than three years prior to filing, but the guarantee was recalled and liability acknowledged through a revival letter within three years[cite: 6]. 3. Whether the NCLT within whose territorial jurisdiction the registered office of the corporate debtor is situated has jurisdiction under Section 60(1) and 60(2) to initiate insolvency resolution against a personal guarantor regardless of his foreign citizenship or overseas residence[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual who executes a personal guarantee for a corporate debtor's debt cannot evade co-extensive insolvency liability under Section 95 of the Code by asserting foreign citizenship or residential status; the non-obstante provisions of the Code override peripheral regulatory statutes, and personal guarantees remain enforceable under Section 60[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(1) and 60(2) vest jurisdiction in the NCLT having territorial jurisdiction over the corporate debtor's registered office to adjudicate insolvency proceedings of its personal guarantor, irrespective of where the guarantor resides or his nationality[cite: 6]; under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, the guarantor's liability is co-extensive and triggered by the guarantee contract terms[cite: 6]; under Article 115 and 137 of the Limitation Act, limitation against a guarantor begins when the guarantee is invoked or recalled, not necessarily on the debtor's NPA date[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The execution of a formal revival letter acknowledging liability within three years of the guarantee, combined with the issuance and service of a formal loan recall notice and statutory demand under Section 95, establishes a subsisting, legally enforceable debt and default within the statutory limitation period[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the guarantee deed contained a specific demand clause, the debt was acknowledged via a revival letter on 10.08.2016, recalled on 11.10.2017, and the statutory demand notice was duly served in October 2020, the Section 95 application filed in 2020 was well within limitation and lawfully admitted[cite: 6].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 239 of 2022 is dismissed[cite: 6]. The admission order dated 20.06.2022 passed by the NCLT Bench-I Hyderabad in CP(IB) No. 401/95 of IBC/HDB/2020 is affirmed[cite: 6]. Connected pending interlocutory applications I.A. No. 512 of 2022 and I.A. No. 513 of 2022 are closed with no order as to costs[cite: 6].
summary: An Australian national appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order admitting a Section 95 insolvency application filed by the State Bank of India against him as personal guarantor to corporate debtor M/s. PPS Enviro Power Private Limited for defaults exceeding Rs. 237 Crores[cite: 6]. The guarantor argued that his foreign citizenship rendered the guarantee void under FEMA Regulation 3A and that the claim was barred by limitation running from the corporate debtor's 2015 NPA date[cite: 6]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under Section 60 of the IBC, jurisdiction depends on the corporate debtor's registered office rather than the guarantor's nationality or residence[cite: 6]. Furthermore, because the guarantee was invoked via a recall notice in 2017 following an acknowledgment of debt in 2016, the petition was filed well within the three-year limitation period[cite: 6].

case_title: IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited & Anr. vs. Abhinav Mukherji & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 356 of 2022 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 358 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited (Appellant/Debenture Trustee); ECL Finance Limited and Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprises Ltd. (Appellants/Debenture Holders/Assignees); Abhinav Mukherji (Respondent No. 1/Homebuyer with 4.43% voting share); Krit Narayan Mishra (Respondent No. 2/Resolution Professional of Palm Developers Pvt. Ltd. replacing erstwhile IRP Manoj Kumar Singh); Palm Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Corporate Guarantor); Saha Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (Principal Borrower / Debenture Issuer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debenture Trust Deed dated 01.07.2016 whereby Saha Infratech issued 110 NCDs of face value Rs. 1 Crore each (aggregating Rs. 110 Crores) subscribed by ECL Finance, secured by an irrevocable Corporate Guarantee dated 02.07.2016 executed by the Corporate Debtor, Demand Promissory Note, Mortgage Agreement over 'Project Encore', and a Revenue Escrow Agreement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim submitted in Form C on 10.02.2020 for Rs. 1,26,96,88,698/- against principal and interest due as of 27.01.2020; overdue default letter previously issued to the Principal Borrower on 03.02.2020 for Rs. 9,16,66,666/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against the Corporate Debtor on 27.01.2020; public announcement on 31.01.2020; Appellants filed Form C on 10.02.2020; IRP constituted CoC on 20.02.2020 admitting Appellants with ~88% voting share; Respondent No. 1 filed IA No. 1610/2020 on 25.02.2020; Appellants issued formal debenture redemption recall notice on 25.03.2020; Corporate Guarantee invoked on 07.04.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Guarantee had not been invoked prior to CIRP commencement or prior to filing Form C; Articles of Association (AoA) of the Corporate Debtor (Clauses 4.1, 5.4, 7.1, 7.2) and Facility Agreement (Clause 6.8) showed that Part II overrode Part I, granting Debenture Holders absolute control over the composition of the Board, deadlock-breaking powers, management appointments/removals, project escrow bank accounts, and power of attorney to execute customer sale deeds; Forensic Audit Report revealed that the Corporate Debtor was used as a conduit to siphon and round-trip Rs. 28 Crores to related entities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II allowed IA No. 1610/2020 on 14.03.2022, holding that Appellants are not financial creditors under Section 5(7) due to lack of direct disbursal, that post-CIRP guarantee invocation was barred by Section 14, and that Appellants were related parties under Section 5(24) disqualified from the CoC under Section 21(2); Appellants appealed under Section 61(1).
legal_issues: 1. Whether an individual allottee/homebuyer has locus standi to challenge the admission of a creditor's claim and the constitution of the CoC without acting exclusively through the Authorised Representative[cite: 7]. 2. Whether a claim arising out of a corporate guarantee can be admitted as a matured financial debt in the CIRP of the corporate guarantor when the guarantee was never invoked prior to the insolvency commencement date or prior to filing the claim[cite: 7]. 3. Whether extensive contractual and governance veto powers over the board, policy decisions, management personnel, and revenue escrow accounts render a lender/debenture trustee a 'related party' under Section 5(24) of the Code, thereby disqualifying it from CoC membership under Section 21(2)[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual financial creditor in a class retains independent locus standi to challenge before the adjudicating authority the illegal admission of claims or improper constitution of the Committee of Creditors; the mandate of an Authorised Representative under Section 21(6A) is strictly confined to attending meetings and casting votes within the CoC[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A claim against a corporate guarantor does not ripen into a matured 'debt due and payable' under Section 3(11) and 3(12) unless the guarantee is validly invoked prior to the insolvency commencement date; invoking a guarantee after the insolvency commencement date is barred by the statutory moratorium under Section 14[cite: 7]; under Section 5(24)(l) and (m), 'control' denotes positive de facto or de jure authority to govern corporate policy, board composition, and financial affairs, irrespective of whether nominee powers were formally exercised[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: When constitutional documents (AoA), sanction letters, and irrevocable powers of attorney vest a debenture trustee with the final authority on deadlocks, budget approvals, and absolute control over revenue escrow accounts to the total exclusion of the corporate debtor's directors, positive control is established on the record[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the corporate guarantee remained uninvoked on the CIRP date and the Appellants exercised pervasive positive control over the debtor company's affairs, the Appellants were rightly classified as related parties excluded from the CoC under Section 21(2) of the Code[cite: 7].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 356 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 358 of 2022 are dismissed[cite: 7]. The order dated 14.03.2022 passed by the NCLT New Delhi Bench-II in IA No. 1610/2020 directing the RP to exclude the Appellants from the CoC and revise their claims is affirmed[cite: 7]. IA No. 1118 of 2022 is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: IDBI Trusteeship Services and ECL Finance appealed an NCLT New Delhi order disqualifying them as financial creditors and excluding them from the CoC of Corporate Debtor Palm Developers Pvt. Ltd. as related parties upon an application by an individual homebuyer[cite: 7]. The NCLAT affirmed the homebuyer's independent standing to challenge CoC membership outside the Authorised Representative[cite: 7]. On merits, the Appellate Tribunal held that an uninvoked corporate guarantee cannot constitute a matured claim, and post-CIRP invocation is impermissible under Section 14 moratorium[cite: 7]. Furthermore, extensive governance rights and control over debtor bank accounts under the Articles of Association constituted positive control under Section 5(24), lawfully barring Appellants from the CoC under Section 21(2)[cite: 7].

case_title: Ariisto Alert Residents Association vs. M/s. Prestige Estates Projects Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ariisto Alert Residents Association (Appellant/registered association of 102 homebuyers in 'Celestia/Fantasia' projects); M/s. Prestige Estates Projects Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Successful Resolution Applicant); Mr. Jayesh Sangrajhka (Respondent No. 2/Resolution Professional); Dipco Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 3/Original Petitioning Operational Creditor); Corporate Debtor is Ariisto Developers Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of residential apartments in proposed high-rise towers 'Fantasia' and 'Celestia' located at Sector-III, CTS No. 19/1-13 ('Ariisto Heaven'), Mulund (West), Mumbai, booked by homebuyers between 2005 and 2006. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total admitted claims against Corporate Debtor were Rs. 2,485 Crores (secured creditors holding over Rs. 1,365 Crores); liquidation value was Rs. 750 Crores; total financial outlay under the approved Resolution Plan was Rs. 1,650 Crores; homebuyers had an 8.5% aggregate voting share in the CoC. 4.
