STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 20.11.2018; Resolution Plan submitted on 24.10.2019; CoC approved the Plan on 13.11.2019 by an 85.48% majority (subsequently rising to 90.68%); NCLT heard MA 4061 of 2019 and reserved orders on 27.10.2020; NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the Resolution Plan and disposed of MA 4061 of 2019 on 23.03.2021; plan was implemented for 1.5 years with Rs. 742 Crores spent on creditor payouts, premiums, and construction. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Authorised representative of homebuyers voted against the Resolution Plan at the CoC meeting; through post-approval outreach, 151 Siesta buyers and 46 Celestia buyers consented to the plan, leaving Appellant representing a minority of 102 buyers (~20% of buyers, under 1% total CoC share); Resolution Applicant adjusted the project layout by shifting Celestia buyers to an adjacent sector three times the size and levied an additional construction escalation rate of Rs. 3,300 per sq. ft. against market values of Rs. 24,000 per sq. ft. carpet area; Appellant simultaneously filed NCLT Application No. 1587 of 2022 seeking implementation of the same plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the Resolution Plan in MA 3714/2019 and disposed of Appellant's objections in MA 4061 of 2019 on 23.03.2021 noting that grievances had been settled; Appellant appealed under Section 61(3) alleging denial of natural justice, breach of RERA, and impermissible post-approval plan modifications.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the approved Resolution Plan was vitiated by a breach of the principles of natural justice and false representations regarding settlement of homebuyer grievances[cite: 8]. 2. Whether an association representing a dissenting minority of homebuyers within a class can challenge the commercial wisdom of the CoC regarding project modifications, relocation of plots, and construction cost escalations under Section 61(3)[cite: 8]. 3. Whether the doctrine of election (approbate and reprobate) estops a creditor from challenging the legality of a resolution plan when it has concurrently applied for its execution and implementation[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Commercial terms concerning architectural alterations, plot relocations, and cost adjustments in real estate insolvency resolution fall squarely within the non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors, and a dissenting minority within a class of creditors cannot upset a plan that accords them rights superior to their statutory liquidation entitlements[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) mandates that dissenting financial creditors are entitled only to the liquidation value of their claims (which was nil for unsecured creditors in this case)[cite: 8]; the Code overrides conflicting provisions of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016[cite: 8]; under Section 61(3), judicial review of an approved resolution plan is strictly confined to statutory non-compliances and cannot be expanded to enforce subjective equitable expectations[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an overwhelming majority of the CoC (90.68%) and over 80% of homebuyers support the plan, and the appellant association concurrently files applications seeking implementation of the selfsame plan, the doctrine of election precludes the appellant from blowing hot and cold to assail its validity[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no error in approving the resolution plan, as all statutory requirements under Section 30(2) were complied with and the commercial wisdom of the CoC cannot be disturbed on equitable grounds, warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 355 of 2021 is dismissed[cite: 8]. The approval of the Resolution Plan by the NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 23.03.2021 is affirmed[cite: 8]. All interim orders stand vacated with no order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: An association representing a minority group of homebuyers challenged an NCLT Mumbai Bench order approving Prestige Estates Projects Limited's resolution plan for Ariisto Developers Pvt. Ltd., alleging denial of natural justice, breach of RERA, relocation of their allotted project plot, and increased construction levies[cite: 8]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT held that technical real estate adjustments and financial terms fall within the unassailable commercial wisdom of the CoC, which approved the plan by a 90.68% majority[cite: 8]. Because dissenting creditors were entitled only to nil liquidation value under Section 30(2)(b), and the appellant had simultaneously sought implementation of the plan, the challenge was legally untenable[cite: 8].

case_title: Darshan Gandhi vs. USV Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Darshan Gandhi is the Appellant (Ex-Director of Lok Housing and Constructions Ltd.); USV Private Limited is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor / Decree Holder); Lok Housing and Constructions Ltd. is Respondent No. 2 (Corporate Debtor) represented by IRP Hemant J. Mehta. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In July 1996, Vipal Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. (VHPL) placed two Intercorporate Deposits of Rs. 25 Lakhs each (totaling Rs. 50 Lakhs) with the Corporate Debtor under a Short-Term Finance Refund Plan; on 10.02.1998, a Tripartite Arrangement was entered into whereby Respondent No. 1 lent Rs. 53,31,170/- to the Corporate Debtor by two cheques to enable the Corporate Debtor to discharge its debt to VHPL. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim of Rs. 52.07 Lakhs; on 17.11.2017/19.12.2017, the City Civil Court at Mumbai decreed Summary Suit No. 7306/2001 in favor of USV for Rs. 52.07 Lakhs with interest at 9% per annum from the date of the suit until realization; loan account originally turned NPA on 26.12.2002. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor made part payment of Rs. 1,23,767/- on 15.04.1998 (inclusive of Rs. 15,972/- interest); debtor acknowledged debt via letter dated 19.06.1998; summary suit instituted in 2001; relief undertaking protection applied from 01.04.2002 to 25.04.2014; fresh summons for judgment taken on 18.02.2017; decree passed on 19.12.2017; Section 7 petition filed on 29.10.2018; right to file reply forfeited on 01.05.2019 after default on multiple settlement adjournments; NCLT admitted Section 7 application on 03.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tripartite agreement dated 10.02.1998; part-payment letter dated 15.04.1998 showing interest payment; audited Balance Sheets of the Corporate Debtor acknowledging the debt continuously from 01.04.2003 through 31.03.2015; independent Chartered Accountant certificate from M/s. IP Mehta & Co.; final unappealed money decree dated 19.12.2017 in Summary Suit No. 7306/2001. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench in C.P. (IB) No. 4135/I&B/MB/2018 admitted the Section 7 petition on 03.06.2019, holding that the debt constituted a financial debt and default was established; Appellant challenged admission under Section 61 asserting limitation, absence of written contract, and impermissible execution of a civil decree.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an unsatisfied civil money decree arising out of commercial financial assistance constitutes a 'financial debt' enabling the decree holder to initiate CIRP under Section 7 of the Code[cite: 9]. 2. Whether the absence of a formal written loan agreement negates the existence of a 'financial debt' when the transaction's commercial nature and consideration for time value of money are established by correspondence and part-payments[cite: 9]. 3. Whether a Section 7 application filed within three years of the passing of a money decree and supported by balance sheet acknowledgments is barred by limitation when the original loan account had become an NPA more than three years prior[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsatisfied final money decree or judgment passed by a competent civil court or tribunal in respect of a commercial loan constitutes a valid financial debt under the Code, providing a fresh cause of action and limitation period to initiate insolvency proceedings under Section 7[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(10) defines a 'creditor' to expressly include a decree-holder, Section 3(11) defines 'debt' as liability in respect of a claim, and Section 3(6) defines 'claim' to include a right to payment whether or not reduced to judgment[cite: 9]; a written contract is not an indispensable prerequisite to prove a financial debt under Section 5(8) if contemporaneous evidence and conduct establish borrowing against time value of money[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The entry of debt in audited balance sheets constitutes a valid acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 9]; furthermore, under the rule in Dena Bank, the passing of a final money decree gives rise to a fresh limitation period of three years under Article 137 from the date of the decree[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the debt originated from an intercorporate tripartite loan, interest had been paid, the debt was acknowledged in audited balance sheets until 2015, and a final money decree was passed on 19.12.2017, the Section 7 application filed on 29.10.2018 was well within limitation and lawfully admitted[cite: 9].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 644 of 2019 is dismissed[cite: 9]. The admission order dated 03.06.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in C.P. (IB) No. 4135/I&B/MB/2018 is affirmed[cite: 9]. All intervention applications (I.A. Nos. 2106, 2660, 4316, 2609 & 2614 of 2019) are disposed of with liberty to the applicants to submit their claims before the Resolution Professional in accordance with law[cite: 9].
summary: The ex-director of Corporate Debtor Lok Housing and Constructions Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by USV Private Limited based on an unsatisfied 2017 civil money decree for Rs. 52.07 Lakhs[cite: 9]. The appellant contended that a decree holder cannot initiate CIRP as a financial creditor, that there was no written agreement showing consideration for time value of money, and that the claim was time-barred since the account became an NPA in 2002[cite: 9]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that an unsatisfied money decree constitutes an enforceable financial debt giving rise to a fresh limitation period, and continuous acknowledgments in audited balance sheets extended the limitation period under Section 18[cite: 9].

case_title: Dr. Periasamy Palani Gounder vs. Mr. Radhakrishnan Dharmarajan & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. Periasamy Palani Gounder (Appellant in Appeals 164 & 219/Promoter & Erstwhile Director of Corporate Debtor Appu Hotels Limited); Dharani Finance Limited (Appellant in Appeal 176/Related Party Unsecured Creditor); Dr. V. Janakiraman (Appellant in Appeal 218/NRI Shareholder); Mr. Radhakrishnan Dharmarajan (Respondent No. 1/Resolution Professional); Mr. M.K. Rajagopalan (Respondent No. 2/Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor operated landmark hotel properties ('Le Meridien' in Chennai and Coimbatore) financed through bank consortium loans led by Indian Bank, with additional financial assistance from Tourism Finance Corporation of India Ltd. (TFCIL). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: TFCIL initiated Section 7 proceedings on default; Corporate Debtor had total financial debt of ~Rs. 390 Crores and operational debt of Rs. 8.52 Crores; Resolution Plan submitted by R-2 offered Rs. 423 Crores against an earlier valuation of Rs. 1,600 Crores; plan provided nil payment to related party financial and operational creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition admitted on 05.05.2020; public announcement on 08.05.2020; first CoC meeting held on 22.06.2020 on 4 days' notice; Form G published in newspapers on 17.08.2020 but never posted on Corporate Debtor's or IBBI's websites; Promoter submitted Section 12A settlement proposal backed by Deutsche Bank term sheet for Rs. 350 Crores on 21.01.2021; 9th CoC meeting held on 22.01.2021 where plan was sent back to RA for revision; revised plan prepared on 25.01.2021 and submitted directly to NCLT on 04.02.2021 without CoC approval; NCLT approved plan on 15.07.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: R-2 was founder and Managing Trustee of Sri Balaji Vidyapeeth, a charitable trust disqualified as an ineligible PRA, yet R-2 used its financials to bolster his own bid; R-2 was Director of International Aviation Academy Pvt. Ltd., which held Rs. 12,03,000/- as unrefunded share application money, attracting deposit default disqualification under Section 164(2)(b); RP's valuers were Delhi-based, conducted no physical verification of assets, and failed to value non-core assets; 9th CoC minutes dated 22.01.2021 showed the plan was sent back for revision to comply with Section 30(2) and was never re-voted upon. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench approved R-2's resolution plan in IA/150/CHE/2021 and dismissed promoter's MA/13/CHE/2021 and related party applications vide common order dated 15.07.2021; Appellants appealed under Section 61(3) alleging gross procedural illegalities, statutory disqualification under Section 29A(e), and unapproved plan submission.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the submission of a revised resolution plan directly to the Adjudicating Authority without placing it before the Committee of Creditors for final voting and approval contravenes Section 30(2), 30(4), and 31(1) of the Code, rendering the plan void ab initio[cite: 10]. 2. Whether the non-publication of Form G on the designated IBBI website and Corporate Debtor's website under Regulation 36A(2) constitutes a material irregularity vitiating the CIRP[cite: 10]. 3. Whether a resolution applicant is disqualified under Section 29A(e) of the IBC read with Section 164(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 and Section 88 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882[cite: 10]. 4. Whether a resolution plan can completely discriminate against and allocate nil value to related party financial and operational creditors while paying unrelated creditors of the same class[cite: 10]. 5. Whether the RP is legally obligated to place a Section 12A withdrawal and one-time settlement proposal before the CoC for consideration and voting[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan that is revised after being considered by the CoC cannot be filed directly before the Adjudicating Authority for approval under Section 31 without being re-tabled, voted upon, and formally approved by the requisite statutory majority of the CoC[cite: 10]; furthermore, related party creditors cannot be subjected to hostile discrimination under a resolution plan solely on the basis of their related party status[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Statutory provisions regulating CIRP practice and procedure are mandatory and cannot be diluted as merely directory[cite: 10]; Section 30(2), 30(4), and 31(1) mandate strict sequence: a plan must be examined by the RP, approved by the CoC by 66%, and only then presented to the NCLT[cite: 10]; the IBC excludes related parties only from the CoC (Section 21) and from acting as resolution applicants (Section 29A), but does not treat them as a separate sub-class for distribution of payments[cite: 10]; Section 164(2)(b) disqualifies directors of companies holding unpaid deposits, triggering Section 29A(e) ineligibility[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical verification of assets by registered valuers under Regulation 35(1)(a) and valuation of non-core assets are indispensable prerequisites to provide reliable data for the CoC's commercial wisdom; naked numbers without valuation reports do not satisfy statutory scrutiny[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan was void ab initio because the revised plan dated 25.01.2021 was never placed before the CoC, Form G was improperly published, the resolution applicant suffered from statutory disqualifications, related parties were unlawfully denied payments, and the Section 12A proposal was improperly withheld from CoC voting[cite: 10].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (CH) (Ins.) Nos. 164, 176, 218 & 219 of 2021 are allowed[cite: 10]. The common order of the NCLT Chennai Bench dated 15.07.2021 approving the Resolution Plan is set aside[cite: 10]. The RP is directed to proceed with CIRP afresh from the publication stage of Form G on the designated websites[cite: 10]. The RP is directed to convene a CoC meeting within 15 days to place the Promoter's Section 12A settlement proposal for voting[cite: 10]. It is declared that claims of related party creditors cannot be discriminated against[cite: 10]. Time spent in appeal is excluded from the CIRP period, with no order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary: Appeals were preferred by the promoter, an NRI shareholder, and a related party creditor challenging an NCLT Chennai order approving a Rs. 423 Crore resolution plan submitted by M.K. Rajagopalan for Appu Hotels Limited[cite: 10]. Setting aside the approval, NCLAT held that the revised resolution plan was void ab initio as it was never placed before the CoC for final approval post-revision, Form G was not published on the IBBI website, valuers failed to physically inspect assets, and the successful bidder was disqualified under Section 29A(e)[cite: 10]. Furthermore, NCLAT held that related party creditors cannot be given discriminatory nil treatment, and the RP was directed to table the promoter's Section 12A settlement offer before the CoC[cite: 10].

case_title: Gautam R. Padival & Ors. vs. Karnataka Theatres Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: TA No. 186 of 2021 (Company Appeal (AT) No. 261 of 2019)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gautam R. Padival & Ors. are Appellants (Minority Shareholders holding 1407 equity shares in R-1); Karnataka Theatres Ltd. is Respondent No. 1 (Unlisted Public Company incorporated in 1945); Respondents No. 2 to 9 are Directors/Promoters of R-1; Respondents No. 10 to 53 are Allottees of the disputed shares; Respondent No. 54 is Charisma Builders represented by Sudhir V. Shetty (Joint Developer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of 984 dormant unsubscribed equity shares (out of 6000 issued shares) at Rs. 2,000/- per share (face value Rs. 100/- plus Rs. 1,900/- premium) via Board resolution dated 07.03.2007; execution of a Joint Development Agreement with R-54 to demolish Jyothi Theatre at TS No. 168, Mangalore, and develop a multi-facility commercial complex approved at the 61st AGM on 08.06.2007 (with R-1 retaining 50% built-up area) and modified at the 62nd AGM on 27.08.2008 (reducing R-1's share to 40%). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Undervaluation and dilution dispute; 984 shares allotted at Rs. 2,000/- per share based on a CA valuation of Rs. 1,313/- that excluded the company's prime real estate, whereas appellants asserted shares were worth over Rs. 30,000/- to Rs. 50,000/- each; JDA terms altered from 50% to 40% built-up area without cash consideration or proper due diligence. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board resolution passed on 07.03.2007; 61st AGM held on 08.06.2007; ROC enquiry report submitted on 07.05.2008/16.05.2008 confirming violation of Section 81; EGM held on 11.02.2008; 62nd AGM held on 27.08.2008; Joint Development Agreement signed on 23.09.2009; Company Petition CP No. 71/2010 filed before CLB Chennai on 08.08.2010. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: List of allottees showing 394 shares went to existing members and 590 shares to 23 new persons, predominantly relatives, daughters of the developer (R-46 and R-47), and acquaintances of interested directors who voted on the resolution; explanatory statement under Section 173 for 61st and 62nd AGMs contained no architectural designs, financial estimates, FAR calculations, or real estate valuation reports; earnest money of Rs. 2 Lakhs accepted from R-54 prior to holding the 61st AGM. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench in C.P. No. 71/2010 (TP No. 24 of 2016) dismissed the petition on 25.06.2019, holding that the 984 shares were not a rights issue and that directors were authorized under Article 4 of the AoA to dispose of them; Appellants appealed to NCLAT under Section 421 alleging oppression and mismanagement.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the allotment of 984 unsubscribed dormant shares after six decades to selected directors, their relatives, and business associates without offering them proportionately to existing shareholders or passing a special resolution violated Section 81(1) and 81(1A) of the Companies Act, 1956 and constituted oppression and mismanagement[cite: 11]. 2. Whether the participation and voting of interested directors in the board meeting approving share allotments to their relatives and acquaintances vitiated the resolution under Section 300 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 11]. 3. Whether passing resolutions to enter into and alter a Joint Development Agreement disposing of the company's sole asset without proper real estate valuation, project reports, or adequate disclosures in the explanatory statement under Section 173 constitutes mismanagement and oppression of minority shareholders[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The allotment of dormant unsubscribed shares to increase subscribed capital constitutes a further issue of capital that must strictly comply with pre-emptive statutory safeguards; directors act in a fiduciary capacity as trustees for all shareholders and cannot exercise allotment powers for nepotism, personal aggrandizement, or altering voting control[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 81 applies to any proposal to increase subscribed capital by further allotment, obligating the company to offer such shares pro rata to existing equity holders under Section 81(1)(a) or obtain approval via special resolution under Section 81(1A)[cite: 11]; private power in the Articles of Association (Article 4) is subordinated to statutory mandates; under Section 300(1), directors interested directly or indirectly in an allotment arrangement are prohibited from participating or voting, rendering interested votes void[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where share valuation completely omits the value of the company's primary real estate asset, allottee rosters demonstrate selective familial ties, and explanatory statements accompanying general body notices lack foundational project metrics, the transactions breach fiduciary standards and establish oppression and mismanagement under the Needle Industries doctrine[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The allotment of 984 shares violated Sections 81 and 300 of the 1956 Act, and the execution of the JDA without fresh land valuation constituted gross mismanagement; while historic operational corporate acts are preserved, the 984 shares are declared void prospectively from the judgment date and a fresh valuation and JDA are required[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 261 of 2019 (TA No. 186 of 2021) is allowed and the NCLT Bengaluru Bench order dated 25.06.2019 is set aside[cite: 11]. The allotment of 984 shares is declared null and void from the date of this judgment, with liberty to R-1 to allot them afresh under the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 11]. R-1 is directed to obtain a fresh current valuation of the land and execute a fresh Joint Development Agreement based on revised terms approved by the Board and General Body within three months[cite: 11]. No order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary: Minority shareholders appealed an NCLT Bengaluru order dismissing their petition alleging oppression and mismanagement against Karnataka Theatres Ltd. regarding the allotment of 984 dormant unsubscribed shares and the execution of a Joint Development Agreement for the company's sole cinema property[cite: 11]. Setting aside the dismissal, NCLAT held that allotting 70-year dormant shares to selected relatives of directors and the builder's family violated Section 81(1) and Section 300 of the Companies Act, 1956 and breached fiduciary obligations[cite: 11]. The Appellate Tribunal declared the allotment of 984 shares void prospectively from the date of the judgment and directed a fresh independent land valuation and a newly negotiated JDA within three months[cite: 11].

case_title: Poonam Kachalia & Ors. vs. CA Kannan Tiruvengadam & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Poonam Kachalia & Ors. are Appellants (Operational Creditors of Hari Machines Ltd.); CA Kannan Tiruvengadam is Respondent No. 1 (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Hari Machines Ltd.); Bank of Baroda, State Bank of India, Union Bank of India, UCO Bank, and Axis Bank are Respondents No. 2 to 6 (Consortium of Banks / Financial Creditors); Pro-Minerals Private Limited (PMPL) is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned to PMPL by Respondent Banks, secured inter alia by three Deeds of Guarantee dated 31.03.2011 executed by Hari Machines Ltd. alongside seven other co-guarantors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by PMPL leading to an outstanding accrued liability of Rs. 2,69,51,45,209/-; in PMPL's CIRP, the consortium received Rs. 37,02,26,590/- under an approved resolution plan submitted by Essel Mining & Industries Ltd., leaving an unpaid balance claim of Rs. 399.1 Crores lodged by the Consortium and admitted by the Liquidator in the liquidation of Hari Machines Ltd. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation of Hari Machines Ltd. commenced on 16.11.2018; CIRP of PMPL commenced on 22.02.2019; NCLT Kolkata approved PMPL's resolution plan on 22.02.2019; Consortium lodged Form D claim with Liquidator; Liquidator admitted claim of Rs. 399.1 Crores; Appellants filed IA (IB) No. 39/CTB/2019 before NCLT Cuttack; NCLT dismissed the application on 24.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Guarantee Deeds dated 31.03.2011; Clause 2.9.5 and Clause 2.9.6 of PMPL's approved Resolution Plan explicitly stipulating that full and final settlement of PMPL's debts was without prejudice to the Financial Creditors' rights to proceed against corporate and personal guarantors for recovery of remaining unpaid balances. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench dismissed Appellants' application IA (IB) No. 39/CTB/2019 on 24.11.2021, upholding the Liquidator's admission of the Consortium's claim; Appellants appealed to NCLAT under Section 61 contending that approval of the principal borrower's resolution plan discharged the guarantor and that proceeding against one co-guarantor violated Section 146 of the Indian Contract Act.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the approval of a resolution plan under Section 31 of the Code discharging the principal borrower operates as a discharge of a corporate guarantor under Sections 134 and 135 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 when creditor rights are expressly reserved in the plan[cite: 12]. 2. Whether a financial creditor is legally entitled under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act to enforce the full residual guaranteed debt against one corporate guarantor in liquidation without proceeding against other co-sureties under Section 146[cite: 12]. 3. Whether operational creditors can challenge the liquidator's admission of a financial creditor's claim via an interlocutory application instead of filing a statutory appeal within 14 days under Section 42 of the Code[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The involuntary discharge of a principal borrower by operation of insolvency law through an approved resolution plan does not ipso facto discharge the independent contractual liabilities of a guarantor where creditor remedies are reserved, and a creditor may recover unpaid balances from any co-guarantor of its choice without being constrained by co-surety contribution rules[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code overrides the Indian Contract Act; under Section 31, an approved resolution plan binds all stakeholders but leaves guarantor liabilities unaffected where expressly carved out (Lalit Kumar Jain doctrine)[cite: 12]; under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, a surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor, and the creditor cannot be dictated to regarding which security or surety to pursue[cite: 12]; Section 42 provides the exclusive appellate remedy against claim admissions or rejections by a liquidator within 14 days[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the resolution plan contains express reservation clauses preserving rights against guarantors, the creditor is entitled to prove the entire unpaid balance in the guarantor's liquidation estate, subject only to the rule against double recovery (no more than 100 pence in the pound)[cite: 12]; co-surety rights under Section 146 arise only between sureties inter se after one has paid more than its proportionate share[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator acted strictly in accordance with Sections 38 to 40 of the Code in admitting the Consortium's claim of Rs. 399.1 Crores, and the Appellants could not bypass Section 42 or dispute the creditor's right to enforce the guarantee[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 91 of 2022 is dismissed[cite: 12]. The order of the NCLT Cuttack Bench dated 24.11.2021 in IA (IB) No. 39/CTB/2019 is affirmed[cite: 12]. No order as to costs[cite: 12].
summary: Operational creditors of Hari Machines Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Cuttack order affirming the Liquidator's decision to admit a Rs. 399.1 Crore claim by a Consortium of Banks based on corporate guarantees for loans availed by Pro-Minerals Private Limited (PMPL)[cite: 12]. Appellants argued that the approval of PMPL's resolution plan discharged the guarantor and that pursuing Hari Machines alone violated co-surety sharing under Section 146 of the Contract Act[cite: 12]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that discharge of a principal borrower under an insolvency resolution plan does not absolve guarantors when rights are expressly reserved[cite: 12]. Furthermore, a creditor's remedy against co-extensive guarantors is unconstrained, and the Liquidator lawfully admitted the claim[cite: 12].

case_title: TLD MEAI FZE vs. Ashish Chhawchharia, Resolution Professional of Jet Airways (India) Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: TLD MEAI FZE is the Appellant (Equipment Manufacturer/Supplier); Ashish Chhawchharia is Respondent No. 1 (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Jet Airways (India) Limited); Jalan Fritsch Consortium is Respondent No. 2 (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of ground support equipment comprising four Ground Power Units (GPUs) and one Conventional Pushback Tractor for deployment at Bengaluru, Chennai, and New Delhi airports under purchase orders dated 14.02.2018 and 08.03.2018 and five invoices dated 25.06.2018 and 09.07.2018, containing explicit title retention clauses. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total equipment purchase price was USD 333,455; Corporate Debtor paid USD 100,036.5 (30% advance) but defaulted on the remaining 70% balance of USD 233,418.5 plus 1% late interest; Appellant lodged a claim in Form B demanding return of equipment and USD 78,909.5 for unauthorized equipment usage. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purchase orders issued February/March 2018; invoices issued June/July 2018; default notice demanding return of equipment issued on 01.06.2019 prior to CIRP; Section 7 CIRP admitted against Jet Airways on 20.06.2019/22.06.2019; Appellant filed Form B on 04.07.2019; RP rejected the claim on 03.09.2019; Appellant filed MA No. 3412 of 2019; CoC approved Jalan Fritsch Consortium's Resolution Plan on 03.10.2020; NCLT approved the plan in IA No. 2081/2020 on 22.06.2021 without deciding MA No. 3412 of 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Five commercial invoices and purchase order terms explicitly stipulated that seller reserved ownership until full and final payment, buyer was prohibited from mortgaging or creating third-party liens, and seller had the right to reclaim goods upon insolvency; Bill of Lading was handed over for cargo delivery; only 30% advance was paid; equipment was entered into the debtor's fixed asset register. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the Resolution Plan in IA No. 2081/2020 on 22.06.2021, treating the equipment as the debtor's assets transferred on an 'as-is-where-is' basis, leaving MA No. 3412 of 2019 undecided; Appellant appealed under Section 61 seeking exclusion and physical return of its equipment.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the delivery of a Bill of Lading constitutes an absolute transfer of title to goods when the underlying contract of sale and invoices contain express retention of title clauses conditioning transfer of ownership on full payment of price[cite: 14]. 2. Whether equipment held in the possession of the corporate debtor under a contract where ownership was retained by the seller forms part of the assets of the corporate debtor under Section 18(1)(f) of the Code[cite: 14]. 3. Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in approving a resolution plan that disposed of third-party assets without adjudicating the owner's pending application for their return[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Assets in the possession of a corporate debtor that are subject to an express title retention clause and where condition precedent regarding full payment of price remains unfulfilled are third-party assets under the Explanation to Section 18(1)(f) of the Code and cannot be included in the debtor's assets or appropriated under a resolution plan[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 19 and 25 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, property in goods passes only when the parties intend it to pass, and a seller may reserve the right of disposal until full payment; delivery of a Bill of Lading transfers constructive possession but does not override contractual title retention conditions[cite: 14]; under Section 18(1)(f) read with its Explanation, third-party assets in possession of the corporate debtor under contractual arrangements are explicitly excluded from the custody and control of the Resolution Professional and cannot form part of the resolution estate[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the specific terms in the purchase orders and commercial invoices proved that the parties intended title to pass only upon full receipt of the 70% balance price; since the balance was never paid, ownership remained vested in the seller[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ground power units and pushback tractor were third-party assets belonging to the Appellant and ought not to have been included in the assets of Jet Airways; the Resolution Professional and SRA are legally bound to hand over the equipment to the Appellant[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 686 of 2021 is disposed of with directions[cite: 14]. The impugned order dated 22.06.2021 is upheld subject to the direction that the Successful Resolution Applicant and the Monitoring Committee must hand over the Appellant's equipment located at Bengaluru, Chennai, and New Delhi airports to the Appellant forthwith[cite: 14]. The claim for usage charges is disallowed, and transportation expenses for returning the equipment shall be borne by the Appellant[cite: 14].
summary: An overseas equipment supplier appealed an NCLT Mumbai order approving the resolution plan for Jet Airways, which treated ground power units and a tractor supplied by the appellant as assets of the airline sold on an as-is basis[cite: 14]. The appellant had received only a 30% advance payment and had explicitly retained ownership under invoice terms pending full payment[cite: 14]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT held that delivery of a Bill of Lading does not transfer title where the contract contains an express retention of title clause[cite: 14]. Under Section 18(1)(f) of the IBC, third-party property held under contractual arrangements cannot be included in the corporate debtor's asset pool, and the SRA was directed to return the equipment[cite: 14].

case_title: Kushal Limited & Ors. vs. Kartik Baldwa & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 678 of 2022 (with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 680 & 681 of 2022)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kushal Limited and its promoters/directors (Sandeep Tulsiram Agarwal, Manoj Agrawal, Kushal Agrawal) are the Appellants (Successful Resolution Applicants); Kartik Baldwa and 63 others are Respondents in Appeal No. 678 (Employees of the Corporate Debtor); Indian Overseas Bank is Respondent in Appeal No. 680 (Lead Bank of Consortium Lenders); Committee of Creditors and Ramchandra Dallaram Choudhary (RP) are Respondents in Appeal No. 681; Rainbow Papers Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution plan submitted by Kushal Ltd. for reviving Corporate Debtor Rainbow Papers Ltd. in response to an Information Memorandum dated 21.02.2018; plan approved by CoC on 06.06.2018/07.06.2018 and sanctioned by NCLT Ahmedabad on 27.02.2019 in IA No. 224 of 2018, effecting the reverse merger of the Corporate Debtor into Appellant No. 1. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics were not specified as monetary defaults of a borrower; instead, Appellants paid an initial upfront sum of Rs. 30.50 Crores and spent Rs. 3.67 Crores as CIRP costs but defaulted on executing the balance obligations under the plan (including payment of employees' provident fund dues and issuing debentures/guarantees to lenders) after alleging that the Corporate Debtor's production capacity was only 1,99,650 MT/annum (GITCO report) instead of 3,59,100 MT/annum stated in the Information Memorandum. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP (IB) No. 88/2017 admitted on 12.09.2017; Information Memorandum issued on 21.02.2018; CoC approved plan on 07.06.2018; NCLT approved plan on 27.02.2019; NCLAT dismissed previous appeals modifying plan regarding PF dues on 19.12.2019; Supreme Court affirmed the order; Appellants filed IA No. 230 of 2020 to recall the approval order after an 18-month delay; NCLT dismissed IA No. 230 of 2020 and allowed IAs No. 229 and 231 of 2020 on 24.03.2021 directing implementation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Information Memorandum containing company profile based on technical reports by MITCON and Indian Agro & Recycled Paper Mills Association; independent technical audit by GITCO commissioned unilaterally by Appellants; stock exchange listing certificates showing installed capacity matching the Information Memorandum; clause 51 of the resolution plan demonstrating Appellants' express agreement to bear past and future tax liabilities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed SRA's application IA No. 230 of 2020 seeking recall of plan approval and refund of Rs. 30.50 Crores, while allowing lender IA No. 229 of 2020 and employee IA No. 231 of 2020 directing immediate execution of the plan; Appellants filed three connected appeals under Section 61 asserting fraudulent misrepresentation.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Resolution Professional committed fraudulent misrepresentation under Section 17 or misrepresentation under Section 18 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 by disclosing the production capacity of the corporate debtor in the Information Memorandum based on earlier independent expert valuation reports[cite: 16]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 or Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 to recall its substantive order approving a resolution plan on allegations of discovered misrepresentation[cite: 16]. 3. Whether a Successful Resolution Applicant can resile from or seek modification/recall of an approved resolution plan after its confirmation has attained finality before the NCLAT and the Supreme Court[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan constitutes a binding contract and statutory decree that cannot be evaded, modified, or recalled at the instance of a Successful Resolution Applicant on belated allegations of misrepresentation, especially where information in the Information Memorandum was compiled in good faith from independent expert technical reports without an intention to deceive[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29 of the IBC obligates the Resolution Professional to disclose 'relevant information' as accurately as reasonably possible based on available corporate records; absent proof of intentional deceit or active concealment, bona fide disclosure of third-party technical data does not constitute fraudulent misrepresentation under Sections 17 or 18 of the Contract Act[cite: 16]; while a tribunal possesses inherent authority to recall orders procured by fraud, Section 420(2) of the Companies Act and Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules do not authorize substantive reviews of validly concluded resolution orders[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish fraudulent misrepresentation warranting recall, the applicant must plead and strictly prove intentional falsehood and lack of due diligence by the RP; where mathematical formulas applied to the applicant's own expert data (GITCO report) confirm the production capacity metrics and the applicant agreed in the plan to absorb contingent liabilities, the plea of misrepresentation fails[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Professional committed no fraud, the SRA failed to exercise pre-bid due diligence, and the plan had attained finality; hence, the recall was rightly refused and directions compelling implementation of the approved resolution plan were legally sound[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 678, 680, and 681 of 2022 are dismissed[cite: 16]. The common order of the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dated 24.03.2021 in I.A. Nos. 229, 230, and 231 of 2020 is affirmed, confirming the dismissal of the recall application and directing the Appellants to immediately implement the approved resolution plan and discharge unpaid dues without costs[cite: 16].
summary: Successful Resolution Applicant Kushal Limited appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing its application to recall the approval of its resolution plan for Rainbow Papers Ltd. and refund its deposited Rs. 30.50 Crores, while directing immediate implementation of the plan in favor of lenders and employees[cite: 16]. The appellant alleged fraudulent misrepresentation regarding the debtor's production capacity in the Information Memorandum[cite: 16]. Dismissing the appeals, NCLAT held that the RP disclosed data based on bona fide third-party reports, which aligned with standard capacity formulas, negating fraud under the Contract Act[cite: 16]. The plan had attained finality before the Supreme Court, binding the SRA to full implementation without excuse[cite: 16].

case_title: K.V. Jayaprakash vs. State Bank Of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K.V. Jayaprakash is the Appellant (Personal Guarantor of the Corporate Debtor); State Bank of India is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor); Ravi Sankar Devarakonda is Respondent No. 2 (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Coastal Projects Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facility of Rs. 774.12 Crores sanctioned by SBI to Coastal Projects Ltd., secured by personal guarantee and mortgage of personal immovable property of the Appellant executed on 26.06.2014, with liability co-extensive with the debtor up to Rs. 164.06 Crores plus interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the Corporate Debtor leading to NPA declaration on 25.01.2017; bank initiated SARFAESI recovery against mortgaged personal properties, culminating in a public auction knock-down on 29.04.2022 in favor of M/s. Bagmane Developers Pvt. Ltd. for Rs. 135.50 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against the Corporate Debtor on 05.01.2018; Liquidation Order passed under Section 33 on 06.12.2018; SBI obtained Section 14 SARFAESI possession order from XXXVII ACMM Bangalore on 03.08.2021; DRT Bangalore dismissed Appellant's Section 17 appeal on 04.10.2021; auction notice issued on 29.09.2021 and 06.10.2021 for auction on 11.11.2021; Appellant filed IA No. 113/CB/2021 before NCLT Cuttack under Section 60(5); NCLT dismissed it on 03.02.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Personal Guarantee dated 26.06.2014 containing clause 7 entitling the Bank to proceed against the guarantor as a principal debtor; SARFAESI sale notices published in Deccan Herald and Prajavani; liquidation claims register showing the mortgaged property belonged exclusively to the guarantor and was excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench dismissed Appellant's IA No. 113/CB/2021 on 03.02.2022, holding that a personal guarantor is a third party unable to invoke Section 60(5) against independent SARFAESI proceedings; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61(1) arguing that moratorium under Section 33(5) barred SARFAESI sales and that subrogation under Section 140 of the Contract Act entitled him to secured creditor status.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to entertain an application by a personal guarantor seeking to restrain independent SARFAESI recovery proceedings initiated by a financial creditor against the guarantor's personal mortgaged property[cite: 18]. 2. Whether the moratorium imposed under Section 14 or the restriction under Section 33(5) of the Code during corporate liquidation interdicts recovery actions against a personal guarantor under the SARFAESI Act[cite: 18]. 3. Whether a personal guarantor whose property is auctioned to discharge the corporate debtor's liability is entitled to be classified as a 'secured creditor' under Section 3(30) of the Code in the corporate debtor's liquidation estate via subrogation under Section 140 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory moratorium and legal restrictions accompanying corporate insolvency resolution and liquidation apply exclusively to actions against the corporate debtor and its own estate, leaving creditors entirely unfettered to pursue independent recovery proceedings against third-party personal guarantors under the SARFAESI Act[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) confers residuary jurisdiction only over questions of fact or law arising directly out of the insolvency resolution or liquidation of the corporate debtor; independent recovery actions under SARFAESI against a personal guarantor's personal assets do not arise out of corporate insolvency (Gujarat Urja doctrine)[cite: 18]; Section 14(3) and Section 33(5) restrict proceedings against the corporate debtor alone, excluding sureties from the protective shield; the non-obstante clause of Section 238 overrides inconsistent provisions of the Indian Contract Act[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To claim secured creditor status under Section 3(30) in a liquidation estate, a party must establish the creation of an express 'security interest' in its favor over the debtor's assets under Section 3(31); subrogation rights under Section 140 of the Contract Act only create an unsecured claim under general law or Section 5(8)(h) and (i), not a security interest[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because SARFAESI proceedings are distinct recovery actions, the moratorium does not protect the personal guarantor, and no security interest was created by the corporate debtor in favor of the guarantor, the NCLT rightly dismissed the application as non-maintainable[cite: 18].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 362 of 2022 is dismissed[cite: 18]. The order of the NCLT Cuttack Bench dated 03.02.2022 in IA (IB) No. 113/CB/2021 is affirmed without costs[cite: 18].
summary: The personal guarantor of Corporate Debtor Coastal Projects Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Cuttack order dismissing his application to restrain State Bank of India from auctioning his personal mortgaged properties under the SARFAESI Act during the corporate debtor's liquidation[cite: 18]. The appellant argued that the Section 33(5) liquidation moratorium barred recovery, that NCLT had exclusive jurisdiction under Section 60(5), and that he was entitled to secured creditor status via Section 140 of the Contract Act[cite: 18]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the statutory moratorium protects only the corporate debtor and not personal guarantors[cite: 18]. Further, SARFAESI proceedings are independent recovery mechanisms beyond Section 60(5) jurisdiction, and the guarantor held no security interest in the debtor's estate[cite: 18].

case_title: Mr. T.S. Murali & Anr. vs. Liquidator Of Helpline Hospitality Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. T.S. Murali and Mrs. Rema Murali are Appellants (Ex-Directors and 100% Shareholders of the Corporate Debtor); Mr. Sarvesh Kashyap is the Respondent (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Helpline Hospitality Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Diversion and siphoning of Corporate Debtor funds to acquire personal real estate; Corporate Debtor and Appellants jointly obtained an ICICI Bank home loan of Rs. 36,59,250/- under agreement dated 30.10.2004, which was utilized to purchase residential property at Plot No. G-158, Sector 41, Noida, registered exclusively in the individual name of Appellant No. 1 via registered sale deed dated 09.02.2005. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rs. 65,29,836.56 was diverted from the Corporate Debtor's bank accounts to service loan EMIs (auto-debited up to 22.07.2013) plus Rs. 20 Lakhs pre-payment on 31.03.2012; statutory service tax liabilities of Rs. 3,91,04,886/- plus penalties totaling over Rs. 8.04 Crores were left in default, while the diverted property had appreciated to a market value of approx. Rs. 4 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 CIRP admitted on 24.04.2017; Corporate Debtor ordered into liquidation under Section 33; Forensic Audit Report submitted on 10.11.2018; Liquidator filed CA No. 840/2018 under Section 66 on 21.12.2018; NCLT ordered attachment and public auction of the Noida property on 20.12.2019; Appellants filed review/modification application CA No. 266/2020 on 07.01.2020; NCLT dismissed review application on 26.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ICICI Bank loan statements showing loan account was in the name of the Corporate Debtor with Appellants as co-applicants and EMIs debited from company accounts; registered sale deed dated 09.02.2005 showing consideration paid via company cheques; audited balance sheets for FY 2007-08 to 2011-12 signed by Appellants as directors despite claiming they resigned in 2006; Service Tax assessment order dated 25.01.2017; Forensic Audit Report establishing fraudulent diversion of company funds for personal estate creation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II in CA No. 840/2018 allowed attachment of the property on 20.12.2019 under Section 66; Appellants sought recall/modification via CA No. 266/2020 offering to refund Rs. 65.29 Lakhs, which NCLT dismissed on 26.02.2021 holding it lacked review jurisdiction and that no error apparent existed; Appellants appealed to NCLAT under Section 61.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the look-back limitation period applicable to avoidance of undervalued or preferential transactions applies to proceedings under Section 66 of the Code for fraudulent trading and diversion of funds[cite: 19]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has statutory power to order the attachment and public auction of an immovable property registered in the name of an ex-director when established that the property was acquired entirely through fraudulent diversion and siphoning of corporate debtor funds[cite: 19]. 3. Whether the NCLT possesses inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 or Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 to review or recall its own final orders passed under Section 66 of the Code[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 66 of the Code, fraudulent transactions and willful siphoning of corporate assets to create personal estates for directors are not subject to any look-back limitation period ('once a fraud, always a fraud'); the Adjudicating Authority possesses comprehensive authority to compel directors to make restitution by attaching and auctioning properties acquired with diverted funds[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66 is distinct from avoidance provisions in Sections 43, 45, and 46, containing no statutory look-back window; wrong labeling of statutory provisions (e.g., citing Section 25(2)(j)) does not invalidate an application where jurisdictional facts establishing fraudulent conduct under Section 66 are present[cite: 19]; Section 238 gives the Code overriding effect over peripheral enactments like the Benami Transactions Act[cite: 19]; neither Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules nor Section 420(2) of the Companies Act vests the Adjudicating Authority with inherent power to review or substantively alter its final orders[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted banking records proving that home loan EMIs and pre-payments were funded entirely from the corporate debtor's bank accounts, coupled with forensic audit findings of intentional fund diversion while corporate statutory dues remained unpaid, conclusively establish fraudulent transactions under Section 66[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the property was purchased entirely with company funds through fraudulent siphoning and the tribunal lacked review jurisdiction, the attachment and auction order was lawful and the review rejection was sound[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 234 of 2021 is dismissed[cite: 19]. The orders of the NCLT New Delhi Bench-II dated 20.12.2019 in CA No. 840/2018 and dated 26.02.2021 in CA No. 266/2020 are affirmed, and the Liquidator is directed to proceed with the liquidation and auction of the attached property without costs[cite: 19].
summary: Ex-directors of Corporate Debtor Helpline Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi orders attaching and ordering the public auction of a residential property in Noida standing in the director's name, and refusing to review the order under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act[cite: 19]. A forensic audit established that the property was acquired using an ICICI Bank loan whose EMIs and pre-payments were funded entirely from company accounts, constituting fraudulent diversion under Section 66 of the IBC while service tax debts went unpaid[cite: 19]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that Section 66 is not governed by any look-back period, and the NCLT has full jurisdiction to attach fraudulently acquired assets and no inherent power to review its substantive orders[cite: 19].

case_title: Manoj Gupta vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
appeal_number: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 43 of 2018 (with Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 47, 49 & 68 of 2018)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Manoj Gupta (Proprietor of M/s. Mahalaxmi Steels) is the Appellant in Appeal No. 43/2018; Sanjay Agencies & Anr. are Appellants in Appeal No. 47/2018; Lahs Green India Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. are Appellants in Appeal No. 49/2018; Saara Traders Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. are Appellants in Appeal No. 68/2018; Competition Commission of India (CCI) is Respondent No. 1; Nagrik Chetna Manch is the Informant/Respondent; Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) is Respondent No. 5; Ecoman Enviro Solutions Pvt. Ltd. and Fortified Security Solutions are Co-bidders/OPs. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Competitive public tenders floated by Pune Municipal Corporation between December 2014 and March 2015 (Tender Nos. 34, 35, 44, 62, and 63 of 2014) for the 'Design, Supply, Installation, Commissioning, Operation and Maintenance of Municipal Organic and Inorganic Solid Waste Processing Plants'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Anticompetitive cartelization and bid-rigging; internal estimated value was Rs. 11.45 Crores, while pre-determined L1 bidder Ecoman bagged contracts for Rs. 14,82,94,580/- (approx. 30% above estimates); CCI imposed a maximum penalty under Section 27(b) of 10% on average three-year total turnover, calculating Rs. 3,36,20,332/- for Mahalaxmi Steels, Rs. 1,51,06,458/- for Sanjay Agencies, and Rs. 42,00,516/- for Lahs Green, before applying lesser penalty reductions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Tenders floated December 2014-March 2015; Information filed under Section 19(1)(a) by Informant on 11.06.2015; CCI passed Section 26(1) investigation order on 29.09.2015; Appellants filed leniency applications under Section 46 in August/September 2016; DG submitted report on 23.11.2016; CCI passed final cease-and-desist and penalty order on 01.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bidders submitted proxy/cover bids orchestrated by Bipin Vijay Salunke to satisfy the mandatory three-bidder criteria; common IP addresses used to upload bids; consecutive Demand Drafts for EMD purchased from the same bank branch; common contact numbers belonging to Ecoman's executive director; confessional statements and admissions in leniency applications accepting submission of proxy cover bids. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI held OPs guilty of bid-rigging under Section 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) and imposed the maximum 10% penalty on total turnover, granting 50% leniency reduction to Mahalaxmi Steels, 40% to Sanjay Agencies, and 50% to Lahs Green; Appellants appealed to NCLAT under Section 53B challenging total turnover calculation and lack of reasons for levying the maximum statutory percentage.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Competition Commission of India erred in imposing the maximum statutory penalty of 10% under Section 27(b) of the Act on the total turnover of the enterprises without providing detailed justification or considering mitigating factors[cite: 20]. 2. Whether the principle of 'relevant turnover' established in Excel Crop Care applies to bid-rigging cartels where cover bidders have no commercial operations or revenue in the infringing product market (solid waste management)[cite: 20]. 3. Whether the NCLAT can direct a criminal/anti-corruption inquiry into the conduct of municipal public officials when collusive bidding reveals prima facie complicity causing wrongful loss to the public exchequer[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the Competition Commission of India enjoys statutory discretion under Section 27(b) to impose penalties up to 10% of turnover, levying the maximum penalty requires specific reasons and an opportunity for the parties to address mitigating circumstances; statutory discretion cannot be exercised arbitrarily or without proportionality[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 27(b) permits penalty imposition on turnover, but penal discretion must adhere to the doctrine of proportionality under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution (Excel Crop Care doctrine)[cite: 20]; where an enterprise participates as a cover bidder outside its regular line of business, applying relevant turnover mechanically to exempt it entirely would defeat the Act's deterrent purpose, but imposing the maximum 10% total turnover penalty without considering mitigating factors constitutes an improper exercise of discretion[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontested admissions of cartel participation in leniency applications under Section 46 operate as conclusive evidence of bid-rigging under Section 3(3)(d), precluding appellants from challenging liability on the merits[cite: 20]; however, the record must reflect that mitigating factors (such as lack of prior infractions, SME status, and degree of cooperation) were considered when selecting the penalty rate[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the findings of bid-rigging were admitted and established by evidence, liability is upheld; however, because the CCI imposed the maximum 10% penalty without giving notice or reasons for adopting the upper ceiling, the quantum of penalty is remitted for reconsideration[cite: 20].
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 43, 47, 49, and 68 of 2018 are allowed in part[cite: 20]. The finding of contravention under Section 3(3)(d) is upheld, but the imposition of penalties is remitted back to the CCI to reconsider the quantum of penalty after giving appellants an opportunity of being heard[cite: 20]. Connected Appeals (Nos. 44, 45, 46, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, and 67 of 2018) are dismissed for non-prosecution[cite: 20]. A direction is issued to the Director General of Police, Maharashtra / DG Anti-Corruption Maharashtra to conduct an inquiry into the role of Pune Municipal Corporation officials[cite: 20].
summary: Appellants appealed against a CCI order finding them guilty of collusive bid-rigging in solid waste management tenders floated by Pune Municipal Corporation and imposing a maximum 10% penalty on total turnover (subject to lesser penalty reductions)[cite: 20]. Appellants argued that the maximum statutory rate was imposed arbitrarily and in violation of the 'relevant turnover' rule in Excel Crop Care[cite: 20]. Upholding the finding of cartelization based on admissions in leniency applications, NCLAT held that the Excel Crop Care turnover restriction cannot completely exempt cover bidders lacking relevant industry turnover[cite: 20]. However, because the CCI levied the maximum statutory 10% penalty without giving reasons or affording a hearing on the upper ceiling, NCLAT remitted the matter for penalty reconsideration and directed an anti-corruption inquiry into municipal officials[cite: 20].

case_title: Mukesh Kumar vs. Ambrane India Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mukesh Kumar is the Appellant (Director and Shareholder of Corporate Debtor MP Promoters Pvt. Ltd.); Ambrane India Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor); Durga Das Agrawal is Respondent No. 2 (Interim Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Oral short-term loan assistance of Rs. 1,01,00,000/- sanctioned by the Board of Directors of Respondent No. 1 vide resolution dated 20.05.2017 under Section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013 at 9% interest per annum compounded on 31.03.2018, repayable on or before 31.03.2018, disbursed in two tranches (Rs. 51 Lakhs via cheque on 26.05.2017 and Rs. 50 Lakhs via RTGS on 03.06.2017). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 01.04.2018 upon non-repayment by the agreed maturity date of 31.03.2018; total claimed default amount as on 31.07.2019 was Rs. 1,21,95,953/- (comprising Rs. 1.01 Crores principal plus contractual interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Formal loan recall/legal demand notice issued on 06.08.2019; Section 7 CIRP petition CP (IB) No. 2607/PB/2019 filed on 26.09.2019; cost of Rs. 50,000/- imposed on Corporate Debtor on 07.04.2021 to file reply; Corporate Debtor filed reply on 20.07.2021; NeSL authentication certificate issued on 04.02.2022; NCLT admitted Section 7 application on 06.04.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board Resolution dated 20.05.2017 recording the 9% per annum interest rate and repayment deadline; bank statement proving disbursement of Rs. 51 Lakhs and Rs. 50 Lakhs; Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheet as of 31.03.2018 reflecting Rs. 1,01,00,000/- as current liability (which the appellant unsuccessfully alleged was advance booking for property 13/13); Information Utility (NeSL) certificate dated 04.02.2022 authenticating the financial debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi admitted the Section 7 petition on 06.04.2022 holding that disbursement and default were authenticated by NeSL; Appellant appealed under Section 61(1) contending that in the absence of a written loan agreement, the transaction constituted an advance for property rather than a financial debt.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the absence of a formal written loan agreement negates the existence of a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the Code when disbursement against consideration for time value of money is established through board resolutions, bank transfer records, and balance sheet entries[cite: 21]. 2. Whether entries in a corporate debtor's balance sheet and authentication by an Information Utility (NeSL) under Section 7(3) constitute conclusive proof of financial debt and default to justify CIRP admission[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A formal written loan agreement is not an indispensable prerequisite to establish a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the Code; an implied agreement for the advance of loan funds with interest and time value of money can be lawfully deduced from contemporaneous corporate board resolutions, banking disbursement trails, Information Utility records, and balance sheet admissions[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7(5)(a), where the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that a financial debt exists, a default exceeding the statutory threshold has occurred, the application is complete, and no disciplinary proceeding is pending against the proposed IRP, admission of the application is the general statutory rule, whereas assigning detailed reasons is mandatory primarily when rejecting an application under the proviso to Section 7(5)[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where bank statements prove disbursement, the lender's board resolution sanctions the transaction at an explicit interest rate with a defined tenure, and an Information Utility (NeSL) issues a certificate confirming debt and default, uncorroborated oral assertions that the funds constituted advance payments for property development cannot rebut the existence of a financial debt[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt of Rs. 1.01 Crores carried consideration for the time value of money, the default on 01.04.2018 was verified, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in initiating CIRP against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 659 of 2022 is dismissed[cite: 21]. The admission order dated 06.04.2022 passed by the NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi in CP (IB) No. 2607/PB/2019 initiating CIRP against MP Promoters Pvt. Ltd. is affirmed without costs[cite: 21]. Delay in filing the appeal is condoned via IA No. 1807/2022[cite: 21].
summary: A director of Corporate Debtor MP Promoters Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by Ambrane India Pvt. Ltd. for default of a Rs. 1.01 Crore short-term borrowing[cite: 21]. The appellant argued that the absence of a written loan agreement precluded classification as a financial debt and claimed the amount was an advance for property purchase[cite: 21]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that a written contract is not mandatory where board resolutions, banking statements, and NeSL certificates establish disbursement for the time value of money at 9% interest[cite: 21]. The debtor's balance sheet confirmed the liability, and default having occurred, admission was justified[cite: 21].

case_title: Anjali Bhardwaj vs. Office of Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi and Haryana & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anjali Bhardwaj is the Appellant (Director and Shareholder of struck-off Company M/s. Millennium Realtech Pvt. Ltd.); Office of Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi and Haryana is Respondent No. 1; Office of Commissioner of Income Tax is Respondent No. 2; M/s. Millennium Realtech Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 3. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation of private real estate company M/s. Millennium Realtech Pvt. Ltd. on 31.01.2006 to engage in construction, real estate development, and project management; company acquired land in 2007 and was party to arbitration proceedings with a builder. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete failure to file statutory annual returns and audited financial statements for financial years following 31.03.2016; company reported nil revenue from operations, nil employees, and paid no GST during the preceding two financial years. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial filings ceased after 31.03.2016; ROC issued show-cause notice in Form STK-1 on 19.07.2019; public notice in Form STK-5 issued on 17.08.2019/09.08.2019; strike-off order published in Form STK-7 under Section 248(5) on 29.10.2019/18.11.2019 dissolving the company; Company filed Section 252 restoration appeal Appeal No. 150/252/ND/2020 before NCLT; NCLT dismissed restoration appeal on 04.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ROC official records and response demonstrating absence of operational revenue and GST details; appellant's explicit admission in paragraph 2.8 of the NCLT appeal memo that inter-se litigation and management deadlock among directors completely prevented board meetings and approval of financial statements since 31.03.2017; arbitral award dated 20.12.2020 rejecting a builder's claim against the company. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-V dismissed Appeal No. 150/252/ND/2020 on 04.03.2022 holding that the company was non-operational and failed to justify restoration under Section 252; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 421 asserting the company held real estate assets and was not a shell company.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a company whose name has been struck off by the ROC under Section 248 for failing to file financial returns for two consecutive years is entitled to restoration under Section 252 on the ground that it holds immovable property or was defending arbitral proceedings[cite: 23]. 2. Whether internal deadlock and shareholder litigation among directors excuse non-filing of statutory annual returns and negate the statutory presumption that the company was not carrying on business or in operation[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To secure revival of a struck-off company under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013, the applicant must establish with cogent documentary evidence that the company was actually carrying on business or in active operation at the time of striking off; mere ownership of immovable assets or ongoing litigation does not suffice to render strike-off action unlawful[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 248 mandates removal where a company fails to file returns for two preceding financial years and fails to obtain dormant status under Section 455[cite: 23]; under Section 250, dissolution does not impede the realization of outstanding claims or discharge of liabilities by a dissolved company, meaning ongoing arbitral claims do not necessitate company restoration[cite: 23]; taking an overly lenient approach under Section 252 without plausible operational proof renders Section 248 redundant[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where company records show nil revenue from operations, zero GST filings, and the appellant expressly admits that management deadlock halted corporate activity and board meetings, the applicant fails to rebut the statutory finding of non-operation[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Millennium Realtech Pvt. Ltd. was entirely defunct and non-operational for the statutory two-year period, and the NCLT committed no error in refusing to restore its name to the register[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 70 of 2022 is dismissed[cite: 23]. The order dated 04.03.2022 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V in Appeal No. 150/252/ND/2020 affirming the strike-off of M/s. Millennium Realtech Pvt. Ltd. is confirmed without costs[cite: 23].
summary: A director and shareholder appealed an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing a restoration petition under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 after the ROC struck off M/s. Millennium Realtech Pvt. Ltd. for failing to file statutory returns after 2016[cite: 23]. The appellant argued that the company was operational, held land assets, and was involved in arbitration[cite: 23]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the company produced nil operational revenue and paid no GST, and the appellant admitted a complete management deadlock since 2017[cite: 23]. Under Section 250, asset realization can proceed notwithstanding dissolution, and the NCLT rightly refused restoration[cite: 23].

case_title: Union Bank Of India vs. Mr. P.K. Balasubramaniam & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union Bank of India (erstwhile Andhra Bank) is the Appellant (Financial Creditor); Mr. P.K. Balasubramaniam is Respondent No. 1 (Personal Guarantor of Corporate Debtor M/s. Tebma Shipyard Limited); State Bank of India is Respondent No. 2 (Financial Creditor / Competing Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities availed by Corporate Debtor M/s. Tebma Shipyard Limited, secured inter alia by personal guarantees executed by Respondent No. 1 in favor of consortium banks including Appellant and SBI. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the Corporate Debtor and Personal Guarantor on credit facilities; specific default amounts were not quantified in the judgment, but exceeded the statutory threshold under Section 95. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellant Union Bank of India filed Section 95 application CP (IB) 33/CHE/2022 on 31.12.2021 (assigned registration by Registry on 09.02.2022); Respondent No. 2 SBI filed Section 95 application CP 5/CHE/2022 against the same guarantor on 03.01.2022 (registered by Registry on 12.01.2022); NCLT heard matters on 07.06.2022, appointing an RP in SBI's petition and dismissing Appellant's petition. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Electronic filing receipts confirming Appellant e-filed on 31.12.2021 and SBI e-filed on 03.01.2022; court order sheets of hearings on 04.03.2022, 01.04.2022, 02.05.2022, and 07.06.2022 demonstrating Appellant never notified the bench that its application was presented earlier in time. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Division Bench-I Chennai on 07.06.2022 appointed an RP in SBI's application CP 5/CHE/2022 and dismissed Appellant's application CP (IB) 33/CHE/2022 under Section 96(1)(b) on the ground that an interim moratorium had attached to the guarantor, granting liberty to proceed in accordance with law; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the commencement of an interim moratorium under Section 96(1)(a) upon the filing of a Section 95 application bars the initiation or prosecution of subsequent Section 95 applications filed by other financial creditors against the same personal guarantor[cite: 25]. 2. Whether an earlier-filed Section 95 application that suffered administrative registration delays by the Registry must take precedence over a subsequent application that was numbered and listed earlier, or whether all creditors are subsumed within the collective statutory insolvency resolution mechanism[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 96 of the Code, the filing of an application to initiate personal guarantor insolvency triggers an interim moratorium on all debts of the guarantor, prohibiting other creditors from initiating or continuing separate legal actions; personal guarantor insolvency is a collective proceeding where all creditors must lodge their claims with the appointed Resolution Professional rather than prosecuting multiple parallel Section 95 applications[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the date of electronic filing constitutes the date of presentation (Basia doctrine), Section 96(1)(b) mandates that during the interim moratorium, creditors of the debtor shall not initiate any legal proceedings in respect of any debt[cite: 25]; the statutory framework under Chapter III (Sections 100 to 105) creates a unified process for public notice, claims consolidation, and repayment plan formulation that covers all creditors of the personal guarantor without multiplicity[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a competing creditor fails to apprise the adjudicating authority across multiple hearings of its prior filing date, an RP is duly appointed in the companion petition, and full statutory liberty is reserved to submit claims under Section 102 and 103, no prejudice is caused to warrant setting back the insolvency process[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The scheme of Chapter III does not permit multiple simultaneous CIRP applications against the same personal guarantor, and since the Appellant is entitled to prove its entire debt before the RP, the dismissal of its separate application with liberty was legally justified[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 293 of 2022 is dismissed[cite: 25]. The order of the NCLT Division Bench-I Chennai dated 07.06.2022 in CP (IB) 33/CHE/2022 is affirmed, confirming the liberty granted to the Appellant to submit its claims before the Resolution Professional appointed in CP 5/CHE/2022 without costs[cite: 25].
summary: Union Bank of India appealed an NCLT Chennai order dismissing its Section 95 petition against personal guarantor P.K. Balasubramaniam on the ground that an interim moratorium had attached under Section 96 following an application by State Bank of India wherein an RP was appointed[cite: 25]. The appellant argued that it had e-filed three days prior to SBI and should have taken precedence[cite: 25]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that personal guarantor insolvency under Chapter III is a collective proceeding that prohibits multiple simultaneous applications against the same debtor[cite: 25]. Because the appellant suffered no prejudice and retained liberty to prove its claims before the RP under Section 103, setting back the proceedings was unwarranted[cite: 25].

case_title: Anheuser Busch Inbev India Limited vs. Mr. Pradeep Kumar Sravanam, Resolution Professional of East Godavari Breweries Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anheuser Busch Inbev India Limited is the Appellant/Financial Creditor; Mr. Pradeep Kumar Sravanam is the Respondent/Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor East Godavari Breweries Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 26] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Brewing Agreement dated 06.02.2015 executed between Appellant and Corporate Debtor under which Appellant advanced Rs. 17.50 Crores, repayable with interest upon termination of the agreement pursuant to Clauses 6.12 and 6.14[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Advance of Rs. 17.50 Crores plus interest at 10% per annum until date of default (03.08.2018) amounting to Rs. 6,10,82,191.78, and default interest at 18% per annum until CIRP commencement (17.11.2021) amounting to Rs. 10,37,34,246.57, totaling a claimed financial debt of Rs. 33,98,16,438.35[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Termination Notice issued by Appellant on 03.08.2018; Arbitration proceedings initiated by Appellant against Corporate Debtor; CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 17.11.2021; Appellant submitted Form C claim on 01.12.2021; Arbitral Tribunal rejected RP's section 14 application and continued arbitration on 14.01.2022; Appellant filed IA No. 155/2022 before NCLT; NCLT dismissed it on 02.12.2022[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Brewing Agreement dated 06.02.2015; Termination Notice dated 03.08.2018; Promoters' personal and related-party corporate guarantees; pending arbitration record where Corporate Debtor filed substantial counterclaims for damages arising from termination of contract which could result in a set-off against Appellant's claims[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Amaravati Bench in IA (IBC) No. 155/2022 dismissed Appellant's application seeking admission of its claim of Rs. 33.98 Crores and induction into the CoC, holding that the RP was justified in keeping the claim in abeyance pending adjudication of the Corporate Debtor's arbitral counterclaims; Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 26].
legal_issues: 1.
