Whether a Resolution Professional possesses the administrative authority under the IBC and CIRP Regulations to keep a financial creditor's claim in abeyance pending the adjudication of an ongoing arbitration proceeding involving substantial counterclaims for damages by the corporate debtor that could result in set-off[cite: 26]. 2. Whether an unadjudicated claim arising out of the termination of a contract must be unconditionally admitted as a financial debt under Section 18 of the Code, entitling the claimant to immediate participation in the Committee of Creditors[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional, possessing purely administrative and non-adjudicatory collation powers, may lawfully keep a creditor's claim in abeyance where the crystallised liability is subject to pending arbitration and substantive counterclaims by the corporate debtor that could result in set-off, until the claim can be determined with legal certainty[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 3(6) defines 'claim' broadly to include disputed rights to payment, Section 18(1)(b) and CIRP Regulation 14 mandate that the RP verify and collate claims based on available records; where a claim is contingent upon an arbitral decision and subject to an unquantified counter-claim, the RP cannot usurp adjudicatory functions to admit an uncertain sum that may conflict with the arbitral award[cite: 26]; unliquidated claims for damages do not constitute a debt presently due and payable until adjudicated by a competent authority (Raman Iron Foundry doctrine)[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where ongoing arbitration records demonstrate that cross-demands and counterclaims exist which have a direct bearing on the pecuniary liability of the parties and may set off the claim, keeping the claim in abeyance pending verification or arbitral determination is justified[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the corporate debtor's counterclaim in pending arbitration could extinguish or alter the appellant's entitlement, the RP committed no error in keeping the claim in abeyance, and the NCLT rightly dismissed the application[cite: 26].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 12 of 2023 is dismissed[cite: 26]. The order of the NCLT Amaravati Bench dated 02.12.2022 in IA (IBC) No. 155/2022 in CP(IB) No. 58/9/AMR/2021 is affirmed[cite: 26]. Connected IA No. 26 of 2023 stands closed without costs[cite: 26].
summary: Anheuser Busch Inbev India Limited appealed an NCLT Amaravati order dismissing its application to compel the Resolution Professional of East Godavari Breweries Pvt. Ltd. to admit its financial claim of Rs. 33.98 Crores and grant it voting rights on the CoC[cite: 26]. The claim arose from an advance under a terminated brewing contract, which was subject to pending arbitration where the debtor had lodged substantial counterclaims[cite: 26]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the RP acted within his administrative powers in keeping the claim in abeyance[cite: 26]. Because the corporate debtor's pending arbitral counterclaims could result in a set-off, the claim could not be admitted with certainty prior to arbitral determination[cite: 26].

case_title: Indra Marshal Power Private Limited vs. Akshaya Irrigation Products Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Indra Marshal Power Private Ltd. is the Appellant/Operational Creditor/Petitioner; M/s. Akshaya Irrigation Products Private Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of 1,495 Indra Marshal Diesel Engine Pump Sets (IMDE Pump Sets) by Appellant to Respondent between 12.11.2013 and 03.10.2014 against purchase orders, e-way bills, and C-Forms[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal outstanding claimed debt of Rs. 2,40,69,233.30 (or Rs. 2,40,73,058/-) plus interest at 18% per annum from the dates of respective invoices, with default arising 30 days post-invoice[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Statutory demand notice issued under Section 434(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 1956 on 23.03.2016; Corporate Debtor replied on 12.04.2016 alleging defective pumps; Appellant filed Winding Up Company Petition No. 311 of 2016 before Telangana High Court on 21.07.2016; High Court transferred the petition to NCLT Hyderabad vide order dated 29.11.2019 in IA No. 1 of 2019; NCLT re-numbered the transferred matter afresh as CP (IB) No. 210/9/HDB/2020 in January 2020; NCLT dismissed it on 30.06.2022[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices, delivery lorry receipts, and Respondent's ledger accounts; letters from agricultural officers and farmers complaining about malfunctioning pump sets; correspondence where Respondent alleged 700 defective pump sets were lying in its godown[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed CP (IB) No. 210/9/HDB/2020 on 30.06.2022 as not maintainable, holding that no mandatory Section 8 notice was issued and that a pre-existing dispute existed; Appellant appealed under Section 61 asserting that a transferred winding up petition cannot be dismissed for want of a Section 8 notice and must be heard from the transfer stage[cite: 29].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a winding up petition transferred from a High Court to the NCLT under the 5th Proviso to Section 434(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 can be dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority for failure to serve a fresh demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC[cite: 29]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority breached judicial discipline by failing to treat the High Court's transfer order as an insolvency proceeding to be adjudicated from the stage before transfer, and by assigning a fresh CP (IB) number and abating the High Court proceedings[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a company winding up petition is transferred by an order of the High Court to the NCLT pursuant to Section 434(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Adjudicating Authority is bound by judicial discipline to treat the proceeding as an insolvency application from the stage of transfer without imposing an artificial requirement of serving a fresh statutory demand notice under Section 8 of the Code[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 applies strictly to cases where notice was not served on the respondent in the winding up petition; under the 5th Proviso to Section 434(1)(c), where notice was served and pleadings were completed in the High Court, the transferred proceeding must be dealt with by the Tribunal as an application for initiating CIRP from the stage before transfer[cite: 29]; the NCLT has no jurisdiction to hold that High Court proceedings abated[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A binding judicial transfer order by a High Court must be followed in letter and spirit; the NCLT cannot bypass the High Court's mandate by re-registering the case as a fresh Section 9 petition and dismissing it for non-compliance with preliminary Section 8 formalities[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's dismissal of the transferred petition for lack of a Section 8 notice was contrary to law and in breach of judicial discipline, necessitating setting aside the order without adjudicating the merits of pre-existing disputes[cite: 29].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 367 of 2022 is disposed of and the impugned order dated 30.06.2022 in CP (IB) No. 210/9/HDB/2020 is set aside[cite: 29]. NCLT Hyderabad Bench is directed to take CP No. 311 of 2016 on its file by assigning an appropriate transfer number, issue notice to the parties, and proceed with adjudication on merits in accordance with law[cite: 29]. Consequent orders dismissing CP (IB) No. 210/9/HDB/2020 shall be passed by the Tribunal upon re-numbering[cite: 29]. Connected IAs are closed without costs[cite: 29].
summary: An operational creditor appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing its petition against Akshaya Irrigation Products for non-service of a Section 8 demand notice and pre-existing disputes[cite: 29]. The petition had originally been instituted as a winding up petition before the Telangana High Court, which transferred the matter to the NCLT under Section 434(1)(c) of the Companies Act[cite: 29]. Setting aside the dismissal, NCLAT held that Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules applies only where notice was not served; for petitions transferred under the 5th Proviso to Section 434(1)(c) after notice, NCLT must hear the matter from the transferred stage without demanding a fresh Section 8 notice[cite: 29]. The matter was remitted to be re-numbered and decided on merits[cite: 29].

case_title: Tarik Klair vs. Registrar Of Companies, NCT Of Delhi & Haryana & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tarik Klair is the Appellant (50% Shareholder and Director of M/s. Opax Web Pvt. Ltd.); Registrar of Companies, Delhi & Haryana is Respondent No. 1; Income Tax Department is Respondent No. 2; Manpreet Singh Sachdeva is Respondent No. 3 (50% Shareholder and second Director of M/s. Opax Web Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation of M/s. Opax Web Pvt. Ltd. on 24.12.2013 as a private IT/software services company with two equal 50:50 shareholders/directors[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total cessation of statutory financial and annual return filings with the ROC after the financial year ending 31.03.2015; balance sheets for FY 2017-18 and 2018-19 reflected Rs. 0.00 under Fixed Assets, Inventories, Trade Receivables, Long-Term Borrowings, and Trade Payables, with a negligible bank balance of Rs. 497.64[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Last annual return filed up to 31.03.2015; show-cause notice Form STK-1 issued on 22.05.2018; Gazette notification in Form STK-5 issued on 18.06.2018; striking off and dissolution notice published in Form STK-7 on 08.08.2018 under Section 248(5); Appellant filed Section 252(3) restoration petition CP No. 49/Chd/Hry/2020 before NCLT; NCLT dismissed it on 27.07.2021[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ROC records showing continuous non-filing for over two years; Income Tax Department confirmation that no ITRs were filed for Assessment Years 2014-15, 2016-17, 2017-18, and 2018-19 (and gross income of only Rs. 2,906/- for AY 2019-20); company never registered under the GST Act; balance sheets prepared unilaterally at Jalandhar without board approval and signed by only one director in violation of Section 134; Respondent No. 3's categorical assertion that complete functional deadlock existed since 2016 due to personal disputes[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed CP No. 49/Chd/Hry/2020 on 27.07.2021 holding that the company was not in operation when struck off; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 421(1) alleging the company had operational turnover and was not a shell entity[cite: 30].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an order of the ROC striking off a company under Section 248(1)(c) can be set aside and the company restored under Section 252(3) on the basis of unaudited balance sheets signed by a single director without approval of the board of directors[cite: 30]. 2. Whether it is 'just' under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to restore a defunct, closely-held private company where an irremediable 50:50 deadlock exists between the two sole directors and one director opposes restoration[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, restoration of a struck-off company cannot be ordered on the basis of unilateral balance sheets that violate statutory approval procedures; where a 50:50 shareholder deadlock exists and the company shows no genuine commercial activity, restoring the company would merely generate further fruitless litigation rather than serve justice[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(3) requires the Tribunal to be satisfied that the company was carrying on business, in operation, or that it is otherwise just to restore it; Section 134 strictly mandates that financial statements be approved by the board of directors and signed by at least two directors before being submitted to auditors; unilaterally drafted accounts lack legal sanctity[cite: 30]; the ROC cannot suo motu confer dormant status under Section 455 without a formal company application under Rule 3 of the Miscellaneous Rules, 2014[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: When financial statements show zero fixed assets, zero receivables, zero GST registration, and non-filing of income tax returns, the applicant fails to establish that the company was carrying on business at the time of striking off[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Opax Web Pvt. Ltd. was completely inoperative and bogged down by an irreconcilable 50:50 deadlock, making the NCLT's refusal to restore the company entirely justified in law[cite: 30].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 115 of 2021 is dismissed[cite: 30]. The order of the NCLT Chandigarh Bench dated 27.07.2021 in CP No. 49/Chd/Hry/2020 is affirmed without costs[cite: 30].
summary: A 50% shareholder and director appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing his petition under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking restoration of struck-off software firm M/s. Opax Web Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 30]. The appellant relied on balance sheets certified by a CA to claim the company was operational[cite: 30]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the balance sheets were invalid under Section 134 as they were signed by only one director without board approval[cite: 30]. Given that the other 50% director confirmed the company was non-operational, no GST registration existed, and an irreconcilable deadlock prevailed, restoration was unwarranted[cite: 30].

case_title: Kanoria Chemical & Industries Ltd. vs. Mr. Vijendra Kumar Jain & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kanoria Chemical & Industries Ltd. is the Appellant (Operational Creditor); Mr. Vijendra Kumar Jain is Respondent No. 1 (Erstwhile Resolution Professional of Transparent Energy System Pvt. Ltd., replacing IRP Ashish Vyas); Transparent Energy System Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 2 (Corporate Debtor / MSME); Mr. Ashok Atre is Respondent No. 3 (Successful Resolution Applicant / Former Director of Corporate Debtor)[cite: 32]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement dated 11.11.2002 for the supply of Multi Stage Evaporators (Effluent Treatment Plant) by Corporate Debtor to Appellant, which generated contractual disputes regarding alleged plant non-performance and culminated in an arbitral award in favor of Appellant on 19.03.2015 for Rs. 6,68,36,789.36 plus interest[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Arbitral award dated 19.03.2015 for Rs. 6,68,36,789.36 plus interest; Appellant filed claim in Form B on 03.06.2019 for Rs. 6,68,36,789.36; IRP initially admitted Rs. 16,78,510.35, but subsequently RP updated the admitted claim in the Information Memorandum to Rs. 11,46,28,813/-; the approved resolution plan allocated 'NIL' (zero) payment to Appellant's claim under Category H[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 9 against Corporate Debtor on 08.03.2019; public announcement on 09.03.2019; Appellant filed Form B on 03.06.2019; R-1 took over as RP in February 2020 and sought updated claim calculations on 21.05.2020; Appellant submitted updated calculations on 16.06.2020; NCLT heard approval application IA No. 07/MB/2021 on 11.02.2021 and approved the resolution plan on 16.04.2021; RP formally notified Appellant of plan approval and nil allocation on 30.04.2021[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitral award dated 19.03.2015; pending execution application before Pune Civil Court and un-stayed Section 34 arbitration challenge before Ankleshwar District Court; Summary of Payments in approved resolution plan categorizing operational creditors into F, G, H, I, J, K, and L without rational explanation; resolution plan text where SRA unilaterally declared the arbitral award 'void ab initio' and 'unlawful' due to an arbitrator's vacancy; registered valuer's report assessing corporate debtor's liquidation value at Rs. 11,43,51,143/-[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench in IA No. 07/MB/2021 approved the resolution plan on 16.04.2021 under Section 31; Appellant appealed under Section 61 asserting discrimination among operational creditors and disqualification of SRA under Section 29A[cite: 32].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an operational creditor whose claim is founded on an un-stayed, valid arbitral award can be arbitrarily assigned to a separate category and allocated 'zero' payment under a resolution plan while other operational creditors of the same class receive substantial payments[cite: 32]. 2. Whether a resolution applicant or RP has the adjudicatory jurisdiction to sit in judgment over an arbitral award, declare it 'void ab initio' in a resolution plan, and extinguish the claim on that basis[cite: 32]. 3. Whether promoters/directors of an MSME corporate debtor are disqualified under Section 29A of the Code from submitting a resolution plan[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the Committee of Creditors may classify operational creditors on rational grounds, it cannot subject an operational creditor holding an un-stayed arbitral award to hostile and arbitrary discrimination by allocating zero payment while paying other operational creditors, nor can a resolution applicant usurp judicial powers to invalidate a binding arbitral award in a resolution plan[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 31 and Regulation 38 mandates fair and equitable treatment of operational creditors; assigning an operational creditor zero payout on the pretext of an un-stayed arbitral challenge violates Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 32]; under Section 240A, the disqualifications under Section 29A(c) and (h) do not apply to MSMEs, allowing former promoters/directors of an MSME corporate debtor to submit a resolution plan[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an arbitral award has not been stayed or set aside by a competent court under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, it remains legally enforceable; inserting clauses in a resolution plan adjudicating the award as void ab initio is unlawful and must be expunged[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA was legally eligible under Section 240A, but the discriminatory zero payout to the Appellant was unsustainable; the plan is modified to pay Appellant the maximum percentage allocated to other operational creditors, with Rs. 1 Lakh costs imposed on the SRA[cite: 32].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 618 of 2021 is allowed[cite: 32]. The approved Resolution Plan is modified: objectionable clauses assailing the arbitral award are deleted, Appellant is directed to be paid the highest percentage of admitted claims paid to other operational creditor categories, RP is reprimanded for failure of duty, and Respondent No. 3 (SRA) is directed to pay Rs. 1 Lakh as litigation costs to the Appellant within 30 days[cite: 32].
summary: An operational creditor appealed an NCLT Mumbai order approving a resolution plan for Transparent Energy System Pvt. Ltd. submitted by its former promoter under the MSME exemption of Section 240A[cite: 32]. The approved plan allocated zero payment to the appellant by unilaterally declaring its arbitral award of Rs. 6.68 Crores 'void ab initio', while other operational creditors received payments[cite: 32]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT held that neither an SRA nor the CoC can usurp judicial authority to declare a valid arbitral award void, nor subject similarly situated operational creditors to arbitrary discrimination[cite: 32]. NCLAT directed payment to the appellant at the highest percentage granted to other operational creditors and imposed costs of Rs. 1 Lakh on the SRA[cite: 32].

case_title: M/s. KK Ropeways Limited vs. M/s. Billion Smiles Hospitality Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. KK Ropeways Limited is the Appellant/Petitioner/Operational Creditor; M/s. Billion Smiles Hospitality Private Limited is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lease/Rent Agreement dated 09.03.2015 under which Corporate Debtor leased commercial food court space ('Shop 2' and basement space at 'Savoy Greens', Jabli, Kasauli, HP) to operate a food counter under the name 'UPSOUTH', agreeing to monthly minimum guarantee rent of Rs. 40,000/- plus CAM charges of Rs. 39,375/-, water, and electricity dues[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of lease rentals and utility charges; dispute referred to arbitration (DIAC Ref. DAC/1854/12-17), resulting in an ex-parte arbitral award dated 29.11.2018 for Rs. 26,33,022/- with interest at 15% per annum; operational debt claimed in Form 5 petition was Rs. 23,02,523/- (with date of default stated as 19.01.2018), while demand notice claimed Rs. 22,39,927.43 and Information Utility record showed Rs. 28,75,314.58[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lease terminated by Corporate Debtor on 20.06.2017 w.e.f. 22.09.2017; arbitration clause invoked on 25.08.2017; ex-parte arbitral award passed on 29.11.2018; Section 8 demand notice issued on 21.02.2019; Corporate Debtor filed Section 34 challenge before Delhi High Court; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 276/BB/2019 filed before NCLT on 20.06.2019; NCLT dismissed it on 27.04.2021[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease Agreement dated 09.03.2015; termination notice dated 20.06.2017; ex-parte Arbitral Award dated 29.11.2018; pending Section 34 petition before the High Court of Delhi challenging the award[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench in CP (IB) No. 276/BB/2019 dismissed the Section 9 petition on 27.04.2021, holding that an arbitral award challenged under Section 34 constitutes a pre-existing dispute under the K. Kishan doctrine and that IBC cannot be used as an execution forum; Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 34].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an operational debt based on an arbitral award remains a 'disputed debt' under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the Code during the pendency of an appeal/application challenging the award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996[cite: 34]. 2. Whether an operational creditor can initiate corporate insolvency resolution under Section 9 of the Code solely for executing and recovering amounts granted under an arbitral award[cite: 34].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of challenge proceedings under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 against an arbitral award establishes that the underlying operational debt is subject to a real, pre-existing dispute, which statutorily mandates the dismissal of an application filed under Section 9 of the Code[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d), the Adjudicating Authority must reject a Section 9 petition if notice of dispute is shown; the filing and pendency of a Section 34 challenge demonstrates that a pre-existing dispute that culminated in an arbitral award continues through the statutory challenge stages until finality under Section 37 (K. Kishan doctrine)[cite: 34]; the Code is designed for corporate resolution, not as an enforcement or money execution substitute for recovering arbitral sums[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The undisputed fact that the corporate debtor has instituted a Section 34 application in a competent High Court to challenge an ex-parte arbitral award is sufficient evidence of a plausible, non-spurious pre-existing dispute without requiring the court to assess the likelihood of success of the challenge[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the arbitral award was sub judice under Section 34 before the Delhi High Court, the claimed operational debt was disputed, and the NCLT committed no legal error in dismissing the Section 9 petition[cite: 34].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 246 of 2021 is dismissed[cite: 34]. The order of the NCLT Bengaluru Bench dated 27.04.2021 in CP (IB) No. 276/BB/2019 is affirmed without costs[cite: 34]. Connected interlocutory applications are closed[cite: 34].
summary: An operational creditor appealed an NCLT Bengaluru order dismissing its Section 9 application against Billion Smiles Hospitality Private Limited, which was filed to recover lease dues of Rs. 23,02,523/- awarded in an ex-parte arbitral award[cite: 34]. The corporate debtor had challenged the award by filing an application under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before the Delhi High Court[cite: 34]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under the Supreme Court's ruling in K. Kishan, the pendency of a Section 34 petition establishes the continuation of a pre-existing dispute, barring CIRP initiation under Section 9(5)(ii)(d)[cite: 34]. Insolvency proceedings cannot be utilized as a summary execution tool for arbitral awards[cite: 34].

case_title: ITC Limited vs. Competition Commission of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: ITC Limited is the Appellant (Acquirer); Competition Commission of India (CCI) is the Respondent; Johnson & Johnson Pvt. Limited ('Seller No. 1') and Johnson & Johnson Pte. Limited ('Seller No. 2') are the Transferors[cite: 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two Brand Purchase Agreements dated 12.02.2015 executed between Appellant and the Sellers for the acquisition of registered trademarks 'Savlon' (Transaction-I) and 'Shower to Shower' (Transaction-II) together with attendant inventories, formulations, technical knowhow, moulds, and promotional materials without acquiring physical factories or employees[cite: 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory non-notification violation; relevant combined turnover attributable exclusively to the target trademarks 'Savlon' and 'Shower to Shower' was Rs. 68.37 Crores, well below the statutory de minimis exemption threshold of Rs. 750 Crores turnover / Rs. 250 Crores assets; CCI imposed a penalty of Rs. 5,00,000/- under Section 43A for failure to notify the combination under Section 6(2)[cite: 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Asset/trademark purchase agreements executed on 12.02.2015; MCA De Minimis Notification S.O. 482(E) issued on 04.03.2011; CCI issued information notice on 11.02.2016; Appellant responded on 08.03.2016; revised threshold notification S.O. 674(E) issued on 04.03.2016; CCI issued notice under Section 20(1) on 07.11.2016; Appellant filed Form-I combination notice under protest on 16.02.2017; MCA clarificatory notification S.O. 988(E) issued on 27.03.2017; CCI unconditionally approved the combination under Section 31(1) on 22.03.2017; show-cause notice under Section 43A issued on 29.03.2017; CCI passed penalty order on 11.12.2017[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Brand purchase agreements dated 12.02.2015; Form I combination notice filed on 16.02.2017; audited financial accounts establishing that the turnover attributable specifically to the acquired trademarks was Rs. 68.37 Crores; MCA Notification dated 27.03.2017 and Press Release dated 30.03.2017 clarifying that target-specific assets and turnover apply when acquiring a portion or division of an enterprise[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI held that acquisition of trademarks constituted acquisition of an enterprise under Section 5(a) and imposed a penalty of Rs. 5 Lakhs under Section 43A for failure to pre-notify under Section 6(2); Appellant appealed under Section 53B challenging the penalty in view of retrospective de minimis target exemptions[cite: 35].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Ministry of Corporate Affairs Notification S.O. 988(E) dated 27.03.2017, clarifying that only the assets and turnover attributable to the specific portion, division, or business being acquired must be considered for De Minimis thresholds under Section 5, operates with retrospective effect[cite: 35]. 2. Whether the acquisition of intellectual property rights/trademarks with an attributable turnover below the de minimis exemption threshold is exempt from mandatory pre-merger notification under Section 6(2), rendering any penalty under Section 43A unlawful[cite: 35].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory exemption notification issued under Section 54 that clarifies the methodology for calculating jurisdictional thresholds by evaluating only the assets and turnover attributable to the specific business, division, or target assets acquired (rather than the seller's total corporate turnover) is clarificatory and curative in nature and applies retrospectively (Eli Lilly doctrine)[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clarificatory notifications issued to remove ambiguities and advance ease of doing business without imposing new liabilities have retrospective effect under established rules of statutory construction (Vatika Township principle)[cite: 35]; where an acquisition of trademarks and related assets falls below the de minimis threshold of turnover and asset value attributable to the target assets, the transaction is exempt from the definition of a combination under Section 5, negating any statutory obligation to notify the CCI under Section 6(2)[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where audited accounts demonstrate that the turnover attributable strictly to the acquired trademarks (Rs. 68.37 Crores) is well below the statutory de minimis limit (Rs. 750 Crores), the target exemption applies, irrespective of the transferor's total global or domestic assets[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the transactions qualified for the de minimis target exemption under the retrospectively applied clarificatory notification, the appellant was under no statutory duty to file a combination notice under Section 6(2), and the penalty of Rs. 5 Lakhs under Section 43A was unsustainable[cite: 35].
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 11 of 2018 is allowed to the limited extent of setting aside the penalty[cite: 35]. The impugned order of the Competition Commission of India dated 11.12.2017 imposing a penalty of Rs. 5,00,000/- on the Appellant under Section 43A is quashed without costs[cite: 35].
summary: ITC Limited appealed a Competition Commission of India order imposing a penalty of Rs. 5 Lakhs under Section 43A for failing to notify its 2015 acquisition of 'Savlon' and 'Shower to Shower' trademarks from Johnson & Johnson under Section 6(2)[cite: 35]. The appellant argued that the transaction qualified for the De Minimis exemption, as the attributable turnover of the acquired brands was only Rs. 68.37 Crores[cite: 35]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT held that the MCA notification dated 27.03.2017—clarifying that only the assets and turnover of the specific business or portion acquired are relevant—is curative and applies retrospectively (following the Eli Lilly ruling)[cite: 35]. The acquisition was exempt, and the penalty was quashed[cite: 35].

case_title: Arvind Garg, Liquidator of Carnation Auto India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Jagdish Khattar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Arvind Garg is the Appellant (Liquidator of Carnation Auto India Pvt. Ltd.); Mr. Jagdish Khattar (since deceased) and his two sons Kunal Khattar and Gautam Khattar, along with widow Ms. Kiran Khattar as legal representatives, are Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt owed by Corporate Debtor Carnation Auto India Pvt. Ltd. to Punjab National Bank, culminating in CIRP and subsequent liquidation order dated 01.08.2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Avoidance of transactions application filed by the Liquidator under Sections 43, 45, 50, and 66 of the Code involving preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions; application dismissed by NCLT on 24.07.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition admitted on 25.09.2017; liquidation ordered on 01.08.2018; avoidance application dismissed on 24.07.2020; Respondent No. 1 Jagdish Khattar expired on 26.04.2021 (notified to tribunal on 12.07.2021); Appellant filed IA No. 2693 of 2021 on 29.11.2021 seeking details of legal heirs; NCLT disposed of IA 2693 on 24.08.2022; details provided via email on 08.09.2022; impleadment application IA No. 3473 of 2022 filed on 12.09.2022; delay condonation application IA No. 4401 of 2022 filed subsequently. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Death certificate and legal heir disclosures showing Ms. Kiran Khattar (wife), Gautam Khattar (son), and Kunal Khattar (son) as Class-I legal heirs of deceased Respondent No. 1. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Liquidator's avoidance application on 24.07.2020; Liquidator appealed under Section 61; during appeal pendency, Respondent No. 1 expired and NCLAT adjudicated applications for condonation of delay (IA No. 4401/2022) and impleadment of legal representatives (IA No. 3473/2022).
legal_issues: 1. Whether the delay in filing an application for impleadment of legal representatives of a deceased respondent beyond the 90-day period under Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1963 is condonable under Section 5 when the appellant lacked knowledge of legal heirs and was prosecuting interim discovery applications during the COVID-19 pandemic exclusion period[cite: 36]. 2. Whether the widow of a deceased respondent qualifies as a legal representative under Section 2(11) of the CPC and Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 to be impleaded in avoidance proceedings under Sections 66 and 67 of the Code[cite: 36].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a party is unaware of the legal representatives of a deceased respondent and pursues discovery applications with due diligence, and where limitation periods stand protected or excluded by Supreme Court suo motu COVID-19 extension orders, delay in filing an impleadment application is condonable upon showing sufficient cause under Section 5 of the Limitation Act[cite: 36]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 2(11) of the CPC, a 'legal representative' includes any person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person or intermeddles with it, which encompasses Class-I heirs under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; the impact of fraudulent transactions under Section 66 and 67 on the estate devolving upon legal heirs is adjudicated post-impleadment[cite: 36]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the appellant filed an immediate application to discover legal heirs upon learning of the death, and filed the formal impleadment motion within days of receiving details, sufficient cause is established to excuse any technical delay, especially when operating under the Supreme Court's limitation exclusion periods[cite: 36]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay in impleadment is condoned, and the legal representatives (widow and sons) are properly brought on record to represent the estate of deceased Respondent No. 1[cite: 36].
operative_order: IA No. 4401 of 2022 (condonation of delay) and IA No. 3473 of 2022 (impleadment of legal representatives) in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 743 of 2020 are allowed[cite: 36]. Ms. Kiran Khattar (wife), Mr. Gautam Khattar (son), and Mr. Kunal Khattar (son) are brought on record as legal representatives of deceased Respondent No. 1, and the amended memo of parties is taken on record[cite: 36].
summary: During the pendency of an appeal filed by the liquidator of Carnation Auto India Pvt. Ltd. against the dismissal of an avoidance application under Sections 43, 45, 50, and 66 of the Code, Respondent No. 1 Jagdish Khattar expired[cite: 36]. The liquidator filed applications for condonation of delay and impleadment of legal representatives (his widow and two sons)[cite: 36]. NCLAT allowed both applications, holding that the delay was sufficiently explained and covered by the Supreme Court's COVID-19 limitation exclusion orders, and that Class-I heirs representing the deceased's estate are proper legal representatives under Section 2(11) of the CPC[cite: 36].

case_title: M/s Tulip Star Hotels Ltd. & Anr. vs. Mr. Anish Niranjan Nanavaty & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Tulip Star Hotels Ltd. (Shareholder/Promoter) and Suspended Management of V Hotels Ltd. are Appellants; Mr. Anish Niranjan Nanavaty (Resolution Professional of V Hotels Ltd.) is Respondent No. 1; Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. (ARCIL) is the Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 2; V Hotels Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 08.03.2002, Corporate Debtor availed a term loan facility aggregating INR 129 Crores from a consortium of banks (BOI, PNB, UBI, Vijaya Bank, Indian Bank, Canara Bank) with uniform interest @13.50% quarterly rest, revised to 12.85% p.a. monthly rest from 01.04.2003. BOI, PNB, UBI, and Vijaya Bank assigned debt to ARCIL in 2009-10. An OTS sanction letter dated 28.02.2011 and Modification Agreement dated 29.09.2011 contemplated settlement for Rs. 150,75,83,970/- with revised interest @22% p.a. compounded monthly from 01.07.2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred when the Corporate Debtor failed to pay instalments under the settlement (including Rs. 17.50 crore due on 30.04.2013 and Rs. 17.50 crore on 31.05.2013). ARCIL issued SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice demanding Rs. 235,46,34,381/- plus 22% interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Settlement revoked by ARCIL via letter dated 17.06.2013. SARFAESI demand notice issued on 10.07.2013. Section 7 IBC application filed on 03.04.2018 and admitted on 31.05.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letter dated 28.02.2011, Modification Agreement dated 29.09.2011, Revocation Letter dated 17.06.2013, orders of DRT/DRAT/Bombay High Court rejecting ARCIL's plea to amend interest to 22% in OA 114/2005, and Supreme Court order dated 03.01.2019 leaving interest determination to the Tribunal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 532 of 2018 admitted on 31.05.2019 leaving interest rate open. RP filed MA No. 2886 of 2019 for determination of interest; Appellant filed IA No. 3114 of 2022 to stay CIRP pending determination. NCLT Mumbai Bench-II on 21.07.2023 allowed MA 2886/2019 fixing interest @22% and dismissed IA 3114/2022, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the rate of interest applicable for determining the financial claim of ARCIL in the CIRP proceedings of the Corporate Debtor should be 22% per annum compounded monthly as per the OTS/Modification Agreement or 14.85% per annum under the original contractual terms following ARCIL's revocation of the settlement agreement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor cannot simultaneously revoke a settlement agreement and enforce the enhanced contractual interest rates or terms that were agreed upon solely as part of that revoked settlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Appellate Tribunal interpreted contractual rights under the CIRP framework, determining that upon formal revocation of an OTS sanction letter, ancillary modification agreements dependent on the sanction cannot survive to impose penal interest rates of 22% p.a.; the debt calculation must revert to the original underlying loan agreements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the terms and interdependence of the Sanction Letter dated 28.02.2011, Modification Agreement dated 29.09.2011, and the Revocation Letter dated 17.06.2013, demonstrating that the higher 22% interest rate was offered strictly in lieu of concessions granted under the OTS. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because ARCIL expressly revoked the OTS settlement on 17.06.2013 and forfeited payments, the 22% rate became unenforceable, and the claim must be redetermined applying the original interest rate of 14.85% p.a.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1114-1115 of 2023 allowed; impugned order of NCLT dated 21.07.2023 set aside. Resolution Professional directed to re-verify ARCIL's claim at 14.85% interest within 2 weeks and place it before the CoC and Successful Resolution Applicant; Successful Resolution Applicant directed to prepare an Addendum within 2 weeks thereafter for CoC approval, to be submitted to NCLT Mumbai with the Resolution Plan approval application. CIRP extended by 60 days to complete the process. IA No. 3022 of 2023 and Contempt Case (AT) No. 21 of 2023 closed with no order as to costs.
summary: Tulip Star Hotels Limited and the suspended management challenged NCLT Mumbai's order fixing ARCIL's claim interest rate at 22% per annum under a revoked OTS settlement and modification agreement. The Appellants contended the interest should be the original contractual rate of 14.85% since ARCIL revoked the OTS on 17.06.2013. NCLAT agreed, holding that a creditor cannot revoke a settlement while selectively enforcing its higher interest rate clause, rendering the modification agreement non-surviving. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the NCLT order, fixed the interest rate at 14.85%, directed redetermination of ARCIL's admitted claim, required an addendum to the approved resolution plan, and granted a 60-day CIRP extension.

case_title: Sabari Realty Private Limited vs. Sivana Realty Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1162 of 2023 (with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1178 & 1179 of 2023)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sabari Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/allottee/shareholder); Sivana Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, formerly Sunshine Housing Pvt. Ltd.); Manish Jaju (Resolution Professional/Respondent No. 1); M/s Kabra Estate & Investment Consultants (Successful Resolution Applicant/Respondent No. 2); Pratik Jayesh Vira / Kalpataru Advisory Services Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant and sister concern held 36.69% equity shares in Corporate Debtor and advanced Rs. 7 Crores loan. Corporate Debtor mortgaged Phase-I (Wings C & D) and Phase-II projects to LIC Housing Finance Ltd. on 15.09.2017 requiring prior NOC for creating third-party rights. Corporate Debtor issued an allotment letter dated 05.04.2018 for 25 flats (12,515.09 sq. ft.) to Appellant without obtaining LIC HFL's NOC, adjusting Rs. 14.64 Crores against loan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose leading to CIRP initiation against the Corporate Debtor; Appellant submitted Form CA for 25 units claiming status as homebuyer/financial creditor in a class while disclosing itself as a related party. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Mortgage executed on 15.09.2017; allotment on 05.04.2018; share transfer agreement dated 31.10.2018; CIRP initiated on 11.08.2020 on application by Spartan Engineering Industries Pvt. Ltd.; Form CA filed 11.01.2021; plan approved by CoC on 22.11.2021 with 99.96% vote share. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Mortgage Deed with negative lien/NOC covenant, Form CA where Appellant admitted being a related party under Section 5(24), MCA/ROC records showing unexecuted share transfer, and Resolution Plan classifying allottees into Affected (no NOC) and Unaffected (with NOC). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V on 19.07.2023 passed three orders: approving Resolution Plan (IA 2981/2021), rejecting Appellant's plan objection (IA 933/2022), and dismissing register rectification (IA 533/2022).
legal_issues: Whether the Appellant was disentitled from CoC membership as a related party; whether an individual dissenting homebuyer can challenge a resolution plan approved by a majority of creditors in class under Section 25A; and whether sub-classifying homebuyers into 'Affected' (allotted without mortgagee NOC) and 'Unaffected' (allotted with NOC) violates Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC, homebuyers as a class are bound by the majority vote of that class, and an individual allottee cannot maintain an independent challenge against the approved resolution plan; furthermore, reasonable inter-se differentiation among allottees based on objective legal criteria (such as valid mortgagee NOC status) does not violate Section 30(2)(e). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(24) and Section 21(2) bar related parties from CoC representation where unrectified company registers and self-declarations establish continuous shareholding; Section 25A mandates that minority class members sail with the majority class decision. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Intelligible differentia test under commercial wisdom of CoC, establishing that units sold in violation of registered mortgage covenants legally differentiate Affected Allottees from Unaffected Allottees. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC acted within its commercial wisdom to cancel defective allotments and re-allot reduced area while curing defects with the secured mortgagee; Appellant's status as a related party and bound class member precluded relief.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1162 of 2023, 1178 of 2023, and 1179 of 2023 are dismissed. Orders of the Adjudicating Authority dated 19.07.2023 approving the Resolution Plan and rejecting IA No. 533 of 2022 and IA No. 933 of 2022 are affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Sabari Realty Private Limited challenged the approval of a resolution plan submitted by Kabra Estate for Sivana Realty, along with the rejection of its objections and rectification application. The Appellant contested its exclusion from the CoC as a related party and assailed the plan's classification of homebuyers into 'Affected' (without mortgagee LIC HFL NOC, receiving 20% area) and 'Unaffected' (with NOC, retaining 100% area). NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that the Appellant had self-declared as a related party, that an individual homebuyer cannot challenge a plan approved by the majority of homebuyers in class, and that sub-classifying allottees based on mortgage compliance was a valid exercise of CoC commercial wisdom.

case_title: Puro Naturals JV vs. Shree Warana Sahakari Bank Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 661-663 of 2023 (with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 651 & 1005 of 2023)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Puro Naturals JV (Successful Resolution Applicant/Appellant); Ritesh R. Mahajan (Resolution Professional/Appellant in Comp App 651/2023); Narayan Shivaji Patil & Ors. (38 Sugarcane Farmers/Creditors/Appellants in Comp App 1005/2023); Shivaji Cane Processors Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Shree Warana Sahakari Bank Ltd. and Kolhapur Urban Co-operative Bank Ltd. (Dissenting Secured Financial Creditors/Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor operated a sugar manufacturing mill. Secured financial facilities were extended by a consortium of lenders and financial institutions secured by company assets, promoter assets, and promoter personal guarantees. Total admitted secured financial debt was Rs. 49,97,14,297/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on debt facilities led ASREC (India) Ltd. to initiate CIRP under Section 7. Total admitted claims across classes stood at Rs. 95,58,50,796/-. SRA offered Rs. 43,82,17,730/- against a liquidation value of Rs. 21,15,61,184/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 18.02.2021. Resolution plan submitted on 02.07.2021, revised on 29.07.2021, and approved at the 6th CoC meeting on 30.07.2021 with 78.03% majority. RP filed approval IA No. 2165 of 2021 immediately thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan clauses C-3(I)-(V), providing Rs. 26.64 Crores for secured creditors with Rs. 2 Crores allocated for assignment/extinguishment of balance debt, promoter personal guarantees, and securities; dissenting financial creditors to be paid in priority over assenting creditors, with SRA undertaking full payment within 90 days. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V vide order dated 01.05.2023 rejected RP's approval application (IA 2165/2021) and allowed objections (IA 112/2022 and IA 963/2022) relying on NCLT Indore's Ujaas Energy order, ruling that a plan cannot extinguish dissenting creditors' personal guarantees without consent.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan approved by the CoC can validly provide for the extinguishment or assignment of third-party personal guarantees and securities of dissenting secured financial creditors without their express consent under Section 30(2)(e); and whether the deferred payout structure to dissenting financial creditors violated Section 30(2)(b) and CIRP Regulation 38(1)(b).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan approved by the requisite majority of the CoC can lawfully provide for the extinguishment, release, or assignment of personal guarantees and security interests granted to secured financial creditors (including dissenting financial creditors), as dealing with security interests forms an integral part of the commercial wisdom of the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) and Regulation 38(1)(b) mandate priority of payment in monetary value relative to assenting creditors, but do not require immediate cash upfront payment at day one if priority of timing and payment terms is preserved. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Adherence to Section 30(2) statutory minimums, verifying that the proposed payout exceeded the liquidation value due under Section 53(1) and satisfied the commercial wisdom threshold endorsed in SVA Family Welfare Trust (Ujaas Energy reversal). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's reliance on the overturned Indore Bench decision was erroneous; the resolution plan fully complied with Section 30(2) and Regulation 38, particularly following the SRA's clarification to disburse 100% of dissenting dues within 90 days.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 661-663 of 2023, 651 of 2023, and 1005 of 2023 are allowed. The NCLT Mumbai order dated 01.05.2023 is set aside. IA No. 2165 of 2021 is allowed, and the Resolution Plan submitted by Puro Naturals JV is approved. IA No. 112 of 2022 and IA No. 963 of 2022 filed by dissenting banks are rejected. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Puro Naturals JV, the RP, and sugarcane farmers appealed against NCLT Mumbai's rejection of an approved resolution plan for Shivaji Cane Processors Limited. The NCLT had rejected the plan because it extinguished promoter personal guarantees of dissenting financial creditors (Shree Warana Sahakari Bank and Kolhapur Urban Co-operative Bank) without consent. NCLAT set aside the order, holding that CoC commercial wisdom encompasses the extinguishment and assignment of guarantees and securities of dissenting creditors under Section 30(2), following the precedent in Ujaas Energy. Finding the payout compliant with Section 30(2)(b) and Regulation 38, NCLAT approved the resolution plan.

case_title: Mr. Sunil Tangri & Anr. vs. Mrs. Ashu Gupta, Resolution Professional of Webtech Packagings India Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1070 of 2021 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1121 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Sunil Tangri and Mrs. Ramni Tangri (Suspended Directors/Promoters of the Corporate Debtor/Resolution Applicants) are Appellants[cite: 6]; Mrs. Ashu Gupta (Resolution Professional, later appointed Liquidator of Webtech Packagings India Pvt. Ltd.) is the Respondent[cite: 6]; M/s Webtech Packagings India Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]; M/s AC Goel Paper Distributing Company Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor[cite: 6]; M/s Siemens Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. is the sole Financial Creditor/sole CoC member[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed operational credit and financial credit facilities, and while experiencing severe financial distress, its management engaged in extensive transactions, including routing funds through related entity M/s Arthah Trading Company, drawing excessive director remuneration, writing off debit balances, disposing of plant assets for undocumented cash consideration, and altering Tally data post-CIRP[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in payments to Operational Creditor leading to Section 9 admission; total provisionally admitted claims were Rs. 4,04,76,290/-; Appellant submitted a resolution plan of Rs. 1,58,07,532/-; while the Forensic Audit Report quantified total fraudulent/misappropriated transactions at Rs. 29,75,73,550/-[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 25.07.2019[cite: 6]; Forensic Audit Report delivered by M/s VMRS & Associates on 22.09.2020[cite: 6]; revised resolution plan approved by CoC on 18.11.2020[cite: 6]; RP filed Section 66 application (IA 102/2021) on 04.12.2020/08.12.2020[cite: 6]; Section 30(6) plan approval application (IA 5756/2020) filed on 29.12.2020[cite: 6]; NCLT passed Section 66 contribution order on 12.11.2021[cite: 6]; NCLT rejected resolution plan and ordered liquidation on 02.08.2023[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic Audit Report documenting 14 specific fraudulent heads totaling Rs. 29,75,73,550/- including stock diversion of Rs. 5,48,50,824/-, related entity transactions of Rs. 24,02,726/-, unprovided doubtful sundry debts of Rs. 2,20,46,314/-, excessive remuneration of Rs. 1,89,14,000/-, unexplained expenses of Rs. 5,91,60,261/-, and 17 post-CIRP journal entries totaling Rs. 8,53,67,678/-[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Court-II) allowed Section 66 application on 12.11.2021 directing Appellants to contribute Rs. 29,75,73,550/- and ordered criminal prosecution[cite: 6]; subsequently, vide order dated 02.08.2023, NCLT dismissed IA 5756/2020 and ordered liquidation under Section 33(1)(b) because the promoter became disqualified under Section 29A(g) pursuant to the 12.11.2021 order[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether the application under Section 66 of the IBC was barred by limitation or vitiated due to delay beyond CIRP model timelines under Regulations 35A and 40A; whether reliance on a Forensic Audit Report without statutory auditor corroboration was legally valid; and whether an order determining fraudulent transactions under Section 66 renders the promoter-applicant ineligible under Section 29A(g) at the stage of plan consideration, mandating plan rejection and liquidation even for an MSME entity under Section 240A[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order passed by the Adjudicating Authority establishing fraudulent or wrongful trading under Section 66 operates as an absolute disqualification under Section 29A(g) of the IBC, which applies continuously throughout the CIRP and prevents an ineligible promoter from having their resolution plan approved, requiring rejection of the plan and mandatory liquidation under Section 33(1)(b)[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A(g) is a non-curable disqualification not exempted for MSMEs under Section 240A; the bar is not restricted solely to the date of submission of the plan but extends to the date of its consideration and approval by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 6]. Furthermore, timelines under Regulation 35A and Regulation 40A are directory and not mandatory[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Findings in an independent expert forensic audit report, evaluated against financial trends, lack of management substantiation, and unadjudicated company balance reconciliations, constitute sufficient evidence of intent to defraud creditors under Section 66[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants were conclusively liable to contribute Rs. 29,75,73,550/- under Section 66, which attracted Section 29A(g) disqualification; because the resolution applicant was ineligible, the plan was rightly rejected and liquidation was lawfully ordered[cite: 6].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1070 of 2021 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1121 of 2023 are dismissed[cite: 6]. The impugned orders of NCLT New Delhi dated 12.11.2021 (directing contribution and criminal prosecution under Section 66/69) and dated 02.08.2023 (rejecting the Resolution Plan and ordering liquidation under Section 33) are affirmed[cite: 6]. Pending interlocutory applications are closed with no order as to costs[cite: 6].
summary: Suspended directors of Webtech Packagings India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against two NCLT New Delhi orders: an order under Section 66 directing them to contribute Rs. 29.75 Crores for fraudulent trading, and a subsequent order rejecting their MSME resolution plan and ordering liquidation due to Section 29A(g) disqualification[cite: 6]. Appellants argued that CIRP model timelines were breached, the forensic audit was uncorroborated, and Section 29A eligibility should be determined only at the date of plan submission[cite: 6]. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that procedural timelines in Regulation 35A are directory, forensic findings established fraudulent diversion, and disqualification under Section 29A(g) persists throughout the CIRP, barring plan approval and necessitating liquidation[cite: 6].

case_title: Jaiprakash Associates Limited vs. Jaypee Infratech Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 302 of 2023 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 507 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jaiprakash Associates Limited (JAL, holding company/construction contractor/Appellant in Comp App 302/2023)[cite: 7]; Jaypee Infratech Limited (JIL, Corporate Debtor under CIRP represented by its Implementation and Monitoring Committee/Appellant in Comp App 507/2023)[cite: 7]; Suraksha Realty Limited and Lakshdeep Investments and Finance Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicants)[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: JAL established JIL as an SPV in 2007 for the Yamuna Expressway Project[cite: 7]. JIL awarded construction contracts to JAL and advanced mobilization funds recoverable against Running Account (RA) bills, alongside Interest Free Maintenance Deposits (IFMD)[cite: 7]. Pursuant to Supreme Court orders in Chitra Sharma, JAL deposited Rs. 750 Crores into Court, which was held to be JAL's property in Jaypee Kensington, subject to an independent reconciliation by Grant Thornton (GT) regarding construction advances[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP was triggered against JIL under Section 7[cite: 7]. Independent reconciliation by GT identified Rs. 536.49 Crores as undisputed amount receivable by JIL/homebuyers from JAL, Rs. 106.90 Crores as disputed IFMD receivable by homebuyers, Rs. 12.26 Crores under mutual dispute, and Rs. 70.89 Crores claimed by JIL under a Land Swap Deal[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: JIL CIRP commenced on 09.08.2017[cite: 7]; Supreme Court Jaypee Kensington judgment pronounced on 24.03.2021[cite: 7]; GT Final Report submitted on 13.08.2021[cite: 7]; NCLT Allahabad/Principal Bench passed impugned order on 07.03.2023 in IA 2593/PB/2021[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Grant Thornton Reconciliation Report dated 13.08.2021, minutes of joint reconciliation meeting dated 24.12.2021 resolving Rs. 12.26 Crores on 50:50 basis, balance sheets of JIL classifying invoked bank guarantees of Rs. 212 Crores as other financial liabilities, and sub-lease deeds executed with ICICI Bank for the Land Swap Deal[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Principal Bench) vide order dated 07.03.2023 directed that out of Rs. 750 Crores and accrued interest, Rs. 649.52 Crores (Rs. 536.49 Cr undisputed + Rs. 6.13 Cr mutually agreed + Rs. 106.90 Cr IFMD) plus proportionate interest be disbursed to JIL/homebuyers, and only Rs. 100.48 Crores plus proportionate interest be refunded to JAL[cite: 7].
legal_issues: What constitutes the true scope and ambit of the reconciliation of accounts between JAL and JIL under the Supreme Court's Jaypee Kensington judgment; whether pre-CIRP claims of JAL (invoked bank guarantees of Rs. 212 Cr, RA bills of Rs. 49.63 Cr, facility management bills of Rs. 2.33 Cr, and hospitality bills of Rs. 1.19 Cr) could be set off against construction receivables of JIL; whether JIL was entitled to recover Rs. 70.89 Crores under a Land Swap Deal; and whether the NCLT could lawfully award proportionate accrued interest on JIL's receivable portion out of JAL's Rs. 750 Crore asset pool[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A court-ordered reconciliation directed specifically to determine excess construction advances recoverable by a corporate debtor from its holding company out of a designated deposit does not extend to adjudicating or setting off the holding company's operational or financial claims against the corporate debtor, which must strictly follow the statutory waterfall and claim collation mechanisms under the IBC[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 and Section 53 prohibit preferential set-offs of pre-CIRP operational debts outside the CIRP process; Supreme Court directions under Article 142 restricted the reconciliation strictly to construction advances under contract, excluding general trade receivables and non-construction land swaps[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Terms of the Supreme Court's mandate in Jaypee Kensington (paras 189-191.1) and verification that advances given by JIL were contractually interest-free, alongside IFMD receipts which also carried no interest covenants[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Rs. 750 Crores deposit and its total accrued interest belong to JAL; since the underlying construction advances and IFMD carried no interest obligations, NCLT had no legal basis to award proportionate interest to JIL; JAL's pre-CIRP counterclaims and JIL's land swap claim of Rs. 70.89 Crores fell outside the scope of reconciliation[cite: 7].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 302 of 2023 is partly allowed by setting aside the direction in Para 111 of NCLT's order awarding proportionate interest to JIL/homebuyers, while rejecting all other set-off claims of JAL[cite: 7]. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 507 of 2023 is disposed of, affirming that findings on issues (a), (b), (d), and (e) favoring JAL were unsustainable, and upholding the rejection of JIL's Rs. 70.89 Crore Land Swap claim[cite: 7]. Out of Rs. 750 Crores, principal sum of Rs. 649.52 Crores is payable to JIL/homebuyers without interest, and the remainder along with the entire accrued interest on the Rs. 750 Crores belongs to JAL[cite: 7]. No costs[cite: 7].
summary: JAL and JIL cross-appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench order appropriating Rs. 649.52 Crores plus proportionate interest to JIL from the Rs. 750 Crores deposited by JAL in the Supreme Court[cite: 7]. JAL sought set-off of Rs. 212 Crores (invoked bank guarantees) and pre-CIRP bills and challenged the grant of interest to JIL[cite: 7]. JIL sought recovery of Rs. 70.89 Crores from a land swap deal[cite: 7]. NCLAT held that reconciliation under Jaypee Kensington was strictly confined to excess construction advances and could not permit pre-CIRP set-offs bypassing the IBC waterfall[cite: 7]. NCLAT upheld the principal appropriation of Rs. 649.52 Crores to JIL, rejected the land swap claim, but set aside the award of proportionate interest, confirming that all accrued interest on the deposit belongs to JAL[cite: 7].

case_title: Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Anuj Jain, IRP of M/s Jaypee Infratech Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax, Circle 5(1)(1), Noida is the Appellant (Operational Creditor)[cite: 8]; Mr. Anuj Jain, IRP of M/s Jaypee Infratech Limited (JIL) is Respondent No. 1[cite: 8]; Suraksha Realty Limited and Lakshdeep Investments and Finance Pvt. Ltd. are the Successful Resolution Applicants/Respondent Nos. 2 & 3[cite: 8]; M/s Jaypee Infratech Limited is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was assessed for income tax; the Department treated land parcel transfers under the Yamuna Expressway Concession Agreement as revenue subsidy, projecting an annual addition of Rs. 3,000 Crores over 36 years (aggregate Rs. 33,000 Crores presumptive liability) and issuing assessment demands for AY 2010-11 and AY 2012-13[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant filed Form B on 28.09.2017 claiming Rs. 3,334.29 Crores (AY 2010-11 demand of Rs. 2,058 Cr, and AY 2012-13 demand of Rs. 1,276 Cr)[cite: 8]. Subsequent ITAT/CIT orders reduced AY 2010-11 demand to NIL, leaving a crystallized demand of Rs. 1157,07,72,480/- for AY 2012-13[cite: 8]. The approved Resolution Plan allocated Rs. 0.10 Crore against the Department's operational claims[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against JIL on 09.08.2017[cite: 8]; Claim filed in Form B on 28.09.2017[cite: 8]; IRP response on claim admissibility issued on 29.01.2018[cite: 8]; Supreme Court recommenced CIRP on 09.08.2018 (Chitra Sharma) and later remitted plan consideration on 24.03.2021 (Jaypee Kensington)[cite: 8]; NCLT New Delhi Special Bench approved Suraksha's plan on 07.03.2023[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form B claim submitted by Department, IRP letter dated 29.01.2018 classifying AY 2012-13 as contingent liability due to pending ITAT appeal, list of creditors dated 29.05.2021 reflecting Department's claim, and approved Resolution Plan Clauses 19.1 to 19.3 allocating Rs. 10 Lakhs[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution plan submitted by Suraksha Realty and Lakshdeep Investments was approved by CoC and sanctioned by NCLT New Delhi Special Bench in IA 2836/2021 on 07.03.2023, while declining blanket extinguishment of income tax proceedings in paras 132-136[cite: 8]; Appellant appealed under Section 61 challenging the adequacy of the Rs. 10 Lakhs payout against its Rs. 1,157 Crore tax claim[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether the claim of the Income Tax Department for AY 2012-13 was non-existent merely because an appeal was pending before ITAT; whether the projected tax liability of Rs. 33,000 Crores stood extinguished by the Supreme Court in Jaypee Kensington; and whether an allocation of Rs. 10 Lakhs against a statutory operational tax claim exceeding Rs. 1,157 Crores violates Section 30(2)(b) and Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC when the liquidation value for operational creditors is nil[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A government authority holding an operational debt is entitled under Section 30(2)(b) to an amount not less than what it would receive under Section 53(1) in the event of liquidation; if the liquidation value apportioned to operational creditors is nil, an approved resolution plan providing a nominal token amount does not violate Section 30(2) or Section 31 of the IBC[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(6) encompasses disputed claims; pendency of an appeal before a tax appellate tribunal does not render an assessment claim non-existent, but its operational character remains subject to the priority and liquidation value limitations of Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53(1)[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the Corporate Debtor's liquidation waterfall under Section 53(1), establishing that secured financial debts exceeded the liquidation value, resulting in zero liquidation value for operational creditors[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Even though the Appellant's claim for AY 2012-13 was validly subsisting and not extinguished, its entitlement under Section 53(1) in liquidation was nil; therefore, the Resolution Plan's allocation of Rs. 10 Lakhs fully satisfied Section 30(2)(b) and did not warrant appellate interference[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 549 of 2023 is dismissed[cite: 8]. The impugned order of NCLT New Delhi Special Bench dated 07.03.2023 approving the Resolution Plan is affirmed with observations[cite: 8]. Interlocutory Applications IA No. 2910 of 2023, IA No. 2331 of 2023, and IA No. 3704 of 2023 are disposed of[cite: 8]. No order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: The Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax challenged the NCLT Special Bench order approving Suraksha Realty's resolution plan for Jaypee Infratech Limited, contending that its crystallized tax claim of Rs. 1,157.07 Crores for AY 2012-13 was wrongfully treated as non-existent and settled for a paltry Rs. 10 Lakhs[cite: 8]. Respondents argued the claim was extinguished under Jaypee Kensington and that the liquidation value was nil[cite: 8]. NCLAT held that while the tax claim was not non-existent or extinguished, the department is an operational creditor[cite: 8]. Since the liquidation value for operational creditors was nil under Section 53(1), the resolution plan providing Rs. 10 Lakhs complied fully with Section 30(2)(b) and required no interference[cite: 8].

case_title: Deputy Commissioner, UTGST, Daman vs. Rajeev Dhingra, IRP of Radha Madhav Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1245 of 2022 (with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1262, 1340 & 1542 of 2022)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Deputy Commissioner UTGST Daman (Appellant in Comp App 1245 & 1340/2022)[cite: 9]; Assistant Commissioner CGST & Central Excise Daman (Appellant in Comp App 1542/2022)[cite: 9]; CRP Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant/Appellant in Comp App 1262/2022)[cite: 9]; Rajeev Dhingra (RP of Corporate Debtor/Respondent)[cite: 9]; Vama Construction Company (Successful Resolution Applicant/Respondent)[cite: 9]; Radha Madhav Corporation Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor underwent CIRP; statutory tax and penalty liabilities arose under UTGST and Central Excise/CGST laws[cite: 9]. SRA submitted a resolution plan of Rs. 36.40 Crores against admitted secured debt of approximately Rs. 533.64 Crores[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP initiated on 22.10.2020; liquidation value was Rs. 57.84 Crores and fair value Rs. 75.65 Crores[cite: 9]. UTGST filed a belated claim of Rs. 26.51 Crores on 09.11.2021; AC-CGST claimed penalty dues of Rs. 37.73 Crores on 02.11.2021[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 22.10.2020[cite: 9]; public announcement on 12.11.2020 fixed claim submission deadline as 25.11.2020[cite: 9]; 90-day extended claim period expired on 24.02.2021[cite: 9]; resolution plan submission deadline expired on 26.10.2021[cite: 9]; plan approved by 100% CoC on 20.12.2021[cite: 9]; NCLT approved plan on 01.08.2022[cite: 9]; NCLT dismissed statutory claims applications on 28.09.2022[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP's written letters to UTGST dated 17.03.2021, 09.07.2021, and 24.08.2021 requesting claims in Form B; post-CIRP show-cause notices and orders dated 26.02.2021 and 20.10.2021 creating new demands; CRP's delayed plan submission lacking EMD and mandatory RFRP documents; approved Resolution Plan allocating Rs. 10 Lakhs for Operational Creditors and Rs. 25 Lakhs for Government dues[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-1 approved Vama's resolution plan in IA 78/2022 on 01.08.2022 (first impugned order)[cite: 9], and consequently dismissed IA 265/2022 (UTGST) and IA 223/2022 (AC-CGST) as infructuous on 28.09.2022 (second impugned order)[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant (CRP) has locus standi under Section 61 to challenge the approval of a resolution plan; whether the RP and CoC committed any material irregularity in rejecting a non-compliant, belated resolution plan; whether the RP is legally obligated under Regulation 12(2) to accept statutory tax claims filed long after the extended 90-day period; and whether the Supreme Court judgment in Rainbow Papers invalidates a resolution plan approved prior to that judgment where tax demands were generated after CIRP commencement[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsuccessful resolution applicant has no locus standi to challenge an approved resolution plan or its implementation under Section 61(1) of the IBC; furthermore, the RP has no legal discretion to admit claims submitted after the expiry of the 90-day window under Regulation 12(2) of the CIRP Regulations, particularly after the CoC has approved a resolution plan[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 12(2) provides a strict outer limit of 90 days from the insolvency commencement date for submission of claims; the Rainbow Papers ruling applies only where statutory demands/recovery proceedings were initiated prior to CIRP, and cannot be extended to post-CIRP assessment orders under prospective overruling principles[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict adherence to statutory CIRP timelines, examination of RFRP non-compliances by the prospective bidder, and proof of timely public notice demonstrating that the RP issued reminders and that tax authorities slept over their claims[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of CRP's defective plan fell within the commercial wisdom of the CoC; the RP lawfully rejected the time-barred claims of UTGST and AC-CGST, and the approved resolution plan did not suffer from any illegality[cite: 9].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1245, 1262, 1340, and 1542 of 2022 are dismissed[cite: 9]. The orders of the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dated 01.08.2022 (approving the Resolution Plan) and dated 28.09.2022 (dismissing the interim applications of the tax authorities) are affirmed[cite: 9]. Parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 9].
summary: Four appeals were filed challenging the approval of Vama Construction Company's resolution plan for Radha Madhav Corporation Ltd. and the rejection of belated statutory claims by UTGST and AC-CGST, as well as an appeal by an unsuccessful bidder (CRP)[cite: 9]. CRP contended its plan was wrongly rejected, while the tax departments argued their claims were improperly excluded contrary to Rainbow Papers[cite: 9]. NCLAT dismissed all four appeals, holding that an unsuccessful bidder lacks locus to assail an approved plan, the RP has no authority to entertain claims filed beyond the 90-day period under Regulation 12(2), and Rainbow Papers was distinguishable as the present tax demands were issued after CIRP commencement[cite: 9].

case_title: Babu Lal Aggarwal & Ors. vs. Manish Kumar & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1093 of 2022 (with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1273 & 377 of 2022 and 967 of 2021)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SAJ Housing Pvt. Ltd. (SHPL, Developer/Appellant in Comp App 1093/2022)[cite: 10]; Babu Lal Aggarwal and Puneet Aggarwal (Suspended Directors of Corporate Debtor/Appellants in Comp App 967/2021, 377/2022, 1273/2022)[cite: 10]; Manish Kumar and Renu Kumar (Financial Creditors/Respondents)[cite: 10]; Ms. Priyanka Chouhan (Resolution Professional, later Liquidator/Respondent)[cite: 10]; M/s Drishti India Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor owned 10 acres of freehold land at village Lakkarpur, Faridabad[cite: 10]. On 20.12.2011, Respondent No. 2 disbursed Rs. 1.90 Crores directly via RTGS into the Corporate Debtor's account with an expectation of benefit from land development[cite: 10]. Subsequently, on 29.05.2012, Corporate Debtor executed a Development Agreement (DA) with SHPL granting 56% built-up rights to SHPL for Rs. 16.15 Crores consideration[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disbursed amount was Rs. 1.90 Crores, reflected as 'long-term borrowing' in Corporate Debtor's balance sheets[cite: 10]. Default occurred on 13.07.2021 upon non-repayment[cite: 10]. SHPL later claimed Rs. 148,33,59,926/-[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application CP(IB) No. 354/2021 admitted on 01.11.2021[cite: 10]; public announcement on 04.11.2021 set claim deadline as 17.11.2021[cite: 10]; 3rd CoC meeting on 19.02.2022 resolved to liquidate the Corporate Debtor[cite: 10]; SHPL filed claim on 25.02.2022, which was rejected on 28.02.2022[cite: 10]; NCLT ordered liquidation on 04.08.2022[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Canara Bank passbook verifying direct RTGS transfer of Rs. 1.90 Crores on 20.12.2011[cite: 10]; audited balance sheet as of 31.03.2020 showing Rs. 1.90 Crores under 'Long-term borrowings'[cite: 10]; letter dated 26.03.2012 referencing development of land[cite: 10]; DA dated 29.05.2012 showing reciprocal profit-sharing between CD and SHPL[cite: 10]; minutes of 3rd CoC meeting noting company had no business operations, no employees, and sole unapproved land asset[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted Section 7 application on 01.11.2021 (first impugned order)[cite: 10]; later, in IA 960/2022, NCLT approved the 100% CoC resolution to liquidate the Corporate Debtor on 04.08.2022, disposing of SHPL's IA 1447/2022 with liberty to claim before the liquidator (second impugned order)[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether a direct advance of Rs. 1.90 Crores reflected as a long-term borrowing qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5(8) on the basis of time value of money, even in the absence of a written interest covenant; whether an investment under a reciprocal Development Agreement constitutes an operational debt or financial debt; and whether the CoC can resolve to liquidate the Corporate Debtor under Section 33(2) before completing 180 days or inviting resolution plans when the business has ceased operations[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance of money made with the expectation of economic return or commercial gain from land development entails the time value of money under Section 5(8) even if interest is not expressly stipulated, constituting a financial debt; additionally, the CoC in its commercial wisdom possesses full statutory discretion under Section 33(2) to resolve to liquidate a non-functional corporate debtor at any stage prior to plan approval[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) encompasses transactions with commercial effect of borrowing; Section 33(2) contains an Explanation empowering the CoC to decide liquidation at any time before plan confirmation, without being mandated to run the entire 180-day CIRP period or invite futile resolution plans[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bank records confirming direct fund disbursement, audited balance sheet entries acknowledging subsisting debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and examination of commercial functionality showing zero operations and employees[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Admission under Section 7 was valid; developer SHPL was a consortium partner entitled only to operational/other creditor status; and the 100% CoC decision to liquidate a non-operating company was a legitimate commercial decision subsuming the initial admission[cite: 10].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1093 of 2022, 1273 of 2022, 377 of 2022, and 967 of 2021 are dismissed[cite: 10]. The second impugned order dated 04.08.2022 ordering liquidation is affirmed and has subsumed the admission order dated 01.11.2021[cite: 10]. The liquidator is directed to proceed with liquidation and allow SHPL to submit its claim before the liquidator[cite: 10]. No order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary: Suspended directors and a real estate developer (SAJ Housing) appealed against the Section 7 admission and subsequent liquidation of Drishti India Limited[cite: 10]. Appellants claimed that a Rs. 1.90 Crore deposit was a non-refundable development deposit lacking time value of money, that SAJ Housing should have been a financial creditor, and that the CoC acted prematurely by voting for liquidation after only 38 days[cite: 10]. NCLAT dismissed all appeals, holding that funds advanced with an expectation of economic gain carry the time value of money under Section 5(8), that developer claims based on profit-sharing are not financial debts, and that under Section 33(2) the CoC has full commercial discretion to liquidate a non-functional company without employees or ongoing business at any stage[cite: 10].

case_title: Securities and Exchange Board of India vs. Mr. Girish Sriram Juneja & Anr.
material_facts: 1.
