FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Chronology of inter-party correspondence, settlement meeting minutes, and requisition notice for EoGM in 2014 relied upon by the petitioners to plead continuous oppression and refute claims of laches. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Transferred petition TP 120/2016 pending before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench. Appellants filed IA 16/2016 seeking dismissal of the petition on grounds of delay, laches, and limitation. By order dated 29.05.2017, NCLT dismissed IA 16/2016, holding limitation to be a mixed question of fact and law reserved for final hearing. Appellants did not appeal that order, but filed IA 259/2017 under Section 420(2) seeking review/recall of the 29.05.2017 order. On 16.02.2018, NCLT dismissed the application for lack of review jurisdiction, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has the statutory or inherent power to review or recall its own substantive orders under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 or Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016. 2. Whether the omission to discuss specific precedents cited in written submissions concerning limitation and laches constitutes a 'mistake apparent from the record' rectifiable under Section 420(2).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The power of judicial review is not an inherent power and must be expressly conferred by statute; the rectification jurisdiction of a tribunal under Section 420(2) is strictly confined to patent, manifest, and self-evident errors apparent on the face of the record without requiring elaborate arguments, and does not permit a rehearing or reconsideration of substantive determinations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Tribunal only to rectify a 'mistake apparent from the record' within two years; it does not confer a power of review. Non-consideration or non-discussion of judicial authorities cited by a party on an issue involving mixed questions of law and fact (such as limitation and delay/laches) cannot be equated with an error apparent on the face of the record. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Distinction between patent, clerical, or self-evident errors striking on mere inspection versus complex points requiring a long-drawn process of reasoning where two opinions are conceivably possible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The application was an impermissible review petition in the garb of rectification; NCLT rightly declined to review its order dated 29.05.2017.
operative_order: All connected Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 105, 107, 108, 110, 111, and 112 of 2018 are dismissed[cite: 7]. Each appeal is dismissed with costs quantified at Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh only) to be paid by the respective Appellants to the State through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs[cite: 7].
summary: Appellants challenged an order of the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissing their applications under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, which sought the recall/review of an earlier order refusing to dismiss an oppression petition on grounds of limitation and laches[cite: 7]. The Appellants contended that failure by the Tribunal to discuss their cited precedents constituted an error apparent on the face of the record[cite: 7]. Dismissing the appeals with costs of Rs. 1 lakh per appeal, the NCLAT held that the power of review is not an inherent power and is absent under Section 420(2)[cite: 7]. Non-discussion of fact-dependent case law does not amount to a manifest error rectifiable under the statute[cite: 7].

case_title: Thota Gurunath Reddy & Ors. vs. Continental Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Thota Gurunath Reddy, an individual promoter-shareholder, along with Paradigm Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (holding 47.88% total equity) are Appellants/Petitioners; Continental Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1; Gleneagles Development Pte. Ltd. (Singapore company holding 51% majority equity) is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Share Purchase Agreement, Share Subscription Agreement, and Shareholders' Agreement all dated 18.02.2015, under which Respondent No. 2 acquired 51% control of Respondent No. 1 for an aggregate consideration of Rs. 293 Crores (Rs. 170 Crores for secondary purchase and Rs. 123 Crores subscription). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement action alleging fund diversion, excessive commissions to overseas associates (Parkway Group), suppression of hospital operations, and attempting to force share dilution via a Rs. 29 Crore working capital call. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreements executed on 18.02.2015; board meeting proposing Rs. 29 Crore capital call held on 26.08.2016; company petition filed in 2016; reference order passed by NCLT on 20.04.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share Purchase and Shareholders' Agreements containing international arbitration dispute resolution clauses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 19/241/HDB/2016 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench under Sections 241-244 of the Companies Act, 2013. Respondent No. 2 filed CA No. 51 of 2016 under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to refer parties to international arbitration. By order dated 20.04.2017, NCLT, sitting as a judicial authority, referred the parties to arbitration. Appellants challenged this reference by preferring an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an appeal lies before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 against an order passed by the National Company Law Tribunal acting as a 'judicial authority' referring parties to arbitration under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. 2. Whether statutory appeals under Section 421 of the Companies Act are barred when an order is governed by the exhaustive, self-contained provisions of Section 50 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an adjudicatory forum exercises jurisdiction as a 'judicial authority' under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the right and forum of appeal must be traced solely from within the Arbitration Act itself; general appellate provisions in the statute constituting the tribunal cannot be invoked to bypass the statutory bar against appeals under Section 50 of the Arbitration Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 50 of the Arbitration Act is exhaustive and forms a self-contained code allowing appeals only against orders *refusing* to refer parties to arbitration under Section 45; an order that *refers* parties to arbitration is non-appealable. Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 applies exclusively to orders passed by the NCLT in its capacity as a 'Tribunal' under the Companies Act, not when functioning as a judicial authority under the Arbitration Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Determination of the source of adjudicatory power under which the impugned order was passed to establish subject-matter appellate maintainability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order referring the dispute to arbitration was made under Section 45 of the Arbitration Act, 1996; hence, the appeal filed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 is fundamentally not maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as not maintainable before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 8]. No order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: Appellants filed an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 against Continental Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. and its majority Singapore shareholder, Gleneagles Development Pte. Ltd.[cite: 8] The NCLT Hyderabad Bench, acting on an application under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, referred the parties to international arbitration pursuant to agreements[cite: 8]. Appellants challenged this order before NCLAT under Section 421 of the Companies Act[cite: 8]. Dismissing the appeal as not maintainable, NCLAT held that an order passed by the Tribunal acting as a 'judicial authority' under Section 45 is governed exclusively by Section 50 of the Arbitration Act, which bars appeals against orders referring parties to arbitration[cite: 8].

case_title: GMB Ceramics Ltd. vs. Spartek Ceramics India Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 258 of 2017 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 160 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pr. Director General of Income Tax and GMB Ceramics Ltd. are Appellants/Creditors; Spartek Ceramics India Ltd. is Respondent No. 1/Sick Company/Demerged Company; Neycer is a connected entity. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Modified Rehabilitation Scheme and demerger scheme formulated under SICA restructuring Neycer and Spartek Ceramics, involving unsecured loan funding to clear creditor liabilities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in respect of unabsorbed income tax losses to the extent of Rs. 77.12 Crores, anticipated capital gains tax revenue loss, and unpaid commercial creditor dues owed to GMB Ceramics Ltd. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demerger scheme sanctioned by BIFR on 20.10.2016. SICA was repealed and SICA Repeal Act, 2003 was notified w.e.f. 01.12.2016. Central Government issued Notification S.O. 1683(E) (Removal of Difficulties Order, 2017) on 24.05.2017 providing a 90-day window to appeal deemed resolution plans before NCLAT. Appeals lodged in 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanctioned demerger scheme dated 20.10.2016 passed in BIFR Case No. 63/2006, granting tax exemptions and restructuring liabilities without consent of the Income Tax department. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Aggrieved by the BIFR scheme dated 20.10.2016, appeals pending before AAIFR abated upon SICA repeal on 01.12.2016. Relying on the Central Government Removal of Difficulties Order dated 24.05.2017 (treating sanctioned BIFR schemes as approved resolution plans under Section 31(1) of the IBC), Appellants directly approached NCLAT under Section 61 read with Section 32 of the IBC.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Central Government, via an executive order under Section 242 of the IBC, can confer appellate jurisdiction upon the NCLAT to hear appeals against BIFR orders by amending the Eighth Schedule to the IBC. 2. Whether an executive notification granting 90 days to appeal can override the mandatory limitation period of 30 days (plus 15 days condonable) prescribed under Section 61(2) of the IBC. 3. Whether a BIFR demerger scheme sanctioned prior to the enactment of the IBC can be legally treated as an approved Resolution Plan under Section 31(1) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory appellate jurisdiction and periods of limitation cannot be created, expanded, or altered by executive orders under a 'removal of difficulties' clause; an executive order that introduces provisions in conflict with substantive legislative enactments is ultra vires and invalid. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 of the IBC restricts the Central Government to removing difficulties in giving effect to the provisions of the IBC itself; it does not authorize the executive to revive abated SICA proceedings, amend the substantive terms of the Eighth Schedule, or alter Section 61(2) limitation limits. Section 61(2) provides a strict 30-day period extendable by at most 15 days, leaving NCLAT without jurisdiction to entertain appeals beyond 45 days. Furthermore, a BIFR scheme never approved by a Committee of Creditors under Section 30(4) cannot be deemed an approved resolution plan under Section 31(1). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison between statutory limitation mandates and executive modifications, and examination of whether the scheme complied with mandatory CIRP approval procedures under Section 30 of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals against the BIFR scheme are barred by limitation and not maintainable under Section 61 of the IBC.
operative_order: Both appeals are dismissed as barred by limitation and not maintainable under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 9]. The impugned scheme dated 20.10.2016 is noted to be illegal as it contravened the law and lacked CoC approval under Section 30(4), but cannot be formally set aside for want of jurisdiction[cite: 9]. Parties are left to raise objections before any court where implementation may be sought[cite: 9]. No order as to costs[cite: 9].
summary: The Income Tax Department and GMB Ceramics appealed to NCLAT against a BIFR demerger scheme dated 20.10.2016 sanctioned under SICA, invoking Central Government Notification S.O. 1683(E) dated 24.05.2017 (issued under Section 242 IBC), which treated BIFR schemes as approved resolution plans under Section 31(1) IBC and allowed 90 days to appeal[cite: 9]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that executive removal-of-difficulty orders cannot alter substantive law or override the mandatory 30+15 day limitation limit under Section 61(2) IBC[cite: 9]. The Tribunal declared that it lacked jurisdiction to entertain the time-barred appeals, observing additionally that BIFR schemes lacking CoC approval cannot constitute valid resolution plans[cite: 9].

case_title: Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs vs. Gitanjali Gems Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 103 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 119 & 124 to 133 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union of India (Ministry of Corporate Affairs) is the Petitioner/Appellant; Gitanjali Gems Ltd. (promoted by Mehul Choksi), Firestar International Ltd., Firestar Diamond International Pvt. Ltd., Diamond R US, Solar Exports, Stellar Diamonds (promoted by Nirav Modi), along with their partners, directors, key managerial personnel, and connected family trusts are Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-crore diamond export and trading operations underpinned by fraudulent LoUs (Letters of Undertaking) and Foreign Letters of Credit (FLCs) obtained from Punjab National Bank without credit limits. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive bank fraud exceeding Rs. 11,400 Crores (escalating beyond Rs. 14,000 Crores), causing wrongful loss to Punjab National Bank through unauthorized overseas SWIFT transactions and Buyer's Credit disbursements. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: PNB registered CBI FIRs on 31.01.2018 and 15.02.2018. MCA directed SFIO investigation on 17.02.2018 under Section 212. MCA filed CP No. 277/2018 before NCLT Mumbai Bench; ex-parte asset restraint order passed on 23.02.2018; modification order vacating restraints on certain independent directors passed on 02.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CBI FIRs detailing fraudulent bypassing of PNB's Core Banking System (CBS) using manipulated SWIFT messages, property schedules showing extensive corporate/personal assets, and SFIO ongoing probe records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: MCA filed CP 277/2018 under Sections 221, 222, 241, 242, 246 r/w 339 alleging prejudice to public interest. NCLT Mumbai Bench granted an interim order on 23.02.2018 freezing assets of all respondent entities, LLPs, trusts, and directors/individuals. On 02.04.2018, NCLT vacated the restraint entirely against five directors/professionals (Sujal Shah, Gopal Krishnan Nair, Suresh Senapathy, Gautam Mukkavilli, and Sanjay Rishi) and partially modified it for others. MCA appealed the exoneration, while individual directors appealed the freeze orders.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Tribunal has jurisdiction under Section 242(4) read with Sections 221, 241(2), 246, 339, and 340 of the Companies Act, 2013 to freeze personal assets of directors, partners, trusts, and individuals during an ongoing SFIO investigation into corporate fraud prejudicial to public interest. 2. Whether the Tribunal can exonerate or vacate interim restraint orders against individual directors prior to the conclusion and submission of the SFIO investigation report.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In proceedings initiated in public interest concerning systemic corporate fraud, the Tribunal possesses plenary interim powers under Section 242(4) read with Sections 221, 246, 339, and 340 to freeze the assets of companies, LLPs, and associated individuals/directors to prevent alienation of assets, and cannot grant premature exonerations while statutory investigations are actively underway. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241(2) read with Section 242 empowers the Tribunal to pass comprehensive orders to protect the public interest; incorporating Sections 339, 340, and 341 mutatis mutandis through Section 246 extends liability and interim injunctive power across individuals, officers, and connected firms. Section 221 read with Section 242(4) cannot be restricted merely to corporate assets when fraudulent diversion of public money to individual accounts/trusts is prima facie evident. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Existence of a prima facie case of large-scale financial fraud, public interest endangerment, and the necessity to preserve assets pending a comprehensive forensic investigation report by the SFIO. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The complete vacation of the freeze against five directors was premature and impermissible before receipt of the SFIO report; however, reasonable monthly allowances for personal subsistence should be permitted to all affected individuals.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 103 and 119 of 2018 are allowed; Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 124 to 133 of 2018 are disposed of[cite: 10]. The NCLT order dated 02.04.2018 exonerating and vacating restraint on Respondents 43, 44, 51, 52, and 53 is set aside[cite: 10]. All named Appellants and Respondents are permitted to withdraw a subsistence allowance of Rs. 1,00,000/- per month from their bank accounts (Rs. 2,00,000/- for Respondent No. 35)[cite: 10]. The blanket restraint order dated 23.02.2018 against removal, transfer, or disposal of funds, assets, and properties shall continue until further orders[cite: 10]. No costs[cite: 10].
summary: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs filed a petition under Sections 241-242 read with Section 221 and 339 of the Companies Act, 2013, concerning the Rs. 11,400+ Crore PNB fraud orchestrated via Nirav Modi and Mehul Choksi entities[cite: 10]. NCLT Mumbai initially froze the personal and corporate assets of all involved companies, trusts, and directors[cite: 10], but subsequently vacated the freeze for five professional/independent directors[cite: 10]. Setting aside the vacation order, the NCLAT ruled that under Section 242(4) read with Sections 221, 339, and 340, the Tribunal has ample jurisdiction to freeze individual assets in public-interest fraud cases and cannot exonerate respondents prior to the submission of the SFIO investigation report[cite: 10]. The freeze was reinstated with a Rs. 1,00,000 monthly subsistence allowance[cite: 10].

case_title: Export Import Bank of India vs. Resolution Professional, JEKPL Private Limited
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 304 of 2017 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 16 of 2018 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 302 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: In CA 304/2017 & 16/2018, Export Import Bank of India (EXIM Bank) is the Claimant/Financial Creditor; JEKPL Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Counter Corporate Guarantor; Jubilant Enpro Private Limited (JEPL) is the Corporate Guarantor; and Jubilant Energy N.V. (JENV, Netherlands) is the Principal Borrower. In CA 302/2017, Axis Bank Limited is the Claimant/Financial Creditor, Edu Smart Services Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor, and Educomp Solutions Limited is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: EXIM Bank disbursed a Dollar Loan facility of USD 50 Million to JENV sanctioned on 13.04.2011/18.05.2011, secured by a Corporate Guarantee from JEPL and a Counter Corporate Guarantee/Supplementary Guarantee executed by JEKPL on 01.08.2011. In Axis Bank's case, a Master Restructuring Agreement dated 25.03.2014 and Corporate Guarantee dated 03.06.2015 were executed by Edu Smart in favor of SBICAP Trustee for consortium lenders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: JENV's loan account was classified as NPA on 17.05.2016 (JEHNV on 01.05.2016). For Axis Bank, default arose from credit facilities aggregating to a verified/claimed default amount of Rs. 396,76,07,676.68. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EXIM Bank recalled JENV's loan facilities on 30.03.2017 and invoked both the Corporate Guarantee and Counter Corporate Guarantee via letters dated 30.03.2017. In Axis Bank's case, public announcements inviting claims were issued on 27.06.2017; claims were lodged in Form C on 22.07.2017 and updated on 11.08.2017 without formal prior guarantee invocation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deeds of Guarantee and Counter Guarantee dated 01.08.2011 stipulating joint and several liability as principal debtors; JEKPL's Annual Report for FY 2016-17 admitting corporate guarantee liabilities; and the Master Restructuring Agreement and Corporate Guarantee dated 03.06.2015 treating the guarantor as principal debtor under Clause 12. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: JEKPL initiated voluntary CIRP under Section 10 (CP No. 24/ALD/2017). The RP rejected EXIM Bank's claim on 04.08.2017, and NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissed EXIM's Section 60(5) application on 27.11.2017 (CA 159/2017) and approved the resolution plan on 15.12.2017 (CA 223/2017). In Edu Smart's Section 7 CIRP (CP IB-102(PB)/2017 initiated by DBS Bank), NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissed Axis Bank's Section 60(5) application on 27.10.2017, holding the claim contingent since the guarantee was not invoked prior to CIRP commencement.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a creditor holding a Counter Corporate Guarantee or uninvoked Corporate Guarantee qualifies as a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8)(h) of the IBC. 2. Whether the invocation or maturity of a corporate guarantee is a mandatory prerequisite for a creditor to lodge a claim or be inducted into the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor holding a guarantee or counter-guarantee obligation backed by underlying financial debt disbursed for the time value of money is a financial creditor; the right to file and collate a claim under the IBC encompasses matured, unmatured, or contingent claims, meaning formal pre-CIRP invocation of a guarantee is not a condition precedent for participating as a financial creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(h) read with Section 5(7) includes counter-indemnity and guarantee obligations arising from borrowings where money is disbursed against consideration for the time value of money, and does not restrict counter-indemnity instruments solely to those issued by banks. Further, 'claim' under Section 3(6) encompasses rights to payment whether matured, unmatured, fixed, or contingent, which does not require an existing 'default' under Section 3(12) as a threshold for claim collation under Section 18(1)(b) or 25(2)(e). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the underlying contracts (Guarantee Deeds, Counter Corporate Guarantee Deeds, and Loan Restructuring Agreements) to verify whether terms bind the guarantor jointly and severally as a principal debtor and whether the debt arose from financial disbursements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: EXIM Bank and Axis Bank are Financial Creditors under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8); their exclusion from the Committee of Creditors was illegal, invalidating any resolution plan approved in their absence without fresh CoC consideration.
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 27.11.2017 and 15.12.2017 passed by NCLT Allahabad Bench, and the order dated 27.10.2017 passed by NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench are set aside. Resolution Professionals and Adjudicating Authorities are directed to treat EXIM Bank and Axis Bank as Financial Creditors and members of their respective Committees of Creditors, convene fresh meetings of the CoC to reconsider compliant resolution plans under Section 30(2) without rebidding, with no order as to costs.
summary: Export Import Bank of India and Axis Bank challenged NCLT orders upholding the rejection of their claims as financial debts and their exclusion from Committees of Creditors. EXIM Bank held a Counter Corporate Guarantee from JEKPL Pvt. Ltd., while Axis Bank held an uninvoked Corporate Guarantee from Edu Smart Services Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, establishing that counter-guarantees fall within financial debt under Section 5(8)(h) and that claim submission under Section 3(6) encompasses unmatured and contingent debts. The Appellate Tribunal ruled that pre-CIRP invocation of a guarantee is unnecessary for CoC inclusion and directed both banks to be inducted into their respective CoCs to reconsider resolution plans.

case_title: Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant/Financial Creditor; Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor; Mohd. Sabir Parvez (Director of Corporate Debtor) is Respondent No. 2; and Mr. M.L. Jain is Respondent No. 3/Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt obligations leading to initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under Section 7 insolvency proceedings in CP (IB) No. 97/7/HDB/2017; exact quantified sum of default is not detailed in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition was admitted on 11.08.2017, with certified order copy made available on 21.08.2017; IRP took charge and CoC was constituted by 15.09.2017. Litigation intervened between 15.09.2017 and 28.02.2018. The statutory 180-day and 270-day CIRP timelines were imminent when CA 93/2018 was filed. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interlocutory timeline records establishing that out of the initial 270 days, approximately 166 days were lost solely due to interim stay orders of NCLT in CA No. 197/2017 (challenging CoC constitution) and the replacement of the Resolution Professional. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CIRP was initiated on 11.08.2017 by NCLT Hyderabad Bench. NCLT granted an interim stay on CoC proceedings on 15.09.2017, which was vacated on 28.02.2018. Upon an application for extension (CA No. 93 of 2018), NCLT Hyderabad passed an interim order on 27.04.2018 merely extending CIRP till 15.05.2018 instead of excluding the litigated stay period, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal has the statutory power to exclude the period lost during judicial stays or unforeseen procedural impediments when calculating the 180/270-day CIRP timeline under Section 12 of the IBC. 2. Whether the 166-day period during which CoC meetings were stayed by the NCLT should be excluded from the corporate insolvency resolution process timeline.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal possesses equitable authority to exclude time lost due to unforeseen litigation hurdles, judicial stays, or vacancy in the office of the Resolution Professional from the statutory CIRP period under Section 12, ensuring the corporate debtor is afforded a viable resolution opportunity before resorting to liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 must be construed purposively to prevent premature liquidation; periods during which CIRP is effectively rendered inoperative through court-mandated injunctions or administrative paralysis do not count toward the substantive 180/270-day statutory duration. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the chronological case record and court orders demonstrating an absolute freeze or total impossibility of proceeding with CIRP activities, such as an interim judicial stay restraining CoC meetings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The 166 days consumed between 15.09.2017 and 28.02.2018 due to the NCLT's interim stay order must be excluded from the computation of the 270 days, and the CIRP timeline is extended accordingly.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 27.04.2018 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench in CA No. 93/2018 is modified. The period of 166 days is excluded from the CIRP timeline, and the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors are granted 166 additional days effective immediately from 08.05.2018 to conclude the CIRP. Appeal disposed of.
summary: Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an interim order of the NCLT Hyderabad Bench that merely granted a brief extension of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. instead of excluding the period during which proceedings were judicially stalled. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and formulated the definitive rule that judicial stay periods, RP vacancy, or litigation delays beyond parties' control can be excluded from calculating the 180/270 days under Section 12 of the IBC. The Tribunal directed the exclusion of 166 days and granted an equivalent period from the date of the order to complete the CIRP.

case_title: Numetal Limited vs. Satish Kumar Gupta & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 169 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 207, 171, 172 & 173 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Standard Chartered Bank and State Bank of India are Financial Creditors; Essar Steel India Limited (ESIL) is the Corporate Debtor (promoted by Mr. Ravi Ruia); Satish Kumar Gupta is the Resolution Professional; Numetal Limited and ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. (AM India) are competing Resolution Applicants. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-crore consortium banking credit facilities extended to ESIL, which defaulted, leading to Section 7 insolvency admission. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amounted to tens of thousands of crores of NPA debt owed by ESIL. Connected NPAs included Uttam Galva and KSS Petron, having aggregate NPA debts of approximately Rs. 7,000 Crores as on 31.03.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 02.08.2017. EOI invited on 06.10.2017; AM India submitted EOI on 11.10.2017 and Numetal on 20.10.2017. Section 29A was inserted via Ordinance on 23.11.2017. First resolution plans were submitted on 12.02.2018; fresh/second round plans submitted on 29.03.2018 / 02.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: On 12.02.2018, Numetal held 25% shares via Aurora Enterprises Ltd. (AEL), 100% owned by Mr. Rewant Ruia (son of promoter Ravi Ruia). AEL divested its 25% shareholding completely on 29.03.2018 to Crinium Bay (VTB), INDO, and TPE. AM India's connected entity, AM Netherlands, held 29.05% shares and co-promoter status in Uttam Galva (NPA > 1 year) and Fraseli/Mittal Investments held management/affirmative control in KSS Global/KSS Petron (NPA). AM Netherlands and Fraseli divested shareholdings in Uttam Galva and KSS Global on 07.02.2018 and 09.02.2018 without paying overdue amounts, placing Rs. 7,000 Crores conditionally in an escrow account. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP disqualified both applicants on 12.02.2018 under Section 29A(c) and (h). In Section 60(5) applications, NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 19.04.2018 confirmed ineligibility of both under Section 29A but remanded to CoC under the second proviso to Section 30(4) to permit AM India 30 days to pay overdue NPA amounts. Both parties appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. How is the expression 'person acting in concert' under Section 29A of the IBC to be defined, and was Numetal ineligible as of 12.02.2018 and 29.03.2018? 2. Can a resolution applicant cure disqualification under Section 29A(c) by merely divesting shareholding/control in an NPA company prior to plan submission without clearing all overdue amounts under the proviso to Section 29A(c)?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of an explicit definition in the IBC or statutes listed in Section 3(37), Regulation 2(1)(q) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011 applies to define 'person acting in concert'; ineligibility under Section 29A(c) attaches as a statutory stigma once an account is classified as NPA for over a year, which can be cured exclusively by paying all overdue amounts and charges under its proviso, and not through eleventh-hour divestment of shares. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A is remedial to purge corporate defaults. Regulation 2(1)(q) has statutory force under SEBI Act Section 30/31. Under Section 29A(c) read with the second proviso to Section 30(4), an applicant who submitted an EOI (first stage of a plan) prior to the 23.11.2017 amendment must be given an opportunity to clear overdues; divestment alone does not wash away the statutory disability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Piercing corporate holding structures and examining shareholding records, voting arrangements, and familial links to determine beneficial ownership, joint action, and exercise of control over NPA companies. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Numetal was ineligible on 12.02.2018 due to AEL's shareholding, but became eligible on 29.03.2018 upon complete exit of AEL. AM India was ineligible under Section 29A(c) due to promoter/control status in Uttam Galva and KSS Petron, which could only be purged by direct payment of overdue amounts, not conditional escrow deposits.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19.04.2018 regarding Numetal's ineligibility as of 29.03.2018 is set aside; Numetal's plan dated 29.03.2018 is declared eligible for CoC consideration. AM India is granted three days (until 11.09.2018) to unconditionally pay all overdue amounts with interest in the accounts of Uttam Galva and KSS Petron. If paid, the CoC shall consider AM India's plan alongside Numetal's. The period from 26.04.2018 to 07.09.2018 spent in appeal is excluded from the 270-day CIRP period. Appeals disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: In the corporate insolvency of Essar Steel India Ltd., the Resolution Professional disqualified Numetal Ltd. and ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. under Section 29A of the IBC. NCLAT held that 'persons acting in concert' under Section 29A is governed by Regulation 2(1)(q) of SEBI SAST Regulations, 2011. Numetal was ineligible during the first bid due to shareholding by the promoter's son's firm (AEL), but became eligible for its second bid on 29.03.2018 after AEL's exit. ArcelorMittal was held ineligible under Section 29A(c) due to promoter and controlling stakes in NPA entities (Uttam Galva and KSS Petron), ruling that share divestment without paying overdue amounts does not cure Section 29A(c) disqualification, granting three days to clear all overdue debts.

case_title: Binani Industries Limited vs. Bank of Baroda & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 82 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 123, 188, 216 & 234 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bank of Baroda is the Financial Creditor; Binani Cement Limited (BCL) is the Corporate Debtor; Binani Industries Limited (BIL) is the promoter/holding company of BCL; Rajputana Properties Pvt. Ltd. (RPPL, an UltraTech competitor) and UltraTech Cement Limited are Resolution Applicants; Vijay Kumar Iyer is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-bank credit facilities and corporate guarantees extended to Binani Cement Limited, which experienced systemic debt servicing failure. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Aggregate verified claims totaled Rs. 7,289.05 Crores, comprising direct financial debts, corporate guarantee exposures, and operational debts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated in 2017 (CP (IB) No. 359/KB/2017). Resolution plans submitted on 12.02.2018. RPPL submitted a revised offer on 07.03.2018; UltraTech submitted a revised offer on 08.03.2018. CoC approved RPPL's plan on 14.03.2018. On 28.05.2018, in its 17th meeting following NCLT directions, CoC unanimously approved UltraTech's plan with 100% voting share. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RPPL's plan offered Rs. 6,932.46 Crores total, providing 100% payment to direct financial creditors, but discriminating against corporate guarantee financial creditors (EXIM Bank given 72.59%, SBI Hong Kong 10%) and allocating only 35% (Rs. 151 Crores out of Rs. 443.23 Crores) to unrelated operational creditors and 0% to related operational creditors. UltraTech's plan offered Rs. 7,950.34 Crores (including Rs. 2,427 Crores offer, Rs. 350 Crores working capital, and 100% payment to all financial creditors and unrelated operational creditors plus 10% interest). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CoC initially approved RPPL's plan on 14.03.2018. Objections were filed by BIL, UltraTech, and operational creditors. By order dated 02.05.2018, NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected RPPL's plan as discriminatory and directed CoC to consider UltraTech's plan. BIL sought termination of CIRP by offering to settle under Section 12A, which NCLT rejected. RPPL and BIL appealed to NCLAT; RP appealed against adverse remarks.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a resolution plan that discriminates between financial creditors similarly situated (direct exposure vs. corporate guarantee beneficiaries) and discriminates against operational creditors by paying them mere liquidation value violates the IBC. 2. Whether the Committee of Creditors is empowered under the Process Document and CIRP regulations to consider and negotiate a revised, higher resolution plan submitted prior to final plan approval to ensure value maximization. 3. Whether a corporate debtor's promoter can unilaterally terminate an ongoing CIRP by offering full settlement without following the mandate of Section 12A.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency resolution plan cannot discriminate between similarly situated financial creditors or treat operational creditors inequitably by relegating them to nominal liquidation value; value maximization of the corporate debtor's assets for all stakeholders is the primary objective of the IBC, and the process is not a recovery mechanism or an auction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) and the IBC scheme mandate a level playing field for operational and financial credit. Regulation 38 cannot override the Code to legitimize discrimination or impose liquidation value on operational or dissenting financial creditors. The CoC's duty under Section 25(2)(h) and Regulation 36B permits flexibility to negotiate and entertain revised offers before final approval to achieve maximization of asset value. Furthermore, Section 12A is non-retroactive and strictly conditional upon 90% CoC voting approval, barring unilateral promoter settlements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparative analysis of the financial distribution matrix across creditor classes to detect unjustifiable disparity and evaluation of the CoC's compliance with procedural rules regarding timeline modifications and plan evaluations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: RPPL's plan was discriminatory and invalid; UltraTech's revised plan offered full value maximization to all stakeholders without discrimination and complied fully with Section 30(2), warranting approval under Section 31.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 123 & 188 of 2018 (preferred by Rajputana Properties Pvt. Ltd.) and Nos. 82 & 216 of 2018 (preferred by Binani Industries Ltd.) are dismissed. Company Appeal No. 234 of 2018 is allowed, expunging all adverse observations against Resolution Professional Vijay Kumar Iyer. UltraTech Cement Limited's revised resolution plan approved by 100% CoC vote is approved under Section 31 of the IBC. Records of CP (IB) No. 359/KB/2017 are remitted to NCLT Kolkata Bench to constitute a monitoring committee and oversee plan implementation. No costs.
summary: In the CIRP of Binani Cement Limited, the NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected the resolution plan of Rajputana Properties Pvt. Ltd. (RPPL) for discriminating between financial creditors and paying operational creditors mere liquidation value, directing consideration of UltraTech Cement Ltd.'s higher offer. Affirming the NCLT, the NCLAT held that the IBC's primary object is asset value maximization and balanced treatment of all stakeholders, prohibiting discrimination against operational creditors or similarly placed guarantee beneficiaries. Dismissing RPPL's and promoter Binani Industries' appeals while setting aside adverse remarks against the RP, the Appellate Tribunal approved UltraTech's revised plan providing 100% payment to all creditors.

case_title: M. Sudarsan Swamy vs. Moana Hong Kong Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M. Sudarsan Swamy is the Appellant/Shareholder; Moana Hong Kong Ltd. is the Petitioner/Respondent who invested over 1 Million USD; Respondent No. 1 is the subject company; Respondent No. 5 is the Managing Director along with other Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Moana Hong Kong Ltd. made foreign investments exceeding 1 Million USD into Respondent No. 1 Company, which later ceased active operations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics are not applicable in this matter as the proceedings concern alleged oppression and mismanagement rather than a financial or operational debt claim under the IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: No Section 8 demand notices, replies, or recall notices were issued; the underlying company petition originated before the Company Law Board, Chennai, prior to its statutory transfer to NCLT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Report of the Bench Officer of the erstwhile CLB, Chennai, indicating statutory records were not maintained in order under Sections 143, 193, 300, and 301 of the Companies Act, 1956; lack of any documentary evidence on record evidencing actual siphoning of funds by individuals or proof that the company was a shell company. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original petition was filed before the CLB under Sections 235, 237, 397, 398, 402, 403, and 405 of the Companies Act, 1956; upon transfer, NCLT Chennai Division Bench passed an order on 19th December 2017 recording at paragraph 39 that the company's funds appeared siphoned, the entity had no business/assets, and that it was admitted to be a shell company.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT had the evidentiary basis and jurisdiction under Section 241 read with Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 to record adverse observations regarding siphoning of funds and declaring the company a shell company based on presumption, and whether it could pass winding-up observations suo motu without an application under Section 273 read with Section 271(e).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adverse adjudicatory findings of fraud, siphoning of company funds, or labeling an entity as a shell company cannot be founded on conjectures, assumptions, or purported oral concessions, but must be strictly supported by tangible evidence on record; furthermore, winding-up orders cannot be issued suo motu under oppression/mismanagement provisions absent a specific prayer under the winding-up provisions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 434(1)(a) requires transferred CLB matters to be disposed of in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013 under Sections 241 and 242; Section 242 permits remedial orders where winding up would unfairly prejudice members, but does not empower the Tribunal to grant winding up or treat an entity as a shell company suo motu without an express petition under Section 271(e) read with Section 273. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied the test of strict evidentiary foundation, holding that a Bench Officer's report highlighting regulatory lapses under Sections 143, 193, 300, and 301 is wholly insufficient to prove actual siphoning of funds or characterize a company as a shell company without specific documentary proof. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The adverse remarks in paragraph 39 regarding siphoning of funds and classification as a shell company were baseless and entered without evidentiary support or jurisdiction, necessitating their deletion.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed in part. The adverse observations made by the NCLT Division Bench, Chennai at paragraph 39 of the order dated 19th December 2017 are set aside. No order as to costs. Registry directed to communicate the order to the concerned NCLT Member (Judicial).
summary: M. Sudarsan Swamy, a shareholder, appealed against paragraph 39 of the NCLT Chennai order dated 19th December 2017, wherein the Tribunal characterized Respondent No. 1 as a shell company and observed that its funds were siphoned off. The NCLAT held that although statutory records were irregular, the record contained no evidence demonstrating siphoning of funds or establishing that it was a shell company. Moreover, in a petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal could not suo motu invoke winding up powers under Section 271(e) read with Section 273 without an explicit prayer. Consequently, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned observations.

case_title: Edelweiss Finvest Private Limited vs. Ramswarup Industries Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Edelweiss Finvest Private Limited is the Creditor/Appellant; Ramswarup Industries Limited is the Corporate Applicant/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debt and settlement proceedings wherein Corporate Debtor committed payment defaults leading to a winding-up petition. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim admitted by Corporate Debtor before the Calcutta High Court was Rs. 9,46,23,000/- with agreed interest at 6% per annum; default date emerged from failure to satisfy payment terms pursuant to High Court order dated 01.02.2010. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Calcutta High Court issued conditional orders on 01.02.2010 and CA No. 168 of 2010 on 09.03.2010; Appellant published newspaper advertisements on 12.11.2012; BIFR reference Case No. 67 of 2012 heard on 24.12.2012 abated on 25.11.2016 via SICA Repeal Act notification; Corporate Debtor filed Section 10 petition thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Calcutta High Court orders dated 01.02.2010, 12.01.2011, and modification order dated 24.08.2012 recording payment of Rs. 15 Lakh and permitting clearance of balance; lack of any High Court order admitting the winding-up petition or directing appointment of a provisional/official liquidator. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CP No. 461 of 2009 filed by Appellant under Sections 433 and 434 of Companies Act, 1956 before Calcutta High Court remained unadmitted; Corporate Debtor subsequently filed CP (IB) No. 349/KB/2017 under Section 10 of IBC before NCLT Kolkata Bench, which admitted the application and imposed a moratorium on 08.01.2018.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate applicant is barred under Section 11(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 from initiating a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 10 during the mere pendency of an unadmitted winding-up petition before a High Court where no order of winding up or liquidation has been passed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory bar under Section 11(d) of the IBC operates only when an actual liquidation order or winding-up order has been made against the corporate debtor; mere pendency of a winding-up petition without admission or an order of winding up does not disentitle a corporate debtor from filing an application under Section 10. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reading Section 11(d) of the IBC alongside amended Section 2(23) and Section 2(94A) of the Companies Act, 2013, the expression 'liquidation order' is synonymous with 'winding up'; ineligibility attaches strictly upon an actual winding up or liquidation order being passed, not at the pre-admission or hearing stage of a winding-up petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the judicial record of the Calcutta High Court in CP No. 461 of 2009 and verified whether any formal order admitting the winding-up petition or directing official liquidation was entered, finding only interim/modification orders regarding installment payments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no order of admission or winding up was passed by the High Court, the Corporate Debtor suffered no ineligibility under Section 11(d), and the Section 10 petition was rightfully admitted.
operative_order: The appeal is found devoid of merit and dismissed. The order dated 8th January 2018 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench admitting the Section 10 application is upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: Edelweiss Finvest Private Limited appealed the NCLT Kolkata order dated 8th January 2018 admitting a Section 10 IBC application filed by Ramswarup Industries Limited. The Appellant argued that the Section 10 petition was barred due to a pre-existing winding-up petition (CP No. 461 of 2009) pending before the Calcutta High Court. The NCLAT reaffirmed its ruling in Unigreen Global, holding that under Section 11(d) of the IBC, a bar arises only where an actual winding-up or liquidation order has been passed. Since the High Court had not admitted the winding-up petition nor ordered liquidation, the Section 10 petition was maintainable, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Pipeline Infrastructure Private Limited vs. Nil
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pipeline Infrastructure Private Limited is the Transferee/Resulting Company (Appellant); East West Pipeline Limited is the Transferor/Demerged Company. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Scheme of Arrangement and Demerger under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 for hiving off and merging the pipeline business of East West Pipeline Limited into Pipeline Infrastructure Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics are not applicable as this proceeding is a corporate restructuring scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First motion company scheme application filed in 2018; impugned order pronounced on 30.08.2018 and delivered on 05.09.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: First Motion Application CSA No. 719 of 2018; draft scheme containing standard vesting recital providing that assets and immovable properties stand transferred and vested by virtue of the sanctioned scheme without further act or deed. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench in CSA No. 719 of 2018 approved the First Motion dispensing with creditors' meetings and directing an equity shareholders' meeting, but inserted paragraph 20 holding that automatic vesting under the scheme is impermissible and mandating separate documentation for transfer of assets under fiscal laws prior to filing with the Registrar of Companies.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT while adjudicating a company scheme application has the jurisdiction to direct the execution of separate transfer documentation for assets under fiscal laws prior to placing the sanctioned scheme before the Registrar of Companies, or whether the court order sanctioning the scheme operates by itself as the instrument of transfer.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order of the company court sanctioning a scheme of amalgamation or demerger operates by force of law as an 'instrument' of conveyance, effecting the transfer and vesting of assets without the requirement of executing separate transfer deeds or conveyances, subject only to payment of applicable stamp duties. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Construing Sections 230 to 234 of the Companies Act, 2013 alongside Section 2(g)(iv) and Section 2(l) of the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958, an order of the NCLT sanctioning a scheme constitutes a conveyance and an instrument; Section 232 effects statutory transfer by judicial decree, rendering additional private conveyancing deeds legally superfluous. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applied the binding precedent of the Supreme Court in Hindustan Lever v. State of Maharashtra, verifying that the statutory scheme and definition of conveyance encompass NCLT sanction orders directly. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's direction requiring separate documentation for transfer of assets before submitting the scheme to the ROC was contrary to law and unsustainable.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The directions and observations contained in Paragraph 20 of the impugned order dated 30th August 2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in CSA No. 719 of 2018 are set aside. The appeal is disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: Pipeline Infrastructure Private Limited appealed against paragraph 20 of the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 30th August 2018 in CSA No. 719 of 2018, wherein the Tribunal ruled that automatic vesting of assets under a demerger scheme is impermissible and mandated execution of separate transfer documentation under fiscal laws before filing with the ROC. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Hindustan Lever and Section 2(g) of the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958, the NCLAT held that an order sanctioning a scheme itself constitutes an instrument of transfer. Consequently, no separate conveyancing documentation is required, and paragraph 20 was set aside.

case_title: Ramprasad Dalmia vs. The Board of Directors, Milkfood Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ramprasad Dalmia is the Appellant/Petitioner holding 105 equity shares; Milkfood Limited is Respondent No. 1 Company; Respondents No. 2 to 5 are Directors/Management of the Company. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Exercise of shareholder governance rights and attendance at the 44th Annual General Meeting of Respondent No. 1 Company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics are inapplicable as the proceedings involve allegations of procedural irregularities in convening an AGM rather than debt recovery. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 44th AGM convened on 26.09.2017; reporting letter along with AGM report sent by Company to BSE on 27.09.2017; statutory Form MGT-15 filed pursuant to Section 121. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Copy of BSE disclosure dated 27.09.2017 recording presence of 25 members in person and 8 by proxy with passing of resolutions based on scrutinizer's report; Form MGT-15 filed with ROC; complete absence of any affidavit, name, or identity of the representative/proxy who attended on the Appellant's behalf; absence of any police complaint regarding alleged intimidation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 271/CHD/PB/2017 under Sections 96 to 98 and 101 to 107 of Companies Act, 2013 alleging the AGM was invalid; NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed the petition at the threshold on 20.12.2017 with Rs. 50,000/- costs, holding Section 96 requirements were satisfied and allegations of procedural coercion were unsupported hearsay.
legal_issues: Whether an individual shareholder can maintain a petition under Section 97 of the Companies Act, 2013 to declare an Annual General Meeting void ab initio and direct reconvening based on unsubstantiated, hearsay allegations of procedural irregularities when the shareholder was not personally present and failed to produce evidence or an affidavit from his proxy.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A company petition challenging the validity or conduct of a shareholder meeting cannot be entertained where the pleadings rest entirely on vague, unverified hearsay allegations of an unnamed proxy without prima facie supporting evidence, affidavits, or established cause of action. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 97 empowers the Tribunal to call or direct the calling of an AGM upon default under Section 96; however, invoking this judicial jurisdiction requires establishing a sustainable prima facie case with clear evidence showing a default occurred. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applied the test of prima facie cause of action and admissible evidence; personal presence of the petitioner or supporting sworn affidavits and identification of authorized proxies/witnesses is essential to establish allegations of procedural illegality or coercion at an AGM. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to disclose the name of his representative, produced no proxy affidavit, lodged no police complaint, and failed to cross the preliminary threshold of disclosing a cause of action, justifying dismissal at the threshold.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The impugned order of the NCLT Chandigarh Bench dated 20th December 2017 dismissing the Company Petition is maintained. No orders as to costs.
summary: Ramprasad Dalmia, holding 105 shares in Milkfood Limited, filed an appeal against the NCLT Chandigarh order dated 20th December 2017 dismissing his petition under Section 97 of the Companies Act, 2013. The Appellant sought to invalidate the 44th AGM held on 26th September 2017, alleging procedural illegalities, absent directors, and intimidation. The NCLAT held that the Appellant was not personally present and failed to disclose his representative's name, file an affidavit from the proxy, or provide any corroborating evidence against the official BSE filings and Form MGT-15. Because no prima facie case or cause of action was established, the dismissal was affirmed.

case_title: SICGIL India Ltd. & Ors. vs. IFB Agro Industries Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SICGIL India Ltd. & Ors. are the Appellants/Acquiring Shareholders; IFB Agro Industries Limited is the Respondent/Petitioner Company. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Acquisition of equity shares of IFB Agro Industries Limited from the open market exceeding 5% shareholding threshold triggering statutory disclosure obligations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics are inapplicable as the matter pertains to non-compliance with statutory shareholding disclosures rather than loan defaults. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Letter sent by 1st Appellant under Regulation 7(1) of SEBI SAST Regulations on 16.01.2004 and received on 22.01.2004 disclosing combined holding reached 5.003%; additional shares acquired on 27.05.2004; continual disclosure under Regulation 13(3) of SEBI PIT Regulations required within 4 working days was delayed and submitted on 17.08.2004 after CP filing. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: BENPOS depository records dated 21.05.2004 demonstrating acquisition of additional 2% equity; disclosure filing submitted to SEBI on 17.08.2004; Company Petition CP No. 550 of 2004 filed before Company Law Board. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IFB Agro filed CP No. 550/KB/2004 under Section 111A of Companies Act, 1956 before CLB Eastern Regional Bench Kolkata; on transfer under Section 434(1)(a) of Companies Act, 2013, NCLT Kolkata Bench by judgment dated 05.07.2017 allowed the petition, barred Appellants from exercising rights beyond 5%, directed Appellants to surrender shares, and authorized IFB Agro to buy back the excess shares at presentation date price or market value.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT exercising jurisdiction under Section 111A(3) of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to Section 59(4) of the Companies Act, 2013) has the jurisdiction to annul share purchases, divest voting rights, and mandate a compulsory buyback of shares acquired in violation of SEBI regulations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory power to rectify a register of members under company law does not confer penal jurisdiction on the Tribunal to annul share transfers, extinguish ownership rights, or order a mandatory buyback of securities; relief is strictly confined to rectifying the register and setting right contraventions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 434(1)(a) mandates transferred petitions to be determined under Section 59(4) of the Companies Act, 2013; Section 59(4) (and predecessor Section 111A(3)) limits the Tribunal's jurisdiction to directing a company or depository to set right contraventions and rectify records, excluding penal sanctions which fall exclusively within SEBI's regulatory domain. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal assessed whether the statutory remedy provided under the section accommodates punitive divestment or forced redemption, holding that jurisdictional scope is strictly circumscribed by the plain statutory text. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by cancelling share transfers and ordering a forced buyback in favour of the company for belated disclosures under SEBI PIT Regulations.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment dated 5th July 2017 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in CP No. 550/KB/2004 is set aside. No order as to costs.
summary: IFB Agro Industries Limited filed a petition under Section 111A of the Companies Act, 1956 alleging that SICGIL India Ltd. and associates acquired equity shares exceeding 5% without adhering to the 4-day disclosure rule under SEBI Insider Trading Regulations, 1992. The NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed the petition, barred voting rights on excess shares, and directed a compulsory buyback by IFB Agro. On appeal, the NCLAT set aside the judgment, holding that under Section 111A of the 1956 Act and Section 59(4) of the 2013 Act, the Tribunal has power only to rectify records and correct register contraventions, not to impose penal forfeitures or order buybacks.

case_title: Raj Singh Chopra & Ors. vs. Jagat Singh Chopra & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Raj Singh Chopra, Narpat Singh Surana, Krishnendu Roy, and Freyaship Services Private Limited are Appellants; Jagat Singh Chopra (father) and Vikram Singh Chopra (son) are Respondents/Original Petitioners. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Family business settlement and corporate governance of Freyaship Services Private Limited (FSPL); conversion of unsecured loans into equity shares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics are inapplicable as the proceedings involve corporate oppression, directorship removal, and unlawful share allotment rather than an IBC debt claim. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Family arbitration award rendered on 22.01.2016; execution modalities signed on 06.07.2016; purported allotment of 26,000 equity shares on 15.09.2016; purported removal of Respondents as directors with effect from 19.10.2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitral award dated 22.01.2016 allotting FSPL to Appellant No. 1; absence of special resolution or Form MGT-14 filed with ROC at the time unsecured loans were raised permitting conversion into equity; total lack of notice or proof of service of Board meetings leading to vacation of office under Section 167(1)(b). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed CP No. 208/KB/2017 before NCLT Kolkata Bench under Sections 58, 59, 241, and 242; NCLT partly allowed the petition on 04.09.2017, cancelling the allotment of 26,000 equity shares to Appellant No. 1 for violating Section 62(3) and restoring Respondents as Directors due to invalid meeting notices.
legal_issues: Whether a private family arbitration award allotting a company to one party automatically extinguishes the directorship and statutory rights of existing directors without following mandatory Companies Act provisions, and whether unsecured loans can be converted into equity shares under Section 62(3) without an antecedent special resolution passed at the time the loans were raised.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The passing of an arbitral consent award dividing corporate holdings does not dispense with statutory governance obligations under company law; directorships cannot be vacated under Section 167 without valid notice of meetings, and debt cannot be converted into equity without a pre-existing option sanctioned by special resolution at the time of borrowing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 62(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 strictly governs loan-to-equity conversions occurring during its operation, requiring an option attached to the borrowing approved by prior special resolution; Section 167(1)(b) applies only where a director absents themselves from validly convened meetings, which strictly necessitates proof of statutory notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The burden of proof rests entirely on the company/directors asserting vacation of office to demonstrate valid dispatch and service of meeting notices; likewise, proof of filed Form MGT-14 and contemporaneous special resolutions is mandatory to sustain share conversion under Section 62(3). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The conversion of 26,000 shares lacked statutory sanction under Section 62(3), and the purported removal of the directors was void because meetings conducted without notice are legally invalid.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The impugned order of NCLT Kolkata Bench dated 4th September 2017 is upheld. Parties remain free to pursue mutual compliance or execution proceedings under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. No order as to costs.
summary: Raj Singh Chopra and others appealed against an order of NCLT Kolkata dated 4th September 2017, which cancelled an allotment of 26,000 equity shares to Raj Singh Chopra and reinstated Jagat Singh Chopra and Vikram Singh Chopra as directors of Freyaship Services Private Limited. Appellants contended that under a family arbitral award dated 22nd January 2016, the company was awarded solely to Raj Singh Chopra. The NCLAT held that an arbitral award does not override statutory company law procedures. Conversion of loans into shares failed to meet Section 62(3) requirements, and removal under Section 167(1)(b) was illegal due to lack of meeting notices.

case_title: Ritemed Pharma Retail Private Limited & Anr. vs. The Official Liquidator & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ritemed Pharma Retail Private Limited is the Transferor Company (Appellant No. 1); Optival Health Solutions Private Limited is the Transferee Company (Appellant No. 2); both are private subsidiaries of Mediplus Health Services Private Limited; Official Liquidator and Regional Director (SER) MCA are Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Scheme of Amalgamation between two private limited companies where the Transferee Company agreed to allot shares at a premium to discharge the purchase consideration (136 shares of Rs. 10 at Rs. 26 premium for every 100 shares held). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics are inapplicable as this matter concerns sanction of an amalgamation scheme under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board resolutions passed on 06.03.2017; meeting dispensation granted by NCLT on 08.05.2017 in CA(CAA) No. 29/230/HDB/2017; Official Liquidator report filed on 10.07.2017; Regional Director affidavit filed on 13.07.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auditor's certificate dated 17.03.2017 certifying draft scheme accounting treatment complied with Section 133 and AS-14; Regional Director report confirming clean regulatory compliance; OL report confirming affairs were not prejudicial to public interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed joint petition CP(CAA) No. 98/230/HDB/2017 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench; by order dated 05.01.2018, NCLT rejected the scheme on the sole ground that Companies Act, 2013 has no explicit provision enabling unlisted/private limited companies to allot shares at a premium in a merger.
legal_issues: Whether an unlisted private limited company is legally entitled under Sections 52, 230, and 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 to issue and allot equity shares at a premium as consideration under a Scheme of Amalgamation, and whether the NCLT can refuse sanction solely because the merging entities are private companies.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Private and unlisted companies enjoy equal statutory freedom under company law to issue shares at a premium as consideration under a scheme of compromise, arrangement, or amalgamation; the sanctioning tribunal cannot reject a scheme conforming with accounting standards by sitting in appeal over commercial wisdom. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 52 applies universally to all companies issuing shares at a premium whether for cash or other consideration; Section 232(3)(i) read with Section 133 and AS-14 contains no restriction barring private or unlisted companies from issuing shares at a premium to reflect net asset value. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applied the Miheer H. Mafatlal doctrine governing sanction of corporate arrangements; where all statutory procedures, meetings, and accounting compliance certificates under Section 232(3)(i) are satisfied, the Tribunal has supervisory, not appellate, jurisdiction over the commercial exchange ratio. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's refusal to sanction the scheme due to lack of an explicit provision for private companies issuing premium shares was erroneous in law, as Section 52 expressly permits premium issuances without distinction.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order of NCLT Hyderabad Bench dated 5th January 2018 is set aside. NCLT Hyderabad Bench is directed to sanction the Scheme of Amalgamation and issue appropriate consequential directions. No order as to costs.
summary: Ritemed Pharma Retail Private Limited and Optival Health Solutions Private Limited appealed the NCLT Hyderabad order dated 5th January 2018 refusing to sanction their Scheme of Amalgamation. The NCLT rejected the scheme solely because the merging entities were unlisted private companies and the Act contained no explicit clause permitting private companies to issue shares at a premium under Section 232. Overturning the decision, the NCLAT held that Section 52 and Section 232 apply uniformly to all companies and permit shares to be issued at a premium for non-cash consideration. Applying the Miheer H. Mafatlal principles, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and directed the NCLT to sanction the scheme.

case_title: Pravin Jain & Ors. vs. Diastar Jewellery Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pravin Jain, Bharti Pravin Jain, and Anuj Pravin Jain are the Appellants/Original Petitioners (holding 19.60% equity independently); Diastar Jewellery Private Limited is Respondent No. 1 Company; Pramod Jain (Managing Director and US citizen) is Respondent No. 2; Rachna Srimal (Director without DIN) is Respondent No. 3[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operation of export-oriented jewelry manufacturing business supplying finished jewelry to US-based affiliated entity Diastar Inc. (wholly owned and managed by Respondent No. 2) based on raw materials and designs[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics under IBC are not applicable as the proceedings involve corporate oppression and mismanagement; however, Rs. 1822.64 Lakhs remained unremitted by Diastar Inc., out of which Rs. 1787.05 Lakhs was written off, alongside mounting statutory liabilities for PF, gratuity, and unpaid bank consortium facilities resulting in NPA classification[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Conditional gift deed and MOU executed on 10.12.2002 and 12.12.2002; joint shareholder board resolution passed on 26.04.2003; subsequent gift deed and Board Resolution executed in favor of Appellants on 16.10.2007; donor Kishanlal Jain expired on 07.04.2009; Appellant issued Section 169 EOGM requisition notice on 26.08.2010[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auditor's reports for FY 2008-2009 and 2009-2010 highlighting non-disclosure of interested party transactions under Section 207(1), non-provision of statutory tax, failure to obtain RBI approval for netting off receivables, and write-off of Rs. 1787.05 Lakhs due to US bankruptcy of Diastar Inc.; corporate registry Form 18 and Form 32 filings showing a parallel entity Diastar India Pvt. Ltd. operating at the identical registered address[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed TCP 79/2010 (originally before the Company Law Board on 08.10.2010) alleging oppression and mismanagement; NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the petition on 01.12.2017 holding that unconditional gift of shares could not be revoked and write-offs due to foreign bankruptcy did not constitute mismanagement[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether writing off substantial export receivables due from an overseas entity owned and controlled by the Managing Director following foreign bankruptcy, coupled with non-payment of statutory dues and total exclusion of minority shareholders, amounts to oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241 and 242, and whether an inchoate conditional gift of shares in favor of a foreign citizen lacking mandatory RBI/FEMA permissions precludes subsequent inter vivos transfer to resident family members[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Siphoning company assets by writing off massive receivables due from a related cross-border entity controlled by the same management without requisite regulatory approvals, failing to provide statutory records, and diverting the business address to a parallel corporate vehicle constitutes gross mismanagement and actionable oppression under company law[cite: 9]; furthermore, a conditional gift of shares to a foreign citizen requiring statutory regulatory approval conveys no vested title if the approval never materializes[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 confer broad remedial powers on the Tribunal to regulate company affairs, supersede or reconstitute board governance under Section 242(2)(h) and (k), and appoint independent administration where winding up would unfairly prejudice members; Section 210 enables judicial requisitioning of Central Government investigations where corporate dealings adversely impact the public interest or national revenue[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied an objective audit and regulatory compliance standard, finding that adverse qualifications in statutory audit reports, deliberate non-cooperation with court-appointed special auditors, and unapproved ledger adjustments of foreign exchange establish a prima facie case of fraudulent mismanagement[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The respondents engaged in oppressive conduct and egregious mismanagement of the company's affairs; title to the disputed 40,77,600 shares legally devolved onto Appellants Nos. 2 and 3, warranting immediate board reconstitution, removal of the Managing Director, and investigation under Section 210[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed and the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai is quashed and set aside[cite: 9]. The matter is remitted to NCLT Mumbai[cite: 9]. Respondent No. 2 is removed as Managing Director (continuing only as Director), and Respondent No. 3 is removed from the directorship[cite: 9]. Appellant No. 1 is appointed Director of the Company[cite: 9]. NCLT Mumbai is requested to immediately appoint an Independent Director with casting vote to take custody of statutory records and administer the company[cite: 9]. A copy of the judgment is forwarded to the Central Government (MCA) to investigate the company's affairs under Section 210[cite: 9]. The Company is directed to record Appellants Nos. 2 and 3 in the Register of Members as joint holders of the 40,77,600 shares since 07.04.2009[cite: 9]. Costs of Rs. 2 Lakhs awarded to Appellants, payable jointly or severally by Respondents Nos. 2 and 3[cite: 9].
summary: Pravin Jain and family appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 1st December 2017 dismissing their petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging oppression and mismanagement in Diastar Jewellery Private Limited[cite: 9]. The NCLAT reversed the dismissal, finding that Managing Director Pramod Jain committed severe mismanagement by siphoning company revenues, writing off Rs. 1787.05 Lakhs in receivables due from his US entity Diastar Inc. without RBI approval, neglecting statutory dues, and running a parallel company at the premises[cite: 9]. The Appellate Tribunal removed Pramod Jain as Managing Director, removed Rachna Srimal as Director, appointed Pravin Jain as Director, directed appointment of an Independent Director, ordered transmission of 40,77,600 shares to Appellants, and referred the matter to MCA for a Section 210 investigation[cite: 9].
